papers.abstract: A user who brings a generalist manipulation policy into their home or office wants it to pick up their objects from their shelves, counters, and tables. Yet even a strong generalist like $\pi_{0.5}$ achieves 0% pickup success in our captured deployment scenes without adaptation, and collecting real demonstrations in every user's environment is prohibitively expensive. We present Splat2Act, an automated real-to-sim-to-real pipeline that personalizes a pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) policy to a specific scene and object set using only a handheld phone scan and images of the user's objects. Unlike prior real-to-sim work that reconstructs individual tabletops, Splat2Act operates on building-scale indoor environments: it builds a photorealistic digital twin with 3D Gaussian Splatting and collision geometry, automatically discovers tabletop and non-tabletop receptacles, constructs feasible pickup tasks, and generates successful demonstrations with a privileged simulation oracle, with only scene and object capture required from a human. Applied to 101 scanned campus environments with a median navigable area of 104.87 m$^2$ and 7 receptacles, the pipeline yields 852 receptacles and over 68,000 pickup demonstrations. We fine-tune $\pi_{0.5}$ in two stages: Stage 1 adapts to hundreds of public object assets, drawn either from the deployment scene alone or from all 101 scenes; Stage 2 personalizes to the user's own objects on the deployment scene's receptacles. Our strongest personalized policy reaches 62.5% aggregate pickup success in the target scene. Deployed on a real Stretch 3, the same policy achieves 63.9% success on a 12-task subset, closely tracking its 66.7% simulated success on those tasks. These results suggest that automated real-to-sim-to-real training can personalize VLA manipulation policies using only simulation-oracle data.
authors: Xiaomeng Ye, Krishna Jaganathan, Gyubeum Lim, Gunjan Chhablani, Muhammad Zubair Irshad, Zsolt Kira
bullets: Addresses the challenge of deploying generalist manipulation policies in new homes or offices, where unadapted pickup success can be ineffective and real-data collection is costly.
Builds building-scale photorealistic digital twins with 3D Gaussian Splatting, collision geometry, receptacle discovery, and automatically generated pickup tasks.
Uses a privileged simulation oracle to produce demonstrations, followed by two-stage fine-tuning on public assets and the user’s objects.
Across 101 scanned campus environments, the pipeline generated over 68,000 pickup demonstrations from 852 receptacles.
The personalized policy achieved 62.5% simulated target-scene success and 63.9% success on a real Stretch 3 evaluation subset, versus 66.7% simulated success on those tasks.

papers.selection_reason: Automated real-to-sim-to-real personalization of VLA manipulation policies using 3D scene capture.
papers.title: Splat2Act: From Captured Scenes to Personalized VLA Manipulation
papers.tldr: Splat2Act personalizes a pretrained VLA manipulation policy to a user’s indoor scene and objects using only a phone scan and object images, achieving roughly 64% real-world pickup success without real demonstrations.

papers.abstract: Pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) models encode broad manipulation priors, yet adapting them to specific tasks requires balancing limited robot interaction, computational resources, and safety constraints. Noise space learning (NSL) adapts flow-matching-based VLAs by learning a context-conditioned distribution over noise while keeping the pretrained VLA fixed. Building on prior noise-steering methods, we formulate NSL as an interface for VLA adaptation that accommodates different learning algorithms and instantiate it with PPO, SAC, and AWR. Theoretically, we provide an information-theoretic analysis of how NSL enables efficient adaptation. Empirically, we study these NSL algorithms on LIBERO, RoboTwin, and four real-robot manipulation tasks under interaction, computation, and execution constraints. Across these settings, we develop a suite of effective NSL variants and derive practical recommendations for choosing among them under different resource and deployment regimes.
authors: Junjie Lu, Chuheng Zhang, Yucen Wang, Yuhua Jiang, Xinyao Qin, Min Xu, Li Zhao
bullets: Addresses VLA adaptation under limited robot interaction, computation, and safety constraints.
Learns a context-conditioned noise distribution as an adaptation interface for flow-matching-based VLAs.
Implements the interface with PPO, SAC, and AWR, while providing an information-theoretic analysis.
Evaluates variants on LIBERO, RoboTwin, and four real-robot manipulation tasks across multiple resource constraints.
Offers practical guidance for selecting NSL variants under different training and deployment regimes.

papers.abstract: Robot policies often convert sensing and control into fixed-rate observation-action sequences, leaving physical time implicit in sequence position. This assumption breaks when observation rates or delays vary, or when inference latency changes. We introduce Chronos Policy, which makes physical time explicit by conditioning on observation capture times and desired action execution times. We study two ways to incorporate time into a diffusion transformer: adding timestamp embeddings to token features, or encoding physical time in positional encoding through time-aware rotary positional encodings (time-aware RoPE). We find that time-aware RoPE is more robust, allowing attention to depend directly on physical time while keeping token content unchanged. During training, we temporally randomize which observations are sampled and when the action chunk begins, exposing the policy to a wider range of sensing and execution schedules that may occur during deployments. This also enables learning from asynchronous, multi-rate data without forcing all measurements onto a fixed temporal grid. Across simulation and real-world experiments, Chronos Policy improves performance on dynamic tasks, where observation-to-action timing is critical, and on multisensory tasks, where the relative timing between observations matters. On standard quasi-static tasks, it preserves nominal performance while improving robustness to changes in sensing and inference timing.
authors: Changhao Wang, Jaden Clark, Shuran Song
bullets: Addresses failures caused by fixed-rate observation-action sequences under changing observation rates, delays, and inference latency.
Conditions a diffusion transformer on observation capture times and desired action execution times.
Compares timestamp token embeddings with time-aware rotary positional encodings; time-aware RoPE is more robust because attention directly uses physical time.
Uses temporal randomization during training to support varied sensing and execution schedules, including asynchronous and multi-rate data.
Improves dynamic and multisensory task performance while preserving nominal performance on quasi-static tasks and increasing timing robustness.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of Chronos Policy. Tokens are paired with their physical times. Time-aware RoPE uses these physical timestamps as positional coordinates, so attention depends on elapsed time rather than sequence index. The diffusion transformer then predicts an action chunk at the requested execution times.

Figure 6: Architecture of Chronos Policy. Proprioceptive, optional force/torque, and noisy action tokens interact through self-attention and attend to image features through cross-attention. Timeaware RoPE encodes observation capture times and queried action times in attention. The transformer iteratively denoises the action chunk.

Figure 1: Timing-related issues in robot policy learning. (a) Real robot systems exhibit multiple sources of temporal variation, including variable sensor sampling rate, observation latency and dropout, inference latency, control frequency, and execution latency. These timing effects matter differently across tasks. (b) In dynamic tasks, the key temporal relationship is between when an observation is captured and when an action takes effect. (c) In multisensory tasks, the key temporal relationship is between when different observations are captured. (d) Even in quasi-static tasks, differences between data-collection and deployment timing can create temporal mismatch. Standard fixed-rate policy representations obscure these distinctions by treating sequence position as a proxy for time.

Figure 5: Real-world evaluation under timing variation. We compare Diffusion Policy, Diffusion Policy with RTC, and Chronos Policy on Dynamic Cup, Peg Insertion, and Pivoting under nominal, observation, inference, and combined timing conditions. Lighter bar segments indicate partial success.

papers.abstract: A central challenge in de novo protein design is generating proteins with desired structural and functional properties. Existing design models typically require a dedicated input representation for each property, limiting the design objectives they support. We develop Prompteina, the first all-atom structure generation model that supports new and broader design objectives specified in natural language, analogous to text-to-image generation. To train Prompteina, we construct Prompteina-Data, a paired text--protein structure dataset of 1.8M structures and 50M+ captions describing global and residue-specific structural and functional properties. We adapt Proteina-Complexa, a pretrained structure generation model, through text-conditioned pretraining and finetuning that aligns residues with their corresponding text. Prompteina outperforms baselines on 15 of 18 structural properties and generates proteins that more closely match descriptions of their intended functions. In binder design, it leads baselines on at least 13 of 20 targets and improves interface confidence by 14\% over the strongest baseline. With iterative in silico feedback, Prompteina's gain over non-iterative generation is 57\% larger than the next-best baseline on the hardest targets. Finally, we experimentally validate Prompteina designs against GM2A, a target with no reported de novo binders. We identify nine binders, with the strongest at an apparent $K_{\mathrm{D}}$ of 107 nM. These results establish natural language as an effective and powerful conditioning interface for protein structure generation.
authors: Joseph Lee, Yanjing Li, Bo Qiang, Gregory Lau, Allyson Ettinger, Noah A. Smith, Rory Donovan-Maiye, David Baker, Hanna Hajishirzi, Pang Wei Koh

Introduces Prompteina, an all-atom structure generator conditioned on natural-language descriptions of global and residue-specific properties.

Outperforms baselines on 15 of 18 structural properties and leads on at least 13 of 20 binder-design targets; iterative feedback further improves performance.
Experimental validation against GM2A identified nine binders, with the strongest showing an apparent KD of 107 nM.

papers.abstract: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) aims to transform interaction experience into persistent improvements, yet external feedback is costly and world-model predictions may become unreliable as policies evolve. We introduce RSI-Anything, a domain-general framework built on JEPA-Anything that uses predictive world models to guide action and learning-data selection. Observed feedback drives policy or workflow improvement and conditional world-model adaptation, while component and compatibility checks govern the retention of updated policy-model pairs. Across diverse computational and scientific domains, RSI-Anything demonstrates substantial gains. In code repair, with the coder fixed, success increases from 26.3% with a static verifier to 29.2% through predictive selection and 31.2% after world-model adaptation, at comparable test usage. Graphical user interface (GUI) evaluations showed higher task completion, while average actions decrease by 39.4%. Across five successive policy versions, laboratory-planning scores more than double from 21.80% to 46.01%. In reaction optimization, RSI-Anything achieves 96.15% mean best observed yield versus 82.16% for Bayesian optimization under the same 40-experiment budget. An end-to-end immune-science application further connects workflow evolution and predictive modeling with therapeutic hypothesis generation. These results demonstrate how predictive world models and retained system updates enable recursive improvement across diverse environments.
authors: Taoyong Cui, Pinxian Zeng, Wanghan Xu, Hao Xiao, Shuhan Xue, Qiang Gao, Wanli Ouyang, Pheng Ann Heng, Zhenfei Yin, Yingcheng Wu, Ling Yang
bullets: Addresses costly feedback and unreliable world-model predictions as policies evolve.
Selects actions and learning data using JEPA-Anything-based predictive world models.
Adapts world models conditionally and retains updated policy–model pairs only after component and compatibility checks.
Reports gains in code repair, GUI task completion, laboratory planning, reaction optimization, and immune-science workflow development.
Scope includes multiple computational and scientific domains; the abstract does not specify broader limitations.],

papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) increasingly analyze and reason about images, yet it remains unclear whether their internal representations faithfully encode the structured relations required for such reasoning. We introduce EICS (Evaluation-Invariant Concept Stability), a metric for testing whether representations consistently encode concepts under controlled one-concept interventions, and CASP-VL (Causally controlled Spatial Perturbations for Vision-Language models), a benchmark of causally controlled spatial perturbations derived from Visual Genome scene graphs. Across multiple VLM architectures, we find that spatial relations are represented substantially less faithfully than lexical information, even when the same models score well above chance on compositional benchmarks. Further analysis shows that the relation is identifiable at the predicate's own tokens but is lost when the sentence is aggregated into a global representation, whether through the (EOS) token or by mean pooling. These findings reveal a systematic failure invisible to output-based evaluation: VLMs do not preserve, in the representation used downstream, relational information that is present in their own input.
bullets: Introduces EICS, a metric for testing concept stability under controlled one-concept interventions.
Introduces CASP-VL, a benchmark of causally controlled spatial perturbations derived from Visual Genome scene graphs.
Across multiple VLM architectures, spatial information is represented less faithfully than lexical information.
Spatial relations remain identifiable at predicate tokens but are lost when representations are aggregated via EOS tokens or mean pooling.
The failure is hidden by output-based and compositional benchmark performance.

figures.caption: Figure 2: A color flip moves the representation across the probe’s decision boundary; a spatial flip does not. Schematic. Left: flipping “red” to “blue” moves the representation into the blue cluster, so a probe trained on original captions predicts the new label (high EICS). Right: flipping “on” to “beneath” leaves the representation inside the “on” cluster, so the probe still predicts the old label (near-zero EICS).

Figure 1: EICS asks whether a representation follows a one-concept change in its input. (I) We edit one concept in a Visual Genome scene graph G, giving G̃. (II) Both graphs are rendered as captions x and x̃ from one template. (III) The text encoder maps each caption to a hidden state. (IV) A linear probe trained only on original captions (V) is tested on the perturbed ones: EICS is how often it predicts the new label, minus chance. The same probe on token counts (dashed) gives the BoW lexical baseline.

Figure 3: Color becomes decodable in the last two layers; spatial relations stay far below the lexical baseline at every layer. EICS by layer for CLIP ViTB/32 (12 color classes, 16 relation classes), averaged over five image-grouped splits; bands span the lowest and highest split. Dashed and dotted lines: the BoW baseline for each concept, averaged over the same splits.

We computed all accuracies with a single script, scoring each caption by its image–text similarity, rather than copying them from prior papers. ARO (Yuksekgonul et al., 2023), SugarCrepe (Hsieh et al., 2023), Winoground (Thrush et al., 2022), What’sUp (Kamath et al., 2023); Ours = CASP-VL + EICS. papers.abstract: Deploying language-model agents onboard mobile robots requires task reasoning and responsive execution within limited compute and memory. We propose BT-Agent, an onboard architecture combining LLM-driven task decisions with predefined behavior-tree (BT) skills. These skills enforce execution conditions and return structured failure feedback. We demonstrate fully onboard operation with a 9B model on a quadruped across five task categories. Intervention tests show that local checks stop ongoing navigation without waiting for another model decision, while the agent remains active to retry or report constraints. To compare agent designs efficiently, we introduce a 161-task multi-fidelity benchmark, evaluated in text on all tasks and in Habitat on 39. Text supports 10.9$\times$ higher evaluation throughput, while simulation reveals how perception and motion failures change task outcomes. BT-Agent's largest success gains over the strongest Act/ReAct baseline occur at 4B and 9B: approximately 10 and 5 percentage points. Ablations identify structured tool calls and informative failure feedback as the most useful components.
authors: Fabio H\"ubel, Adam Lilja, Yue Yin, Siming He, Claire Tomlin, Shankar Sastry, Jonas Frey, Marco Pavone

Shows its largest gains over Act/ReAct at 4B and 9B, and finds structured tool calls plus informative failure feedback most useful.

papers.abstract: We present HorizonNav, a video diffusion-based framework for anticipatory robot navigation that transforms a single RGB image and a text prompt into a geometrically aligned representation of plausible surrounding 3D space. Given the initial observation and a textual description of the reconstruction objective, a vision-language model, guided by designed instructions, interprets the scene and constructs structured prompts for a video diffusion model. The resulting video sequence provides plausible future observations of the environment, which are subsequently processed using monocular ORB-SLAM3 for camera pose estimation and Video Depth Anything for dense depth prediction. Our central contribution is a geometry-guided depth alignment stage that combines the estimated camera poses with triangulated visual landmarks to constrain dense depth predictions across multiple views. This alignment improves the geometric consistency of the reconstructed 3D environment, addressing inconsistencies that temporal coherence of the generated video alone cannot resolve. The experimental evaluation of navigation in imagined 3D environment shows that across a 19-scene horizon study, planning-feasible scenes increase from 13/19 at P20 to 15/19 at P81, while successful RRT trials increase from 62/90 to 75/90. In a separate corridor study, 6 of 25 evaluable generated-camera trajectories violate the reconstructed collision constraints; RRT planner recovers feasible alternatives in 5 of those 6 cases. A larger archive contains 58 usable reconstructions from 67 attempted cases, of which 36 support a downstream plan and 22 do not, exposing reconstruction and free-space failure modes rather than hiding them without lidar. Across 15 corridor reconstructions, the mean reconstruction error is approximately 0.30 m at matched structural landmarks.
authors: Hajira Amjad, Valerii Serpiva, Viacheslav Liubimov, Didar Seyidov, Dzmitry Tsetserukou
bullets: Generates plausible future views from one RGB observation plus a textual reconstruction objective.
Uses a vision-language model to guide prompts for video diffusion, then applies ORB-SLAM3 and Video Depth Anything.
Aligns dense depth with camera poses and triangulated landmarks to improve multi-view geometric consistency.
In a 19-scene horizon study, planning-feasible scenes rose from 13/19 to 15/19, and successful RRT trials from 62/90 to 75/90.
The approach remains subject to reconstruction and free-space failures; matched-landmark error was approximately 0.30 m across 15 corridor reconstructions.

papers.abstract: Comics are one of the great visual records of the twentieth century: hundreds of thousands of pages in which a mass readership saw its leaders, its wars and its heroes. Most of this record has never been studied as a whole; comics scholarship proceeds one book at a time. We argue that artificial intelligence, including generative models, can change this to the benefit of the medium itself. We propose PAGE, a framework that makes artificial intelligence an instrument for comics research. It parses every scan into panels, text and a bibliographic record; annotates each page with a vision-language model that follows a written codebook, as a human coder would; grounds samples of these readings in human annotation; and explains change across an archive, with estimates controlled for publisher and genre. We demonstrate the framework on 3,929 American comic books (1938--1956) and 87 volumes of Japanese manga, in three studies, each resting on a different capability. The first pairs text search with visual reading to recover how a mass medium portrayed political power. The second measures the page's visual form across an industry and recovers the hand of individual artists. The third follows who speaks across two comics traditions, checked against human annotation. Beyond research, the same instruments can make archives searchable by what is drawn, open comics to blind and low-vision readers, and help preserve fragile collections and credit uncredited artists. We outline a research agenda in which artificial intelligence strengthens the study, preservation and reach of the medium.
bullets: Addresses the limits of book-by-book comics scholarship across vast American comics and Japanese manga archives.
Parses scans into panels, text, and bibliographic records, then applies codebook-guided vision-language annotation grounded in human checks.
Demonstrates three studies of political representation, visual form and artists’ styles, and speaking roles across comics traditions.
Applies the framework to 3,929 American comic books from 1938–1956 and 87 manga volumes.
Potentially supports searchable archives, accessibility for blind and low-vision readers, preservation, and attribution of uncredited artists.

The same objects can serve readers, archives and artists through discovery, attribution, access, preservation and teaching.

papers.abstract: When solving complex spatial reasoning tasks, ordinary humans naturally revisit the scenes from task-relevant viewpoints and mentally reconstruct the spatial layouts from those viewpoints. But can Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) proactively think in the same way? We term this ability Active Spatial Mentalization (ASM), an intrinsic component of visual intelligence that remains substantially underdeveloped in current LVLMs. To bridge this gap, we introduce SpatialASM, a scalable framework to internalize ASM into LVLMs through training-time spatial simulation. SpatialASM employs an allocentric novel-view generator to ground hypothetical viewpoints in visual evidence and produces two complementary forms of supervision: i) explicit ASM trajectories that teach LVLMs when and how to adaptively invoke view planning and imagination during spatial reasoning, and ii) automatically-constructed perspective-taking tasks that further strengthens viewpoint-conditioned scene imagination. On seven benchmarks spanning relatively perception-oriented spatial understanding to more challenging tasks requiring multi-image, cross-view and viewpoint-transformation reasoning, SpatialASM yields performance gain on LVLMs of four LVLM backbones in spatial reasoning while retaining their original general vision capabilities. The experimental results demonstrate that our approach improves average accuracy across the seven spatial benchmarks. And the synthesis of ASM trajectories provides a scalable pathway to alleviate the scarcity of spatial Chain-of-Thought (CoT) supervision for eliciting active viewpoint exploration and mental scene simulation.

papers.abstract: A central challenge in embodied recursive self-improvement is enabling agents to convert interaction history into capabilities that persist beyond one world and transfer to later tasks. A saved memory or successful final action does not by itself establish that a reusable capability was acquired; evaluation must separate capability change from carried-over resources, unequal source exposure, and early execution failures. We construct MC-EvoBench as a controlled Minecraft benchmark with a fixed catalog of 19 registered evolution chains, including 12 primary evaluation chains and seven calibration or probe chains, together with three graph-aligned paired probe families for transfer. The benchmark represents each task as a task-state graph, defines stage-level environment verifiers, assigns matched source and target roles, resets the target world, and permits only a declared agent artifact to cross the source-target boundary. For each probe, no-prior, related, unrelated, and shuffled source conditions are evaluated under matched environment-step budgets and five seeds; we report TSR, WGP, and VMP and retain provenance records. The benchmark reveals a consistent direct-capability gap between controller and planner-backed variants, while related experience yields no stable transfer: it does not improve either tool probe, its small wood-species gain hinges on one seed, and all intervals include zero. Stage audits further show that early wood-collection and crafting bottlenecks often leave later capabilities unobserved. MC-EvoBench thus offers a controlled testbed for durable, transferable embodied capabilities. Code and data are available at https://github.com/xzw-ustc/mc-bench-open-source
authors: Jingwei Song, Zhisheng Chen, Bingfan Zeng, Jing Tang, Yubo Hou, Jinhao Jing, Zhengwei Xie, Linfeng Zhang
bullets: Tests whether interaction history yields reusable skills rather than merely preserved resources or successful actions.
Uses 19 registered evolution chains, task-state graphs, stage verifiers, reset target worlds, matched source conditions, and provenance tracking.

Finds a consistent direct-capability gap between controller and planner-backed agents, while related experience shows no stable transfer.
Stage audits identify early wood-collection and crafting failures that can prevent later capabilities from being observed.

papers.abstract: Generalist robot policies are trained with imitation learning and are bounded by the quality and coverage of their demonstrations. Reinforcement learning can improve and extend them, either by fine-tuning the policy weights or by training a small module to steer the input noise of a frozen generative policy. When tasks arrive sequentially, both approaches suffer from catastrophic forgetting. Fine-tuning on a task degrades prior tasks, and steering only shifts forgetting to the shared steering module. We propose Dream to Remember (D2R), which continually steers a frozen generalist policy toward new tasks, while retaining its earlier skills. As the steering module learns a new task, a frozen pretrained world model rehearses prior tasks through imagined rollouts, anchoring the module to its earlier behavior without a replay buffer or new data. When the world model is faithful enough, D2R learns the new task entirely in imagination. Otherwise, it learns the task in the environment while using the world model only to rehearse prior tasks. On CALVIN, D2R improves eight tasks in sequence entirely in imagination, raising average success from 63.7% to 74.8%, while LoRA fine-tuning on the same sequence drops it to 11.7%. With a frozen off-the-shelf generalist policy and world model, $\pi_0$ and A2World, D2R learns unseen LIBERO-90 tasks in the environment while keeping $\pi_0$'s performance on the LIBERO suites it was fine-tuned on, even though the world model is not accurate enough for policy optimization. Finally, on a real Franka robot, D2R improves three tasks in sequence entirely in imagination while retaining the earlier improvements.
authors: Bahey Tharwat, Iman Nematollahi, Marvin Alles, Xingyuan Zhang, Akshay L Chandra, Abhinav Valada
bullets: Addresses catastrophic forgetting when adapting robot policies to sequentially arriving tasks.
Learns a steering module for a frozen generative policy rather than changing the policy weights.
Uses a frozen pretrained world model to rehearse prior tasks via imagined rollouts, avoiding replay buffers or additional data.
Can learn new tasks entirely in imagination when the world model is sufficiently accurate; otherwise, it combines environment learning with imagined rehearsal.
Demonstrated on CALVIN, LIBERO, and a real Franka robot, retaining prior abilities while improving sequentially added tasks.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of D2R. (a) Steering in imagination: A small steering module learns to shape the noise fed to the frozen policy through RL in a frozen world model. (b) Rehearsal in the world model: The world model imagines rollouts of prior tasks, where a KL penalty anchors the module to its earlier behavior. (c) Simulator or memory: A faithful world model supports both learning and rehearsal, while a coarser one can still support rehearsal as learning moves to the environment.

Figure 1: Dream to Remember (D2R): We adapt a frozen generative policy sequentially by steering its input noise with a small module trained inside a learned world model. While the module learns the current task, the same world model regenerates imagined rollouts of prior tasks, and we regularize the module toward its previous behavior on those states. Skills thus accumulate without revisiting prior tasks on the robot or storing their trajectories. Rehearsal requires less world model fidelity than optimization, allowing even a model too coarse for learning a new task to preserve prior skills.

Figure 3: Continual steering on LIBERO. Diagonal cells show the success when each task is learned, and cells below show the forgetting, the points lost after each later stage. DSRL forgets each task as soon as the next is learned, instruction KL reduces this, and D2R keeps the tasks to the end.

Figure 4: Continual steering on a real Franka robot. Heatmaps follow Figure 3, with the success rate when each task is learned on the diagonal and the forgetting score below it. D2R retains prior gains across the sequence, whereas DSRL without rehearsal loses about half of them. Adaptation occurs entirely in imagination, with the robot used only for evaluation.

papers.abstract: How well can vision-language models (VLMs) reason about what is missing from an image? We study this question with OccludeBench, a manually curated benchmark for recovering fully occluded objects from the visual evidence that remains. OccludeBench distinguishes direct cases, where the hidden object must be recovered from a specific physical cue such as a shadow or reflection, from inferential cases, where it can be inferred from broader scene context. Across five VLMs, accuracy averages 42.7% on direct cases versus 62.7% on inferential cases, exhibiting a 20.0-point gap. Humans attain higher accuracies of 63.4% versus 68.5% for direct and inferential images, respectively, with no significant gap. To locate this failure, we introduce OccludeTrace, a four-stage diagnostic that isolates where the visual reasoning process breaks down. The bottleneck emerges when models must recover the relevant object from the projection within the full image: they succeed on only 50% of failed examples, compared with 91% of examples they answer correctly. Extended reasoning, tool use, and few-shot prompting yield inconsistent improvements and do not reliably eliminate the gap. In contrast, an inpaint-then-confront intervention, which prompts models to first generate a candidate hidden object and then evaluate that hypothesis against the visible physical cue, reduces the gap to a statistically non-significant difference for both models with image-generation capabilities. Together, our results establish a tractable, controlled diagnostic for isolating how VLMs reason about visual content that is missing from an image.
authors: Jasin Cekinmez, Addison J. Wu, Ryo Mitsuhashi, Linrong Cai, Xingyu Fu, Zhuang Liu
bullets: Benchmark separates direct cases, relying on shadows or reflections, from inferential cases based on broader scene context.

OccludeTrace identifies recovering the hidden object from its projection in the full image as the main bottleneck.

Inpaint-then-confront reduces the direct–inferential gap to a statistically non-significant difference for models with image-generation capabilities.

papers.abstract: LiDAR-inertial odometry (LIO) is widely used for real-time localization and mapping, but its reliability can degrade substantially in subterranean environments affected by smoke, dust, and other airborne obscurants, whereas radar remains comparatively robust. This article presents a one-class temporal learning framework for LiDAR degradation detection and reliability-aware localization under such conditions. A broad set of degradation-sensitive cues, including spatial, cross-modal, geometric/motion, intensity, and measurement-recency features, is evaluated to characterize changes in LiDAR sensing quality. Their temporal evolution is modelled over sliding windows using an LSTM autoencoder trained exclusively on nominal operation, enabling deviations from healthy sensor behaviour to be detected without requiring labelled degradation data. The resulting LiDAR reliability estimate governs adaptive selection between LIO and radar inertial odometry (RIO), retaining LIO during reliable sensing and transferring localization authority to RIO when degradation is detected. The framework is evaluated using real-world ground robot data collected in GNSS-denied subterranean tunnels under nominal and dense-smoke conditions. Experimental results demonstrate degradation detection, adaptive modality switching, and continued localization output under severe LiDAR degradation. A feature family ablation study further shows that a reduced feature representation can improve degradation-aware localization performance in the evaluated dense-smoke scenarios, highlighting the importance of feature parsimony in one-class sensor degradation detection. The code will be released as open source to support reproducibility and further research.
authors: Moumita Mukherjee, Avijit Banerjee, Anton Koval, George Nikolakopoulo
bullets: Targets LiDAR reliability loss caused by airborne obscurants in GNSS-denied underground settings.
Uses spatial, cross-modal, geometric/motion, intensity, and recency cues modeled over time.
Trains an LSTM autoencoder only on nominal data, avoiding labeled degradation examples.
Controls switching between LIO and RIO, preserving LIO when healthy and transferring authority to radar when degraded.
Real-world tunnel experiments show degradation detection, adaptive switching, and continued localization under dense smoke; a reduced feature set improved performance in the evaluated scenarios.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Proposed reliability aware LMRIO framework. Asynchronous LiDAR, IMU, LIO, and RIO measurements are temporally synchronized and encoded into a Twelve dimensional degradation sensitive feature representation(fη). Consecutive normalized feature vectors(f̄η) form a temporal sequence processed by an LSTM autoencoder trained on nominal operation. Reconstruction errors are used to infer LiDAR degradation and adaptively select between LIO and RIO.
Fig. 1: Conceptual framework for LiDAR degradation-aware adaptive localization under airborne obscurants.

Fig. 4: Trajectory comparison across the four experimental scenarios. Under nominal conditions, LMRIO closely follows LIO for both the P-shaped and round-tunnel traversals (a,c). Under dense smoke, the P-shaped traversal exhibits severe LIO divergence following LiDAR degradation (b), while the roundtunnel traversal shows stale LiDAR-based localization (d). In both degraded cases, LMRIO selects RIO during unreliable LiDAR operation, preserving a continuous localization output.

Fig. 3: Localization trajectories and LiDAR maps for the P-shaped and round-tunnel traversals. Under nominal conditions, LMRIO closely follows the LIO estimate in both trajectories (a,c). In dense smoke, the P-shaped traversal exhibits pronounced LIO divergence as LiDAR quality deteriorates (b), while the round-tunnel traversal shows stale LiDAR measurements and loss of LiDAR-based localization updates (d). In both degraded cases, LMRIO switches to RIO during intervals identified as unreliable, maintaining a consistent localization output.

Fig. 5: Raw and smoothed LSTM-autoencoder reconstruction errors with the nominal threshold. Nominal traversals remain largely below the threshold despite transient fluctuations (a,c), whereas dense-smoke traversals show pronounced or sustained error growth associated with LiDAR degradation (b,d). The smoothed error drives learned degradation detection, while LiDAR recency is evaluated independently.

Fig. 6: Estimator-selection traces across the four experimental scenarios. LIO remains selected throughout nominal operation (a,c). Under dense smoke, the degradation detector triggers a transition to RIO in the P-shaped traversal (b), while the LiDAR-recency criterion activates RIO when measurements become stale in the round-tunnel traversal (d). The switching variables ∆LIO and ∆RIO indicate the active localization modality.

papers.abstract: Memes play a central role in modern online communication, especially in contexts of political conflict where visual and textual cues combine to convey persuasive messages. We study persuasive technique detection in Ukrainian memes using vision-language models (VLMs). We introduce UkrMeme, a dataset of 200 organically produced Ukrainian wartime memes annotated for persuasion techniques, and PTM-UA, a Ukrainian translation of a subset of the Propaganda 950 benchmark that preserves original visual content while translating meme text. We evaluate VLMs in a zero-shot prompting setup across image, text, and multimodal inputs using hierarchical F1 metrics. Finally, we compare Layer-wise Relevance Propagation (LRP) and model-generated token attributions and analyze the semantic categories of evidence emphasized by each explanation method.

papers.abstract: State-space models (SSMs) maintain a fixed-size recurrent state, but reading and writing it at every decoding step can bottleneck hybrid models. This eager state management causes large state I/O with low arithmetic intensity, leaves speculative decoding no cheap rollback, and feeds state quantization error into subsequent recurrent updates. We introduce ReplaySSM, which unrolls the recurrence to represent the state as a checkpoint and a buffer of recent SSM inputs. This separates output computation from checkpoint updates. By updating the checkpoint periodically, ReplaySSM avoids state writes on most steps and roughly halves the dominant state memory traffic. Keeping recent inputs also makes speculative rollback a buffer-pointer operation and enables output-only verification without materializing intermediate states. The same separation allows a low-precision checkpoint to serve output computation on most steps while a higher-precision checkpoint serves recurrent updates, so rounding error in the low-precision copy never enters later updates. We implement ReplaySSM in vLLM for Mamba-2 and Gated DeltaNet. At serving batch size 256, it accelerates standard decoding by $1.20$--$1.47\times$ over a tuned vLLM baseline across four hybrid models, and delivers about $1.8\times$ the throughput of vLLM's speculative decoding on the two 120B-class models. Separate state precisions also reduce output KL divergence and downstream accuracy losses compared with a shared low-precision checkpoint.
authors: Ze-Wei Liou, Harris Nover, Amey Naik, Andrii Skliar, Igor Shovkun, Ido Shahaf, Tri Dao
bullets: SSM state I/O can bottleneck decoding because each step reads and writes a fixed-size recurrent state.
ReplaySSM represents state with a periodic checkpoint plus a buffer of recent inputs, avoiding most state writes and roughly halving dominant state-memory traffic.
Input buffering makes speculative rollback a pointer operation and supports output-only verification without materializing intermediate states.
Separate low-precision output and high-precision update checkpoints prevent rounding errors from propagating through recurrent updates.

figures.caption: Figure 1: ReplaySSM overview. Top: conventional decoding loads and stores the full state at every step. ReplaySSM unrolls the recurrence to separate output computation from checkpoint updates: it caches recent SSM inputs and folds them into the checkpoint periodically, avoiding full-state writes on most steps. Bottom: three challenges of conventional decoding, and how ReplaySSM addresses each. (1) SSM layers can bottleneck hybrid models up to 100K tokens (Nemotron-3-Super-120BA12B-NVFP4, batch size 256, one B300); ReplaySSM roughly halves their state traffic. (2) State rollback, expensive to support in conventional speculative decoding, becomes a buffer-pointer move. (3) A low-precision checkpoint serves outputs while a high-precision one carries the recurrence, so rounding error no longer re-enters the recurrence.

papers.abstract: Low-bit inference on accelerators with native 4-bit support requires quantizing both weights and activations to realize the full throughput gains these formats provide. While post-training weight quantization has been extensively studied, activation quantization remains considerably more challenging and typically requires calibration data. In this work, we introduce DUALQUANT, a dual-scale, calibration-free post-training quantization framework that directly minimizes the weight-reconstruction Mean Squared Error (MSE) and, as an immediate by-product, yields per-channel activation rescalings prior to activation quantization. Our key observation is that the scaling factors obtained by minimizing weight-reconstruction error provide effective activation rescalings, enabling competitive activation quantization without calibration data. We formulate DUALQUANT as a non-differentiable weight-reconstruction problem and develop an efficient solver based on variable splitting and block coordinate descent, where each subproblem admits a closed-form update. DUALQUANT provides a unified algorithm supporting a wide range of formats, including the full MX family and NVFP4. To our knowledge, DUALQUANT is the first dual-scaling method to formally support MX and NV block formats. Across Llama and Qwen models evaluated on WikiText-2, C4, and zero-shot downstream tasks, DUALQUANT matches or exceeds the accuracy of calibration-based SmoothQuant across most models and formats, and substantially outperforms calibration-free baselines, with large gains for MX and NV block formats. We validate these gains with a real packed W4A4 inference path for Llama-3.1-8B on an RTX 4090. The resulting implementation closely matches the accuracy of fake quantization while delivering up to 2.61x memory reduction and up to 2.46x throughput speedup over BF16.
authors: Mahsa Salmani, Sayeh Sharify, Hesham Mostafa
bullets: Targets the challenge of activation quantization, which typically requires calibration data to preserve LLM accuracy.
Derives per-channel activation rescalings from weight-reconstruction MSE minimization, avoiding calibration data.
Uses variable splitting and block coordinate descent with closed-form subproblem updates.
Supports diverse formats, including the full MX family and NVFP4, with reported gains especially for MX and NV block formats.
On Llama-3.1-8B with packed W4A4 inference, achieves up to 2.61× memory reduction and 2.46× throughput speedup versus BF16.

papers.abstract: Training long-horizon language model agents requires assigning credit to intermediate decisions from sparse terminal feedback. Within a finite group of sibling rollouts, useful action comparisons depend on their context, evidence for both alternatives, and how that evidence enters learning. We propose Matched-Context Group Policy Optimization (MCGPO), a procedure for constructing weighted action preferences from already collected trajectories. MCGPO defines comparison contexts with pre-action state summaries and observed rubric progress, annotated by task rules. Two-action support selects among ordered exact and coarse matching rules. Fixed folds separate candidate decisions from the terminal outcomes used to orient their preferences, and support-dependent evidence weights scale an auxiliary pairwise objective alongside shared GraphGPO task learning. MCGPO reuses rollout data and each response's original history, preserving critic-free training. Across six environment-backbone settings with three training seeds each, MCGPO improves mean success over matched GraphGPO: by 0.47-1.46 percentage points on ALFWorld and WebShop with Qwen2.5-1.5B and 7B, and by 3.96 and 5.16 points on WebShop with Qwen3-4B and 8B. The ALFWorld gains build on baseline success above 92%, where remaining headroom is limited. Integrated success improves in three of four Qwen2.5 settings. Three-seed factorial controls support opposite-fold evidence and evidence weighting; joint state-rubric matching achieves the highest mean in all four representation-control settings.
authors: Chenxu Zhang, Yaorui Shi, Wenlong Zhang, Jianchao Tan, Zihan Wang, Yiming Cheng
bullets: Addresses credit assignment when agents receive feedback only at the end of long tasks.
Builds weighted two-action comparisons using pre-action state, rubric progress, and exact or coarse context matching.
Uses fixed folds to prevent candidate decisions from being oriented by the same terminal outcomes, while retaining critic-free training.
Improves mean success over matched GraphGPO across six environment–backbone settings, with gains ranging from 0.47 to 5.16 percentage points.
Joint state–rubric matching performs best across the tested representation controls; gains are smaller where baseline success already exceeds 92%.

papers.abstract: On-policy self-distillation promises to replace the sparse outcome signal of verifiable-reward RL with dense token-level credit: a teacher conditioned on the reference solution scores the student's own rollout, and the resulting distributional shift is distilled back into the policy. We investigate whether this scoring signal actually contains corrective credit. Using gold error spans in student rollouts, we test the two signals consumed by self-distillation objectives, the full-distribution KL and the token log-ratio, for two properties: whether they localize errors and whether they push probability away from erroneous student tokens. They exhibit neither of these properties nor can they reliably distinguish correct from incorrect rollouts within the same problem. We argue that this failure is structural: locating an error in a reasoning trace is itself a search problem, while a scoring teacher is never explicitly asked to perform that search. The same model, with the same privileged information, localizes errors substantially better when allowed to generate a critique. This forms the motivation for \emph{critique-conditioned self-distillation}: first generate a critique of the current rollout, then condition the scoring teacher on that critique. The resulting signal localizes errors, is corrective within error spans, and shifts probability toward tokens that initiate backtracking such as ``Wait'', ``But'', and ``Actually''. We further show that the critique is useful both at test time, where resuming a wrong rollout with the critique in context converts math problems the model cannot solve by sampling, and in cold-start GRPO, where it provides an advantage signal on prompts for which verifiable rewards alone provide none.
authors: Mayug Maniparambil, Ayush Rai, Ekansh Verma, Noel E. O'Connor, Fergal Reid
bullets: Full-distribution KL and token log-ratio signals neither localize errors nor reliably distinguish correct from incorrect rollouts.

Critique-conditioned self-distillation generates a critique before scoring the rollout, producing corrective signals within error spans.
The critique shifts probability toward backtracking tokens such as “Wait,” “But,” and “Actually.”
At test time and in cold-start GRPO, critiques help recover from wrong rollouts and provide useful advantages when verifiable rewards are absent.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces critique-conditioned self-distillation for reasoning LLMs, improving training signals and test-time reasoning; relevant to LLM training and reasoning.
papers.title: A Privileged Teacher That Only Scores Cannot Search: Critique-Conditioned On-Policy Self-Distillation for Reasoning
papers.tldr: Scoring-only privileged teachers fail to find and correct reasoning errors, while generating a critique first enables effective error localization and corrective self-distillation.

papers.abstract: World-action models (WAMs) predict a robot's actions together with the observations those actions will produce. However, the strongest models rely on video diffusion transformers that are far too computationally expensive for resource-constrained edge devices. We present SmolWAM, a latent WAM that we derive from the 2B-parameter Cosmos Policy by keeping its pretrained trunk and rebuilding its inference interface: single-frame visual latents, cached text features that preserve the trunk's attention sinks, 12 of 28 transformer blocks, and 1,008 tokens from which actions and future visual latents are read out in one rectified-flow step. Trained in 3.6 GPU-hours, SmolWAM succeeds in 95.5% of 400 LIBERO episodes at 57 ms and 2.3 TFLOP per 16-action chunk with 2.4 GiB of GPU memory, 11x faster than its teacher with 18.5x fewer FLOPs and 3.2x less memory, and its world head still forecasts scene motion.
authors: Timi Owolabi, Hikmah Olawore, Frances Adelakun, Ayotomiwa Oyewumi
bullets: Targets the high computational cost of video-diffusion world-action models on resource-constrained edge devices.
Rebuilds a pretrained 2B-parameter model’s inference interface using visual latents, cached text features, 12 transformer blocks, and a single rectified-flow step.
Achieves 95.5% success across 400 LIBERO episodes with 57 ms inference latency and 2.4 GiB of GPU memory.
Runs 11× faster than its teacher while using 18.5× fewer FLOPs and 3.2× less memory.
Its world head retains the ability to forecast scene motion.

papers.abstract: Cooperative multi-agent tasks often impose constraints on a shared objective or collective safety. A team level violation cost function can measure this constraint outcome, but does not distinguish which agents' actions most strongly influence that violation. We present SafeDiSTL, a constrained multi-agent reinforcement learning framework that allows for credit assignment even with joint constraint measurements. We use Signal Temporal Logic (STL) robustness to measure episode-level violation through running-maximum cost increments. Smooth full-episode robustness and differentiable dynamics provide action sensitivities, which allocate each cost increment across agents at the same decision time. These sensitivities account for delayed effects when weighting agents' shares of each cost increment. We study the framework in cooperative payload transport, connected navigation, and networked traffic control tasks. SafeDiSTL achieves 1.6-5.1x the safe-success rate in transport, improves navigation safe-success by 11.1%, and delivers 50-68% more throughput in traffic when compared to constrained baselines. Results demonstrate a strong improvement of the learned policy in dealing with shared constraint while retaining the performance of unconstrained policies.
authors: Hongrui Zheng, Aditya Singh, Rahul Mangharam
bullets: Addresses joint constraints whose team-level violation costs do not reveal which agents caused them.
Uses Signal Temporal Logic robustness with running-maximum cost increments to measure episode-level violations.
Applies differentiable dynamics and full-episode sensitivities to allocate delayed constraint effects among agents.
Evaluated on payload transport, connected navigation, and networked traffic control.
Reports 1.6–5.1× higher safe-success in transport, 11.1% better navigation safe-success, and 50–68% higher traffic throughput than constrained baselines.

papers.abstract: Efficient attention mechanisms, such as linear and sliding window attention, aim to reduce the computational complexity of Transformers from quadratic to linear. However, their degraded in-context recall often necessitates interleaving full attention layers, leaving the quadratic bottleneck unresolved in long-context processing. To address this, we introduce Orthros attention, which shifts the efficiency paradigm from structural allocation to phase-aware decoupling. As a unified module, it dynamically switches its computation pattern across different phases of sequence processing, enabling linear complexity prefilling and full attention decoding. Our design grants Orthros attention a lower asymptotic complexity compared to vanilla Transformers in prevalent long-context scenarios characterized by heavy prefilling and light decoding. Beyond theoretical formulation and complexity analysis, extensive empirical evaluations demonstrate Orthros's superiority across multiple dimensions. First, we validate its fundamental language modeling capabilities, demonstrating scalability across varying model sizes and strong competitiveness in comprehensive architectural comparisons. Second, Orthros exhibits exceptional conversion feasibility via a data-efficient Transformer-to-Orthros conversion, yielding performance that even surpasses the original Transformer. Finally, Orthros achieves a $21.9\times$ prefilling speedup over Transformers with end-to-end inference gains, while preserving long-context capabilities, as demonstrated by near-perfect 128K needle-in-a-haystack results and Transformer-level performance on real-world in-context recall tasks. Overall, these advantages in high performance, flexibility, and efficiency position Orthros as a promising candidate to succeed the Transformer in industrial applications.
authors: Yuhong Chou, Zehao Liu, Yuqi Pan, Qian Liu, Xianwei Chen, Zhongzhu Zhou, Jibin Wu
bullets: Addresses degraded in-context recall in efficient attention methods that still require costly full-attention layers.
Dynamically switches computation patterns by sequence-processing phase rather than statically mixing attention structures.
Achieves lower asymptotic complexity in long-context workloads dominated by prefilling.
Reports up to 21.9× prefilling speedup with end-to-end inference gains.
Preserves long-context performance, including near-perfect 128K needle-in-a-haystack results and Transformer-level real-world recall.

papers.abstract: Scaling generalist robotic policies is limited by the high cost of collecting embodied interaction data. Large-scale egocentric human videos offer a rich alternative, but they lack robot action labels, and existing action annotation methods are often noisy under real-world visual complexity and diverse manipulation dynamics. We introduce LAPT-Scale, a scalable latent action pre-training paradigm with two components: LAPT-Scale-LAM learns continuous latent actions by explaining frame-to-frame visual transitions in human videos and uses them as human-derived supervision, while LAPT-Scale-Policy trains a VLA policy through human-video latent-action pre-training, target-robot embodiment alignment, and task-specific post-training. Unlike prior vector-quantized LAMs, LAPT-Scale-LAM uses a continuous latent space to preserve fine-grained motion and interaction dynamics. We further combine perceptual, semantic, and optical-flow alignment signals to improve transition-level supervision beyond pixel reconstruction. Trained on 23.3K hours of egocentric video, LAPT-Scale-LAM provides implicit action supervision for policy pre-training, yielding consistent scaling gains and improving real-robot success from 63.3% to 85.0% as annotated human video scales from 1K to 5K hours. The learned policy also generalizes to unseen visual conditions.
authors: Zhiyuan Xiang, Peidong Liu, Mingyang Li, Jiawei Li, Wenhow Li, Wenbo Ding, Xiang Deng
bullets: Addresses the high cost of collecting robot interaction data and the lack of action labels in human videos.
Learns continuous latent actions from frame transitions using perceptual, semantic, and optical-flow alignment signals.
Pre-trains a vision-language-action policy, aligns it to the target robot embodiment, and applies task-specific post-training.
Trained on 23.3K hours of egocentric video, it improves real-robot success from 63.3% to 85.0% when annotated human video increases from 1K to 5K hours.
The resulting policy generalizes to unseen visual conditions.

papers.tldr: LAPT-Scale uses continuous latent actions learned from large-scale human videos to pre-train generalist robot policies, substantially improving real-robot performance as video data scales.

papers.abstract: Long-context serving runs out of KV memory before the hardware reaches its useful throughput. HiSparse stores history in host memory and fetches only the selected entries, but it uses one cache budget at every load and does not handle draft-model speculative decoding such as DSpark and DFlash2. We present Adaptive DHiSparse, which supports speculative decoding over hierarchical sparse KV and adapts residency to load. It protects the required working set, retains additional history while GPU memory is spare, and recovers the rest through exact fused retrieval. DSpark and DFlash2 keep their proposal and acceptance rules: queries share missing-row retrieval, draft KV uses a window-bounded ring, and verification staging is reused across layer groups. At 100K context and concurrency 128, GLM-5.3 with DFlash2 delivers 793 output tokens/s per decode GPU, 1.45$\times$ HiSparse and 1.27$\times$ non-speculative adaptive serving. Held to the same latency bounds as HiSparse, it sustains up to 4$\times$ the concurrency and 2.3 to 3.7$\times$ the output, depending on the per-token bound. On DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash at 500K context and concurrency 512, Adaptive DHiSparse with DSpark delivers 1.85$\times$ the output of resident serving with DSpark. In a load step, optional residency reduces host fetches from 14.2% to 1.4% of selected rows at low load and releases memory under pressure.
bullets: Addresses KV-memory exhaustion and fixed cache budgets in long-context serving, including compatibility with DSpark and DFlash2.
Protects the required working set, uses spare GPU memory for extra history, and exactly retrieves missing entries from host memory under pressure.
Reuses speculative-decoding mechanisms such as shared missing-row retrieval, window-bounded draft-KV caching, and verification staging across layers.

At 100K context and concurrency 128, achieves 793 output tokens/s per GPU with GLM-5.3 and DFlash2; the abstract reports higher throughput and concurrency than HiSparse and non-speculative adaptive serving.
At low load, optional residency reduces host fetches from 14.2% to 1.4% of selected rows, while memory is released as load increases.

figures.caption: Figure 3 | One speculative round over the KV hierarchy. The drafter, conditioned on target features, extends the anchor D into a block, and the target model verifies its 𝐾 queries in one pass. Here E and F are accepted, G is rejected, and the correction G∗ opens the next round. (1) Draft KV is held in a ring bounded by the drafter’s window. (2) For each request and KV source, the resolver handles the top-𝑘 selections of the 𝐾 queries together, so each distinct missing row is copied from host once (a is selected by three queries, b by two), and each query still attends over its own selection. (3) Rows that do not fit the hot cache go to a staging arena, reused across layer groups after its readers finish and promoted rows are copied back. (4) The target writes the rows of all 𝐾 queries to the tail. Acceptance commits the computed rows of the anchor and the accepted drafts; the rejected row is dropped and G∗ has no row until the next forward. Host backup of the committed rows follows verification. Sizes are illustrative (𝐾 = 4, 𝑘 = 3).

Figure 9 | Output and host fetches against the hot-cache budget. (a–d) Output per decode GPU and (e–h) share of selected rows fetched from host, for HiSparse and Adaptive HiSparse as 𝐵/𝑘 varies, without speculation. GLM-5.3 runs at 100K context on one prepared prefix, and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash at 500K on 16 prepared prefixes.

Figure 2 | One decode step and where its KV lives. The indexer reads index state and emits the top-𝑘 positions, colored here by where each row is found. The resolver first takes rows that are in the tail or in optional history (1), then scans the hot cache (2). A row found in none of them is copied from host DRAM into the hot cache (3) before attention reads the selected rows. Optional history holds imported history in reclaimable capacity of the KV pools, drawn schematically as one divider that moves with load. The hot cache and the tail are kept per request and KV source and are never lent. Host backup can be deferred while HBM is spare: a row without host backing stays protected on the GPU, so every missing row has host backing. A lookup skips steps 2 and 3 only when every selected row resolves in step 1. Row positions are illustrative.

Figure 4 | GLM-5.3 serving at 100K context. (a) Output throughput against offered concurrency, (b) mean TTFT and (c) mean TPOT against output throughput. Color gives the KV policy and filled markers add DFlash2. TTFT in (b) is on a logarithmic axis. Adaptive DHiSparse uses static blocks of 8 at C4 to C32, 6 at C64 and 4 at C128 and C256.

(a) Allocated request slots. (b) Coverage: ready optional history over eligible history. (c) Share of selected rows fetched from host. One-second counters shown in five-second bins. The dashed line is the least-squares fit, 49.4 GB/s (𝑅2 = 0.9992). One query’s top-𝑘 over the 32 requests of a call is 37.75 MB, so disjoint selections fetch eight such payloads and shared selections one. (b) DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash at 500K, single-query resolver with no host miss: time against hot-cache size for two batch sizes. The dotted line is the direct path at batch 8. (c) The same resolver at 𝐵 = 4,096 with and without 77 host misses per request. Error bars span the minimum and maximum of nine timings in (a) and the 10th to 90th percentiles in (b) and (c). papers.abstract: Standard Policy Gradient (PG) algorithms suffer from high estimation variance because they rely on Monte Carlo updates. While off-policy variance reduction mitigates this problem, establishing optimal sample complexity currently requires either restrictive assumptions, such as uniformly bounded importance weights, or impractical second-order operations. In this work, we introduce Loopless Variance-Reduced PG (LVR-PG), a unified theoretical framework that abstracts a class of first-order estimators that integrate recursive updates with defensive importance sampling, including known estimators such as PAGE-PG and STORM-PG. We prove that this algorithmic class achieves $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\epsilon^{-2})$ last-iterate global convergence under weak gradient domination for general parametric policies. We establish this guarantee using purely first-order updates, with minimal assumptions and without gradient preconditioners. By extending state-of-the-art lower bounds to continuous parametric policies, we establish an $\Omega(\epsilon^{-2})$ sample complexity limit, confirming our framework is minimax-optimal up to logarithmic factors and horizon terms.
authors: Leonardo Cesani, Matteo Papini, Marcello Restelli
bullets: Addresses the high variance of Monte Carlo policy-gradient estimates and limitations of existing off-policy variance reduction methods.
Unifies recursive estimators with defensive importance sampling, including PAGE-PG and STORM-PG.
Proves last-iterate global convergence with approximately O(ε⁻²) sample complexity for general parametric policies under weak gradient domination.
Uses only first-order updates, without bounded importance weights or gradient preconditioners.
Extends lower bounds to continuous parametric policies, showing the rate is minimax-optimal up to logarithmic factors and horizon terms.

papers.abstract: Linearizing softmax attention offers a route to efficient Transformer inference, but preserving pretrained attention remains challenging. We identify an important source of approximation error overlooked by standard linearization methods: a small number of outlier dimensions contribute disproportionately to query-key dot products and account for a large fraction of the approximation error. Motivated by this heterogeneity, we propose Outlier-Aware Attention Linearization (OAL), a dimension-aware method for constructing quadratic attention approximations. Starting from a second-order Taylor approximation, we introduce a Hadamard-product formulation that makes individual query-key contributions explicit. This formulation relaxes globally shared coefficients to support dimension-specific linear terms and cross-dimensional quadratic interactions while preserving separable evaluation. To retain this flexibility with fewer parameters, OAL groups dimensions with similar contribution scales to share coefficients, while allowing distinct treatment of the few outliers. The resulting positive quadratic kernel is calibrated against pretrained attention outputs and admits linear-time evaluation with respect to sequence length for fixed head dimensions. On Qwen2.5-0.5B, OAL reduces frozen-attention output relative MSE by approximately 8.9% compared with DiJiang. Replacing middle-layer attention modules and jointly fine-tuning the kernel coefficients with LoRA further lowers WikiText-103 perplexity from 31.71 to 27.50 compared with a learned global quadratic, while improving accuracy on PIQA, HellaSwag, and ARC-E. These results demonstrate the value of outlier-aware dimension grouping for both attention approximation and pretrained-model conversion. The code is available at https://github.com/wuqianyue09/OAL

On Qwen2.5-0.5B, OAL reduces frozen-attention output relative MSE by approximately 8.9% versus DiJiang.

papers.abstract: Large language models struggle to reliably identify and correct errors in their own reasoning. Unlike prior training-based approaches that fine-tune an LLM to generate revisions or feedback, we learn where to intervene in failed rollouts and determine how to redirect them. To choose where to intervene, we train a 130K-parameter MLP head on a frozen encoder using only final-answer correctness. For redirection, we find that under a fixed generation budget, the tested inline injections fail to reliably redirect reasoning, whereas presenting the same instruction in a new user turn changes the model's course. The resulting correction framework, UPTURN (User-Prompt TURN injection at a learned position), requires no LLM fine-tuning: it retains a selected prefix, injects an instruction as a new user turn, and regenerates the suffix. Across four reasoners and six math benchmarks, UPTURN improves average accuracy in every setting over a 32-rollout baseline. It outperforms self-correction and reflection-token injection baselines under matched correction budgets, transfers across reasoners and to GPQA-Diamond without retraining, and complements GRPO and self-correction methods.

papers.abstract: Curriculum learning typically organizes training samples from easy to hard. In GRPO, medium-difficulty samples are attractive for online selection because they are more likely to yield informative group-relative learning signals, and prioritizing them can improve training efficiency. However, it remains unclear whether persistently selecting such samples also leads to the strongest final model performance, or whether training can benefit from progressing toward harder samples. Meanwhile, sample difficulty changes as the policy evolves, so fixed difficulty estimates can become misaligned with the current policy. We therefore re-estimate sample difficulty under the current policy and, inspired by the easy-to-hard principle of curriculum learning, design and evaluate a staged curriculum that progressively shifts the active difficulty band toward harder samples. Experiments on GSM8K show that persistent medium-difficulty selection does not achieve the strongest observed performance. Across three random seeds, progressing to a moderately harder difficulty band improves test accuracy to $0.6591 \pm 0.0077$, compared with $0.6449 \pm 0.0024$ for the fixed-medium curriculum. However, further progression to a harder difficulty band reduces accuracy to $0.6405 \pm 0.0053$. These results show that staged difficulty progression can outperform persistent medium-difficulty selection, but its benefit is non-monotonic. Effective GRPO curricula can therefore benefit from progressing beyond medium difficulty, while avoiding excessive progression toward overly difficult samples.}
authors: Ronghan Li, Fei Chen, Mingyu Lu
bullets: Persistent medium-difficulty selection is efficient for generating informative group-relative signals but is not optimal for final performance.
The method re-estimates sample difficulty under the evolving policy and progressively shifts the active difficulty band.
On GSM8K, the moderately harder curriculum reached 0.6591 ± 0.0077 test accuracy versus 0.6449 ± 0.0024 for fixed-medium selection.
Further progression to a harder band reduced accuracy to 0.6405 ± 0.0053 across three random seeds.
The benefit of difficulty progression is non-monotonic, indicating a need to avoid overly difficult samples.

figures.caption: Fig. 2 Comparison of the training paradigms considered in this study. Standard GRPO uses the full training set without difficulty-based selection. The static curriculum uses a fixed easy-to-hard ordering determined by the initial solvability estimate P0(x). The fixed-medium curriculum reselects samples online according to the current-policy success rate while keeping difficulty band B3 fixed. The staged curriculum reselects samples online while moving the active difficulty band through B1 → B2 → B3 → B4 → B5.

Fig. 1 Motivation and research questions for difficulty-aware training in GRPO. (a) The usefulness of a training problem depends on its current solvability: overly easy or hard problems tend to yield weak group-relative learning signals, whereas intermediate-solvability problems are more likely to produce informative comparisons among sampled responses. (b) Sample difficulty depends on the current policy and can change across difficulty bands as training proceeds, making precomputed difficulty estimates potentially stale. (c) Intermediate-solvability samples are therefore natural candidates for online selection and are emphasized by recent difficulty-aware selection strategies. This motivates two questions examined in this study: whether precomputed difficulty estimates remain aligned with the evolving policy, and whether persistently selecting the medium-difficulty band is sufficient or the curriculum should progress to harder difficulty bands during training.

papers.abstract: The Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus (ARC) is increasingly used to evaluate whether neural networks can infer task-specific transformations from few demonstrations. Recent ARC models differ in architecture, but also in broader training and evaluation protocols, including pretraining data, data augmentation, test-time setup, and optimization budgets, making conclusions about architecture benefits debatable. In this work, we study how the performance of the vision-inspired VARC and recursion-based TRM models is affected by pretraining and test-time training (TTT) budgets under a common inductive protocol on ARC-AGI-1. We cross five pretraining budgets with four TTT budgets for each test task. Each budget specifies a task-variant count and total sample presentations, defining the controlled training budgets. We observe that increasing TTT sample presentations improves the standard ARC pass@2 metric in all settings for both models. Increasing the TTT task-variant count consistently helps only TRM, whereas VARC often performs better with fewer variants. VARC also remains competitive without pretraining, while TRM benefits much more from it. These results show that pretraining and TTT budgets affect ARC evaluation and motivate reporting at comparable budgets.

papers.abstract: Automating biological laboratories requires robots to perform dexterous tool interactions under realistic visual conditions while handling dynamic experimental phenomena, presenting significant challenges for robotic manipulation. To enable systematic evaluation under these conditions, we introduce AutoBio+, a simulation benchmark and framework for dexterous manipulation in realistic biological laboratory environments. AutoBio+ comprises 14 tasks across 4 robot embodiments, spanning functional tool use, precision manipulation, language-conditioned visual grounding, and instrument operation. We introduce controllable dynamic experimental phenomena, including flames, vapor, and bubbles, to capture the evolving visual conditions of laboratory procedures. To further enhance environmental realism, we develop a hybrid rendering pipeline that integrates interactive simulated foreground objects with Gaussian-splatting backgrounds reconstructed from 6 real laboratory scenes. For efficient large-scale data generation and evaluation, we further build a parallel simulation framework on top of mjlab, proposing Parallel Finite-State Machine (PFSM) and integrating batched rendering with decoupled trajectory replay for demonstration generation and model-independent closed-loop policy evaluation. Our evaluation reveals substantial variation in policy performance across tasks, exposing distinct strengths and weaknesses of current manipulation policies. Real-world experiments further demonstrate a reduced sim-to-real gap, supporting the validity of AutoBio+ for realistic manipulation evaluation. Supplementary materials are available at https://autobio-plus.github.io/AutoBioPlus.
authors: Xuanye Wu, Yue Shi, Yongcan Yang, Yiqun Wang, Zhaoqi Wan, Dayu Xia, Jiezhang Cao, Xiangfei Li, Yao Mu, Guangtao Zhai

Provides scalable evaluation through parallel finite-state machines, batched rendering, and decoupled trajectory replay.
Finds substantial task-dependent variation in policy performance, with real-world experiments indicating a reduced sim-to-real gap.

papers.selection_reason: Benchmark and framework for dexterous manipulation in realistic laboratory environments.
papers.title: AutoBio+: Benchmarking Dexterous Manipulation with Dynamic Experimental Phenomena in Realistic Laboratories
papers.tldr: AutoBio+ is a realistic simulation benchmark for evaluating dexterous robot manipulation in biological laboratories with dynamic visual phenomena and diverse tool-use tasks.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are rapidly improving on long-horizon scientific and olympiad tasks. Recent systems have produced a Lean-formalized resolution of the Navier--Stokes problem and autonomous solutions to four open questions in the Erd\H{o}s Conjectures database. Yet neither system releases both its underlying model and complete inference stack. More broadly, a single agent session remains brittle on difficult problems: early errors can propagate, missing domain knowledge can stall progress, and apparent success can mask a misinterpretation or weakening of the original task. We introduce HOA (Humanize Olympiads Agent), an open, flow-level framework that coordinates multiple agent sessions through three complementary feedback channels. First, an independent reviewer evaluates each candidate and provides actionable feedback. Second, a structured wiki supplies task-specific knowledge that may be missing or unreliable in model pretraining. Third, a verifier checks generated Lean proofs against trusted challenge statements. With GPT-5.6 Sol, HOA achieves perfect scores on the IMO, IPhO, and IOI 2026, near-full marks on the IChO 2026 problem set, and solves all 672 problems (100%) on PutnamBench. On the Lean-Eval leaderboard, HOA ranks first, solving 251 of 304 problems (82.6%). We further evaluate HOA with open models. Using Kimi-K3, HOA achieves full scores on the IMO, IPhO, and IOI, and a gold-level score of 97.1% on the IChO. These results closely match the closed-source GPT-5.6 Sol + /Goal baseline on the IMO and IPhO, while exceeding it on the IChO and IOI, demonstrating that systematic feedback can help bridge substantial differences in base-model capability.
authors: Zhengyang Zhang, Jing Xiong, Hongzhou Lin, Juihui Chung, Zijian Zhang, Song Han, Sihao Liu, Ligeng Zhu
bullets: Targets brittleness in single-session agents, including error propagation, missing knowledge, and task misinterpretation.
Uses three feedback channels: actionable independent review, a task-specific structured wiki, and trusted Lean-proof verification.
With GPT-5.6 Sol, reports perfect scores on IMO, IPhO, and IOI 2026, near-full IChO marks, and 672/672 PutnamBench problems.
Ranks first on Lean-Eval, solving 251/304 problems (82.6%).
With Kimi-K3, achieves full IMO, IPhO, and IOI scores and 97.1% on IChO, suggesting feedback can compensate for weaker base models.
