papers.abstract: Attention Residuals (AttnRes) enables content-dependent retrieval over network depth, which can be viewed as single-stream softmax attention along the depth axis. Inspired by the success of multi-head attention along the sequence axis, we introduce Multi-Stream Attention Residuals (MSAR), an extension of AttnRes that generalizes this mechanism to multi-head depth attention, yielding substantial performance gains with minimal additional overhead. MSAR draws stream diversity from sequence context through multi-scale causal convolutions, allowing different heads to retrieve historical representations through distinct contextual views while preserving the integrity of the hidden representation. The retrieved streams are combined through lightweight adaptive mixing to generate the single-stream layer input. By retaining single-stream sources and expanding them on demand, MSAR supports multi-stream computation without requiring persistent multi-stream storage or communication. Across all 12 downstream benchmarks at the 18B and 28B MoE scales, MSAR consistently outperforms prior residual variants, including standard residual connections, manifold-constrained Hyper-Connections (mHC), and AttnRes. Scaling-law experiments yield an iso-loss compute speedup of $1.58\times$ over the standard residual baseline, compared with $1.35\times$ for AttnRes and $1.30\times$ for mHC. These results make MSAR a promising residual architecture for large-scale pre-training.
authors: Xiaohan Qin, Xiangdong Zhang, Tuo Dai, Sunan Zou, Huaijin Wu, Yebin Yang, Zhuo Xia, Lin Yao, Yuliang Liu, Junchi Yan
bullets: Addresses the limited single-stream retrieval of prior residual architectures across network depth.
Uses multi-scale causal convolutions to give attention heads distinct sequence-context views.
Adaptively mixes retrieved streams into a single layer input while avoiding persistent multi-stream storage or communication.
Outperforms standard residuals, mHC, and AttnRes across 12 downstream benchmarks at 18B and 28B MoE scales.
Achieves a reported 1.58× iso-loss compute speedup over standard residuals, versus 1.35× for AttnRes and 1.30× for mHC.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies issue sparse targets whose arrival at the robot controller is delayed and irregular, so a reasonable predicted action can still produce abrupt motion near people. Remedies are evaluated on different streams, delays and metrics. JitterVLA replays identical commands and arrival traces through alternative controllers, isolating the controller's effect. We apply it to synthetic reaches, hand trajectories from 20 people, three open VLA pipelines (838 episodes) and a physical UR3. Interpolation lowered modeled p99 jerk for every source, by 83% (615 to 106 m/s^3) on human motion with 200 ms delay, at a 2.0 cm tracking cost, and the effect replicated on 598 new episodes; jerk-limited generation lowered jerk further at a larger cost. Entropy-discontinuity associations had opposite, replicated signs in two pipelines, and entropy gating helped in one but not the other. On the UR3, interpolation lowered accelerometer-derived jerk by 3.0-14.0% in all six exploratory pairs, while a position-derived metric did not resolve the contrast. JitterVLA supports screening before human-centred studies; code and data will be released.
authors: Faith Ogunwoye, Didar Seyidov, Konstantin Gubernatorov, Dzmitry Tsetserukou
bullets: VLA commands arrive sparsely and irregularly, potentially causing abrupt motion near people.
The benchmark isolates controller effects by replaying the same commands and arrival traces across alternatives.
Interpolation reduced modeled p99 jerk by 83% on delayed human-motion traces, with a 2.0 cm tracking cost; jerk-limited generation reduced jerk further at greater cost.
Results across three VLA pipelines showed inconsistent links between entropy discontinuities and motion quality, and entropy gating helped only one pipeline.
On a physical UR3, interpolation reduced accelerometer-derived jerk in all six exploratory pairs, while a position-derived metric did not show the same contrast.

papers.abstract: Dynamic vocabularies built on-the-fly via Lempel-Ziv-Welch (LZW) compression let a language model represent the same text in fewer tokens, but prior work shows that this efficiency comes at a cost to reasoning and perplexity. We show that this quality gap is not a fundamental price of compression but can be substantially closed through targeted improvements to the compression layer and LZW codec, without modifying the underlying pretrained language model. Our analysis reveals four key issues: (1) LZW's compression algorithm creates an implicit conflict between the input embedding and the output embedding, a tension that a single shared embedding cannot resolve; (2) naively applying RoPE to LZW-compressed sequences ignores that merged tokens can span multiple tokens; (3) merging certain tokens (notably digits) disproportionately hurts downstream accuracy; and (4) dynamic vocabularies introduce an inherent segmentation ambiguity that confounds standard evaluation. We address these through decoupled input/output dynamic embedding layer, size-aware RoPE positioning, and a modified LZW codec supporting selective merges and multi-view segmentations. Across four models, our recipe improves perplexity on every corpus we evaluated as well as mathematical reasoning accuracy, closing roughly half the quality gap between zip2zip and the uncompressed baseline at a similar compression ratio on general text. This represents a significant step toward lossless adaptive-vocabulary compression for language models.
authors: Saibo Geng, Andrea Gentilini, Xinxian Ma, Nathan Ranchin, Yunzhen Yao, Robert West
bullets: Identifies four issues: shared input/output embeddings, RoPE misalignment for merged tokens, harmful digit merging, and segmentation ambiguity.
Uses decoupled input/output dynamic embeddings, size-aware RoPE, selective token merges, and multi-view segmentations.
Improves perplexity across all evaluated corpora and improves mathematical reasoning accuracy across four models.
Closes roughly half the quality gap between compressed zip2zip and the uncompressed baseline at a similar general-text compression ratio.
Targets adaptive-vocabulary compression while preserving the underlying model.

Figure 1: Why LZW induces prefix-aligned output codes. (a) The LZW dictionary is prefixclosed: an entry is registered only after its own prefix, so the entries available at a given position form a chain under the prefix order ({AB,ABC,ABCD}), all sharing the same first constituent. (b) The mirror image—a suffix-closed dictionary {CD,BCD,ABCD}—never arises under LZW. (c) Consequence for the language model: at a single decoding position the output hyper-encoder must score every member of such a chain against the same hidden state, which pushes their unembedding vectors toward one another and imposes a prefix-aligned geometry on f out ϕ .

Non-canonical input triggers the guard: SKIP (no entry, the candidate already exists), RESUME (the deferred entry is created on the next code), and EARLY EXIT (a novel combination is reached partway through the expansion). Both cases emit the same base-token sequence.

papers.selection_reason: Inference-time token compression via dynamic LZW vocabularies and token merging directly targets token-level efficiency.
papers.title: zip2zip++: Towards Inference-Time Token Compression with Minimal Quality Loss
papers.tldr: zip2zip++ reduces the quality loss of inference-time LZW token compression through targeted embedding, positional, codec, and evaluation improvements—without changing the pretrained language model.

papers.abstract: Large Audio Language Models (LALMs) achieve strong performance on speech-text tasks, but standard audio encoders produce hundreds of tokens for even short audio clips. Because self-attention scales quadratically in sequence length, this inflates inference-time compute substantially. Current training-free token compression methods prune or merge tokens based solely on coarse attention or feature similarity. However, treating audio tokens as generic, isotropic features smooths over spectral transitions, destroying fine-grained phonetic transitions essential for decoding speech. In contrast, speech signals exhibit highly structured temporal patterns where information density peaks at acoustic transitions. We propose AudioTETRIS, a training-free, two-stage framework that uses the audio encoder's representation geometry as an acoustic prior for token importance before applying attention-based compression. Instead of discarding encoder structure after the encoding stage, AudioTETRIS propagates this prior directly into the LLM decoder to compute a per-token fused score. This score drives progressive top-$k$ token selection across decoder layers without requiring additional training or auxiliary models. Evaluated on Qwen2-Audio-7B, Phi-4-Multimodal, and Audio Flamingo 3, AudioTETRIS retains near-uncompressed performance on several speech tasks using only 25% of audio tokens, matches or surpasses full-token accuracy at moderate compression rates, and consistently outperforms existing training-free baselines.
authors: Shreya Sajid, Anna Vettoruzzo, Joaquin Vanschoren
bullets: Targets the high inference cost caused by hundreds of audio tokens and quadratic self-attention.
Uses encoder representation geometry to identify transition-rich, information-dense tokens.
Fuses acoustic-prior and decoder attention signals into per-token importance scores.
Progressively selects top-k tokens across decoder layers without training or auxiliary models.
Evaluated on three audio LLMs, it retains near-uncompressed speech-task performance and outperforms training-free baselines.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of AudioTETRIS. A phoneme-transition-aware acoustic prior wt is computed from the audio encoder’s hidden states via the transitional distance dt = ∥ht − ht−1∥22, preserving phoneme transitions yhard (§4; left). Token pruning occurs in two stages: Stage 1 injects wt as a static acoustic prior from the encoder’s hidden states; Stage 2 computes a depth-adaptive LLM attention score, fusing intra-audio attention in early layers with cross-modal (text-to-audio) attention in later layers (right). The two scores are fused into a single importance score, and top-k selection retains the most salient tokens at each pruning layer ℓ.

Figure 8: Schematic of the phoneme-transition-aware prior pipeline. Top: audio waveform with forced-alignment phoneme segments. Second row: per-token encoder hidden states ht, colored by phoneme membership. Third row: raw derivative dt (bars) and the Gaussian-smoothed transition score bt (line). Bottom: ground-truth transition labels, shown as discrete spikes yhard and their Gaussian-smoothed form ysoft, used to compute rhard and rsoft.

This shift motivates our layer-dependent pooling rule in Eq. 3.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) is a key driver for Large Reasoning Models, but it is vulnerable to "zero-reward collapse", a training failure where a sudden increase in task difficulty causes the learning signal to vanish. We argue that the conventional approach of discarding these failed trajectories is wasteful, as they contain valuable diagnostic information about the model's cognitive gaps, a bright side that can be leveraged for recovery. Existing solutions, however, often regress to static, "off-policy-style" interventions like pre-defined hint libraries or perform post-hoc refinement, failing to provide the adaptive, forward-looking guidance needed to escape the collapse. To address this, we propose a paradigm shift towards on-policy pedagogical intervention and introduce MENTOR, a multi-agent framework that acts as a live mentor. MENTOR diagnoses the root cause of failure in real-time and dynamically generates targeted, instructional prompts to guide the learning agent's next attempt. As a plug-and-play module, MENTOR integrates seamlessly into existing policy optimization pipelines like GRPO without modifying the training infrastructure. Extensive experiments on math and code generation show that MENTOR effectively mitigates zero-reward collapse, outperforming state-of-the-art baselines. Notably, it achieves massive average relative gains of up to 78.3% on Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct over its base model.
authors: Guanlan Yue, Hang Yu, Xiaoyong Huang, Ruipeng Li, Wei Zhang, Bingchang Liu, Rui Wang
bullets: Zero-reward collapse can occur when task difficulty rises sharply, causing learning signals to disappear.
Failed trajectories contain diagnostic information but are often discarded or handled with static, off-policy interventions.
MENTOR is a multi-agent live mentor that identifies failure causes and generates adaptive guidance for the next attempt.
It is designed as a plug-and-play module for policy optimization pipelines such as GRPO.
Experiments in math and code generation report improved recovery and gains of up to 78.3% on Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct over its base model.

papers.abstract: Pre-trained robot policies, such as Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models, provide a strong foundation for generalist robotic manipulation, but adapting them to new tasks with only a few demonstrations remains challenging. Directly fine-tuning a pre-trained policy often achieves strong in-distribution performance, yet it can distort the representations learned during pre-training and weaken the model's generalization ability under out-of-distribution shifts. We propose Retrieval-Anchored Representation Alignment (RARA), a two-stage adaptation method, to address this issue. First, RARA retrieves representation features from pretraining with similar task intent and motion, and aligns the policy's representations of the target demonstrations with the pre-trained representations of the retrieved demonstrations. Second, RARA fine-tunes the policy on the target demonstrations while limiting how much its representations of the retrieved demonstrations change during fine-tuning. By reducing the representation mismatch before action learning and preserving pre-trained knowledge during adaptation, RARA limits unnecessary representation drift during fine-tuning. Experiments with Diffusion Policy and GR00T on 13 tasks in RoboTwin, RoboCasa, and on a real robot show that RARA improves the average success of fine-tuning by 9.5 points in-distribution and 13.6 points out-of-distribution, and outperforms all compared baselines. Project page: https://shua-kang.github.io/RARA_robot/
authors: Xuhui Kang, Sung-Wook Lee, Yan Zhuang, Tianle Zhong, Yen-Ling Kuo
bullets: Addresses representation drift and weakened out-of-distribution generalization when adapting pre-trained robot policies with few demonstrations.
Uses a two-stage process: retrieve similar pre-training features and align target representations, then fine-tune while constraining changes to retrieved representations.
Evaluated with Diffusion Policy and GR00T across 13 tasks in RoboTwin, RoboCasa, and on a real robot.
Improves average fine-tuning success by 9.5 points in-distribution and 13.6 points out-of-distribution, outperforming compared baselines.

papers.abstract: Humanoid tennis requires reactive whole-body coordination under rapidly changing ball dynamics, yet collecting task-specific motion-capture demonstrations that cover diverse approach states, contact locations, and timing conditions is costly. Inspired by how humans acquire new skills by combining reusable motor experience with task-specific demonstrations, we present ATHLETE, a framework for learning reactive humanoid tennis from generic locomotion data and ordinary tennis videos. ATHLETE combines LAFAN1 locomotion with video-derived striking motions and uses Trajectory-Guided Motion Matching (TGMM) to construct diverse task-conditioned whole-body references. These references are transformed into a reactive policy through physics-based teacher--student learning with online DAgger distillation, followed by PPO fine-tuning for the tennis task. The resulting policy responds directly to robot and ball observations without requiring reference-motion inputs at deployment. On a real humanoid robot, ATHLETE achieves forehand and backhand hit rates of $90.00\%$ and $86.67\%$, respectively, and enables multi-shot rallies with human players. These results demonstrate that ATHLETE can learn dynamic humanoid tennis skills from reusable locomotion data and video demonstrations. Result videos and code can be found at https://anonymous.4open.science/w/ATHLETE2027/.
authors: Zhihao Tian, Zifan Wang, Enzheng Zhu, Xun Yang, Jialong Qin, Mengbo Wang, Junwei Liang
bullets: Addresses the costly need for extensive task-specific motion-capture data covering diverse tennis states.
Uses Trajectory-Guided Motion Matching to build task-conditioned whole-body references from locomotion data and ordinary tennis videos.
Distills these references into a reactive physics-based policy with online DAgger, then fine-tunes it with PPO.
The deployed policy uses only robot and ball observations, without reference-motion inputs.
On a real humanoid, it achieves 90.00% forehand and 86.67% backhand hit rates and supports multi-shot rallies.

papers.abstract: We present Rationally Linearized Multilayer Perceptrons(RaLiMPs), a new approach to efficiently linearizing MLPs using low-degree rational approximations of standard activation functions. Inspired by polynomial-based MLP linearization, we show that rational approximations can provide accurate representations at substantially lower degree. RaLiMPs exploit these approximations to construct kernel representations with narrow bottlenecks, enabling efficient composition across MLP layers. We provide theoretical guarantees for the resulting approximation and evaluate RaLiMPs across applications ranging from implicit 3D models to large language models. Our experiments demonstrate favorable accuracy--efficiency tradeoffs, with RaLiMPs achieving competitive or improved accuracy while substantially reducing inference cost.

papers.abstract: Anticipation of vessel trajectories is an essential task when navigating at sea. This applies to both human navigators and autonomous surface vessels. Trajectory forecasting enables sub-routines such as collision avoidance to assess the situation and react accordingly in time. This paper investigates Transformer and Performer models for trajectory prediction of surface vessels in confined waters. Using widely available position data from the Automatic Identification System (AIS), candidate models are trained and evaluated. Historical information on how other vessels have moved in the local area surrounding each agent is conveyed using positional heat maps. The heat maps are generated using Kernel Density Estimation (KDE) and encoded with a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) before entering the Transformer models. The models are trained with quantile loss to efficiently obtain a model-aware prediction interval, as this is crucial for timely collision avoidance. The proposed model architectures are shown to greatly outperform previous work while the inclusion of local heat maps enables the prediction of vessel movement that is not otherwise indicated from the previous positions.

papers.abstract: Multimodal language models (MLLMs) exhibit promising spatial reasoning capabilities, yet the internal mechanisms supporting them remain poorly understood. We uncover S-Space, a linear representation subspace in which object-token representations encode continuous coordinates along horizontal, vertical, and distance axes. Although we identify these axes by differentiating spatial-answer scores with respect to object-token activations, S-Space is intrinsic rather than induced by specific data or prompts, remaining readable under non-spatial questions. We show that S-Space functions as an internal spatial workspace of MLLMs. Perception encodes object locations into it, forming spatial representations that can be directly read out to support accurate spatial judgments. Internal reasoning transforms it for changing viewpoints. Verbal responses selectively access it, evidenced by causal interventions that alter spatial judgments while largely preserving non-spatial responses. Case studies further show that S-Space assigns locations to unseen entities and the observer, and connects physical directions with abstract linguistic meanings, suggesting both the capabilities and limitations of large-scale language training. Finally, we use S-Space as a diagnostic tool for spatial reasoning failures. Direction-word readouts reveal systematic coupling between cardinal and image-relative reference frames. More importantly, a perception-computation decomposition exposes a key bottleneck: MLLMs can form capable spatial representations, yet fall short in the spatial transformations required to reason reliably across viewpoint changes.
authors: Zhiyuan Shi, Xiang Li, Xingzhuo Guo, Shangchen Miao, Weiliang Chen, Qiyu Dai, Jinshan Ren, Jiangran Lyu, Fangfu Liu, Mingsheng Long, Jialong Wu
bullets: Object-token representations encode continuous horizontal, vertical, and distance coordinates in a linear subspace.

Causal interventions show that modifying S-Space changes spatial judgments while largely preserving non-spatial responses.
Diagnostics indicate that unreliable spatial reasoning stems mainly from deficient viewpoint-related spatial transformations, not representation formation.

papers.title: S-Space: Exploring Spatial Workspace in Multimodal Language Models

papers.abstract: Action-conditioned world models offer a promising foundation for generalist robotic intelligence by predicting the consequences of actions. However, existing robotic datasets provide limited coverage of the diverse interaction dynamics required for generalizable world modeling. Large-scale egocentric human videos offer complementary interaction experience, yet the embodiment gap between human hands and robotic manipulators hinders effective cross-embodiment learning. Meanwhile, the predominance of successful demonstrations leaves failure dynamics substantially underrepresented, limiting the ability of world models to anticipate unsuccessful executions. To address these limitations, we introduce HF-WM, an action-conditioned world model that combines Human interaction learning with Failure-aware post-training. To bridge the embodiment gap, we develop a dual-branch framework that couples video generation with auxiliary pointflow prediction, using stabilized pointflow as a unified motion representation across human and robot interactions while suppressing egocentric camera motion. To improve failure modeling, we further perform Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) post-training on perturbed actions derived from successful demonstrations, guided by action alignment and physical plausibility rewards, enabling the model to learn plausible failure dynamics without paired ground-truth videos. Extensive experiments demonstrate that HF-WM achieves state-of-the-art performance in action-conditioned video generation and exhibits strong utility for policy evaluation in downstream robotic tasks.
authors: Peiyan Tu, Cong Wang, Hanxin Zhu, Xin Jin, Zhibo Chen
bullets: Addresses limited interaction diversity, the human–robot embodiment gap, and the underrepresentation of failures in robot datasets.
Uses a dual-branch model combining action-conditioned video generation with auxiliary pointflow prediction.
Employs stabilized pointflow to represent motion across human and robot interactions while reducing egocentric camera-motion effects.
Applies GRPO post-training to perturbed actions, guided by action-alignment and physical-plausibility rewards, without paired failure videos.
Experiments report state-of-the-art action-conditioned video generation and strong utility for downstream robotic policy evaluation.

papers.abstract: In machine learning, a self-attention dynamics describes the attention mechanism of transformers, and is obtained treating the layer index of a transformer as time index. Even though naturally discrete-time, this dynamical system is most often studied in continuous-time. Scope of this paper is to provide a thorough investigation of the discrete-time version of the self-attention dynamics: a complete classification of its equilibria is given, and their stability properties are studied, in both the single-head and the multihead case. We show that in both cases the main attractor of the dynamics is a consensus equilibrium aligned with the principal eigenvector of the value matrix (in the single-head case, a corresponding matrix of weights in the multihead case), even though other locally asymptotically stable bipartite equilibria can be show to exist at least in the single-head situation. The behavior is confirmed by looking at the learned weight matrices of a real transformer.
bullets: Studies self-attention dynamics using the transformer layer index as discrete time.
Classifies equilibria and analyzes their stability for both single-head and multihead attention.
Identifies consensus equilibria aligned with the principal eigenvector of the value matrix or a related multihead weight matrix as the main attractors.
Shows that locally asymptotically stable bipartite equilibria can also occur, at least in the single-head case.
Observations are supported by examining learned weight matrices from a real transformer.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Example of bipartite consensus with d = 3 and n = 10. (a): when a very small perturbation is applied to a locally asymptotically stable bipartite consensus point (aligned with v1), the system returns to the bipartite equilibrium. (b): when a larger perturbation is applied to the same bipartite consensus point, the trajectory escapes towards one of the two the consensus points associated to the principal eigenvector v1. The two tokens in blue and green “migrate” to the antipodal point, thereby achieving consensus.

Fig. 1. Example of single-head self-attention dynamics with d = 3 and n = 10. Top panel: the trajectory of the 10 tokens is shown on the sphere S2. The solid dot is the endpoint of a trajectory, i.e., the consensus point reached by all tokens. Lower panel: the correlation corr(xi,v1) tends to 1 as consensus is achieved (all tokens become aligned with the principal eigenvector v1). The black dotted line is the mean correlation over the 10 tokens.

Fig. 3. Example of real shared-weight transformer: ALBERT. (a): Inter-token distance for 103 experiments. (b): Correlation between xi(t) and v1 for t = 1, . . . , 24 over multiple experiments. (c): Histogram of the correlation between xi(T ) and v1 at T = 24 over 103 experiments.

papers.selection_reason: Provides a theoretical analysis of self-attention dynamics in Transformers, contributing to the understanding of LLM architectures.
papers.title: Asymptotic Analysis of Discrete-Time Self-Attention Dynamics in Transformers
papers.tldr: This paper rigorously analyzes discrete-time self-attention as a dynamical system, classifying its equilibria and showing that consensus aligned with a principal eigenvector is the main attractor.

papers.abstract: Runtime failure monitors for robot policies are typically evaluated by how accurately they distinguish failed from successful executions. Yet an accurate alarm may arrive too late for recovery, while an unnecessary intervention may disrupt an execution that would otherwise succeed. We introduce RESCUE, a counterfactual framework for evaluating whether a monitor's alarms enable useful interventions. By restoring simulator and policy states at execution checkpoints, RESCUE compares alternative actions, identifies the latest checkpoint satisfying a specified recovery criterion, and evaluates whether acting on alarms reduces expected task-completion cost. We evaluate RESCUE with OpenVLA-OFT and $\pi_{0.5}$ over LIBERO-Spatial and LIBERO-Plus using 128,340 counterfactual branches. Recoverability depends on the state--intervention pair rather than on robot state alone: at $\tau=0.5$, 14 of 66 OpenVLA-OFT/LIBERO-Plus failures contain a recoverable checkpoint under continuation, compared with 34 of 66 under continuation or scripted recovery, while recovery reduces recoverability in other conditions. On the primary strong-policy conditions, favourable detection scores do not establish lower intervention cost. Under the evaluated stop-and-reset model, even an idealised detector can afford only a 2.0--3.3% false-alarm rate before unnecessary resets outweigh the savings from stopping failures early. These results show that monitor value depends jointly on the intervention available and the workload in which it is deployed.
authors: David Ahmedt-Aristizabal, Abdelwahed Khamis, Mohammad Ali Armin, Lars Petersson
bullets: Motivation: alarms can be too late to enable recovery, or can disrupt executions that would have succeeded.
Method: restore simulator and policy states at checkpoints, compare counterfactual interventions, and find the latest recoverable checkpoint.
Contribution: a framework for measuring recoverability and intervention cost jointly with monitor performance.
Findings: recoverability depends on the state–intervention pair; favourable detection scores do not necessarily reduce intervention cost.
Scope/limitation: under the evaluated stop-and-reset model, ideal detectors tolerate only a 2.0–3.3% false-alarm rate before resets become counterproductive.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Measuring recoverability and its dependence on intervention. At τ = 0.5, step 48 is the last recoverable checkpoint, while step 56 no longer satisfies the recovery criterion. Right: Median recoverability horizons (circles), interquartile ranges (bars), and median runtime-monitor alarm times (black symbols) across policy settings. Continue and escalate denote CONTINUE and scripted RECOVER; ticks show median horizons at τ = 0.3 and τ = 0.7. On OpenVLA-OFT/LIBERO-Plus, 14/66 failures contain a qualifying checkpoint under CONTINUE, 33/66 under RECOVER, and 34/66 under their union.

Fig. 3. Monitor alarms often arrive after the recoverability horizon. Across four policy settings, left: fraction of alarmed failures whose alarm occurs after the horizon, with 95% Wilson confidence intervals; right: alarm-minus-horizon lag, with medians and interquartile ranges. Positive lag indicates late detection. Results include failures for which both an alarm and a recoverability horizon are defined under the corresponding intervention. Purple denotes CONTINUE; amber denotes scripted RECOVER, labelled “escalate” in the figure.

papers.selection_reason: Counterfactual evaluation of VLA runtime monitors for robot policy recovery; directly relevant to embodied VLA and robot learning.
papers.title: RESCUE: Is This Alarm Worth Acting On? Counterfactual Evaluation of VLA Runtime Monitors
papers.tldr: RESCUE evaluates robot runtime alarms by whether acting on them actually improves task outcomes, not merely by detection accuracy.

papers.abstract: Nonlinear model predictive control (NMPC) can be applied to large nonlinear systems with complex objectives while enforcing constraints, but the cost of solving the underlying optimization problems limits real-time application for systems with fast dynamics or many states. Neural networks can reduce this online cost by approximating the control law, but may violate constraints and typically require many precomputed optimizer solutions for training. The learning-based iterative solver for constrained optimization (LISCO) instead learns to predict primal-dual steps toward satisfaction of the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) conditions through self-supervised training without precomputed solutions, but its dense, monolithic architecture grows with the prediction horizon. We remove this horizon dependence by exploiting the temporal structure of the problem in the solver architecture, which makes the network size independent of the horizon while leaving the training loss and the solver iteration unchanged. A closed-loop resampling strategy further aligns the training distribution with closed-loop operation at no additional sampling cost. On an economic NMPC benchmark of a CSTR cascade, the proposed solver scales to larger problems than monolithic LISCO and achieves median speedups of up to a factor of four over IPOPT. In closed loop, it achieves comparable control performance to IPOPT with no observed constraint violations.
bullets: Addresses the high online optimization cost of NMPC for large or fast nonlinear systems.
Uses a temporal-decomposition architecture to predict primal-dual KKT steps without network growth as the prediction horizon increases.
Retains LISCO’s self-supervised training and iterative solver procedure, requiring no precomputed optimizer solutions.
Adds closed-loop resampling to better match training data with deployment conditions without extra sampling cost.
On a CSTR cascade benchmark, scales to larger problems, reaches up to 4× median speedups over IPOPT, and achieves comparable closed-loop control with no observed constraint violations.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a scalable learned iterative solver for Nonlinear MPC using temporal decomposition, fitting 'Robot Learning and Manipulation' through robotic control and learned planning.
papers.title: A Scalable Learned Iterative Solver for Nonlinear MPC via Temporal Decomposition
papers.tldr: A temporally decomposed learned solver makes constrained nonlinear MPC scalable with horizon-independent network size while maintaining IPOPT-like control performance and avoiding observed constraint violations.

papers.abstract: Multimodal LLMs can fail to read text embedded in an image's coarse structure (text a human recovers by squinting) and report that no text is present. We name this class Squint Text and study it as a recognition deficiency, motivated by cases from a production moderation pipeline. We introduce SquintBench, comprising 1076 production-derived moderation images, and SquintCtrl, a controlled synthetic suite for mechanism diagnosis. Frozen-weight analysis shows that hidden text leaves a coarse signal while glyph identity is weakly represented; identity becomes substantially more accessible when the correct spatial regions are supplied, implicating spatial selection as a major bottleneck. Suppressing high-frequency content also improves reading at a fixed visual-token budget, while visual token count may also contribute. These findings motivate Squint OPSD: a frozen teacher receives a downscaled view and the ground-truth transcription as privileged context, and its token-level distributions supervise a student along on-policy trajectories. At inference, the student reads the original image alone. Squint OPSD reaches 88.61 ANLS on SquintBench, versus 26.50 for the unadapted backbone, 24.44 for the best general-purpose model on the original view, and 68.60 at best for an off-the-shelf model under a downscaled view. These results substantially narrow the gap between available visual evidence and its generated read-out without auxiliary views at inference.
authors: Chen Peng, Shan Huang, Jianbo Huang, Linrui Qin, Qibo Sun, Mengwei Xu
bullets: Introduces Squint Text: embedded text that humans can recover by squinting but MLLMs may report as absent.
Releases SquintBench with 1,076 production-derived moderation images and SquintCtrl for controlled diagnosis.
Finds that text location is a major bottleneck: supplying correct regions improves glyph identity, while suppressing high frequencies can help at fixed visual-token budgets.
Proposes Squint OPSD, which distills token-level supervision from a frozen teacher using privileged downscaled views and transcriptions, while the student uses only the original image at inference.
Achieves 88.61 ANLS on SquintBench, compared with 26.50 for the unadapted backbone and 68.60 for the best off-the-shelf model using a downscaled view.

papers.selection_reason: Diagnoses and improves MLLM text reading via spatial selection and privileged distillation; fits multimodal LLM research.
papers.title: When MLLMs miss what humans read: diagnosing and learning to read squint text
papers.tldr: The paper shows that MLLMs often miss faint, coarse “squint text” because of spatial-selection and visual-token bottlenecks, and improves recognition through teacher-guided distillation.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement Learning (RL) substantially improves planning performance in autonomous-driving Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models. However, existing RL methods rely on scalar trajectory rewards that measure overall quality but fail to identify specific planning errors or provide actionable correction signals. In long-tail scenarios, errors in scene understanding, behavior selection, and trajectory execution are compressed into a single score. We observe that Reflective Guidance turns trajectory evaluation into explicit diagnoses and corrective instructions, substantially improving planning accuracy. Yet such guidance requires an initial prediction and its evaluation results, making it unavailable for direct single-pass inference. We propose Reflect-VLA, which treats Reflective Guidance as training-time privileged information and internalizes its planning benefits through Dual-Path On-Policy Self-Distillation (Dual-OPSD). Unlike scalar-reward optimization, Dual-OPSD uses the driving score only to route student-generated trajectories. It distills dense token-level corrective distributions from the teacher for risky trajectories while applying self-imitation to preserve reliable ones. To provide reliable corrective distributions on student rollouts, the teacher is progressively constructed through Driving-Knowledge Pretraining, Planning-and-Refinement SFT, and Self-Refinement Rejection Sampling. At inference time, Reflect-VLA generates trajectories in a single pass without explicit guidance or iterative refinement. Experiments on NAVSIM v1/v2 and Bench2Drive demonstrate competitive planning performance while reducing training time by over 90% compared with RL.
authors: Yuechen Luo, He Chong, Fang Li, Shaoqing Xu, Hexin Zhang, Ruiqi Zhang, Ziying Song, Lei Yang, Zhi-Xin Yang, Fuxi Wen
bullets: Scalar trajectory rewards provide limited, non-actionable feedback for specific planning errors, especially in long-tail scenarios.
Dual-Path On-Policy Self-Distillation uses driving scores to route student rollouts, distilling token-level corrections for risky trajectories and self-imitation for reliable ones.
A progressively built teacher supplies corrective guidance through knowledge pretraining, planning/refinement supervised fine-tuning, and self-refinement rejection sampling.
At inference, the model plans in a single pass without explicit reflection or iterative refinement.
Experiments on NAVSIM v1/v2 and Bench2Drive show competitive planning performance and over 90% lower training time than RL.

papers.abstract: Speech recognition on low-cost microcontrollers is, in practice, limited to keyword spotting or a fixed list of commands. We present O\'ido, an inference engine that runs open-vocabulary English speech recognition entirely on an ESP32-S3 (240 MHz dual-core Xtensa LX7, 512 KB of SRAM, 8 MB of PSRAM, 16 MB of flash, no neural accelerator). O\'ido executes a 13M-parameter Conformer-CTC model with int8 weights, per-frame dynamic int8 activations and int8 attention on the chip's SIMD instructions, with a schedule designed around flash and PSRAM bandwidth. On LibriSpeech test-clean/test-other the on-device arithmetic reaches 3.70%/8.23% word error rate (WER), within 0.12 points of full precision, and 3.33%/7.15% with an on-chip 1.3M-parameter language model; a transducer head gives 2.99%/6.67% and an int4 variant fits in 8.3 MB. This is 2.3-2.8x fewer errors than the vendor's recognizer on the same chip, and fewer than Whisper tiny.en and Moonshine tiny in full precision on a laptop, including in real noise and reverberation. Measured on a physical board, the firmware runs at 1.97x the duration of the audio on one core, with transcripts identical to an instruction-exact emulator: accurate, but not yet real time (a 4 s command is transcribed about 8.7 s after it ends). The two-core schedule gives wrong results on silicon and is disabled. A streaming variant shows partial text while the speaker talks and delivers the final text 4.1-11.1 s after clips of 3.6-10.6 s (7.2-22.4 s in utterance mode) at 4.86%/11.03% WER; a Spanish model makes 34-60% fewer errors than multilingual Whisper tiny. Code and models are released.
authors: Daniel Varela S\'anchez, Guillermo Mart\'in-Coello Ju\'arez
bullets: Addresses the limitations of low-cost microcontrollers, which typically support only keyword spotting or fixed commands.
Runs a 13M-parameter Conformer-CTC model using int8 quantization, SIMD-optimized attention, and flash/PSRAM-aware scheduling.
Achieves 3.70%/8.23% WER on LibriSpeech test-clean/test-other, with improved results from language-model and transducer variants.
On a physical board, runs at 1.97× audio duration on one core; streaming provides partial transcripts but still has multi-second latency.
Code and models are released; the two-core schedule is disabled because it produces incorrect results on silicon.

papers.abstract: Collective Autonomous Vehicle (AV) route choices in real-world traffic networks can create externalities for Human-Driven Vehicles (HDVs), as routes that benefit AVs may increase travel times for other road users. To address this, we introduce a social component, the marginal cost, to the selfish travel time AV reward. Marginal cost captures an AV's impact on other road users by comparing their travel times with those in a counterfactual simulation in which the AV is removed. We study AV route choice in mixed-autonomy traffic settings using Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL), where AVs learn routing policies through repeated interactions with the traffic environment. Experiments on the real-world networks of Ingolstadt and Provins show that incorporating marginal cost into the AV reward not only limits the increase in HDV travel times and shortens AV travel times relative to selfish AV routing, but also improves overall system performance. In Ingolstadt, selfish routing of 40\% AVs increases the travel times of other vehicles by 1.7\%, and this drops to 1.1\% when the social reward is included. Interestingly, not only does overall system performance improve, but the AVs are also better off when acting socially.This effect is consistent across tested cities, penetration rates, and replications, yet when the weight of the social component in the reward increases, the system fails to reach the desired performance. For a more scalable approach to social AV routing in mixed-autonomy traffic, we compute the marginal cost only for the AVs whose route choices most affect the traffic system. This reduces the number of counterfactual simulations and achieves similar performance at a significantly lower computational cost. Our results suggest that AV routing should go beyond selfish rewards and, for the benefit of all traffic participants, include a social component in its objective.
authors: Anastasia Psarou, Mikolaj Rams, Blazej Torbus, Rafal Kucharski
bullets: Selfish AV route choices can increase travel times for human-driven vehicles in mixed-autonomy traffic.
The method estimates each AV’s impact by comparing traffic with and without that AV in a counterfactual simulation.
Experiments on Ingolstadt and Provins show lower human-driver delays, shorter AV travel times, and better system performance with social rewards.
For 40% AV penetration in Ingolstadt, the human-driver travel-time increase falls from 1.7% to 1.1%.
Computing marginal costs only for the most influential AVs preserves similar performance at lower computational cost; excessive social-reward weighting can hurt performance.

However, computing marginal cost requires additional counterfactual simulations for each AV, adding computational cost. (C) To reduce this burden, we introduce selective marginal cost reward shaping, which computes marginal cost rewards only for a subset of the most impactful AVs. This preserves some of the benefits for AVs and HDVs’ travel times while reducing the number of counterfactual simulations.

papers.abstract: Earnings call transcription presents a realistic continual learning scenario where Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) systems are updated with new recordings but risk catastrophic forgetting of previously learned financial speech patterns. Adapting Whisper-small from a general-domain speech corpus to the Earnings22 benchmark reveals the opposite: all evaluated methods exhibit improvement on held-out financial speech from the same domain during adaptation rather than forgetting. This task complementarity makes regularization counterproductive. Nevertheless, when regularization is warranted, a layer-wise mini-Kronecker-Factored Approximate Curvature (mini-KFAC) approximation seems to achieve lower word error rates (WERs) and more stable optimization than standard diagonal Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC). The results suggest that task complementarity should be assessed before applying continual learning constraints, and prefer mini-KFAC EWC over diagonal EWC when needed.
bullets: Studies continual learning for earnings-call ASR when adapting Whisper-small to financial speech.
All evaluated methods improve held-out speech from the same domain during adaptation, indicating task complementarity.
Regularization is therefore counterproductive for this adaptation scenario.
When regularization is needed, layer-wise mini-KFAC EWC appears to yield lower WER and more stable optimization than diagonal EWC.
The findings recommend checking task complementarity before imposing continual-learning constraints.

papers.abstract: Traditional system identification typically involves two steps: initially, training data is processed to estimate a model of the system of interest; then, the model is used to predict outputs for new input queries. In contrast, recent in-context learning approaches learn a meta model that maps directly from training data and query inputs to outputs in a zero-shot fashion, bypassing explicit model estimation. This approach leverages a meta model trained offline, on large sets of synthetically generated data, to emulate the behavior of a system identification algorithm. In this work, we advance this meta-learning framework for system identification in three directions. First, we develop a unified probabilistic meta-identification architecture that combines a Transformer-based encoder-decoder with tailored mechanisms for handling long training sequences, enabling calibrated predictions over long horizons. Second, we show how a pre-trained meta model can act as an uncertainty-aware synthetic data generator for classical system identification, providing task-specific data that regularize parametric models when real data are scarce. Third, we systematically evaluate the framework on standard nonlinear system identification benchmarks and on a challenging out-of-distribution scenario, demonstrating competitive accuracy with state-of-the-art methods and strong generalization, including cases where input-only adaptation is sufficient to handle significant distribution shifts.
authors: Matteo Rufolo, Dario Piga, Filippo Pura, Marco Forgione
bullets: Replaces explicit per-task model estimation with a meta-model that maps training data and query inputs directly to predictions.
Uses a Transformer encoder-decoder with mechanisms for long sequences and calibrated long-horizon predictions.
Generates task-specific synthetic data to regularize classical parametric models when real data are limited.
Achieves competitive accuracy on nonlinear system-identification benchmarks and generalizes to challenging distribution shifts.
Input-only adaptation can be sufficient under significant distribution changes.

papers.abstract: End-to-end planning in complex scenes must model diverse driving intentions and select the most appropriate trajectory using scene context and future risks. However, multi-query regression may collapse to one mode, while anchor-based and generative planners share a scaling bottleneck: small candidate sets limit maneuver coverage or discovery of high-quality trajectories, whereas large sets increase generation and scoring costs. We propose ManeuverFlow to generate trajectories for distinct intentions in one step and evaluate and refine them using current and future evidence. The model selects relevant maneuver modes, draws corresponding noise from the Gaussian mixture prior, and maps it to intention-specific trajectories through a maneuver-routed mixture-of-experts MeanFlow field. Current features and future features predicted by the world model are aggregated along each candidate path into trajectory-specific evidence for PDM-factor prediction. Using the same evidence, the refiner predicts local Frenet residuals for selected candidates; refined and retained candidates are then jointly re-scored for selection. With a lightweight TransFuser-style ResNet-34 backbone, ManeuverFlow achieves 90.6 PDMS and 90.1 EPDMS on NAVSIM v1/v2 navtest, respectively. On WorldEngine's recent 3DGS closed-loop benchmark, it attains the highest listed PDMS$^\ast$ scores of 75.19 and 74.58 under logged and IDM-controlled traffic, respectively. Code: https://github.com/wyh-autonomy/maneuverflow.
authors: Yuhao Wei, Yong Chen, Chen Yang, Yingchen Wang, Delin Ouyang, Lingfeng Qi, Qi Lan, Zhanhua Zhang, Jie Li, Guofa Li
bullets: Addresses mode collapse and the cost–coverage trade-off of small versus large candidate sets.
Uses maneuver-routed mixture-of-experts MeanFlow to map maneuver-specific Gaussian-mixture noise to trajectories.
Aggregates present and world-model-predicted future features along each path for trajectory-specific scoring.
Refines selected candidates with local Frenet residuals before joint re-scoring.
Reports strong performance on NAVSIM v1/v2 and the WorldEngine 3DGS closed-loop benchmark.

papers.abstract: Forecasting desertification has received far less attention than mapping it. We use a convolutional LSTM (ConvLSTM) trained on ten annual Earth Observation (EO) variables (2000-2023) over the semi-arid state of Cear\'a, Brazil, on a 256x206 grid at roughly 2.2 km resolution, to measure how much of the year-to-year evolution of a MapBiomas-derived degradation index (IDV) can be predicted from satellite data. The network predicts a bounded change on top of the last observed state, is trained in two stages (single-step, then recursive rollout) and is evaluated on a contiguous spatial and temporal holdout. State-wide mean IDV rose from 0.238 to 0.350 between 2000 and 2023, about 0.005 per year, but cell-level change is dominated by year-to-year jumps, and a gradient-boosting model given all channels explains only 4.7% of its variance. Against this ceiling, the ConvLSTM lowers RMSE relative to persistence by 1.6% one year ahead and 4.4% four years ahead in a held-out southern band (p < 0.001), beats persistence with a constant drift and reproduces 53-69% of the regional drift. Drift-aware baselines only help from the third year onward, by up to 4.4% in RMSE at six years. An earlier formulation that redrew the whole field each year predicted changes unrelated to the observed ones (correlation -0.06) and produced a spurious decline when run recursively. Channel knockouts suggest that elevation and EVI degrade the forecast, while slope and aspect have no measurable effect. Monte Carlo dropout and stochastic scenario maps convey the uncertainty that the expected-value forecast hides. Under climatological forcing, mean IDV rises from 0.350 in 2023 to 0.370 in 2030. EO-based desertification forecasting is therefore reliable for the regional trend, not for individual cells.
authors: Filipe Moura Da Silva, Cl\'aubio Landney Lima Bandeira
bullets: The study tests how observable and forecastable year-to-year changes are in a MapBiomas-derived degradation index across semi-arid Ceará, Brazil.
A ConvLSTM predicts bounded changes from the previous state using ten annual EO variables, with single-step training followed by recursive rollout.
On a spatial and temporal holdout, it improves RMSE over persistence by 1.6% at one year and 4.4% at four years, while reproducing 53–69% of regional drift.
Cell-level variability is largely unpredictable: an all-channel gradient-boosting model explains only 4.7% of variance, and forecast skill mainly reflects regional trend.

Uncertainty maps from Monte Carlo dropout and stochastic scenarios reveal variation hidden by expected-value forecasts; climatological forcing projects mean IDV increasing from 0.350 in 2023 to 0.370 by 2030.

papers.abstract: Reliable real-time failure detection is critical for deploying learned robotic policies, yet defining failures explicitly is infeasible in open-world settings. This motivates failure detection from nominal demonstrations alone. Existing methods, however, struggle to balance robustness to benign variations with the ability to capture semantic and interaction-level errors. We introduce Robot-WATCHDOG, a self-supervised framework that models manipulation scenes as object-centric spatio-temporal graphs. Building on this representation, we investigate two complementary failure scores: Trajectory Projection and Correlation (TPC), a non-parametric measure of geometric deviation and relational consistency, and GnnT, a Graph Attention Network with a Transformer that predicts future object states. We evaluate both on a public benchmark and on a new dataset of semantically complex manipulation tasks, across six tasks and ten random seeds. Both scores outperform image-based failure detectors, particularly on semantic and interaction-level failures. TPC provides the strongest performance in AUPR and MCC on both dataset averages, with low variance across seeds. Qualitative results are made available at https://cea-list.github.io/Robot-WATCHDOG/.
authors: Quentin Rolland, Fabrice Mayran de Chamisso, Jean-Baptiste Mouret
bullets: Addresses open-world failure detection without requiring explicitly labeled failures.
Introduces two self-supervised scores: TPC for geometric and relational deviations, and GnnT for predicting future object states.
Evaluated on a public benchmark and a new semantically complex manipulation dataset spanning six tasks and ten random seeds.
Both methods outperform image-based detectors, especially for semantic and interaction-level failures.
TPC achieves the strongest average AUPR and MCC with low variance across seeds.

papers.abstract: Kernel Ridge Regression (KRR) is a theoretically sound algorithm for nonparametric learning, which is also often used to investigate properties of deep learning. However, the exact KRR formulation incurs time and memory costs preventing applicability to large datasets, motivating the development of approximate solvers. These algorithms rely on (i) iterative methods, to avoid the computational burden of direct solutions; (ii) sketching or batching, to reduce the problem size; and (iii) preconditioning, to accelerate convergence. While crucial for fast convergence, preconditioning incurs memory costs that can be managed by lowering the number of free parameters of the model, potentially at the expense of expressivity and hence accuracy. To address this challenge, we propose BLOKS, a Conjugate Gradient-based solver for Nystr\"om-sketched KRR built around a novel preconditioner that combines a block Jacobi approximation with sketching. The BLOKS preconditioner has memory cost independent of both the dataset size and the number of parameters, allowing scaling to large models. We provide a memory-efficient, GPU-accelerated implementation and show that BLOKS achieves excellent accuracy while retaining favorable time/memory complexity. Indeed, on standard large-scale datasets used to benchmark kernel solvers, BLOKS achieves comparable or better performances than state-of-the-art methods.
authors: Giordano Vitale, Giacomo Meanti, Marco Rando, Blanca Ayuso de Dios, Lorenzo Rosasco
bullets: Targets the time and memory barriers of exact kernel ridge regression on large datasets.
Uses a Conjugate Gradient solver for Nyström-sketched KRR with a block-Jacobi preconditioner augmented by sketching.
The preconditioner’s memory cost is independent of both dataset size and model parameter count.
Provides a memory-efficient, GPU-accelerated implementation.
Reports excellent accuracy and comparable or better performance than state-of-the-art kernel solvers on standard large-scale benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence is beginning to automate scientific discovery, yet physical robot-policy research still relies on scientists and engineers to interpret experimental failures and decide how controllers should be revised. We present EndoRSI (Endoscopic Recursive Self-Improvement), a human-governed, self-improving robotic research system in which the embedded EndoForge coding agent iteratively develops and refines endoscopic robot policies using evidence from physical experiments. Physical execution remains isolated within a safety-constrained runtime under human authorisation. In motorised endoscopy, validation evidence first caused the agent to reject an initial action representation, while subsequent physical experiments falsified an offline-supported insertion strategy by revealing hazardous closed-loop behaviour absent from the source data. Failed physical rollouts were then incorporated into policy revision; insertion success subsequently increased from 2/21 in the first generation to 17/21 in the fourth. The frozen final policy retained competence across visual and hardware shifts and was the best performing autonomous policy across six independent ex-vivo porcine specimens. These results show that physical robot interaction can serve as experimental evidence for agent-driven robot policy research.

papers.abstract: Translating language into humanoid motion requires coordinating body parts, determining motion duration, and producing references suitable for robot execution. We introduce PartiGen, a part-aware latent diffusion framework that incorporates anatomical structure into a shared whole-body motion representation. Part-specific attention processes anatomically masked frame features, and its outputs are fused to combine local limb information with whole-body context. Conditioned on text and motion history, the model generates motion primitives autoregressively. Forward-kinematics supervision encourages kinematic consistency, while a learned end-of-sequence predictor selects a frame-level endpoint after generation. On HumanML3D retargeted to the Unitree G1, PartiGen achieves a segment-level FID of 3.165, a 16.8% reduction over TextOp, and improves R@1 by 1.4 percentage points. In the duration study with 16-frame primitives, endpoint prediction reduces mean absolute duration error from 12.471 to 3.080 frames compared with a fixed-length cutoff. We further evaluate robot execution using a pretrained, frozen GRIT tracker: 409 of 500 generated references (81.8%) pass the posture-based stability screen in MuJoCo. Following simulation screening and manual selection, 26 of 27 attempted motions are judged successful on the real G1.
authors: Chuxuan Huang, Zhanxiang Cao, Tianyue Zhan, Haoyang Li, Yang Zhang, Liyun Yan, Chenlin Ming, Keqi Zhu, Yizhi Chen, Shengcheng Fu, Zihao Zhou, Xinyi Peng, Kaixuan Zhang, Boyang Xing, Jiawei Bao, Yang Yang, Yue Gao

papers.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have become the standard architecture for frontier LLMs. The multiple parallel experts in each transformer block theoretically enable expert specialization according to categories such as domains, languages, or modalities during pretraining. However, when data is imbalanced across categories, minority categories can become concentrated in a small fraction of the expert pool or spread inefficiently across them, effectively limiting their available capacity. In this work, we demonstrate that category-conditioned expert-selection biases can preferentially route tokens from different categories toward specialized expert pools. By applying biases based on input category, we provide a simple way to induce soft category-aligned specialization. This intervention encourages categories toward distinct expert subsets while retaining cross-category sharing when useful. More importantly, it enables the over-allocation of expert capacity to categories that would otherwise be disadvantaged by data scarcity. We observe performance improvements across modalities, low-resource languages, and code in models up to 10.6B parameters. At our smallest and largest model scales, these gains are equivalent to allocating 18.5% and 2.7% additional baseline training tokens, respectively. Overall, our results show that expert biases can serve as a lightweight control for category-level expert allocation, making room for low-resource categories while retaining standard MoE inference.
authors: Ayush K. Tarun, Clara Meister, Antoine Bosselut
bullets: Data imbalance can leave minority categories with too little effective expert capacity or inefficiently distributed experts.
The method applies input-category biases to expert selection, inducing soft specialization into category-aligned expert pools.
The approach supports over-allocation of experts to disadvantaged categories without changing standard MoE inference.
Improvements are reported across modalities, low-resource languages, and code for models up to 10.6B parameters.
Reported gains correspond to the benefit of 18.5% and 2.7% additional baseline training tokens at the smallest and largest scales, respectively.

figures.caption: Figure 2: COAX effectively coaxes category-aligned routing. In-group routing fraction: the fraction of a token’s top-K selected experts that belong to its designated subset Pct . Figure 1: Given an input category, COAX adds a category-conditioned bias α to the routing scores of a designated subset of experts before top-k selection. This bias softly encourages tokens from the same category to route to a common expert set, promoting category-specific specialization, while leaving all experts available when the learned routing scores sufficiently favor them. The mechanism is applied across MoE layers during pretraining, but the biases can be removed at inference time.

Figure 3: COAX does not sharpen the learned router. Router entropy over all 128 experts, averaged across tokens and layers, for the 3B-A654M model on the four-language mixture from Section 5.1. Entropy is computed before adding the category bias and therefore reflects the router’s learned scores. Both models sharpen during training, but the COAX-trained router remains consistently flatter, suggesting that its performance gains arise from changes in expert learning rather than a better, more discriminate router.

Figure 4: COAX’s gain does not decay over training steps. papers.abstract: Classifier-free guidance (CFG) is a standard technique for improving conditional generation in diffusion models, yet its activation schedule is usually selected heuristically. In practice, most existing CFG-based methods rely on a pre-defined activation policy throughout inference, while recent dynamic variants often depend on hand-designed schedules without a principled theoretical explanation of when conditional information is most useful. In order to understand how the informational relevance between conditioning inputs and the score function evolves over the course of generation, we explore when guidance should be activated from an information-theoretic perspective. In this work, we formulate the diffusion trajectory as a time-dependent information bottleneck and show that the effectiveness of conditional information is not uniform throughout sampling, but becomes significantly stronger after a critical stage characterized by a Fisher-information balance condition. Motivated by this insight, we propose a training-free dynamic CFG strategy for inference. Rather than prescribing a fixed schedule in advance, our method constructs a stochastic process from conditional and unconditional score statistics and activates guidance when the estimated guidance gain crosses a prescribed threshold. This yields an adaptive activation rule that aligns condition injection with the underlying generation dynamics, while also recovering interval-based guidance as a limiting special case. Extensive experiments across diverse architectures and tasks, demonstrate that our method is effective, robust, and broadly applicable. Beyond empirical improvements, our framework provides an interpretation of dynamic guidance methods and a principled foundation for inference-time control in conditional diffusion models.

papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) struggle to answer questions over long interaction histories, where relevant evidence may be scattered across distant sessions. Existing memory systems typically construct and maintain sophisticated memory representations offline, before user queries are observed, incurring substantial overhead and limiting their ability to adapt memory construction to query-specific information needs. In this paper, we propose T$^2$Mem, a Test-Time Memory construction framework that defers memory construction to inference and progressively builds memory along the reasoning process. Specifically, T$^2$Mem extracts lightweight episode-level metadata offline to capture key events and temporal associations as retrieval cues, while retaining links to the original interactions to facilitate the reconstruction of dependencies across episodes. At test time, the LLM adaptively retrieves and organizes metadata and raw interactions, progressively constructing query-specific memory as reasoning unfolds. Experiments on LoCoMo and LongMemEval show the effectiveness of T$^2$Mem by consistently outperforming strong baselines across different backbone LLMs while substantially reducing the overhead of memory construction. Further analysis demonstrates that deferring memory construction to inference enables the memory construction process to dynamically adapt to the information needs of individual queries. All code is available at https://github.com/OpenBMB/T2Mem.

papers.abstract: Existing real-world reinforcement learning methods improve robot policies by combining human corrections with autonomous rollouts. However, accumulated experience varies in its value for policy improvement, and even successful trajectories can contain inefficient or redundant behavior, motivating more selective experience reuse. To this end, we propose Evo-RL, an iterative reinforcement learning method that combines human interventions with advantage-guided experience selection. Evo-RL uses human corrections and experience with positive estimated advantages from successful trajectories to iteratively refine the policy. To support learning from these different experience sources, we introduce RW-RL-Dataset, which spans over 1,000 hours across four robot embodiments. On a real-world high-precision manipulation task, Evo-RL improves attempt success rate over RECAP by 30.46\%. Our code, model checkpoints, and dataset are publicly available.

Code, checkpoints, and dataset are publicly available.

papers.abstract: Mamba-3 introduces input-dependent rotations into recurrent state updates, but their contribution beyond state retention remains unclear. We interpret these ro- tations as underdamped second-order dynamics, providing a framework for in- vestigating the role of oscillation in sequence modeling. Controlled comparisons show that underdamped dynamics outperform non-oscillatory damping regimes on state-tracking tasks, while language-model pretraining demonstrates benefits for long-context prediction and length generalization. Interventions in pretrained models further establish the importance of learned phase, and state analysis sug- gests that rotation regulates how retained information combines with incoming up- dates. Taken together, these findings identify underdamped dynamics as a useful mechanism for recurrent computation and suggest that oscillation supports long- context processing by regulating how information accumulates.

papers.abstract: Attention sinks are tokens or positions that consistently receive disproportionate attention mass, often beyond what their semantic content would suggest. Despite extensive study in large language models, their behavior and functional relevance in text-to-image (T2I) Transformers remain largely unexplored. To fill this gap and better understand how text-to-image Transformers allocate and route attention, we explore this phenomenon of text-to-image transformers across bidirectional diffusion models and causal autoregressive models. Specifically, we explore whether attention sinks exist, where they emerge, and how they functionally influence generation. Through systematic attention analysis and targeted interventions, we identify that attention sinks emerge in both bidirectional diffusion and autoregressive models but exhibit distinct patterns. The autoregressive model concentrates attention on the first and global-scale tokens, whereas the bidirectional models develop sinks near modality boundaries, within text regions, and at spatial corners. Moreover, these patterns vary across generation stages and are localized to a sparse subset of layers and heads. To assess their functional relevance, we perturb sink-related heads and token positions. It turns out that perturbing sink-ranked heads produces larger average changes than non-sink comparisons, while some sink-position perturbations have limited effects on bidirectional model scores. We further introduce register tokens to redistribute attention sinks and find that several configurations preserve or modestly improve generation performance. Overall, attention sinks are architecture-, inference-stage-, and component-dependent phenomena, providing a basis for mechanistic analysis and principled attention design in text-to-image transformers.

papers.abstract: Tool-using agents increasingly require a common substrate for building, training, evaluating, distilling, and maintaining agentic systems, yet existing tooling typically addresses these stages in isolation. We present AgentTune, a source-available Python library that provides a unified framework for developing and optimizing tool-using agents. At its core, AgentTune introduces a two-tier EventLog representation that preserves agent trajectories while supporting consistent projections for training, evaluation, and auditing. Building on this substrate, the library provides a shared agent runtime, tool-calling reinforcement learning, agentic distillation, retrieval-augmented generation, decision workflows, evaluation utilities, and a designed path toward self-healing agents. These components are exposed through composable interfaces so that agent strategies, training methods, evaluation procedures, and recovery mechanisms can be combined without requiring separate representations or pipelines. We demonstrate the framework across agentic tasks including legal contract search and domain-specific applications, illustrating its use for trajectory-based optimization, tool-use evaluation, and cross-task agent development. AgentTune is released as a source-available library at https://github.com/Lexsi-Labs/AgentTune
authors: R E Zera Marveen Lyngkhoi, Abhivansh Gupta, Vidushee Vats, Ram Mohan Rao Kadiyala, Vinay Kumar Sankarapu, Pratinav Seth

Demonstrates applications in legal contract search and domain-specific tasks, including trajectory optimization and tool-use evaluation.
Released as a source-available Python library; the self-healing-agent pathway is presented as a design direction.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces AgentTune, a unified framework for training and optimizing tool-using LLM agents, which is a key paradigm for embodied AI and LLM agents.
papers.title: AgentTune: A Unified Training Lifecycle for Tool-Using LLM Agents
papers.tldr: AgentTune unifies the development, training, evaluation, distillation, and maintenance of tool-using LLM agents through a shared trajectory representation and composable interfaces.

papers.abstract: Motivated by the success of large language models (LLMs) with broad generalizability and robustness to noisy or unreliable pre-training data, we explore in-context prediction of PDE solution fields using approximate pre-training data. In addition, inspired by the posterior predictive mean-based inference mechanism of the in-context learning in prior-data fitted networks (PFNs), we propose PDE-PFN, a prior-data fitted neural solver that approximates the posterior predictive mean of PDE solutions via in-context learning. PDE-PFN builds on a PFN architecture with self- and cross-attention mechanisms of Transformer and is pre-trained on noisy approximate solutions generated by physics-informed neural networks, serving as diverse but not necessarily exact priors. Through experiments on a range of two-dimensional PDEs, we demonstrate that PDE-PFN achieves empirical generalization across heterogeneous equations, robustness under noisy priors, and zero-gradient-update in-context inference capability. PDE-PFN achieves competitive or improved predictive accuracy relative to the evaluated baselines while supporting flexible context and query representations.
authors: Jaehyeon Park, Mingu Kang, Dongseok Lee, Woojin Cho, Kookjin Lee, Anthony Gruber, Youngjoon Hong, Noseong Park
bullets: Targets generalizable PDE solution prediction using approximate, noisy pre-training solutions.
Approximates the posterior predictive mean through a PFN architecture with self- and cross-attention.
Pre-trains on diverse solutions generated by physics-informed neural networks rather than exact data.
Experiments on two-dimensional PDEs show heterogeneous-equation generalization and robustness to noisy priors.
Provides competitive or improved accuracy against evaluated baselines with flexible context and query representations.

figures.caption: Figure 1: The overall workflow of PDE-PFN. Our model performs in-context learning (ICL) based on given observations (i.e., context) to infer solutions. Even when trained with an approximated PINN prior, our method can improve over noisy approximate pretraining data.

papers.selection_reason: Develops PDE-PFN, a prior-data fitted neural solver using in-context learning and Transformers, applicable to modeling physical dynamics and leveraging LLM-style architectures.
papers.title: PDE-PFN: Prior-Data Fitted Neural PDE Solver
papers.tldr: PDE-PFN is a Transformer-based prior-data fitted neural solver that uses in-context learning to predict PDE solution fields from noisy approximate prior data without gradient updates.

papers.abstract: Serving a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model pays for expert precision twice: the resident footprint pays for every expert the router can reach, while each batch-one decode step pays only for the experts it selects. These are two different rate functionals over the same per-expert widths, yet published per-expert MoE allocators constrain only the first. We call the difference the store-read gap; in the released BitsMoE checkpoint, 2.54 bits per weight (bpw) of storage become 7.50 bpw of decode traffic. We propose DuoRate, which stores once and reads per workload. Offline, it stores one uniform tier of a prefix-readable weight stream and bakes a distortion tensor. Online, it profiles a workload's own prefill without labels and solves a Lagrangian rate-distortion allocation under the decode functional; routing frequency provably cancels from every per-expert decision, and the solve costs one dot product per expert and a bisection. A deployment therefore keeps a single artifact that prefill reads at the stored rate and decode reads at the workload's own rate. On Qwen3-30B-A3B, DuoRate reading 2.3 bpw exceeds every 2-bit-class baseline by 6.3 to 47.0 points of average accuracy, and at 2.9 bpw it matches 4-bit formats that read 1.4-1.6 bpw more. The advantage is largest under long decoding: on GSM8K, DuoRate at 2.9 bpw matches or exceeds every 4-bit format and trails BF16 by only 0.25 points, and at 2.6 bpw it still matches or exceeds the 4.5-bit NF4 and FP4. Against controls in its own format, the allocation alone is worth 0.07-0.11 bpw of read rate. Code will be released upon publication.
authors: Mengqi Guo, Zhe Wei, Yuan Yuan, Jiunn Bin Lim, Boyi Pan, Michael Bi Mi
bullets: MoE serving has separate storage and decode-rate costs, but prior allocators optimize only storage.
DuoRate stores one uniform, prefix-readable artifact and uses workload-specific, label-free profiling to allocate decode precision online.
Its optimization reduces to one dot product per expert plus bisection; routing frequency cancels from individual expert decisions.
On Qwen3-30B-A3B, it outperforms 2-bit-class baselines at 2.3 bpw and approaches 4-bit-format accuracy at 2.9 bpw.
Benefits are strongest for long decoding; on GSM8K, 2.9 bpw trails BF16 by only 0.25 points and remains competitive at 2.6 bpw.

figures.caption: Figure 1: The DUORATE pipeline. Stage 1 (offline, once) stores one uniform tier of a prefixreadable stream and bakes the distortion tensor S. Stage 2 (per workload) profiles the workload’s own prefill without labels, scores every expert and tier by one dot product, and takes a per-expert Lagrangian argmin with one shared λ, from which fe cancels; a bisection on λ meets the read budget B. Serving: prefill pays Rstore, decode pays Rread.

Figure 2: Frequency cancellation (Proposition 1, Corollary 1); illustrative values. (a) For two experts eightfold apart in f , supporting lines of slope −λ to de and −λfe to fede touch the same tier, so the argmin does not depend on f . (b) On the read set {p2, p3, p4} the thresholds fix one family of tier maps; routing frequencies f and g only change where the bisection stops.

Figure 4: What the allocation alone is worth (WikiText-2). (a) Perplexity against the budgeted read rate: DUORATE, random mixtures of two adjacent tiers (every draw), the interpolated uniformtier null (dashed) and tables re-solved from a disjoint split (hollow). Brackets: gap to the strongest mixture; arrows: extra read rate the mixture needs to match (dotted: extrapolated); blue ticks: each table at its stored rate. (b) Gap to the null placed at either rate, with 95% bootstrap intervals.

Figure 3: Average accuracy (MMLU-Pro, MMLU, GSM8K) against the rate read per activated weight at batch-one decode. (a) Every row of Table 1. (b) The top-left corner: DUORATE at 2.9 bpw sits with the 4-bit formats, which read 1.4–1.6 bpw more. Hollow markers are stored rates joined to read rates: BITSMOE stores 2.54 and reads 7.50; DUORATE stores 4.27 and reads 2.9.

Table 1: Results on Qwen3-30B-A3B-Base. BPW is the rate read per activated expert weight at batch-one decode (for DUORATE, the read budget); DUORATE stores 4.3. ∗BITSMOE stores 2.5; 7.5 is its read rate. GSM8K is strict match; AVG. is the mean of MMLU-Pro, MMLU and GSM8K. Bold is the best in each group.
