papers.selection_reason: Proposes DuoRate, a two-rate precision allocation strategy for Mixture-of-Experts serving, optimizing memory and compute efficiency for large language models.
papers.title: DuoRate: Two-Rate Per-Expert Precision Allocation for Mixture-of-Experts Serving
papers.tldr: DuoRate allocates per-expert precision for both storage and workload-specific decode traffic, substantially improving MoE accuracy at low read rates.

papers.abstract: Agentic workloads resend long contexts that barely change between calls. Prefix caching now skips most of their prefill, yet every request must still be tokenized in full before the cache can even be consulted. Tokenization, a CPU stage long treated as negligible, becomes the largest part of time-to-first-token (TTFT), and a frontend that tokenizes for a whole GPU fleet limits how many GPUs it can feed. We present GraphTok, a GPU tokenizer that runs the entire encoding pipeline, from pre-tokenization through byte-pair encoding (BPE) merging to token-ID assembly, as one replayable CUDA graph. GraphTok reproduces the reference token IDs bit-for-bit on GPT-2, Llama 3, Qwen 2.5, DeepSeek-V3, and Gemma 3, hands short inputs to a CPU engine where the GPU cannot win, and plugs into unmodified vLLM and NVIDIA Dynamo. GraphTok encodes one million GPT-2 tokens in 1.7-3.2 ms including data transfers, and on Llama 3 it is 4.7-6.0x faster than gigatoken, the strongest CPU tokenizer. On TokTier's own single-request benchmark, it is 2.6-3.9x faster than gigatoken and up to 18.1x faster than TokTier. In vLLM with a cached prefix, it lowers mean TTFT by 2.1-2.4x. The largest gain is capacity. Within a 2 s P99 target, one Dynamo frontend with GraphTok sustains 518 requests/s of 121k-token traffic, the busiest-hour load of 56 GPUs, against 296 with gigatoken and 18.5 with the default tokenizer. Across 121k to one million tokens, this is 1.75-2.5x the load gigatoken sustains, with a P99 up to 64x lower where gigatoken's tail breaks.
authors: Mohammad Siavashi, Pascal Schwinte, Ali Banaei, Gerald Q. Maguire Jr., Marco Chiesa, Dejan Kosti\'c
bullets: Agentic requests resend mostly unchanged long contexts, but full CPU tokenization occurs before prefix-cache lookup and becomes a major TTFT bottleneck.
GraphTok performs pre-tokenization, BPE merging, and token-ID assembly on GPUs, while routing short inputs to CPU when more efficient.
It reproduces reference token IDs bit-for-bit across GPT-2, Llama 3, Qwen 2.5, DeepSeek-V3, and Gemma 3, and integrates with unmodified vLLM and NVIDIA Dynamo.
It reduces cached-prefix mean TTFT by 2.1–2.4× in vLLM and sustains substantially higher frontend load under a 2-second P99 target.
The approach targets long-input, high-throughput serving; short inputs may remain on the CPU path.

papers.selection_reason: GPU tokenizer reduces TTFT and increases LLM serving capacity, fitting efficient AI.
papers.title: Taking Tokenization off the Host for Agentic LLM Serving
papers.tldr: GraphTok moves full tokenization from CPU to a replayable CUDA graph, substantially reducing TTFT and increasing the request capacity of agentic LLM serving.

papers.abstract: Partial differential equation (PDE) surrogate modeling often relies on either dense observations or access to governing equations/physics constraints. In practice, observations can be sparse and partial, and the underlying physics may be partially specified or unavailable. We introduce SBNO, an equation-free paired-data diffusion bridge matching framework that learns conditional operators for both forward and inverse PDE problems under partial observations. SBNO uses diffusion Schr\"odinger bridge matching to learn a pair of time-dependent drifts from a mask-aware endpoint coupling that preserves empirical input-solution pairing during training and supports both PDE-task directions within a single framework. At inference time, SBNO produces a deterministic point reconstruction by integrating the probability-flow ODE constructed from the learned drift pair, without inference-time observation or PDE guidance-weight tuning. On five PDE benchmarks with 5% observations, SBNO achieves superior or comparable accuracy to baselines while demonstrating lower test-instance error dispersion. Furthermore, SBNO is at least $9.7 \times$ faster and reduces GPU memory by at least $4.3 \times$ compared to guided-diffusion baselines.

papers.abstract: 6D pose estimation of novel objects without CAD models remains an open challenge: model-free methods must build the object representation from scratch during onboarding and have long trailed their model-based counterparts. We present NovaSplat, a model-free pipeline that closes this gap. From a short smartphone video captured at onboarding, we train a 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) model that serves both as a template source for detection and coarse pose estimation and as a differentiable backbone for pose refinement. Our refiner optimizes the object-to-camera pose with combined photometric and geometric losses under a continuous rotation parametrization free of gradient singularities. On a household-object benchmark, NovaSplat surpasses all model-based methods. On a challenging industrial benchmark with textureless and specular surfaces, it outperforms all model-free competitors while substantially narrowing the gap to model-based ones. We further introduce NovaSplat-Lite, an inference variant that is $3.1\times$ faster at negligible accuracy cost. Code will be made available at \href{https://github.com/POSE-Lab/novasplat}{https://github.com/POSE-Lab/novasplat}.
authors: Georgios Floros, Evangelos Sartinas, Orestis Vangelis, Maria Pateraki
bullets: Addresses the challenge of estimating poses for unseen objects without CAD models.
Uses an onboarding video to train a 3DGS model for detection, coarse pose estimation, and differentiable refinement.
Refines object-to-camera pose with combined photometric and geometric losses and a continuous, nonsingular rotation representation.
Outperforms model-based methods on a household-object benchmark and model-free methods on a challenging industrial benchmark.
NovaSplat-Lite achieves 3.1× faster inference with negligible accuracy loss.

papers.abstract: The escalating environmental footprint of the Information and Communication Technol- ogy (ICT) sectorwith global Data Center electric- ity usage potentially reaching 3% by 2030 and the imperative for real-time responsiveness in smart buildings demand a foundational shift towards Edge Computing. This article proposes a holis- tic architectural and algorithmic approach for cre- ating autonomous, resilient, and privacy-preserving learning systems within smart buildings, advancing the core concept of the building itself as the data center. Our contributions, demonstrating originality compared to conventional centralized systems, are structured around three main pillars: 1) Validation of resilient data acquisition chains using the af- fordable Arduino ecosystem (Uno R4 WiFi/BME280) and secure persistence solutions including centralized archiving (Node-RED/MySQL) and secure remote transfer (Python/rsync/SSH). 2). The proposal of a lightweight, KOptim orchestration framework, inter- operable with the FIWARE standard, for the dynamic management of Service Level Agreements (SLA). 3) The adaptation and experimental valida- tion of the Generalized Hebbian Algorithm (GHA) for Principal Component Analysis (PCA) on low- power microcontrollers,We introduce and compare an iterative learning strategy using data buffers, featuring sorting and explicit preservation of extreme samples to maintain diversity. Experimental results on the high-dimensional Tour Perret sensor data confirm that this novel method, despite introducing a necessary temporal complexity of O(W log W ) due to sorting, achieves convergence and final result quality that is visually equivalent to processing the entire dataset in full memory, reliably identifying two distinct operational states.
bullets: Addresses ICT energy use and the need for real-time smart-building responsiveness by treating the building as a local data center.

Adapts Generalized Hebbian Algorithm PCA to low-power microcontrollers using buffered, sorted data while preserving extreme samples.
On Tour Perret sensor data, the method identifies two operational states with quality visually equivalent to full-memory processing, at added O(W log W) temporal complexity.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) exhibit complementary capabilities, yet selecting the most suitable expert for a given image-question query remains challenging due to heterogeneous multimodal inputs and varying expert strengths. Existing routing approaches rely on text-based cues or static model profiles, failing to capture fine-grained visual evidence and expert-specific failure patterns. To address this, we propose MHR-Router, a multimodal heterogeneous retrieval-enhanced adaptive routing framework for VLM inference. It accurately dispatches each multimodal query to the most suitable VLM expert via local retrieval evidence. MHR-Router consists of two stages: (1) Multimodal Routing Representation, which fuses frozen multimodal features into a comprehensive query representation; and (2) Heterogeneous Retrieval-Enhanced Adaptive Routing, which retrieves expert-specific success and failure memories as local evidence and employs a shared scorer to adaptively select the optimal expert. Experiments show that MHR-Router effectively achieves heterogeneous modality routing and consistently improves accuracy over traditional baselines.

bullets: Addresses the challenge of selecting among VLM experts with complementary strengths and heterogeneous failure patterns.

papers.abstract: Memory-augmented assistants retrieve evidence from stored conversations and documents to answer queries. Most embedding-based retrievers compare single-vector representations of queries and memories, even when relevance depends on a small part of the content. Such local evidence can be matched to queries using the contextual token representations already computed by the same embedding models. Our method uses sparse token matching to improve retrieval without additional training. Each query token retrieves a small set of matching tokens across candidate memories. The matching scores are aggregated for each memory and combined with whole-memory similarity to rank memories. An optional low-rank query adapter can be trained with supervision while keeping the encoder and stored memory representations fixed. Our method improves retrieval across eight benchmarks and multiple model families without additional training. Query adaptation further increases the gains to 13.3 and 14.3 percentage points in average Recall@10 and NDCG@10 on Qwen3-Embedding-4B. These retrieval gains translate into higher question-answering accuracy on long-term memory benchmarks.
authors: Han Luo, Zhan Zhuang, Xu He, Jujia Zhao, Yu Li, Suqin Yuan, Dong Li, Lei Feng
bullets: Addresses the weakness of single-vector retrieval when relevance depends on small parts of a memory.
Matches each query token to candidate-memory tokens and aggregates scores with whole-memory similarity.

Improves retrieval across eight benchmarks and multiple model families; adaptation further raises Recall@10 and NDCG@10 on Qwen3-Embedding-4B.

papers.abstract: Set-based language model routing aims to increase the coverage of the event where at least one model answers a query correctly while controlling the number of inference calls made. Existing risk-controlled routing policies bound the all-miss risk (the probability that every model in the selected set fails) by calibrating a single conformal threshold and applying it to a nested family of model sets. Because each model is scored in isolation, these policies ignore the dependence structure of model failures. Models that share training data or architecture tend to fail on the same queries, so two individually strong models can be jointly redundant while a weaker but complementary model covers the queries that the others miss. To account for this dependence, which existing risk-controlled policies ignore, we propose CopRoute, which orders models by how many new queries each one answers correctly beyond those already selected, decides per query how far down that order to go, and then picks the smallest cutoff that still meets the target risk. We show that CopRoute's ordering attains, on the design data, the best guarantee any efficient fixed-ordering algorithm can give for the average number of calls to the first correct model, and that a separate calibration step certifies the all-miss risk of the deployed sets. On RouterBench and RouterEval, CopRoute attains the fewest certified calls on nine of ten datasets at a target risk of 0.05 and on eight of ten at 0.10, making up to 79 percent fewer calls (median 24 percent) than the state-of-the-art risk-controlled policy at the same certified all-miss risk.

On RouterBench and RouterEval, it achieves the fewest certified calls on 9/10 datasets at risk 0.05 and 8/10 at risk 0.10.
It reduces calls by up to 79%—24% at the median—relative to the compared risk-controlled policy at the same certified risk.

papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) reveals versatility and convenience during VLM post-training, providing dense supervision for student from teacher. However, we observed an anomaly that the distilled VLM could still answer the questions accurately even when the related visual regions were masked or replaced with noise. Building on this observation, our quantitative and qualitative experiments demonstrate that OPD, which uses the answer as a hint, has failed to teach students to genuinely seek out and rely on visual evidence. Our theoretical analysis suggests that this failure arises from a shortcut enabled by the lack of visual constraints during distillation. To address the issue, we introduce Contrastive Vision On-policy Distillation (CV-OPD), which compares teacher distributions induced by positive and negative crops while conditioning on the same student prefix and augments optimization with a margin-based contrastive constraint, which is modulated with discrepancy gating across token and sample level. Specifically, CV-OPD first introduces a negative teacher unrelated to the answer and designs a Contrastive Divergence Loss (CDL) that constrains the feature distribution of student by contrasting the positive and negative teachers, correcting how the student exploits visual regions. The CV-OPD introduces a Discrepancy Aware Gate (DAG) that uses token-level and sample-level discrepancies to select visually relevant tokens for optimization, directing the student's attention toward visual content. Extensive experiments across a broad range of fine-grained visual benchmarks demonstrate that CV-OPD substantially alleviates shortcut and consistently improves the visual reasoning capabilities of existing VLMs.
authors: Haowei Wang, Hao Lin, Qi Zhu, Jiayi Ji, Deyi Ji, Liujuan Cao, Rongrong Ji
bullets: OPD can produce accurate answers even when relevant image regions are masked or replaced with noise, revealing weak visual grounding.
CV-OPD contrasts teacher outputs from answer-relevant positive crops and unrelated negative crops under the same student prefix.
Its Contrastive Divergence Loss encourages students to distinguish useful from irrelevant visual features.
A Discrepancy Aware Gate selects visually relevant tokens using token- and sample-level discrepancies.
Experiments on broad fine-grained visual benchmarks show reduced shortcut behavior and improved visual reasoning in existing VLMs.

papers.abstract: Memory-dependent manipulation requires a policy to track execution state and recover visual evidence that is no longer observable. We propose dual-stream memory for vision-language-action policies, assigning these requirements to complementary representations. A task-agnostic Gated DeltaNet compresses history into one temporal token, supervised by progress prediction and action-conditioned feature reconstruction. A task-conditioned retriever retains frames above a fixed relevance threshold; linear multi-scale fusion encodes each frame into sixteen spatial tokens. We then freeze the temporal compressor and jointly optimize retrieval and policy learning. Across sixteen RoboMME tasks, the complete model achieves 49.22% mean success versus 44.51% for the published FrameSamp+Modul reference, improving fourteen tasks and all four suite means. On four real-robot tasks, mean success reaches 62.5% versus 37.5%, with the largest gains on repeated actions requiring execution-stage discrimination. These results support combining execution context with selective visual access, while failures under cup swaps expose persistent identity tracking as an unresolved requirement.
authors: Yang Wang, Ping Liu, Ruiyu Wang, Xuhua Chen, Lingfeng Zhang, Tao Zhang
bullets: Targets manipulation tasks where execution state must be tracked and previously visible evidence recovered.
Uses a task-agnostic Gated DeltaNet temporal compressor with progress prediction and action-conditioned reconstruction.
Adds a task-conditioned frame retriever and encodes selected frames with 16 spatial tokens; the compressor is frozen during joint retrieval-policy training.
On 16 RoboMME tasks, mean success is 49.22% versus 44.51% for FrameSamp+Modul; real-robot mean success is 62.5% versus 37.5%.
Cup-swap failures indicate persistent object-identity tracking remains unresolved.

papers.abstract: In this paper, we propose Data-Adaptive Mahalanobis Cross-Head Attention (DAMCHA), a simple and effective attention mechanism that generalizes Multi-Head Attention (MHA) through the lens of metric learning. Standard MHA implicitly learns a static, head-wise Euclidean similarity corresponding to the diagonal blocks of a unified cross-head metric matrix, discarding all off-diagonal interactions across heads. DAMCHA addresses this limitation via two key innovations. First, it learns the full cross-head metric matrix, inducing a Mahalanobis-like similarity that explicitly captures inter-head interactions beyond the restricted block-diagonal structure of MHA. Second, it parameterizes the metric matrix as an input-dependent function, enabling the attention geometry to dynamically adapt to the intrinsic manifold structure of the data rather than remaining fixed after training. We further introduce principled regularization strategies, most notably stack-wise parameter sharing, to ensure computational efficiency and stable optimization. DAMCHA serves as a drop-in replacement for MHA and its variants in various Transformer architectures, delivering superior expressive power and learning performance with comparable or reduced computational overhead. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DAMCHA-based Transformers consistently outperform competing baselines across a range of benchmark tasks. Code is available at https://github.com/erwinmsmith/DAMCHA.
authors: Zhenke Duan, Xin Li, Jiqun Pan, Dong Xiaofei, Hanwen Ning, Xinyuan Song
bullets: Generalizes multi-head attention by learning a full cross-head metric instead of a block-diagonal, head-wise Euclidean metric.
Makes the metric input-dependent so attention geometry can adapt to the data’s intrinsic structure.
Uses regularization, including stack-wise parameter sharing, to support stable optimization and computational efficiency.
Acts as a drop-in replacement for MHA and its variants across Transformer architectures.
Experiments report consistent improvements over competing baselines on benchmark tasks with comparable or lower computational overhead.

papers.abstract: Cross-tokenizer on-policy distillation (OPD) requires aligning teacher and student sequences before their scores can be compared. Decoded-text alignment provides such correspondence at the chunk level, but leaves a distinct problem unresolved: credit alignment. A chunk-level signal specifies how much a span should change, but not how that signal should be distributed across student tokens, while tokens without teacher correspondence remain unconstrained. We propose CAST (Chunk-aware credit Assignment with Selective Token Anchoring), a shift-or-stay framework that addresses both issues. For aligned chunks, CAST redistributes each chunk's advantage across student tokens using predictive uncertainty and local teacher-signal smoothness, emphasizing learning opportunities supported by locally consistent teacher feedback while preserving the chunk's total advantage. The resulting weights exactly solve a KL-regularized credit-allocation problem. For unaligned positions, CAST selectively anchors the student to its initial policy through a KL penalty, limiting drift where teacher supervision is unavailable. Because credit assignment is separated from chunk construction, CAST also applies to punctuation-defined or fixed-length chunks under shared tokenization. Across six mathematics, science, and code benchmarks, CAST improves the average over the strongest evaluated baseline by $2.45$ and $1.32$ points for cross-tokenizer transfer from Qwen3-8B to Mistral-7B and Llama-3.1-8B, respectively, and by $2.10$ points for shared-tokenizer transfer to Qwen3-1.7B.
authors: Jingru Yang, Jinhang Wu, Minjing Shi, Shengfeng He, Xuyan Li, Man Tan, Biye Li
bullets: Addresses the unresolved credit-alignment problem: distributing chunk advantages across student tokens and constraining unaligned positions.
Redistributes each chunk’s advantage using predictive uncertainty and local teacher-signal smoothness, while preserving the total advantage.
Uses selective KL anchoring to the student’s initial policy where teacher supervision is unavailable.
Separates credit assignment from chunk construction, supporting decoded-text, punctuation-defined, and fixed-length chunks.
Across six math, science, and code benchmarks, improves over the strongest evaluated baseline by 2.45, 1.32, and 2.10 points in the reported transfer settings.

papers.abstract: In-context-learning Tabular Foundation Models (TFMs) are uniquely suited to scenarios with limited resources or privacy constraints, as they solve new tasks without additional training. However, their architecture consists of multiple transformer blocks, resulting in high computational and memory footprints. Meanwhile, traditional alternatives like Gradient-Boosted Decision Trees (GBDTs) remain highly competitive and run efficiently on CPUs, suggesting that tabular tasks may not inherently require deep architectures. This contrast raises a fundamental question: can TFMs be simplified by removing architectural redundancies without sacrificing performance? To answer this, we introduce a closed-form, label-free affine translator that replaces a contiguous window of up to 96% of the blocks, leaving the rest unchanged. Evaluating eight frontier TFMs on 171 classification datasets, we reveal that tabular transformers are vastly overparameterized: replacing half of a model's blocks costs at most $0.002$ median AUROC across all architectures, with the half-depth TabFM still outperforming every other full-depth TFMs and tuned GBDTs. Furthermore, different model families are overparameterized in different ways: TabPFN-3 relies on its encoders, maintaining performance regardless of which single block is retained. Other single-axis models spread computation thinly, needing only their first block, while dual-axis models concentrate it in one critical block. Ultimately, removing depth saves up to 1.5B parameters, speeds up GPU inference by up to $6\times$ at a median cost of $0.03$ AUROC, while a single-block TabPFN-3 serves cached queries $2.4\times$ faster using $6\times$ less memory at negligible cost.
bullets: The work addresses the high resource demands of deep in-context-learning tabular transformers.
A label-free, closed-form affine translator replaces up to 96% of contiguous transformer blocks without retraining.
Across eight TFMs and 171 classification datasets, removing half the blocks costs at most 0.002 median AUROC.
Shallower models can save up to 1.5B parameters and provide up to 6× faster GPU inference, with a median 0.03 AUROC cost.
Different model families concentrate useful computation differently, so the best retained blocks vary by architecture.

papers.abstract: Can a vision model learn what words mean from pixels alone? We show that the two largest DINOv3 vision transformers organize words rendered in images by word meaning, despite being pretrained using self-supervision on images only, without paired captions, class labels, or other language supervision. We derive word representations from embedding differences between word images and matched controls, then test whether semantically related words are neighbors within each model's embedding space, while controlling for spelling similarity. We find that brand names in the same industry group together, as do nouns from the same semantic domain. Country-capital pairs exhibit consistent vector offsets, similarly to word embeddings trained on text. These word representations also align with the representations of the visual object categories they name. DINOv3-H and DINOv3-7B are, to our knowledge, the first self-supervised vision models to show substantial semantic structure for rendered words. Comparisons with text and speech encoders reveal shared structure among representations of the same words. Contrastive alignment with either encoder further strengthened DINOv3-H's word-level semantic structure, while leaving the other finetuned vision models largely unchanged. Image-only training can therefore teach vision models not just what words look like, but also how their meanings relate.
authors: Anders Gj{\o}lbye, Sebastian Ray Mason, Stella Frank, Lars Kai Hansen
bullets: DINOv3-H and DINOv3-7B organize rendered words by semantic meaning without captions, labels, or language supervision.
Word representations are extracted by comparing embeddings of word images with matched controls while controlling for spelling similarity.
Brands in the same industry and nouns in the same semantic domain cluster together; country-capital pairs show consistent vector offsets.
Word representations align with the visual object categories named by those words and share structure with text and speech encoders.
Contrastive alignment further strengthened DINOv3-H’s word semantics, while effects on other finetuned vision models were limited.

papers.abstract: On-Policy Distillation (OPD) has emerged as a powerful paradigm for transferring reasoning capabilities from frontier models to smaller models, while extending its success to multi-turn agentic environments remains challenging. We study agentic OPD through interaction states, distinguishing the objective task and executed action-observation record from the internal semantic trajectory of student reasoning. Through this lens, we identify two roles of student reasoning in multi-turn OPD: prior reasoning distorts teacher supervision, while current reasoning shapes the action alternatives sampled at the same state. Specifically, at matched interaction states, removing prior student reasoning improves teacher continuation success and changes the teacher's token-level targets, with larger continuation gains at later turns. Meanwhile, resampling complete reasoning-action responses yields greater action diversity at the same state than resampling actions under a fixed reasoning trace. We introduce State-Grounded On-Policy Distillation, a framework that grounds teacher supervision in interaction states and reallocates the sampling budget to generate multiple complete reasoning-action responses at states with high response entropy, while retaining full-history student generation. Comprehensive evaluations across ALFWorld, ScienceWorld and WebShop demonstrate that State-OPD achieves the highest macro-average success rate among the evaluated methods for both Qwen3-1.7B and Qwen3-4B students. Notably, for Qwen3-4B, State-OPD raises macro-average success from 26.07\% with the strongest baseline to 31.74\% and surpasses its Qwen3-32B teacher on ALFWorld Seen. Further analyses reveal that State-OPD achieves higher task success with fewer supervised turn responses and substantially reduces persistent failed-action repetition; qualitative traces illustrate decision revision based on interaction feedback.
authors: Zhentao Zhang, Yanzhao Zheng, Yanlin Liu, Yuanqiang Yu, Tianze Xu, Chao Ma, Jihuai Zhu, Lelun Wu, Baohua Dong, Hangcheng Zhu, Ruohui Huang, Gang Yu
bullets: Problem: Standard on-policy distillation struggles in multi-turn agents because prior student reasoning can distort teacher supervision and fixed reasoning traces limit action diversity.
Method: Separate interaction states from internal reasoning, remove prior student reasoning when querying teacher continuations, and allocate sampling to high-entropy states.
The framework retains full-history student generation while generating multiple complete reasoning-action responses at selected states.
Across ALFWorld, ScienceWorld, and WebShop, State-OPD achieves the highest macro-average success among evaluated methods for both Qwen3-1.7B and Qwen3-4B.
For Qwen3-4B, macro-average success increases from 26.07% with the strongest baseline to 31.74%; analyses also show fewer supervised turn responses and less repeated failed actions.

papers.abstract: Video generation supports digital content creation, with applications in virtual avatars, AI-driven filmmaking, interactive game engines, and world models. State-of-the-art systems achieve controllability primarily through image-to-video (I2V) generation, in which an injected anchor image determines the identity, composition, and style of the resulting video. In modern pipelines, this anchor is synthesized by a text-to-image (T2I) generator. This raises a largely overlooked question: Are images obtained directly from the T2I model truly suitable for current video models? Our analysis shows that anchor aesthetic and quality scores are weakly correlated with downstream video quality. The structure-and-texture score is negatively correlated with I2V video quality in both the visual and motion dimensions. Fine-tuning the T2I model on an image reward accordingly yields anchors with visibly denser structural and character detail: they score higher on image metrics, yet lower the video reward on every I2V model we test and change downstream motion unpredictably. We therefore introduce Golden Anchor Learning (GAL), to our knowledge the first framework for learning golden anchors by optimizing a T2I generator with downstream video feedback. GAL evaluates candidate anchors through the videos they induce under a frozen I2V model and converts video rewards into image-level preferences for DPO fine-tuning of the T2I generator. On all four I2V models, GAL raises the VBench average by $2.97\%$--$8.46\%$ over the untuned generator. The rendered clips also score higher under VideoReward-Overall, and their extracted frames under HPSv3 and UniPercept. GAL yields consistent motion gains across all four I2V models, as measured by a $5.62\%$--$38.24\%$ increase in VBench dynamic degree. Although GAL is trained only on HunyuanVideo-1.5 renders, these gains extend to the other three I2V models.
authors: Jinyuan Xu, Shitong Shao, Lichen Bai, Zikai Zhou, Guoxi Huang, Nantheera Anantrasirichai, Zeke Xie
bullets: Image aesthetic and quality scores poorly predict the quality of videos generated from an anchor image.
Fine-tuning the image generator solely on image rewards can worsen video quality and produce unpredictable motion.
GAL evaluates candidate anchors through videos from a frozen I2V model, then uses video-derived preferences for DPO fine-tuning.
Across four I2V models, GAL improves VBench average by 2.97%–8.46% and dynamic degree by 5.62%–38.24%.
Although trained with HunyuanVideo-1.5 renders, GAL’s gains transfer to three other I2V models.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of GAL. Training (top): For each prompt, we sample K = 4 anchor images from the T2I generator, render each into a video with a frozen I2V model, and score the videos with a frozen video-reward model. We use these scores to construct image-level preference pairs and fine-tune only the upstream T2I generator with cross-modal DPO. Video rendering, scoring, and pair construction are performed offline. Inference (bottom): The fine-tuned T2I generator produces anchor images that improve video quality, while the downstream I2V model remains unchanged.

Aesthetics and quality are nearly uncorrelated with every video axis, and structure/texture is anti-correlated with visual and motion quality.

We therefore use it as the default variant. Metrics and parentheses follow Table 2.

For each of the 72 official VBench dynamic-degree prompts, we sample 12 seed-conditioned sibling anchors from the same T2I generator and render them with each frozen I2V model under a fixed downstream setting. VBench returns a binary label d ∈ {0, 1} for each rendered clip. We report the overall dynamic fraction and the prompt-averaged within-prompt variance across the 12 seeds. Low variance means that changing the seed-conditioned anchor rarely changes the binary dynamic/static decision for the same prompt. papers.abstract: Learning new tasks in multimodal continual instruction tuning can cause catastrophic forgetting of previously acquired knowledge. Although multi-expert LoRA distributes learning across experts, updates to a dense low-rank expert can still affect many output features. We introduce Monarch-MoE, which replaces the dense factors in LoRA experts with block-diagonal factors connected by a fixed permutation. This structure provides blockwise gradient isolation: individual block-pair updates affect only one output block, while connections between all input and output blocks are maintained. To make these compact experts practical on memory-limited hardware, we combine batched computation, fused forward operators, and an optimized backward pass. Across three continual-learning methods evaluated on MLLM-DCL and UCIT with LLaVA-1.5-7B, Monarch-MoE improves first-task retention while reducing adapter parameters by approximately 75% and 50%, respectively. In the main comparison, first-task forgetting is as low as 0.52 percentage points on MLLM-DCL and 0.10 on UCIT, with method-dependent trade-offs in final performance. Our implementation supports fine-tuning and inference on a single 24 GB RTX 4090, with lower measured memory use and competitive runtime in the evaluated settings. Together, these algorithmic and systems improvements make structured experts a practical option for continual adaptation on memory-limited hardware.
authors: Xi Zhang, Boyu Diao, Zesen Chen, Ruiqi Liu, Hangda Liu, Yongjun Xu
bullets: Targets catastrophic forgetting when learning new multimodal tasks.
Replaces dense LoRA factors with block-diagonal factors linked by a fixed permutation, isolating updates by output block while preserving global connectivity.
Uses batched computation, fused forward operations, and an optimized backward pass for memory-limited hardware.
Across MLLM-DCL and UCIT with LLaVA-1.5-7B, reduces adapter parameters by approximately 75% and 50%, respectively, while improving first-task retention.
Runs fine-tuning and inference on a single 24 GB RTX 4090, with method-dependent trade-offs in final performance.

papers.abstract: Actions specify what a robot should execute, but do not describe what those commands will achieve. Vision-language-action (VLA) policies nevertheless learn primarily by predicting action chunks from images, language, and state. We introduce Action--Future Coupled Effect Learning (AFCE), which makes a future-grounded physical Effect the policy's primary prediction target. An offline tokenizer constructs temporally ordered Effect tokens from demonstrated actions, realized robot responses, and sparse visual transitions. Reconstruction objectives encourage the representation to retain executable detail and observed physical change. A flow-matching VLA predicts Effects from current images, instruction, and robot state, while a state-conditioned decoder converts them into action chunks. Embodiment-specific interfaces allow single- and dual-arm tasks to share the Effect model. On DexJoCo, AFCE achieves $50.97\%$ overall success, improving over $\pi_{0.5}$ and UVT by 11.82 and 15.21 percentage points, respectively. It leads on all five bimanual tasks, highlighting the value of Effect supervision for coordinated dexterous manipulation. The project page is available at https://afceproject.github.io/AFCE-Web/.

papers.abstract: Time-series foundation models use the same network depth for every input, although forecasting windows differ in structure and difficulty. We test whether whole Transformer blocks can be removed at inference time in two pretrained models: Chronos-Bolt and TimesFM 2.5. Our bypasses avoid the original block computation and preserve the dense model exactly when all blocks are enabled. Masks are selected only on calibration windows and evaluated on 1,088 held-out windows from ETTh1, Traffic, Weather, and Exchange. At moderate sparsity, Chronos-Bolt with 7/11 candidate blocks and TimesFM with 16/20 blocks show little change in mean relative forecasting quality across datasets while reducing median A100 batch-1 latency by 11.2% and 13.4%. More aggressive TimesFM skipping accelerates inference further but substantially harms Traffic and Weather. Across both models, different equal-budget masks win on different windows, and a retrospective oracle significantly improves over the best static mask on every dataset. However, dataset-specific masks transfer inconsistently, and Chronos representations do not support reliable unseen-domain routing. These results establish cross-architecture structured redundancy and input-dependent opportunity, but not a deployable dynamic inference method.

papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a target policy on its own rollouts using token-level supervision from a stronger teacher, but typically relies on the teacher being substantially more capable than the target. Recent work relaxes this requirement by transferring the relative policy difference between an expert and a reference policy rather than the expert's absolute distribution. Yet it remains unclear which differences provide useful supervision and which targets can benefit from them. We develop a unified view in which the log-probability ratio between a proxy expert and a proxy reference defines an implicit reward for KL-regularized policy optimization. This formulation induces an on-policy update for the target, recovers conventional OPD as a special case, and enables any-to-any transfer across models that differ in scale, training stage or generation. Our systematic experiments yield three findings. First, a stronger expert is not necessarily a better source of supervision: differences induced by task-specific training, including reinforcement learning and supervised fine-tuning, transfer consistently, whereas those arising from model scale alone transfer weakly or not at all. Second, the expert and reference serve complementary roles: the expert provides the capability to be transferred, while the reference filters out shared behavior and isolates the relevant residual. Third, even a useful difference does not transfer to every target: success requires the induced update to move the target toward the expert and generalize beyond sampled rollouts. Raw policy distance does not predict transferability, whereas an appropriate reference can rescue otherwise unsuccessful transfer. These results characterize when relative policy differences provide effective supervision for OPD.
authors: Rong Wu, Daocheng Fu, Yu Yang, Xuemeng Yang, Siqi Li, Shu Zou, Yao Zhu, Botian Shi, Bo Zhang, Cong Zhang, Pinlong Cai, Jianbiao Mei
bullets: Frames the log-probability ratio between a proxy expert and reference as an implicit reward for KL-regularized target updates.
Generalizes conventional on-policy distillation and supports transfer across models differing in scale, training stage, or generation.
Task-specific changes from reinforcement learning or supervised fine-tuning transfer more reliably than differences caused by model scaling alone.
The expert supplies transferable capability, while the reference removes shared behavior and isolates useful residuals.
Transfer succeeds only when the update moves the target toward the expert and generalizes beyond sampled rollouts; suitable references can rescue failed transfers.

papers.abstract: Fast rollout generation for long-context reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) requires reducing KV-cache traffic without changing the response groups used for policy optimization. In our profiled RLVR workloads, attention accounts for 72--76\% of autoregressive decoding kernel time. Sparse attention reduces these reads, but sampling directly from a sparse policy changes the response groups used for learning. For group-relative optimization, we show that even exact response-wise reweighting does not generally recover the expected dense-policy update because the advantage of each response depends on the rewards of other group members. We propose Self-Sparse Speculative Rollouts (S$^3$R). It uses sparse attention to propose tokens, then generates responses through full-attention verification and exact speculative sampling. Drafting and verification share the same policy parameter, eliminating the need to train or update a separate drafter. The resulting response groups follow the dense-policy distribution. Under S$^3$R, we characterize speedup conditions and the costs of drafting and verification. We found that dense verification still requires the complete historical KV cache. A KV-aware scheduler therefore limits KV-cache repeated offloading and restoration while maintaining rollout parallelism. % OR thrashing In a matched ablation with an aggressive sparse drafting budget, S$^3$R maintains stable training while direct sparse sampling with training-side correction becomes unstable. On long-context mathematical reasoning, S$^3$R achieves $1.39\times~1.35\times$ the end-to-end training throughput of autoregressive rollouts on Qwen3 model, with comparable task performance.
authors: Yuhang He, Hongyu Ge, Zihan Lin, Siyi Liu, Yongqi Zhang

S$^3$R uses the same policy for sparse drafting and full-attention verification, avoiding a separately trained drafter.
A KV-aware scheduler reduces repeated KV-cache offloading and restoration while preserving rollout parallelism.

On long-context mathematical reasoning, it reports 1.35–1.39× end-to-end training throughput with comparable task performance.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) under partial observability typically re- lies on recurrent networks to encode temporal information, with the recurrent module trained jointly with the policy or value function. This raises a natural question: is learning the recurrent network actually necessary? In this paper, we investigate whether a frozen recurrent network can provide sufficient memory for solving par- tially observable Markov decision processes (POMDPs). Motivated by the theoretical foundations of Reservoir Computing (RC) and Generalized Reservoir Computing (GRC), we study a simple archi- tecture that combines a fixed recurrent network with a trainable nonlinear output module. We evaluate this approach across tasks with varying memory demands, observation modalities, and action spaces. Surprisingly, frozen recurrent networks support recall over hundreds of steps and achieve competitive control performance across diverse POMDPs, while using less than half the number of trainable parameters required by their fully trainable counterparts. These results suggest that learning the recurrent memory module is not always necessary for solving POMDPs. Frozen recurrent networks therefore provide a simple, parameter-efficient, and sur- prisingly strong baseline for partially observable RL. Our source code is available at https://github.com/Aphlios/FRN-POMDP
authors: Zekang Wang, Zhe He, Gaojie Jin
bullets: Partially observable RL commonly trains recurrent memory jointly with policy or value functions.

They achieve competitive control performance while requiring less than half as many trainable parameters as fully trainable recurrent models.
The approach is proposed as a simple, parameter-efficient baseline, though its effectiveness is evaluated within the studied POMDP tasks.

papers.abstract: Autonomous landing of unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) on unmanned surface vehicle (USV) is difficult in high sea states. Existing hierarchical landing methods often infer future USV motion only implicitly from short observation histories, which limits their ability to adapt to severe and rapidly changing sea conditions. This paper presents a prediction-informed hierarchical control framework. A pretrained model is developed to explicitly predict the USV attitude during high-level landing decisions. The prediction helps identify suitable landing windows and choose the right touchdown time, while a conventional low-level flight controller maintains UAV stability and tracks motion commands. To evaluate the framework under realistic disturbances, a real-sim validation setup is constructed in which USV-motion data collected in real sea conditions are transferred to a MuJoCo USV. The experiments demonstrate the feasibility of using explicit attitude prediction to improve landing-window selection and support timing-aware UAV landing planning in rapidly varying marine environments.

Combines high-level planning with a conventional low-level flight controller for UAV stability and command tracking.

papers.abstract: While reinforcement learning with verifiable reward (RLVR) enhances reasoning in large language models, its efficacy in long-horizon multimodal tasks remains underexplored. Visual Sudoku puzzles pose a representative challenge, requiring multi-step deductive reasoning over both local constraints and global dependency chains. To this end, we introduce FG-Sudoku, a fine-grained benchmark categorized by grid size and required deductive steps. Evaluations reveal that frontier MLLMs fail on complex long-range dependencies (e.g., 9*9 puzzles). During post-training, this near-zero success rate causes severe reward sparsity, halting standard RLVR. We propose Adaptive Curriculum Group Relative Policy Optimization (AdaC-GRPO) to overcome this. Unlike rigid or prior-based schedules, AdaC-GRPO dynamically constructs training batches by tracking the model's "Zone of Proximal Development" via online rollout accuracy. Experiments demonstrate that AdaC-GRPO enables Qwen2.5-VL-7B to approach the performance of Gemini-2.5-Flash while bridging 62.2% of the overall accuracy gap to Gemini-2.5-Pro, with its generalizability further validated across InternVL-3.5 and Qwen3-VL.
authors: Sida Li, Yuanxin Liu, Linli Yao, Shicheng Li, Xu Sun, Haoli Bai, Xiaohui Li

AdaC-GRPO dynamically selects training batches using online rollout accuracy to track the model’s learning frontier.
Enables Qwen2.5-VL-7B to approach Gemini-2.5-Flash and close 62.2% of the accuracy gap to Gemini-2.5-Pro.
Generalization is validated across InternVL-3.5 and Qwen3-VL.

papers.abstract: World models enable large language model (LLM) agents to anticipate action effects and make informed decisions. For generalization, it is desirable for such world models to transfer efficiently to new environments with similar interaction structure and underlying dynamics. Recent approaches encode world dynamics as symbolic rules or executable programs, whose compositional structure in principle affords transfer, but still organize such knowledge around environment-specific objects. To address this limitation, we introduce RoleWorld, a symbolic world modeling approach which uses reusable prototypes and environment-specific parameter values as functional role abstractions to represent how objects behave in interactions. From interaction trajectories, a teacher LLM extracts role prototypes and executable transition rules defined over role instances, together with a skill that guides the actor LLM to use role information in decision making. In a target world, without the teacher, the actor uses this skill together with its current role assignments and parameter estimates, and actively tests a role instance hypothesis through interaction when its uncertainty affects the current decision. Feedback from each action refines role assignments and estimates parameter values online, with no LLM parameter updates and the transition rules held fixed. Experiments on MARS benchmark show that RoleWorld enables robust generalization across environments with significantly altered object behavior, suggesting that functional role abstractions can serve as an effective component for knowledge transfer in world modeling. authors: Boyuan Xiao, Pu Wang, Ji Feng, Yao-Xiang Ding
bullets: Targets efficient generalization to new environments with similar interaction structures but altered object dynamics.

Experiments on the MARS benchmark show robust cross-environment generalization under substantially changed object behavior.

papers.abstract: Power sampling improves large language model (LLM) reasoning at test time by sampling from a sharpened version of the base model's distribution. Its sampler, PowerMH, is slow because its Metropolis--Hastings (MH) updates are sequential: each accept/reject decision sets the state from which the next proposal is generated. Prior work reduces this cost by changing the sampler or the model (e.g., sequential Monte Carlo, approximate lookahead, distillation). We propose Predictive SubTree Prefetching (PreSTO), which accelerates PowerMH by prefetching future proposals and provably leaves its MH transition kernel unchanged. PreSTO views future MH outcomes as a tree of accept/reject decisions: in each model call, it generates the proposals of a \textit{prefetched subtree} of this tree in one batch, then follows the realized path with the original MH acceptance rule. We also observe that MH reaches only a sparse, nearly unary part of each prefetched subtree, we further design a \textit{predictive traversal rule} that chooses the subtree to maximize the predicted number of completed transitions. Across seven datasets and five base LLMs, PreSTO achieves median speedups of $1.71\times$, $1.91\times$, and $2.33\times$ on PowerMH and its follow-ups EntropyCut and MultiTryMH, respectively; on the first two, it makes a median of $3.9\times$ fewer model calls, each only $2.1\times$ longer. On LCB V6 with Qwen3.5-9B, the predictive traversal rule is a further $1.25\times$--$1.37\times$ faster than the default breadth-first traversal.
authors: Nan Jiang, Panagiotis Theodoropoulos, Wei Deng
bullets: PowerMH is slow because sequential Metropolis–Hastings decisions require each proposal to depend on the previous outcome.
PreSTO organizes possible future accept/reject outcomes as a tree and prefetched subtrees of proposals in parallel model calls.
A predictive traversal rule selects subtrees expected to complete more MH transitions, exploiting the sampler’s sparse, nearly unary paths.
Across seven datasets and five base LLMs, it reports median speedups of 1.71× for PowerMH, 1.91× for EntropyCut, and 2.33× for MultiTryMH.
For LCB V6 with Qwen3.5-9B, predictive traversal is 1.25×–1.37× faster than breadth-first traversal.

papers.abstract: Scaling robot manipulation policies requires large amounts of diverse, action-labeled data, yet collecting such data in the real world remains expensive and difficult to scale. Existing methods either depend on human teleoperation, rely on simulation with limited visual realism, or use human videos that lack embodiment-specific annotations. In this paper, we introduce Grounded-Dreamer, a framework for synthesizing physically grounded robot manipulation data with video world models while avoiding human teleoperation demonstrations. Grounded-Dreamer combines the visual realism of generative video models with simulator physics engines. Starting from a small set of real images depicting robot task initial states, our method automatically reconstructs task-relevant objects and camera geometry, aligns them in simulation, and collects physically valid trajectories. These trajectories are used to post-train both a video world model and an inverse dynamics model, enabling the generation of visually realistic robot manipulation videos and corresponding robot actions from real images. To filter physically implausible rollouts, Grounded-Dreamer replays generated trajectories in the reconstructed simulation and retains only those that successfully complete the tasks. The real-world robot policies are trained solely on the grounded synthetic trajectories without any human demonstrations. Empirical results in real-world tasks demonstrate that Grounded-Dreamer can synthesize physically grounded data and substantially facilitate policy learning without requiring human teleoperation effort.
authors: Feng Jiang, Shu Chen, Yuanfei Wang, Yuan Li, Zhenhao Shen, Jiaqi Liang, Yang Chen, Lei Wei, Chen Xie, Ruihai Wu
bullets: Addresses the cost and scalability limits of collecting real-world robot demonstrations.
Reconstructs task objects and camera geometry from a small set of real initial-state images, then aligns them in simulation.
Post-trains a video world model and inverse dynamics model to generate realistic manipulation videos and robot actions.
Filters synthetic rollouts by replaying them in simulation and retaining only task-successful trajectories.
Uses only grounded synthetic data to train real-world policies, which facilitates policy learning in real-world tasks.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of Grounded-Dreamer. Our framework automates the generation of massive, high-fidelity robot data from a small number of real-world reference images. By combining generative world models with simulation-based verification, Grounded-Dreamer produces data that is both visually realistic and physically consistent. This simulation verification loop effectively filters out the physical hallucinations common in purely generative approaches, allowing robot policies to be trained directly on scalable synthetic data that transfers robustly to complex real-world scenarios.

Figure 2: The Grounded-Dreamer Pipeline. Given several real-world reference images, our pipeline first reconstructs physically aligned simulation scenes and objects. Within these environments, task data is automatically collected and processed with interaction-aware masking to fine-tune Cosmos-Predict 2.5 as the core data generation model. An image refinement model then synthesizes diverse initial frames by combining reconstructed assets with real scene backgrounds and object appearances. Conditioned on these frames, the generation model produces manipulation videos, which are converted into action trajectories using an Inverse Dynamics Model (IDM). Finally, all synthesized trajectories are replayed in simulation for closed-loop verification, filtering out physically inconsistent samples before policy training and real-world deployment.

papers.abstract: We present Neurograf v1, an experimental end-to-end Romanian-first language-model pipeline developed to investigate the feasibility of training language models from scratch for a lower-resource European language. The pipeline comprises RoSfera, a 635 GB Romanian corpus containing 175.7 million documents; an 80k byte-level BPE tokenizer; five decoder-only models ranging from 160M to 6B parameters, trained on 131 billion tokens; three instruction-tuned assistants; and two contrastively trained embedding models. Training and evaluation were conducted using computing infrastructure at ELI-NP/IFIN-HH. The model family exhibits consistent scaling of validation loss and increasing Romanian factual and cultural knowledge with model size. On the 1,000-question WWTBM benchmark, Neurograf-6B achieves 69.89% accuracy on Romanian-context questions, while Neurograf-3.2B reaches 67.38%. Compute-optimal analysis yields a parameter-scaling exponent of approximately 0.423. Neurograf v1 serves as an experimental demonstrator rather than a production system. The study identifies practical challenges involving diacritic preservation, corpus quality, data composition, and tokenization efficiency, while demonstrating the feasibility of developing Romanian-first base models, instruction-following assistants, and semantic embedding models within a unified training pipeline.

On the 1,000-question WWTBM benchmark, the 6B and 3.2B models achieve 69.89% and 67.38% accuracy on Romanian-context questions, respectively.
Identifies challenges in diacritic preservation, corpus quality, data composition, and tokenization efficiency; the system is an experimental demonstrator, not a production model.

papers.abstract: LLM-as-a-Service has become a dominant paradigm for accessing large language models without requiring local deployment. However, the process raises severe privacy concerns when user queries may include sensitive or confidential contexts. Differential privacy (DP) provides a principled approach to protecting such inputs, but existing DP inference methods are primarily designed for short- or moderate-context settings and struggle with million-token-scale inputs due to limited context capacity and severe utility degradation under DP perturbation. In this paper, we propose DP-MIND, a memory-guided framework that scales differentially private inference to million-token contexts. DP-MIND enables private long-context inference by locally perturbing the input and processing it chunk by chunk with a compact memory that preserves task-relevant information across the sequence. To make this memory robust to DP noise, we optimize the memory construction policy directly on perturbed inputs using reinforcement learning, guided by both final answer correctness and memory consistency. We further recover perturbation-corrupted answer spans through a local denoising module without exposing the original context to the external model. We provide theoretical privacy analysis of DP-MIND and further conduct extensive empirical analysis across multiple long-context benchmarks with context lengths up to the million-token scale, demonstrating that DP-MIND consistently outperforms existing DP and long-context inference baselines in both scalability and utility.
authors: Zhihao Liu, Yitian Cheng, Shuang Liu, Rui Wen, Yuke Hu, Zhan Qin
bullets: Addresses privacy and utility challenges in LLM-as-a-Service for sensitive, million-token inputs.
Processes perturbed inputs chunk by chunk while a compact memory preserves task-relevant information across the sequence.
Uses reinforcement learning to make memory construction robust to differential privacy noise, optimizing correctness and memory consistency.
Applies local denoising to recover perturbation-corrupted answer spans without revealing the original context to the external model.
Theoretical and empirical analyses across long-context benchmarks show improved scalability and utility over existing DP and long-context inference baselines.

papers.abstract: Collecting dexterous manipulation demonstrations for each robot hand requires repeated task-specific data acquisition. We ask whether one shared corpus of natural human demonstrations can instead serve as a reusable data interface for different dexterous hands, without collecting task demonstrations on each target robot. We present Human2Dex, a wrist-centric human demonstration interface that separates shared human observation and motion semantics from embodiment-specific execution. It aligns observations through local hand-appearance adaptation and a shared 21-point hand representation with consistent structural semantics across human and robot observations. It constructs executable supervision by retargeting fused human hand motion to each target hand, and introduces the Grasp-Pocket Interaction Representation (GPIR) to express tracked objects relative to a hand-centered Functional Grasp Pocket. The corpus is converted into separate training sets for Linker O6 and Wuji, while action labels, normalization, training, and diffusion-policy checkpoints remain hand-specific. Across six real-world tasks, Human2Dex achieves 109/120 (90.8%) successes on Linker O6 and 97/120 (80.8%) on Wuji. Across both hands, Human-Raw achieves 63/240 (26.3%) successes, whereas the complete Human2Dex configuration achieves 206/240 (85.8%). These results support the use of wrist-centric human demonstrations as a reusable interface across calibrated dexterous hands while retaining embodiment-specific policy learning. The project website is publicly available at https://human2dex.pages.dev/.
authors: Jiachen Zhang, Yuanyuan Li, Shaqi Luo
bullets: Addresses the need to repeatedly collect task demonstrations for each robot hand.
Uses local hand-appearance adaptation and a shared 21-point hand representation to align human and robot observations.
Retargets human motion to each hand and introduces GPIR for hand-centered object representation.
Evaluated on six real-world tasks: 90.8% success on Linker O6 and 80.8% on Wuji.
The complete configuration reaches 85.8% success across both hands, versus 26.3% with raw human demonstrations.

papers.title: Human2Dex: Dexterous Robot Learning from Wrist-Centric Human Demonstrations
papers.tldr: Human2Dex reuses wrist-centric human demonstrations to train policies for different dexterous robot hands, achieving high real-world task success without robot-specific data collection.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models and world action models (WAMs) have advanced robotic policy learning by building on pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) and video generative models (VGMs), respectively. Yet VLAs learn without explicit supervision from future world states, while WAMs that condition actions on predicted futures incur extra inference cost and let visual prediction errors propagate into actions. We present Forward Dynamics Models (FDM), a family of robotic action models that couples action and future world-state prediction through an action-to-future paradigm. Future prediction is conditioned on action features, never the reverse: end-to-end training lets ground-truth future states supervise the policy through these features, while prediction errors cannot propagate into actions. At inference, FDM skips future generation entirely, avoiding its computational cost. The paradigm is backbone-agnostic, and we instantiate it with both VLM and VGM backbones. Experiments in simulation and on real robots demonstrate the effectiveness of FDM across both backbone families, achieving a state-of-the-art 99.4% average success rate on LIBERO and absolute gains of up to 13% over VLA and WAM methods on real-world tasks.
authors: Zipei Ma, Junzhe Jiang, Jiahui Zhang, Juntong Zhang, Chun Gu, Bozhou Zhang, Jiankang Deng, Xiatian Zhu, Li Zhang
bullets: Addresses the lack of explicit future-state supervision in VLAs and the inference cost and error propagation of WAMs.
Uses an action-to-future paradigm: predicted futures condition on action features, not vice versa.
End-to-end training lets future-state prediction supervise the policy without allowing prediction errors to affect actions.
Backbone-agnostic design is instantiated with both vision-language and video-generative backbones.
Demonstrates a 99.4% average success rate on LIBERO and up to 13% absolute gains over VLA and WAM methods on real-world tasks.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of our Forward Dynamics Models. The context expert encodes visual observations and the instruction to guide the action expert. During training, the generation expert predicts future states from context and action features; its loss backpropagates through these action features to complement action imitation. This asymmetric connection lets future supervision shape the policy while keeping action prediction independent of predicted futures. At inference, the action expert generates actions using the required context features, skipping future generation.

Inference latency is measured on one NVIDIA H100 GPU.

Figure 1: Architectural comparison of action prediction and future supervision. (a) VLA predicts actions directly from the current observation and instruction. (b) A future-conditioned WAM conditions action prediction on predicted future video, requiring future generation at inference. (c) FDM conditions future prediction on context and action features through action-to-future learning. During training, action imitation and future prediction are jointly optimized; the future loss backpropagates through action features to supervise the policy. At inference, FDM denoises action chunks using only the current observation and instruction, skipping the future-generation branch marked as training only while retaining context processing.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a new action model paradigm coupling action and future prediction, relevant to VLA and robot learning.
papers.title: Forward Dynamics Models
papers.tldr: Forward Dynamics Models train robot policies with future-state supervision while avoiding future generation at inference, improving efficiency and performance.

papers.abstract: Continual post-training faces a dual challenge of acquisition and retention: models must learn new capabilities while preserving prior knowledge. While Self-Distillation Fine-Tuning (SDFT) mitigates this using self-supervision with in-context demonstrations, it relies on strong in-context learning and instruction-following abilities. Consequently, SDFT fails on smaller models critical for low-latency, on-device use. To enable continual learning at smaller scales, we first identify the root cause of failure. We show that poor acquisition and forgetting correlate linearly with the post-trained model's distribution shift, revealing the necessity of in-distribution learning. We thus introduce Synthetic Self-Distillation (SynthSelf), imitating SDFT's in-distribution rewrite by outsourcing the task to a minimally larger, same-family aligner. Coupled with off-policy supervision and rejection sampling, this provides the high-quality supervision small models require without breaking their original distribution. Evaluations spanning 4 acquisition datasets (including a mixture) and 14 retention benchmarks show SynthSelf consistently outperforms 6 methods (including off- and on-policy distillation) across 3 small model scales. Extensive further analyses confirm SynthSelf paves the way toward effective small-model continual learning.
authors: Woosung Koh, Hyunsoo Lee, Kyungjae Lee, Haeju Park, Dahyun Lee, Dasol Hwang, Moontae Lee
bullets: Small models struggle with standard self-distillation because they lack strong in-context learning and instruction-following abilities.
The authors link poor acquisition and forgetting to distribution shift during post-training, motivating in-distribution learning.
SynthSelf uses a minimally larger, same-family aligner to generate in-distribution rewrites, combined with off-policy supervision and rejection sampling.
Across 4 acquisition datasets, 14 retention benchmarks, and 3 small-model scales, SynthSelf consistently outperforms 6 compared methods.
The approach targets low-latency and on-device continual learning, though its scope is evaluated within the reported small-model and benchmark settings.

papers.abstract: Large audio-language models (LALMs) frequently exhibit object hallucination, affirming absent sounds. The dominant mitigation, Audio-Aware Decoding (AAD), contrasts logits under real audio against an all-zero "blank" waveform, flagged by prior review as out-of-distribution. We introduce a black-box causal test that isolates the claimed evidence itself: localize a claim's evidence region via CLAP similarity, remove it by spectral gating, and compare against a random-window control across a 2x2x2 grid on three LALMs. On Qwen2-Audio-7B, localized ablation's raw AUROC trails blank's (0.613 vs. 0.721); this is a duration confound, not a localization failure, since blank removes the entire clip versus the grid's 2-4 s. Holding duration fixed, localization beats random removal at every cell on both models. Raw detection value remains model-dependent, especially on Audio Flamingo 3. The same evidence corrects decoding: contrastive decoding combining blank and language-prior contrasts, gated and ensembled, raises Qwen2-Audio accuracy from 57.1% to 71.9%, beating AAD alone. A unified causal-grounding profile does not transfer between models, indicating different grounding regimes. The source code and a detailed report of our findings, including identified limitations, are available at https://github.com/khalooei/causa.
bullets: LALMs may hallucinate absent sounds; Audio-Aware Decoding’s blank-audio comparison can be confounded by removing the entire clip.
The study localizes evidence with CLAP similarity, removes it via spectral gating, and compares it with random-window removal across multiple models and conditions.
After matching removal duration, localized ablation outperforms random removal, but raw detection behavior varies by model.
Combining blank and language-prior contrasts improves Qwen2-Audio accuracy from 57.1% to 71.9%, outperforming AAD alone.
Grounding profiles do not transfer consistently between models; the study reports limitations and releases code.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes audio grounding and hallucination in large audio-language models, fitting multimodal LLM research.
papers.title: Does Location Matter? A Black-Box Causal Audit Reveals Model-Dependent Audio Grounding in LALM Hallucination
papers.tldr: A black-box causal audit shows that audio-grounding evidence and hallucination mitigation are model-dependent, while duration-controlled localization and combined contrastive decoding improve reliability in tested settings.

papers.abstract: Visual agents for symbolic graphics reasoning depend on executable world representations, yet continued improvement remains bottlenecked by ambiguous supervision from final renders. Recent agentic systems refine scenes through repeated interaction, but they lack mechanisms to recursively extract actionable evidence from execution traces, overlooking which proposed symbolic edits survived, disappeared, or interfered during program execution. To address this, we propose VETR (Verified Execution Trajectories for Refinement), a framework that enables agentic recursive self-improvement over executable world representations for symbolic graphics reasoning. Within each task, VETR retains aligned program/render records with bounded runtime observations and introduces an execution refiner that compiles observed writes and state changes into constrained alternative programs. The refiner validates their endpoints and preservation conditions against captured runtime state; the ordinary visual verifier then assesses goal relevance. Repair construction makes no additional language-model calls, but can require additional executions. Evaluations on BlenderGym (280 tasks) and BlenderBench (27 released tasks) with GPT-5.6-luna and Qwen3.8-27B show that VETR consistently outperforms existing refinement strategies, including BlenderAlchemy and VIGA. Controlled ablations evaluate the contributions of execution refinement and role-asymmetric evidence organization under fixed generator-interaction caps.
authors: Yingbo Ma, Kuangshi Ai, Gordon Dai, Chenglong Yu, Chaoli Wang, Hua Shen
bullets: Addresses ambiguous supervision from final renders by identifying which symbolic edits persist, vanish, or interfere during execution.
Maintains aligned program/render records with bounded runtime observations and compiles state changes into constrained alternative programs.
Validates repaired programs against runtime endpoints and preservation conditions, then uses visual verification for goal relevance.
Evaluated on BlenderGym and BlenderBench with two language models; consistently outperforms prior refinement strategies, including BlenderAlchemy and VIGA.
Ablations examine execution refinement and role-asymmetric evidence organization under fixed generator-interaction limits.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Conceptual overview of VETR. VETR refines scenes through execution-grounded evidence, bridging a scene program, its execution trace, and the realized 3D scene. Given a start and goal image, the system performs iterative updates guided by observed writes and realized bindings. This evidence-supported refinement targets viewpoint alignment, appearance (lighting/material) editing, and geometry and placement adjustments. Runtime checks test supported effects, while visual feedback guides subsequent proposals toward the goal.

Figure 2: Execution-evidence refinement before visual assessment. Each complete program executes from B. The private refiner constructs alternatives, compiles supported changes and compatible bindings, and checks their realization relative to the candidate’s reference record. For the numerical channel, Wh contains selected cells, Ch \ Wh contains captured cells to preserve, and properties outside Ch are not covered by that contract. Goal-image comparison occurs only in the ordinary visual verifier. Delivery, shortcuts, and the six-execution cap are specified in Algorithm 1. Repair construction makes no additional language-model calls.

Figure 3: Qualitative comparison of visual editing. Columns display the goal, start, VIGA final output, and VETR final output across three editing categories: light (color), geometry (chair position & orientation), and shape (facial expression). Red arrows and boxes highlight local regions of comparison. Reported values denote PL ×100 (lower is better). VETR achieves near-zero PL in the displayed light and geometry tasks and lower error in the displayed shape task. These output comparisons illustrate visual fidelity, not an independent verification of the refiner’s runtime mechanism.

Comments summarize observed changes and feedback; ellipses omit unchanged or lengthy code. Scores are N -CLIP × 100 (↓).

papers.selection_reason: Execution-grounded self-improvement for agents refining symbolic 3D graphics, relevant to embodied agentic reasoning and 3D scene manipulation.
papers.title: VETR: Execution-Grounded Self-Improving Agent for Symbolic Graphics Reasoning
papers.tldr: VETR improves symbolic graphics agents by using execution traces to verify and repair programs for more reliable self-improvement.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive robot policies rely on action tokenizers to convert continuous action chunks into compact sequences of discrete prediction targets. Existing tokenizers can reconstruct action chunks from discrete codes, but often leave implicit what each individual token contributes to the reconstructed action. We introduce Residual Action Tokenization (ReAT), which gives each token an explicit role in refining the current action reconstruction. It uses the decoded reconstruction as feedback to construct the next token from the remaining action error. This closes the loop between encoding and decoding, making each new token responsive to the errors left by the actual decoded prefix. Across 19 manipulation tasks spanning three simulation benchmarks and real-world settings, 8-token ReAT policies outperform the evaluated baselines in task success; on LIBERO, even 4-token ReAT surpasses the evaluated 8-token action-tokenization baselines at half the token budget. These results suggest a path toward action tokenization that supports self-corrective policy learning, helping autoregressive policies learn to progressively refine their own action plans.
authors: Dijia Zhan, Zhuo Li, Xuemiao Xu, Sun Zheng, Jinyi Li, Wenjun Wang, Jie Tang
bullets: Addresses the unclear contribution of individual tokens in existing action tokenizers.
Builds each next token from the remaining action error after decoding the current prefix.
Evaluated across 19 manipulation tasks in three simulation benchmarks and real-world settings.
ReAT policies with 8 tokens outperform evaluated baselines; on LIBERO, 4 tokens outperform 8-token baselines.
Supports progressively refined action plans with fewer prediction tokens.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Architecture of ReAT. Top left: residual tokenization with reconstruction feedback across tokens. Top right: residual encoding and draft-conditioned decoding in one residual refinement iteration. Bottom: an observation-conditioned policy predicts tokens, whose prefixes are decoded by the frozen tokenizer.

Figure 1: Comparison of action-token decoding strategies. Full-sequence decoding requires all M tokens, while ordered prefix decoding reconstructs a complete action chunk from any nonempty prefix. ReAT combines the existing draft with each new token to produce a learned correction. Orange arrows indicate the corrections applied to the previous reconstruction in ReAT; target trajectories are shown only for reference.
Figure 5: LIBERO reconstruction error versus token length. Raw-action MSE on validation chunks; percentages give policy success. Dashed links: observed Pareto front. FAST uses mean token length.
Figure 4: Three benchmark domains. Simulator renders (LIBERO, MetaWorld, RoboCasa).

Figure 6: Real-world bucket stacking. Left: a successful ReAT sequence on the X-Trainer arm. papers.abstract: AI agents depend on repeated decisions to accomplish tasks, with large language models (LLMs) commonly serving as their core decision makers. The recent emergence of Jev offers an opportunity to make these decisions faster and at lower cost. However, it remains unclear whether such local savings can be translated into efficient and reliable task completion. In this paper, we investigate this efficiency transfer across five agents in two representative application settings, embodied tasks in ALFWorld and mobile app use in AndroidWorld. Across 4,500 task executions, we jointly evaluate task effectiveness, decision-level and task-level resource use, and execution behavior. Experimental results show that Jev integration substantially reduces decision cost and latency across all five agents, with task-level gains varying by workflow. Task success remains close to baseline levels on ALFWorld and declines more substantially in two mobile agents. Auxiliary reasoning and additional interactions absorb decision savings, while failed recovery and premature completion limit successful delivery. Mean cost per successful outcome increases in one agent even as spending per attempt falls. These findings highlight the importance of preserving progress, supporting recovery, and verifying completion when integrating efficient decision models into agent workflows. Their practical value should be assessed through successful task delivery, recovery behavior, and resources per delivered outcome.

Efficiency should be measured by successful outcomes, recovery behavior, and resources per delivered task—not per-attempt spending.
