papers.abstract: People often learn how an unfamiliar object moves through a small exploratory push, using its response to guide their next motion. Inspired by this behavior, we study humanoids pushing carts whose mass and caster stiffness are initially unknown. Our object-centric framework closes online estimation, flow-based planning, and whole-body control into a loop, creating a tension: replacing the plan whenever the belief shifts disrupts the maneuver under way, while keeping it strands the robot on a path its evidence has ruled out. Belief-Overlap Partial Inversion (BOPI) scales revision to agreement, inverting the flow under the old belief only as far as the beliefs disagree before reconstructing under the new one. Across 18 simulated goals it lowers pooled final position and yaw error by roughly 33% and 47% against fixed-depth replanning, and on hardware it translates and turns a non-holonomic cart.
authors: Chen Yu, Sudarshan S Harithas, Juan Borbon, Dingqi Zhang, Jiuguang Wang
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between disruptive full replanning and continuing along invalidated plans.
Combines online object-property estimation, flow-based planning, and whole-body control.
Partially inverts the old plan only where old and new beliefs disagree, then reconstructs the remainder under the new belief.
Across 18 simulated goals, reduced pooled final position error by roughly 33% and yaw error by 47% versus fixed-depth replanning.
Hardware experiments demonstrated translation and turning of a non-holonomic cart.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. An object-centric estimation–planning–control framework. Online estimation informs object planning and whole-body control (trajectory waypoint tracking). papers.abstract: Recent work on large audio-language models (LALMs) explores adaptive reasoning to balance accuracy and efficiency. However, existing approaches often rely on coarse-grained difficulty estimation, overlooking the diverse factors that determine reasoning effort. We address this limitation by deriving five-dimensional difficulty scores and compressed reasoning traces from complementary offline assessments. Based on this characterization, we propose SWEAR, a difficulty-aware reasoning framework that learns difficulty signals during supervised fine-tuning and uses reinforcement learning to adapt reasoning allocation across reasoning stages. Experiments on MMAU-test-mini and MMAR show that SWEAR improves accuracy while substantially reducing generated tokens, shortening reasoning for easy instances without sacrificing performance on difficult ones.
authors: Yixuan Li, Minghao Lv, Xuenan Xu, Zihao Zheng, Mengyue Wu
bullets: Addresses coarse difficulty estimation in adaptive reasoning for large audio-language models.

(c) Curriculum RL progresses from easy to hard while jointly optimizing task quality, format, rating-conditioned section-length rewards, and teacher-anchored rating calibration under reference-policy KL regularization. papers.abstract: Third-person human videos offer a scalable alternative to task-specific reward engineering, teleoperation, and manually scripted demonstrations for humanoid loco-manipulation. Recent video-to-humanoid systems have shown that noisy human motion, object trajectories, and contacts can be extracted from unstructured videos and refined into deployable skills. However, a key gap remains for contact-rich imitation: the task is often defined by world-frame contacts whose poses, timing, and speed must survive embodiment mismatch and runtime scene changes. Towards this, we present VICAR (Video Imitation with Contact-Aware Retargeting), a pipeline for learning humanoid interactive skills from third-person human videos. The system first recovers human motion, reconstructs task-relevant obstacles from monocular video, and then retargets the motion to a humanoid while preserving global contact poses, motion speed, and collision clearance. Unlike retargeting methods that only remove penetration or preserve local interaction geometry, our formulation represents user-specified contact poses and collision clearance as high-priority Lagrangian penalty terms and optimizes the full motion to remain smooth through contact-rich transitions. The resulting motions are used to train a contact-conditioned motion generator whose inputs include movable contact points enabling runtime adaptation to new contact positions. We demonstrate the framework on ten diverse third-person video skills, including six table-tennis serves, three object-pickup tasks, and ladder climbing, and deploy the learned skills on hardware. These results suggest that contact-preserving retargeting is a practical step toward humanoids that learn useful interactive behavior by watching humans.

bullets: Addresses contact-rich imitation under embodiment mismatch and changing runtime scenes.

papers.abstract: Safety-aligned large language models (LLMs) remain vulnerable to jailbreaks and can over-refuse benign requests. Understanding these failures requires distinguishing harmfulness recognition from the computation that writes refusal. We reframe this as a pathway question and make it measurable on residual-stream updates in decoder-only Transformers, separating the harmfulness information a module update exposes from the change it produces in readable refusal evidence. Across 18 Base-Instruct pairs spanning Qwen, Llama, and Gemma, harmfulness is decoded more readily from attention updates, particularly in early layers, whereas MLP updates contribute more strongly to harm-selective refusal writing in aligned models. Post-training strengthens MLP refusal writing in all 18 pairs without systematically improving harmfulness decodability, while positive MLP writing becomes more concentrated in deeper layers after post-training. Across six reasoning-enabled models, harmfulness remains decodable during reasoning while strong refusal writing concentrates at answer onset, a pattern that persists with reasoning disabled. Causal interventions further support this pathway: resetting downstream MLP updates to their clean values substantially reduces the refusal shift caused by upstream attention interventions. Building on these findings, we introduce Sentinel, which combines an attention-derived perception score P with an MLP-derived decision score D. Their joint profiles characterize jailbreaks and over-refusals, and conditional routing with both signals achieves a lower aggregate error rate than single-signal routing and evaluated fixed reminders across eight models.
authors: Zixuan Weng, Haoqi He, Weifei Jin, Yue Huang, Yang Bai

In reasoning-enabled models, harmfulness remains detectable during reasoning, but refusal writing concentrates near answer onset.
Causal interventions support attention-to-MLP dependence, and Sentinel’s combined perception and decision signals outperform single-signal routing and evaluated fixed reminders across eight models.

papers.tldr: The study finds that attention mainly recognizes harmfulness, while MLPs convert that signal into refusal behavior, enabling a two-signal safety monitor called Sentinel.

papers.abstract: Corpus-level long-context reasoning requires agents to acquire and integrate evidence across document collections that exceed their context windows. Existing agent harnesses enable incremental access to these corpora, but acquired evidence and evolving conclusions often remain entangled in a growing interaction history. This implicit state management can lead to two coupled failure modes: unbounded exploration, where retrieval expands the interaction history without resolving decision-relevant information gaps, and evidence-state drift, where previously acquired evidence or subsequent corrections fail to inform the current conclusion. We present LongHarness, a model-agnostic harness that makes the interaction between acquired evidence and evolving conclusions explicit. Its core mechanism, Evidence-Conclusion Coevolution, uses unresolved conclusions to guide exploration toward missing information, while newly acquired evidence strengthens or revises the conclusions that directed the search. LongHarness couples this process with Evidence Lifecycle Management, which keeps accumulated evidence current and traceable throughout the interaction. Together, these mechanisms focus retrieval on remaining information needs and keep conclusions aligned with current evidence. We evaluate LongHarness on OfficeQA Pro V1 and V2, AA-LCR, and LongBench v2 using GLM-5.3-Flash and Qwen3.8-Flash. Compared with direct reasoning using the same backbone, LongHarness improves GLM-5.3-Flash exact match on OfficeQA Pro from 15.8% to 60.2% on V1 and from 4.4% to 61.1% on V2. Against state-of-the-art agent harnesses, it surpasses Claude Code by 12.0 percentage points on V1 and Codex by 18.9 points on V2. With Qwen3.8-Flash, LongHarness reaches 61.7% on V1, outperforming Claude Code by 8.3 points and Codex by 12.0 points.

papers.abstract: Processing a long sequence does not guarantee that distant information remains usable. As context grows, a fixed-size memory must retain many associations, connect information across positions, and preserve relevant structure without being overwhelmed by everything it observes. These are distinct requirements: a memory may store more information without representing the relationships needed for retrieval, and it may transport those relationships without preserving the ones that matter. Thus, the challenge is not simply extending context length, but constructing a memory that remains usable as context grows. We study this problem in large-chunk test-time training (TTT) and identify two basic failures: single-step writes accumulate interference, limiting capacity, while self-associative writes cannot form cross-position bindings. We introduce Double-Take (DT), which repairs these failures with multi-step unpinned updates and cross-position mixing, and adds bidirectional change-sensitive writes for selective retention. Capacity alone leaves end-to-end recall at the $0.10$ chance floor; adding binding raises it to $0.92$. Trained only on $32\,\mathrm{kb}$ genomic contexts, DT reaches $0.927$ AUROC at $131\,\mathrm{kb}$ and $0.856$ near $1\,\mathrm{Mb}$, while transferring zero-shot from human to mouse. Together, these results identify capacity, binding, and selectivity as three requirements for usable long-range memory.
authors: Vakul Raghavan, Utkarsh Grover, Mingyang Mao, Chengwen Wang, Xiaomin Lin
bullets: The work argues that extending context is insufficient: memory must retain information, bind distant positions, and selectively preserve relevant structure.
It identifies interference from single-step writes and the inability of self-associative writes to form cross-position bindings.
Double-Take addresses these issues with multi-step unpinned updates, cross-position mixing, and bidirectional change-sensitive writes.
Adding binding improves end-to-end recall from the 0.10 chance floor to 0.92, while models trained on 32 kb genomic contexts generalize to 131 kb and nearly 1 Mb.
The method also transfers zero-shot from human to mouse, supporting the role of capacity, binding, and selectivity in long-range memory.

papers.abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) agents have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in tackling complex tasks through agentic workflows. However, manually designing these workflows is labor-intensive and lacks flexibility to adapt to diverse queries. While automated workflow optimization is a promising direction, existing methods often incur expensive API costs during training-phase feedback collection. Furthermore, they fail to adaptively reuse high-quality workflows, which creates a bottleneck for both performance and cost-effectiveness. To address these limitations, we propose CB-Orchestrator, an adaptive framework that decouples workflow generation from selection. In the first stage, we construct a diverse pool of candidate workflows via evolutionary search. In the second stage, we formulate workflow selection as a Contextual Bandit problem, which enables sample-efficient learning by balancing exploration and exploitation, thereby significantly reducing the feedback required for training. During inference, the model adaptively selects the optimal workflow tailored to each query. Evaluations across five diverse benchmarks demonstrate that CB-Orchestrator consistently outperforms all baselines. Notably, on the MATH dataset, CB-Orchestrator achieves better performance than strong recent baselines while reducing training-phase API token overhead by no less than 40.55% and total end-to-end training (including workflow pool generation) token overhead by no less than 29.73%.

papers.abstract: KV-cache reuse in large language model serving is commonly limited to exact prompt prefixes, preventing reuse when the same retrieved document appears after different system prompts, conversation histories, or dynamic metadata. We present KV-Repurpose, an open-source, vLLM-based system for developing and evaluating segment-wise KV-cache reuse beyond exact prefixes. The system combines cache-aware segment scheduling, prompt construction, capacity management, workload generation, and runtime monitoring. Experiments on long-context benchmarks show that naive segment reuse largely preserves output quality for single-document question answering and summarization, while exposing clear limitations in cross-document reasoning. Under a Zipfian RAG-style workload in which 20% of requests share a fixed prefix, KV-Repurpose achieves a substantially higher token-level cache hit rate than prefix caching at the same 30 GB cache capacity, 63.9% versus 3.3%, resulting in lower TTFT. Even with 1 TB of cache capacity, prefix caching reaches only a 17.9% hit rate in this workload. Source code is available under the Apache-2.0 license at https://github.com/taiga333/eval-kv-repurpose.
authors: Taiga Ikeda, Daisuke Miyashita, Jun Deguchi

papers.abstract: Radiology reports are essential for diagnostic reasoning and patient care, yet their manual preparation is time-consuming and cognitively demanding. Automatic radiology report generation (RRG) offers a scalable alternative, but existing models often produce lengthy, unstructured narratives that overlook diagnostic cues and multi-view information. We present Clinical-Knowledge Guided Disease-aware Visual-Textual Alignment for QA-Style Radiology Report Generation (CliQ-RRG), a unified two-stage framework for interpretable and clinically grounded reporting. In Stage 1, CliQ-RRG employs a Disease-aware Visual-Textual Alignment module that aligns image and text representations using predicted disease embeddings, reinforced by a Prior-Guided Attention Module (PrAM) to capture multi-view dependencies across current and prior scans. In Stage 2, GraphRAG-guided retrieval augments intermediate textual representations with graph-grounded clinical evidence, and a large language model restructures them into concise, interpretable question-answer (QA) pairs with diagnostic summaries. Experiments on two public chest X-ray benchmarks demonstrate that CliQ-RRG consistently outperforms prior methods across both lexical and clinical metrics, generating accurate and clinically coherent QA-style radiology reports. Code is available at: https://github.com/chandravardhan-singh-raghaw/CliQ-RRG.

bullets: Targets lengthy, unstructured reports that may miss diagnostic cues and multi-view information.
Stage 1 uses disease-aware visual-textual alignment and prior-guided attention to model current and prior scans.
Stage 2 applies GraphRAG-guided clinical retrieval and an LLM to produce QA pairs with diagnostic summaries.
On two public chest X-ray benchmarks, it outperforms prior methods on lexical and clinical metrics.
The approach is evaluated specifically for chest X-ray reporting and depends on clinical-knowledge retrieval.

papers.abstract: Large language model agents increasingly operate in long-horizon environments where early mistakes can trigger cascading failures and trap agents in dead-end trajectories. Agents must therefore be able to proactively recover from such states and turn their exploratory experience into guidance for subsequent decisions. We introduce ReTRAIL, a framework that enables agents to rewind the environment to earlier states while preserving valid progress and carrying forward knowledge learned from abandoned exploration. The environment state moves backward while the agent's knowledge continues to move forward. ReTRAIL trains a shared policy with two complementary signals: State-Anchored GRPO compares alternative continuations from revisited states to improve execution, while a branch-advancement reward guides reflection through the progress of subsequent exploration. Experiments across four interactive benchmark MineSweeper, Sokoban, ALFWorld and ScienceWorld show that simply adding a rewind primitive provides limited benefit and can even degrade performance. In contrast, ReTRAIL enables agents to rewind from unproductive states and use insights from abandoned branches to guide subsequent exploration. These results demonstrate the value of coupling environment rewinding with experience reuse within an ongoing task for long-horizon task solving. The code is available at https://github.com/whi497/ReTRAIL.
authors: Ziang Ye, Wentao Shi, Lei Chen, Zhengzhou Cai, Yu Wang, Zhiyuan Yao, Zihan Wang, Xierui Song, Fuli Feng, Yixin Cao
bullets: Long-horizon agents can suffer cascading failures when early mistakes lead to unproductive trajectories.
ReTRAIL rewinds environments to earlier states, preserves valid progress, and carries learned experience forward.
It trains a shared policy using State-Anchored GRPO for comparing alternative continuations and a branch-advancement reward for guiding exploration.
Across MineSweeper, Sokoban, ALFWorld, and ScienceWorld, rewind alone offered limited or harmful benefits, whereas ReTRAIL improved recovery and exploration.
The approach focuses on coupling environment rewind with experience reuse within the same task.

papers.abstract: Multi-robot coordination is essential in applications such as coverage, target tracking, and information gathering, where robots must jointly select actions to maximize team performance. Submodular maximization provides an effective framework for such coordination, and resilient variants further account for robot failures or adversarial removals. However, existing methods typically overlook the impact of robot loss on the communication network, which may disconnect the surviving team and prevent continued coordination. To address this issue, we introduce Resilient $k$-Connected Submodular Maximization, which jointly considers task performance, resilience, and communication connectivity. The resulting feasible family is not a matroid, preventing the direct application of classical curvature-greedy guarantees. We overcome this challenge through a Menger-based connectivity reduction, a connectivity-aware greedy algorithm with a feasibility-preserving fallback, and a new curvature-based analysis that captures the cost of enforcing connectivity through a single factor $\rho$. Our method achieves a worst-case post-failure objective within a factor of $[\max(1-\nu_f(\mathcal{I}),h(N,\beta))]^2 \rho \frac{1}{\kappa_f}(1-e^{-\kappa_f})$ of the optimal connectivity-respecting resilient assignment, while recovering the classical unconstrained guarantee in the appropriate limits. Experiments on multi-robot target tracking validate the proposed method and characterize the practical impact of connectivity constraints.
authors: Yoonjae Hwang, Hojune Kim, Ellen Novoseller, Guangyao Shi, Gaurav S. Sukhatme
bullets: Addresses the risk that robot loss disconnects the surviving communication network, halting coordination.
Introduces Resilient $k$-Connected Submodular Maximization, jointly modeling task performance, failure resilience, and communication connectivity.
Uses a Menger-based connectivity reduction, connectivity-aware greedy selection, and a feasibility-preserving fallback.
Provides curvature-based worst-case guarantees that account for connectivity costs through a factor $\rho$ and recover classical guarantees in limiting cases.
Experiments on multi-robot target tracking evaluate the method and the practical effects of connectivity constraints.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: The core structural conflict in multi-robot deployments. (Left) Aerial teams face adversarial attacks or failures removing up to β nodes. (Middle) Existing frameworks treat requirements in isolation, in which standard resilient maximization risks post-attack fragmentation, while standard connectivity assumes a failure-free environment. (Right) Our framework resolves this by achieving simultaneous adversarial resilience and (β+1)-vertex-connectivity, ensuring the surviving team remains structurally connected and performant.

Fig. 2: Post-attack topology after removing 3 bait robots from an 8-robot team. (a) Resilient Only [8]: unconstrained S2 (resilient set) selection leaves survivors fragmented (κ = 0, 2 components); 36/56 possible 3-robot failures would disconnect them. (b) RES-CON: adding a k-connectivity constraint (k = 4) keeps survivors fully connected (κ = 7), with 0/56 possible failures.

Fig. 3: Realized price of connectivity ρ (solid: median; shaded band: interquartile range) and fallback-firing frequency (dashed) versus communication density, for β = N/4 (left) and β = N/2 (right). The dotted verticals mark the (β+1)-connectivity percolation threshold. Above the threshold ρ is a flat 1.0 and the fallback frequency collapses to zero. Below it, ρ degrades as the fallback activates.

Fig. 4: Margin (realized ratio − squared bound) over the (κf , β) plane, where the non-negativity certifies the squared factor. Every cell is positive, indicating the squared bound holds across the entire swept plane on non-degenerate instances.
Fig. 5: Worst-case-survivor disconnection rate versus communication density (normalized to the percolation threshold).

Fig. 6: Cumulative worst-case tracking below threshold (rc/rmove = 5.2). Resilient-Only accrues the most tracking value by ignoring connectivity, while RES-CON accepts a modest tracking reduction in exchange for roughly halved disconnection

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a resilient multi-robot coordination framework using submodular maximization with $k$-connectivity constraints, offering a technically meaningful optimization approach for multi-agent navigation.
papers.title: Failure-Resilient Multi-Robot Coordination with $k$-Connectivity Constrained Submodular Maximization
papers.tldr: A connectivity-aware submodular optimization framework enables multi-robot teams to remain coordinated and effective despite robot failures or adversarial removals.

papers.abstract: Recurrent-depth language models improve inference-time reasoning by repeatedly applying a shared network to refine internal representations, but the additional recurrent computation also increases inference cost. This overhead is particularly pronounced during long-context prefill, where the full input sequence is repeatedly processed across recurrent depth. Weight-and-activation quantization offers a natural way to accelerate this computation through lower-precision arithmetic, yet repeatedly applying quantized computation introduces numerical perturbations that accumulate along the recurrent trajectory. We systematically analyze how such errors propagate across recurrent depth and show that quantization errors introduced earlier are attenuated by more subsequent recurrent steps and therefore have a smaller effect on the final representation. Matched-budget experiments strongly support this prediction, showing that placing quantized computation earlier in recurrent depth consistently yields the best fidelity. Based on this insight, we introduce RAMP (Recurrent Adaptive Mixed Precision), which performs early recurrent refinement using low-precision weight-and-activation computation and restores high precision for terminal refinement. Across context lengths up to 4K, RAMP preserves near-full-precision prefill quality while achieving up to 1.16x end-to-end first-prefill speedup on an NVIDIA H100, corresponding to a 13.9% latency reduction.
bullets: Quantization errors introduced earlier in recurrent depth are attenuated by later refinement steps.
Matched-budget experiments find that assigning low precision to early recurrent steps gives the best fidelity.
RAMP applies low-precision weight-and-activation computation early, then restores high precision for terminal refinement.
Across contexts up to 4K, RAMP achieves up to 1.16× end-to-end first-prefill speedup on an NVIDIA H100.
The reported evaluation focuses on prefill efficiency and quality preservation at context lengths up to 4K.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of RAMP. RAMP executes the shared recurrent block Fθ using FP8 weight-and-activation computation during early recurrent refinement and restores BF16 computation for the final recurrent steps. The dashed line marks the precision switch, while the recurrent architecture and total recurrent depth remain unchanged.

Figure 3: Quality preservation and end-to-end prefill efficiency of RAMP. (a) WikiText prefill fidelity at 4K context under different precision schedules. RAMP uses 24 FP8 recurrent steps followed by 8 BF16 steps, while Early-BF16 uses the same precision budget in the opposite order. Restoring BF16 computation for terminal refinement substantially reduces the NLL deviation from BF16-32. (b) WikiText fidelity and H100 first-prefill efficiency across context lengths. The green curve reports end-to-end first-prefill speedup over BF16, while the blue curve reports paired WikiText tail-64 ∆NLL relative to BF16-32. RAMP preserves near-BF16 fidelity across context lengths up to 4K while reaching approximately 1.16× first-prefill speedup at long context.

Figure 1: Empirical validation of depth-dependent quantization error propagation. (a) Perturbation survival as a function of injection depth. Both Gaussian perturbations and INT8 quantization-residual perturbations exhibit substantially lower survival when injected earlier in recurrent depth, while perturbations introduced near terminal depth retain a larger fraction of their initial error. Error bars denote the original 95% confidence intervals. (b) Precision-placement comparison under the same budget of 24 FP8 and 8 BF16 recurrent steps. Each point represents one of 20 frozen random precision schedules, with the horizontal axis indicating the mean depth of its BF16 steps and the vertical axis showing final hidden-state relative error. Moving BF16 computation toward later recurrent depth is associated with lower final error. RAMP places all eight BF16 steps at the end and outperforms all 20 random schedules, whereas the reverse (Early-BF16) schedule places all eight BF16 steps at the beginning and produces substantially larger error.

papers.selection_reason: Mixed precision for efficient prefill in recurrent-depth LMs, directly relevant to efficient AI.
papers.title: RAMP: Recurrent Adaptive Mixed Precision for Efficient Prefill in Recurrent-Depth Language Models
papers.tldr: RAMP speeds up long-context prefill in recurrent-depth language models by using low precision early and high precision late, preserving near-full-precision quality with up to 13.9% lower latency.

papers.abstract: Evaluating deep learning optimizer is challenging because confounding factors such as hyperparameter tuning and optimizer-model co-design often obscure true algorithmic performance. We present results of the updated AlgoPerf V1 benchmark, in which we evaluate a new set of training algorithms on wall-clock time-to-target across nine workloads on fixed hardware. This report focuses on the results of the benchmark's self-tuning ruleset, which requires submissions to use a single configuration across all workloads. Out of the 13 submissions in PyTorch and JAX, Schedule-Free AdamW ranked first. In addition to the wall-clock scores, we also analyze the trade-offs between step efficiency and wall-clock execution, revealing that matrix-preconditioned and two-loop methods achieve good sample efficiency but require more aggressive computational optimizations to be competitive in runtime. Finally, our hyperparameter saliency and retention analyses show that the learning rate and momentum are highly sensitive across domains and algorithms, highlighting the need for methods that are more robust against hyperparameter tuning and can generalize well to new tasks.
authors: Priya Kasimbeg (Alice), Ahmed Khaled (Alice), Aahlad Chandrabhatta (Alice), Yifan Wang (Alice), Andy Liu (Alice), Niccol\`o Ajroldi (Alice), David Tweedle (Alice), Xingyu (Alice), Yang, Isaac Patole, Frank Schneider, George E. Dahl
bullets: The benchmark evaluates training algorithms by wall-clock time-to-target across nine workloads on fixed hardware.
Its self-tuning ruleset requires one configuration to be used across all workloads, reducing workload-specific tuning advantages.
Schedule-Free AdamW ranked first among 13 PyTorch and JAX submissions.
Matrix-preconditioned and two-loop methods showed good sample efficiency but needed stronger computational optimization for competitive runtime.
Learning rate and momentum were highly sensitive across domains, motivating more robust, transferable optimizers.

papers.selection_reason: Evaluates training algorithms (optimizers) for efficiency on a new benchmark, highlighting the trade-offs between step efficiency and wall-clock execution. This contributes to the understanding of computational efficiency in deep learning.
papers.title: Towards Easier-to-Tune Training Algorithms: New Results from AlgoPerf
papers.tldr: AlgoPerf V1 finds that Schedule-Free AdamW performs best under a single self-tuning configuration, while hyperparameter robustness remains a key challenge.

papers.abstract: Multi-view representations enable pretrained image and video vision-language models to understand 3D scenes, but their long visual token sequences make inference costly. Redundancy arises both from repeated observations of the same scene regions across views and from processing all visual tokens at every LLM layer, regardless of their relevance to the current computation. We propose GeoGR, a two-stage framework that jointly compresses scene representations and visual computation. At the projector level, GeoSemZip consolidates cross-view observations into 3D voxel tokens and combines semantic saliency with spatial coverage to construct a compact scene representation. Unselected voxel features are aggregated into contextual anchors to retain scene information that would otherwise be discarded. At the LLM level, we identify an effective visual computation window and observe that query-conditioned token relevance remains locally stable but changes over longer layer intervals. Guided by these findings, GroupRoute combines late entry and early exit with recoverable group-wise skipping. Low-relevance tokens bypass complete LLM layers while retaining their hidden states and can rejoin the active group at subsequent anchor layers selected under a computation budget. For compression-aware post-training, we construct a compact dataset of 67K samples by retaining 30% of the original training pool. With this protocol, GeoGR retains 95.2% and 96.8% of the dense post-trained models' performance on LLaVA-OneVision-7B and Video-3D LLM-7B, respectively, while accelerating LLM prefill by $6.8\times$ and $6.1\times$. These results demonstrate the consistent effectiveness of GeoGR across 3D VLMs with and without explicit 3D spatial encoding, highlighting a favorable performance-efficiency trade-off. The code is available at https://github.com/EIT-NLP/GeoGR.
authors: Yongxin Zheng, Hao Wu, Fang Li, Hu Fu, Peiran Yin, Xudong Wang, Haozhe Hu, Xinghao Chen, Yunpu Ma, Wei Zhang, Xiaoyu Shen
bullets: Addresses high inference cost from repeated cross-view observations and processing all visual tokens at every LLM layer.
GeoSemZip builds compact 3D voxel-token representations using semantic saliency and spatial coverage, while retaining discarded information in contextual anchors.
GroupRoute uses late entry, early exit, and recoverable group-wise skipping to adapt visual computation to token relevance.
Using a 67K-sample compression-aware post-training set, GeoGR retains 95.2% and 96.8% of dense-model performance on two 7B 3D VLMs.
It accelerates LLM prefill by 6.8× and 6.1×, demonstrating applicability to models with and without explicit 3D spatial encoding.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of GeoGR. (1) Projector-level Compression: GeoSemZip consolidates crossview observations into 3D voxel tokens using depth and camera poses. Saliency-based selection preserves dominant tokens, while Morton-order sampling selects contextual anchors that aggregate unselected voxel features by cosine similarity. The compressed visual tokens are combined with text tokens to form the LLM input. (2) LLM-level Compression: GroupRoute confines visual computation to an intermediate-layer window through Late Entry and Early Exit. Within this window, Recoverable Group-wise Skipping routes query-conditioned token groups through or around complete LLM layers. Skipped tokens retain their hidden states and can resume computation after regrouping at subsequent anchor layers. Text tokens remain active throughout the LLM.

papers.selection_reason: Compresses 3D visual tokens and skips LLM layers for efficient 3D VLMs, directly relevant to token pruning and multimodal efficiency.
papers.title: GeoGR: Spatial-Semantic Token Compression and Group Routing for Efficient 3D VLMs
papers.tldr: GeoGR makes multi-view 3D vision-language models substantially faster by compressing redundant scene tokens and selectively routing visual tokens through LLM layers while preserving most performance.

papers.abstract: Self-evolving agents are increasingly used to improve language model systems without human intervention through either weight updates or harness improvements. Existing approaches typically pursue these directions separately: some methods update model weights using self-generated experience, while others rewrite the harness that defines how an agent uses prompts, tools, context, and execution feedback. However, these approaches overlook the relationship between model weights and the agent harness. To connect these processes and ensure effective and smooth agent self-evolving, we propose Evo$^2$, a framework for weight-harness co-evolution. For harness updates, we design a unified dual-role pipeline that a single policy serves as both a Proposer, which writes harness edits, and a Reflector, which diagnoses their effects and guides revision. For weight updates, harness modifications and their execution outcomes guide the training of both the Proposer and the Reflector. We further develop EvoTIDE, a training pipeline that recovers usable trajectories through edit extraction and prefix continuation, then combines SFT with interleaved GRPO across the two roles. Extensive experiments across three coding benchmarks demonstrate that Evo$^2$ significantly outperforms existing self-evolution methods. It achieves 82.1% on Polyglot and 48.3% on SWE-bench Verified, compared with 62.6% and 41.0% for the strongest baseline, respectively. We also show that the evolved harnesses transfer to different tasks without further evolution and rank first in cross-benchmark evaluations. Our dual-role harness improvement framework is also able to extend to self-evolution with proprietary models, improving a GPT-5-mini agent's performance from 24.4% to 48.3%. These results demonstrate the applicability of the framework Evo$^2$ across domains and its broad transferability across models and tasks.
authors: Chejian Xu, Shujian Zhang, Wenxuan Zhou, John Lambert, Beck Chen, Bo Li, Andrew Hard, Rajiv Mathews
bullets: Addresses the gap between approaches that separately update model weights or agent harnesses.
Uses a dual-role policy as both a Proposer of harness edits and a Reflector that diagnoses outcomes and guides revisions.
Introduces EvoTIDE, which recovers training trajectories through edit extraction and prefix continuation, combining SFT with interleaved GRPO.
Achieves 82.1% on Polyglot and 48.3% on SWE-bench Verified, exceeding the reported strongest-baseline results of 62.6% and 41.0%.
Evolved harnesses transfer across tasks; the framework also improves a GPT-5-mini agent from 24.4% to 48.3%.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) inherit powerful priors from pretrained video generation models, but their variational autoencoder (VAE) representations are optimized for visual reconstruction rather than manipulation. External visual representations can improve manipulation, but existing methods couple representation choices with different integration mechanisms, obscuring their individual effects. We systematically compare visual representations, five integration mechanisms, and feature combinations under controlled settings. Our study yields three main findings. First, strong general-purpose visual representations provide broader robustness gains and can match or outperform representations pretrained for specific visual capabilities. Second, channel-wise joint prediction achieves the highest average success rate; further analyses suggest that future-feature prediction and the action expert's effective use of added visual information contribute to its gains. Third, additional sources should be selected for the task-relevant information they contribute beyond existing representations, as the same source can help one combination but harm another. However, even the best evaluated composition provides a smaller additional gain than the initial improvement from adding a strong general-purpose representation to the VAE-only baseline. We instantiate the resulting Representation Recipe as R$^2$-WAM. It achieves state-of-the-art performance on RoboCasa GR1 Tabletop with an 84.7% success rate and reaches 92.8% on RoboTwin 2.0, improving over the VAE-only baselines by 5.9 and 2.2 percentage points, respectively. Taken together, these findings suggest that future work should prioritize stronger general-purpose visual representations and more effective mechanisms for integrating them into WAMs, with feature composition serving as a supplementary route to improvement.
authors: Kai Liu, Jiangran Lyu, Tingyu Deng, Yixin Zheng, Jingtian Wan, Wenbo Cui, Mi Yan, Yizhou Zhou, Haoran Li, Dongbin Zhao, Zhizheng Zhang, He Wang
bullets: Compares visual representations, five integration mechanisms, and feature combinations under controlled settings.

Additional representations help only when they add task-relevant information beyond existing features; composition gains are secondary.
R²-WAM reaches 84.7% on RoboCasa GR1 Tabletop and 92.8% on RoboTwin 2.0, improving over VAE-only baselines by 5.9 and 2.2 points.

papers.abstract: Continual learning requires models to accumulate past experience and transfer it to new tasks. Despite substantial research on continual learning, existing work remains largely confined to non-embodied settings, without extending to embodied environments. To address this gap, we introduce EmbodiedCLBench, the first benchmark in embodied simulation for evaluating the continual learning capability of self-evolving agents. With compositional generalization as the core evaluation principle, our benchmark evaluates whether agents can first learn from basic tasks and then recombine the acquired skills to solve complex, unseen advanced tasks. Based on EmbodiedCLBench, we conduct extensive experiments across multiple agent harnesses and learning methods, revealing consistent limitations and distinctive behaviors. Our results show that while advanced tasks can be hardly solved under zero-shot setting, the experience from basic tasks enables consistent improvement. Such benefit from the experience remains stable even if the task complexity increases. However, this improvement does not scale accordingly with the number of learning samples, and current agents cannot extract meaningful information from additional experience. Collectively, our findings highlight continual learning as a fundamental yet underexplored capability, and our benchmark offers valuable resources for designing effective self-evolving agents in embodied environments. Our code and dataset are available at https://pku-value-lab.github.io/EmbodiedCLBench-homepage.
authors: Jie Huang, Yanan Chen, Ruixun Liu, Kaichen He, Xinyi He, Rui Huang, Zilong Zheng, Zhenliang Zhang, Yiwu Zhong
bullets: Evaluates continual learning through compositional generalization: agents learn basic tasks before tackling unseen advanced tasks.
Experiments span multiple agent harnesses and learning methods, revealing consistent limitations and distinct behaviors.
Experience from basic tasks consistently improves performance on advanced tasks, including as task complexity rises.
Agents struggle in zero-shot settings and fail to gain proportional benefits from increasing amounts of experience.
The benchmark supports research on more effective self-evolving embodied agents.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of the construction process of EmbodiedCLBench. During task generation, basic tasks connect a few atomic actions into simple household operations, and advanced tasks combine elements from multiple basic tasks into compositional tasks. For each task, a state-transition graph is built, with each graph node as an intermediate state and paired with action options and a first-person-view image. During evaluation, the agent observes the current state and selects from candidate actions. After each selection, the agent transitions to the next node on the graph.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has become a dominant paradigm for enhancing LLMs' reasoning capabilities. Yet long-horizon autoregressive rollouts introduce a fundamental limitation: local policy mismatch can compound into severe state distribution shift over trajectories. Existing LLM RL methods, such as GRPO and GSPO, control policy mismatch at the token or sequence level, but overlook this trajectory-induced shift, causing training instability and eventual collapse as the horizon grows. To close the state distribution gap, we propose Trajectory-Aware Policy Optimization (TAPO), a principled framework that theoretically derives the state-distribution correction from the off-policy policy gradient and incorporates it into the RL objective. TAPO further employs a geometric-mean estimator for variance reduction, together with a length-aware dynamic clipping that prevents overly deviated updates across the trajectory. Extensive experiments demonstrate that TAPO significantly surpasses existing LLM RL algorithms across eight competition-level benchmarks, achieving up to 48% and 12% improvement over GRPO on mathematical reasoning and algorithmic coding, with substantially enhanced training stability.
authors: Zhicheng Cai, Weinan Dai, Yuyan Zhou, Wei-Ying Ma, Ya-Qin Zhang, Hao Zhou
bullets: Long autoregressive rollouts amplify small policy mismatches into severe state distribution gaps.
Existing methods such as GRPO and GSPO mainly constrain token- or sequence-level mismatch, leaving trajectory-induced shift unaddressed.
TAPO derives a state-distribution correction from the off-policy policy gradient and adds it to the RL objective.
A geometric-mean estimator reduces variance, while length-aware dynamic clipping limits overly large trajectory-level updates.
Across eight competition-level benchmarks, TAPO improves over GRPO by up to 48% on mathematical reasoning and 12% on algorithmic coding, with more stable training.

As response lengths increase, GRPO and GSPO exhibit growing KL divergence and eventual training collapse, while TAPO maintains controlled KL divergence and stable improvement.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning has become the foundational paradigm for enhancing the reasoning capabilities of LLMs. Yet the dominant approach, Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), relies on a geometrically degenerate clipping proxy that cannot adapt its resistance to policy shifts, leading to premature clipping and degraded exploration. Subsequent variants alleviate these issues through fragmented and heuristic modifications. We propose Generalized Proximal Policy Optimization (GPPO), a principled and unified framework for understanding and designing LLM RL algorithms through the lens of divergence. We establish a generalized $f$-divergence trust-region theory with a monotonic performance improvement guarantee, and show that different $f$-divergences induce distinct geometries and policy update dynamics. We further introduce novel estimator topologies that provide more faithful divergence estimates than the conventional single-sample Monte Carlo estimation. Under this framework, PPO and recent variants such as DAPO, DPPO, and RIPO emerge as special cases, establishing a principled two-dimensional design space of {Divergence $\times$ Estimator}. Extensive experiments on eight competition-level math and coding benchmarks show that both dimensions are critical. The best-performing GPPO instantiation surpasses standard GRPO by up to 50% and 14% on math and coding, delivering SOTA performance.
authors: Zhicheng Cai, Xinyuan Guo, Hanlin Wu, Weinan Dai, Yuyan Zhou, Wei-Ying Ma, Ya-Qin Zhang, Hao Zhou
bullets: PPO’s fixed clipping proxy can cause premature clipping, limiting policy adaptation and exploration.
GPPO develops an $f$-divergence trust-region theory with a monotonic performance-improvement guarantee.
It introduces improved estimator topologies for more faithful divergence estimation than single-sample Monte Carlo methods.
PPO, DAPO, DPPO, and RIPO are framed as special cases in a two-dimensional Divergence × Estimator design space.
Experiments across eight competition-level math and coding benchmarks show gains of up to 50% and 14% over standard GRPO, respectively.

papers.selection_reason: Unifies LLM reinforcement learning algorithms through f-divergence theory, with direct implications for LLM reasoning training.
papers.title: Generalized Proximal Policy Optimization: Unifying LLM RL Algorithms from the Perspective of Divergence
papers.tldr: GPPO unifies LLM reinforcement-learning algorithms through generalized divergence-based trust regions and achieves strong gains on math and coding benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Softmax-based multimodal emotion recognition methods often assign high confidence even when sensor data are corrupted or contradictory, for example when facial expressions suggest positive valence while vocal prosody indicates negative arousal. We present an Evidential Multimodal Transformer with Dempster-Shafer Fusion (EMT-DS) that addresses this problem through formal uncertainty quantification. EMT-DS models predictions as Subjective Opinions (Dirichlet distributions), separating epistemic uncertainty (lack of evidence) from aleatoric uncertainty (sensor noise). Modality-specific transformer encoders produce belief mass distributions that are fused with Dempster's Rule of Combination, which normalizes the joint belief mass by a conflict coefficient 1/(1-c), so that contradictory evidence is explicitly quantified as conflict and the fused prediction becomes diffuse rather than being forced into an unjustified consensus. Under subject-independent and speaker-independent evaluation on four benchmarks, EMT-DS achieves 84.3% accuracy on IEMOCAP versus 81.7% for the best baseline (p < 0.01), 82.4% on DEAP under leave-one-subject-out evaluation versus 78.1%, and 96.8% on the highly imbalanced KEMDy20, and it improves accuracy on CMU-MOSEI by 2.4 points over the strongest evidential baseline. In controlled ablation, it reduces Expected Calibration Error from 0.153 (softmax transformer) to 0.042. It maintains 71.2% accuracy under severe Gaussian noise on audio features (sigma = 1.0), where attention baselines drop to 45.3%, and degrades gracefully when entire modalities are absent. The fusion step has O(MK^2) complexity, compared with O(M^2 d^2) for cross-modal attention. The learned conflict metric also flags likely errors: reviewing 20% of samples captures 80% of misclassifications, which supports selective prediction in clinical and safety-critical systems.
bullets: Addresses overconfident predictions caused by corrupted, missing, or contradictory sensor signals.
Uses modality-specific Transformer encoders with Subjective Opinions (Dirichlet distributions) to separate epistemic uncertainty from aleatoric noise.
Fuses belief masses with Dempster’s Rule, quantifying inter-modal conflict and producing more diffuse predictions when evidence disagrees.
Across four benchmarks, reports improved accuracy and calibration, including 84.3% on IEMOCAP and an Expected Calibration Error reduction from 0.153 to 0.042.
Shows robustness to severe audio noise and missing modalities; conflict scores also support selective review of likely errors.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Overall architecture of EMT-DS. Modality-specific encoders (e.g., Wav2Vec2, ViT-B/16, BERT/KoELECTRA, and a physiological 1D-CNN) extract features hm ∈Rd from heterogeneous inputs such as audio, video, text, and physiological signals. Evidential heads generate Subjective Opinions ωm = (bm,um,am) by predicting Dirichlet parameters via softplus-activated layers (Eq. 5), yielding belief masses and uncertainty (Eq. 9). The Dempster-Shafer fusion module iteratively combines opinions (Eqs. 12, 13), computing conflict c to quantify cross-modal disagreement. The fused opinion produces final class probabilities via Eq. 2.

Fig. 2: Confusion matrices for EMT-DS on the three benchmark datasets. Diagonal elements represent correct classification rates. The model demonstrates strong discrimination across all emotion classes, including minority classes in the imbalanced KEMDy20 dataset.

Fig. 3: (Left) Average uncertainty by modality on KEMDy20. Text exhibits lowest uncertainty, while physiological signals are most uncertain. Fusion substantially reduces uncertainty. (Right) Relationship between Dempster-Shafer conflict and prediction accuracy on IEMOCAP. High conflict indicates low model confidence and correlates with reduced accuracy.

Fig. 5: Evidential output layer architecture. Feature representation hm ∈ Rd undergoes linear projection Wmhm + bm followed by softplus activation and an L1 evidence cap to produce the bounded evidence vector em (Eqs. 5–6). Dirichlet parameters αm k = emk + 1 define concentration and strength Sm = ∑ k α m k (Eq. 8). Subjective Opinion components are derived as bmk = emk /S m, um = K/Sm, and amk = 1/K (Eq. 9), satisfying ∑ k b m k + um = 1.

Fig. 4: Sensitivity analysis of key hyperparameters on IEMOCAP. (a) KL annealing coefficient λt peaks at 0.8. (b) Conflict regularization λc optimal at 0.10. (c) Learning rate plateau between 1×10−4 and 5×10−4.

Fig. 7: Error detection under selective review (horizontal axis: percentage of data reviewed; vertical axis: percentage of total errors detected). Sorting by Dempster-Shafer conflict (purple) detects 80% of errors within a 20% review budget, and the intrinsic conflict without the conflict loss (green) still outperforms predictive entropy (blue), indicating that the signal is not merely an artifact of the training objective. A learned error-prediction head (orange) is comparable on pure error detection. Operating points are fit on a disjoint calibration split.
Fig. 6: Reliability diagram comparing EMT-DS (green) and standard Softmax (red). EMT-DS is well-calibrated (ECE=0.042), while Softmax is overconfident (ECE=0.153).

Fig. 2: Scalability analysis: (left) training time per epoch in seconds and (right) inference throughput in samples per second, as a function of the number of modalities. EMT-DS exhibits linear scaling.

papers.abstract: In repeated human-AI interaction, a single observation can be quoted, summarized, and returned to a model as multiple reports, making repetition look like independent corroboration. We study whether language models can use supplied report lineage to update according to evidence provenance rather than report count. We introduce Latent Quotient Evidence Training (LQET), a relational objective that combines sparse Bayesian supervision with constraints that encourage stable predictions when reports add no new evidence and consistent updates to the same new evidence across relay histories. On a controlled binary benchmark, LQET reduces new-evidence update RMSE by 41-44% and log-odds drift after eight relay steps by 89-91% relative to task-only training across Qwen3-4B and Phi-4-mini, with three paired training seeds per backbone. The gains extend to a closed-loop simulation in which model confidence controls how many relayed reports re-enter the model's context in later rounds. By grounding belief updates in supplied provenance, LQET offers a route toward dynamic human-AI systems in which influence follows new evidence, not the number of times the same evidence returns.
authors: Tianyi Huang, Eric Liu, Jay Chong, Emily Yin, Wanqi Zhao
bullets: Addresses repetition bias in human-AI feedback loops, where one observation may appear as multiple corroborating reports.
Uses report lineage with sparse Bayesian supervision and relational consistency constraints.
Encourages stable predictions when relays add no evidence and consistent updates across different relay histories.
On a controlled binary benchmark, LQET reduced new-evidence update RMSE by 41–44% and eight-step log-odds drift by 89–91% versus task-only training.
Benefits also extended to a closed-loop simulation where model confidence controls future report relaying.

papers.abstract: Learning-based methods have demonstrated strong performance in mapless robot navigation. However, a learned policy remains restricted to the embodiment on which it was trained. Many cross-embodiment navigation methods require time-consuming online training and can still underperform target-specific policies. In fact, demonstrations collected on a source embodiment already contain navigation experience that is potentially reusable for deriving a policy for each target embodiment, but the embodiment mismatch prevents these demonstrations from directly serving as valid supervision for the target. In this article, we present CeDR-Nav, a cross-embodiment demonstration recasting framework that trains a dedicated navigation policy for each target embodiment from existing source demonstrations without online data collection. Geometry-consistent scaling with per-demonstration validity assessment converts the source demonstrations into target training data, and a target-specific Gaussian mixture policy generates feasible avoidance maneuvers for each target embodiment. Extensive quantitative simulations and real-world deployments across multiple robot platforms demonstrate the effectiveness of CeDR-Nav, with an average success-rate gain of 13.8 percentage points over DRL-DCLP in cross-embodiment simulations and target-specific policy training completed within seconds.
authors: Xianghui Wang, Xinming Zhang, Yiwei Qian, Siwei Cheng, Shanze Wang, Dan Zhang, Wei Zhang
bullets: Addresses the embodiment mismatch that makes source-robot demonstrations invalid for target-robot supervision.
Uses geometry-consistent scaling and per-demonstration validity checks to recast source data for each target embodiment.
Trains a target-specific Gaussian mixture policy to produce feasible collision-avoidance maneuvers.
Validated in simulations and real-world deployments across multiple robot platforms.
Reports a 13.8-percentage-point average success-rate gain over DRL-DCLP in cross-embodiment simulations, with training completed within seconds.

papers.abstract: Empowerment measures the capacity of an agent to actively control its environment. In this work, we explain the connection between skill learning and empowerment. While skill learning is not empowerment, we introduce a simple scalable recipe for empowerment maximization: empowerment corresponds to the number of executable skills from a state, so maximizing empowerment corresponds to reaching states that are good starting points for many skills. Our recipe applies to arbitrary underlying skill learning methods. Whereas most prior work on empowerment looks at tabular settings, this recipe enables us to study empowerment at a scale where we can realize theoretically-predicted but empirically-elusive properties of empowerment (e.g., gathering resources, environment modification, survival). Experiments show that empowerment maximization unlocks interesting emergent properties, such as building a house in Crafter. Website and code at \href{https://empowerment-geometry.github.io/scaling-empowerment/}{this https url}.
authors: Catherine Ji, Vivek Myers, Joshua Lin, Alexandra Wingate, Sergey Levine, Benjamin Eysenbach
bullets: Connects empowerment with skill learning while distinguishing the two concepts.
Defines empowerment operationally as the number of executable skills available from a state.
Proposes a simple recipe that works with arbitrary underlying skill-learning methods.
Scales empowerment studies beyond tabular environments to realize theoretically predicted behaviors.
Demonstrates emergent behaviors, including house building in Crafter.

papers.title: Scaling Empowered Agents
papers.tldr: A scalable approach to empowerment maximization guides agents toward states from which they can execute many diverse skills, producing emergent behaviors such as resource gathering, environment modification, survival, and house building.

papers.abstract: Language-model agents are used for specialized work such as financial research, healthcare and law. Such agents are often capable enough for a task but still miss its details. In finance, for example, these details include which filing reports a figure or how a company discloses a metric. Retraining the agent to learn these details is expensive, and often impossible when the agent is a closed or shared system. Writing the missing know-how into the agent's prompt makes the prompt long and identical for every input, although different inputs need different guidance. We propose to learn to generate this guidance instead. A small advisor model reads each input and writes structured advice, which is appended to the prompt of a frozen executor. The advisor is trained with hindsight, following work on distillation with privileged information. On a training pool with graded answers, we analyse the executor's failures, run it under several strategies to see which one worked on each input, and let a teacher that sees the grades and the traces write the advice that would have helped. The advisor then learns, by supervised fine-tuning, to write that advice from the input alone. Because the student is a separate small model rather than the executor, it is cheap to train and adds little latency. We call this approach hindsight structured advice distillation (HSAD). On FrontierFinance, a public benchmark of expert-written financial research queries, an 8B advisor raises the qualification rate of Samaya's proprietary research agent, which already leads the benchmark's leaderboard, from 52.9% to 56.6%. This is above the agent's own high-effort configuration, at 37% lower cost per query. We study the generalization of the proposed approach, and in particular show that HSAD also improves results on WebShop, BIRD text-to-SQL and ExpertLongBench.
bullets: Targets specialized tasks where agents miss domain-specific details and full retraining is costly or impossible.
A teacher analyzes graded answers, executor traces, and strategy outcomes to create helpful structured advice.
A separate advisor learns to generate this advice from the input alone, then appends it to the frozen executor’s prompt.
On FrontierFinance, an 8B advisor raises qualification from 52.9% to 56.6% and exceeds the executor’s high-effort setting at 37% lower query cost.
The approach also improves results on WebShop, BIRD text-to-SQL, and ExpertLongBench.

papers.abstract: Learning from Demonstrations (LfD) enables robots to learn object manipulation directly from human demonstrations. In contrast to resource-intensive and labor-intensive teleoperation, egocentric demonstrations are easy to collect, enabling scalable data collection. Manipulated objects are often partially occluded in everyday environments, yet prior egocentric demonstration-based methods that require no robots or specialized teaching devices do not explicitly address occlusions. To fill this gap, we propose EgoReveal, a framework that learns viewpoint-repositioning together with manipulation actions from egocentric human demonstrations to reposition the viewpoint and obtain target visibility under partial occlusions. EgoReveal instantiates this as two imitation policies: one predicts the future camera-arm pose sequence from the current view and camera-arm pose, and the other predicts the future control commands from object keypoints and a history of control commands. EgoReveal switches between the two based on target visibility. In experiments where the manipulated object is partially occluded initially, EgoReveal repositions the camera to obtain visibility and completes the task more reliably than fixed-camera baselines.

bullets: Addresses partial object occlusions, which prior robot-free egocentric demonstration methods do not explicitly handle.
Uses two imitation policies: one predicts camera-arm repositioning, and the other predicts manipulation controls.

Experiments show more reliable task completion than fixed-camera baselines when objects are initially occluded.

papers.abstract: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) remains a widely used approach for post-training large language models, because fixed demonstrations can directly introduce desired reasoning strategies and behavioral patterns. Yet forcing a model to imitate externally provided trajectories may also interfere with behaviors already supported by pretraining, limiting generalization beyond the training distribution. Recent dynamic SFT methods mitigate this issue by reweighting token-level supervision according to model-side signals such as predictive probability, prior support, or distributional compatibility. However, model compatibility is not equivalent to learning value: a token that is weakly supported by the current model may either be an undesirable mismatch or precisely the task-specific decision that the demonstration is intended to teach. We propose CIG-SFT, an information-theoretic framework that estimates the task-conditioned information carried by each demonstrated token. Under teacher forcing, we compare the token likelihood from a frozen reference model with and without access to the task input while keeping the gold solution prefix fixed. The resulting conditional information gain quantifies how much the task itself reduces uncertainty about the demonstrated decision. We then convert this information into a KL-regularized projection of the current policy and derive an equivalent scalar-weighted SFT objective whose logit gradient exactly matches that of the projected target. Across mathematical reasoning and code-generation benchmarks, CIG-SFT consistently outperforms standard SFT and recent adaptive fine-tuning baselines, with particularly strong improvements in generalization to challenging evaluation distributions, while requiring neither additional training data nor online rollouts.
authors: Yuxuan Gu, Kequan Niu, Xiaocheng Feng, Yun Li, Yiqiao Yang, Bing Qin
bullets: SFT can over-imitate demonstrations and disrupt useful behaviors learned during pretraining.
CIG-SFT estimates each token’s task-conditioned information gain using a frozen reference model with and without task input, while fixing the gold prefix.
These information scores define a KL-regularized target and an equivalent scalar-weighted SFT objective.
Across math reasoning and code generation benchmarks, it outperforms standard SFT and adaptive fine-tuning baselines, especially on challenging distributions.
The method does not require additional training data or online rollouts.

papers.abstract: Visual interventions provide a training-free way to reduce hallucinations in multimodal large language models. However, an intervention may have little leverage at some layers and may damage a correct answer even when it changes the output. We investigate where visual interventions retain leverage and when they improve predictions. First, we apply the same visual-residual edit at successive decoder layers, matching its RMS strength across depth. Across six checkpoints from three model families, we observe a persistent drop in intervention effect and define its operational onset for this edit as the \textbf{Evidence Anchoring Boundary (EAB)}. With boundaries fixed on calibration queries, held-out effects on disjoint evaluation queries before EAB are $13.78\times$--$26.10\times$ larger than those after it. Comparison with intermediate readouts shows that the edit can lose leverage before answer preferences stabilize. Second, we compare counterfactual subtraction across presence, attribute, and relation questions. Subtraction can correct a misleading preference, leave a decision unchanged, or remove a preference supporting the correct answer. Based on these observations, we develop calibrated selective routing, which preserves the original prediction unless calibration supports an intervention for the question type. It improves full-set attribute accuracy by $1.56$--$1.81$ percentage points across three checkpoints, while universal subtraction is neutral or harmful.

papers.abstract: Accurate daily precipitation forecasts are important for weather-sensitive decisions. Although recent Weather Foundation Models (WFMs) have achieved significant progress, they are trained on reanalysis data, which exhibit regional and intensity-dependent biases. Since retraining WFMs on observation-based targets is costly, we study Dynamics-Precipitation Decoupling, a plug-and-play framework that uses a separately trained generator to map non-precipitation forecasts from a frozen weather model to observation-aligned daily precipitation. Its key challenges are to capture heterogeneous rainfall distributions and align daily accumulations with atmospheric signals that evolve across space and time. To address them, we train a diffusion generator conditional on atmospheric states and satellite-gauge estimates of precipitation. A multi-scale recurrent encoder summarizes atmospheric evolution, while cross-attention aligns atmospheric and precipitation features during denoising. Extensive evaluation of various backbones, including Pangu-Weather, GraphCast, and HRES, on global and regional forecasting shows improved daily precipitation accuracy and event detection, with better representation of localized accumulation patterns. Global ensemble evaluation shows lower Brier scores than ENS and training-from-scratch GenCast at all reported lead times, with lower CRPS in most comparisons. Remarkably, a heavy-rainfall case study using 2,288 stations in China further supports improved daily accumulation patterns and event detection against ground observations.

papers.abstract: Video editing models achieve strong performance in modifying appearance, backgrounds, styles, and motions, empowered by large-scale training data. Beyond general scenarios, professional motions are significant in performance, sports, and martial arts. This paper focuses on professional motion editing, which involves fine-grained motion technique and temporal structure. Given professional motion names but lacking detailed descriptions, existing models often fail to generate professional motions, such as incorrectly lifting the front wheel under a Stoppie instruction. To address this challenge, we introduce MotionCoach, a trained multimodal agent that uses multi-turn tools and performs self-verification, producing a grounded prompt and a reference clip as reliable and sufficient multimodal guidance to inject external professional motion knowledge into video editing models. To supply training data, we build a data pipeline to construct trajectories. We cold-start the agent on MotionCoach-SFT-10k and apply Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) on MotionCoach-RL-2k with rewards on the motion guidance prompt, the motion outcome video, and the format. For evaluation, we introduce VPMEBench, comprising 314 professional motion editing tasks with fine-grained references and annotations. Extensive experiments show that MotionCoach improves the overall score from 55.1 to 65.6 on Seedance 2.0 and from 51.2 to 64.5 on MiniMax-H3. Learning to construct multimodal guidance enables precise professional motion editing without retraining video editing models.

papers.abstract: We introduce MVGraph, a benchmark for evaluating large vision-language models (LVLMs) on multi-graph reasoning where the evidence required by a query is distributed across multiple interrelated visual graph views. Although such evidence commonly resides in source-specific graphs, temporal snapshots, or local observations, existing graph reasoning benchmarks remain confined to a single self-contained structure, assessing only graph perception and reasoning while leaving the alignment and composition of evidence across views underexplored. MVGraph comprises 8k instances spanning 8 \textit{graph-theoretic} tasks, abstracted from two multi-graph scenarios (partial and temporal graph views). Each problem is programmatically constructed and verified to be unsolvable from a single view. Beyond end-to-end evaluation, we decompose multi-graph reasoning into four complementary capabilities---Perception, Alignment, Composition, and Reasoning---and design 29 diagnostic tasks with 64k instances to probe each one, along with golden intermediate representations for evaluating the intermediate process. Across 15 LVLMs, we reveal the difficulty of multi-graph reasoning and identify cross-view edge alignment and relation-level composition as prominent bottlenecks through stage-oriented diagnostics. Meanwhile, temporal constraints and increasing view counts expose further capability boundaries. Code and data are available at https://github.com/AAAndy-Zhu/MVGraph.

Evaluates 15 LVLMs and identifies cross-view edge alignment and relation-level composition as key bottlenecks.
Temporal constraints and more numerous views further expose capability limits.

papers.abstract: Embodied agents must translate multimodal observations and user requests into executable actions while adapting to product constraints, changing goals, and execution feedback. We present JoyInside-VLM-Agent, a ReAct-style multimodal agent developed through product-conditioned trajectory construction and staged policy learning for robotic platforms and smart hardware. A closed-loop sandbox generates multimodal interaction trajectories covering goal revisions and failure recovery, which are checked against execution outcomes and semantic criteria. Supervised fine-tuning and multi-teacher on-policy distillation precede reinforcement learning with DPER (Dual-Source Privileged On-Policy Self-Distillation with Token-Level Evidence Routing). DPER routes token-level evidence between a frozen privileged teacher and a privileged student sharing the rollout policy's parameters, modulating reward-derived token advantages while preserving their signs. Training rewards combine generative process evaluation, multi-judge rankings, and task-queue consistency. JoyInside-VLM-Agent achieves a BFCL v4 overall score of 77.44, exceeding the evaluated baselines; results on the other public benchmarks are mixed. On JoyInside-Devices and JoyInside-Robotics, the evaluated system, which includes domain-specific skill refinement, leads the baselines on all reported metrics. Two real-world quadruped case studies illustrate visually grounded search, replanning after execution failure, and explicit failure reporting.

Combines generative process evaluation, multi-judge rankings, and task-queue consistency for training rewards.

Scores 77.44 on BFCL v4 and leads reported metrics on JoyInside-Devices and JoyInside-Robotics, while results on other public benchmarks are mixed; quadruped case studies demonstrate search, replanning, and failure reporting.

papers.abstract: This paper introduces MathVis, a benchmark designed to evaluate LLMs' ability to visualize frontier mathematical problems and perform diagram-assisted reasoning. The benchmark consists of 512 tasks, each comprising a mathematical statement, a reference diagram, executable TikZ or SVG code, a Gold Intermediate Representation (IR), atomic rubrics, and error codes. Through rigorous evaluation, GPT-6-Astra, Claude Fable 5, and Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview achieve pass@1 scores of 31.25%, 26.56%, and 22.85%, respectively. We found that although the tasks require visualization, LLMs produce outputs dominated by formal languages, symbols, and graphics programs, rather than explicit diagram-mediated reasoning. Furthermore, while the solutions generated by LLMs may contain all the necessary elements, they are often visually confusing to humans. Ultimately, this benchmark aims to visualize mathematical problems and promote research on enabling LLMs to simplify their reasoning via visual diagrams.

papers.abstract: Decoder hidden states from different layers of large language models (LLMs) often encode complementary information. However, existing speculative decoding methods typically rely on a small set of target-model layers chosen using fixed, position-based heuristics. Selecting an optimal subset of layers is inherently a combinatorial problem, making exhaustive evaluation infeasible even for moderately deep models. In this work, we present a principled framework for multi-layer hidden-state selection for speculative decoding based on two complementary criteria: informativeness, measured through matrix-entropy analysis, and diversity, quantified using centered kernel alignment (CKA). We investigate layer-wise Shannon entropy, aggregate entropy under hidden-state concatenation, and pairwise CKA dynamics across depth, revealing distinct geometric and informational compartments within decoder representations. Motivated by these findings, we propose entropy and CKA-based layer selection algorithms that favor hidden-state sets that are both highly informative and minimally redundant. As part of this framework, we introduce token-entropy filtering, which removes hidden states associated with low predictive-entropy tokens, thereby improving the quality of layer-selection statistics. In EAGLE3-style speculative decoding, our selected sets outperform fixed baseline choices, including the default $[2, N//2, N-3]$ rule, while providing a clearer explanation of why some defaults can remain competitive. Our results provide a practical recipe for multi-layer hidden-state selection for speculative decoding, insights into the geometry and information in LLM decoder states, and a foundation for extending similar analysis to related applications.
authors: Raghavv Goel, Sudhanshu Agrawal, Mukul Gagrani, Risheek Garrepalli, Mingu Lee
bullets: Existing methods often use fixed, position-based layer subsets, while optimal selection is combinatorial and costly to evaluate exhaustively.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models provide a unified framework for visual understanding, language grounding, and robot control, yet anticipating how the scene will evolve beyond the current observation can provide additional information for control. Action supervision alone does not explicitly encourage such anticipation, while future-image prediction entangles task-relevant motion with largely static appearance. To address these limitations, we introduce Evo-World, a lightweight VLA model that augments policy learning with future motion prediction through optical-flow supervision, thereby providing a task-relevant predictive signal focused on motion rather than appearance. We further design the training procedure to preserve these predictive representations during policy learning, regulating representation diversity while decoupling representation learning from action optimization. Across simulation benchmarks, Evo-World demonstrates strong performance, achieving a tier-averaged success rate of 91.1% on Meta-World MT50 , with a 13.0% relative improvement over the non-predictive baseline. On real-world AgileX robots, Evo-World outperforms the evaluated baselines across single-arm and bimanual manipulation tasks while using only 0.87B parameters and delivering lower GPU memory usage and higher inference efficiency. These results demonstrate that future motion prediction through optical-flow supervision provides an effective and lightweight approach to enhancing the predictive capabilities of VLA models.
authors: Zile Zhong, Yuxin Du, Tao Lin, Haoxiao Wang, Wei Dai, Binhua Zuo, Bo Zhao

Achieves a 91.1% tier-averaged success rate on Meta-World MT50, a 13.0% relative gain over a non-predictive baseline.
Shows stronger performance than evaluated baselines on real-world single-arm and bimanual AgileX tasks with 0.87B parameters, lower GPU memory use, and higher inference efficiency.
