papers.abstract: Large language models have achieved remarkable advances in complex reasoning. However, scaling reasoning post-training with ever-larger corpora can substantially increase training cost without proportional performance gains. In this study, we therefore ask: how far can reasoning supervision be compressed without sacrificing capability? To this end, we propose an uncertainty-guided progressive contraction framework that concentrates supervision and optimization on the reasoning trajectories most valuable for learning. Specifically, rather than treating a teacher-generated chain-of-thought (CoT) as a single realized path, we construct uncertainty-profiled reasoning supervision by building Monte Carlo reasoning trees around intermediate reasoning states to expose process-level uncertainty. This uncertainty first contracts the original corpus into a compact teacher-informed pool. A second, learner-aware contraction then performs online routing during SFT, concentrating optimization according to the student's evolving learning state. Together, the two stages progressively contract both supervision and optimization, substantially reducing the student training budget. Experiments across diverse reasoning benchmarks and LLM families show that our method uses as little as 0.22% of the optimization budget of full-data SFT, over 450x less training exposure, while maintaining or improving reasoning performance. Notably, our framework generalizes well across heterogeneous student families, black-box teachers, and weak-to-strong transfer. This indicates that it is not only a way to accelerate training but can also enhance reasoning capability.
authors: Suorong Yang, Jiaxin Wang, Jiaming Su, Chentao Yue, Furao Shen, Peng Ye, Soujanya Poria
bullets: Targets the high cost and diminishing returns of scaling reasoning post-training data.
Builds Monte Carlo reasoning trees to estimate process-level uncertainty around teacher-generated chains of thought.
Progressively contracts training in two stages: teacher-informed data selection, then learner-aware online routing during SFT.
Uses as little as 0.22% of the full-data SFT optimization budget—over 450× less training exposure—while maintaining or improving performance.
Works across diverse benchmarks, LLM families, black-box teachers, and weak-to-strong transfer.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) excel across diverse tasks, benefiting from knowledge priors, in-context reasoning, and test-time computation. Despite these strengths, single-model reasoning remains vulnerable to error propagation, as later steps depend on the model's earlier outputs, leaving reasoning blind spots difficult to independently reassess. To address this limitation, we develop \textit{collaborative learning}, encompassing the construction of heterogeneous collaborators and the learning of effective cross-model collaboration. Specifically, \textit{model slicing} replaces a large model with smaller, heterogeneous models under a comparable parameter budget, enabling prior reasoning to be reassessed across distinct model parameterizations. \textit{Pyramid supervision} combines protocol distillation with step-level supervision to refine reasoning and interaction decisions throughout collaboration. We evaluate our approach across four task categories: multi-hop question answering, mathematical reasoning, code generation, and open-ended constrained generation. The trained heterogeneous models achieve comparable or better task performance than the original large model and established multi-agent baselines, including reinforcement-learning-based methods, while also achieving higher inference efficiency than the multi-agent baselines and exhibiting differentiated collaboration patterns across tasks. These findings show that learned collaboration turns model heterogeneity into complementary reasoning capabilities.
authors: Yuheng Wang, Runde Yang, Zhuohan Bao, Qiran Zhang, Huatao Li, Yiyang Zheng, Lin Wu, Jingru Fan, Shu Yao, Yihan Li, Zhi Li, Chen Qian
bullets: Targets error propagation and blind spots in single-model reasoning.
Uses model slicing to create heterogeneous collaborators within a comparable parameter budget.

Reports comparable or better performance than the original large model and established multi-agent methods, with higher inference efficiency than those baselines.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have shown strong promise in robotic manipulation, yet their post-training still predominantly relies on trajectory-level supervised imitation over robot demonstrations. While effective for learning feasible actions, this paradigm supervises policies to reproduce expert actions at each step, biasing them toward demonstration-specific action paths and providing limited guidance for recovering toward task-progress states once execution deviates from demonstrated trajectories. To address this limitation, we propose OGPO, an Offline Goal-conditioned Policy Optimization framework for recoverable VLA post-training. Instead of treating offline demonstrations merely as step-wise action labels, OGPO adaptively relabels trajectories with semantic key states and constructs goal-conditioned process rewards to optimize the policy for reaching these task-progress states. In this way, OGPO shifts VLA post-training from trajectory-level action imitation to key-state reachability learning, enabling policies to acquire a more robust ability to complete goal states from feasible off-demonstration states without requiring additional online interaction. Experiments on LIBERO and MetaWorld show that OGPO consistently improves VLA policy performance over standard supervised fine-tuning. Moreover, evaluations on LIBERO-Plus and our proposed LIBERO-ReAct, a mid-execution perturbation benchmark, further demonstrate that OGPO achieves stronger robustness and goal-directed recoverability under distribution shifts and recoverable off-demonstration states.
authors: Xule Gao, Xi Wang, Zehua Zang, Rui Wang, Changwen Zheng, Chuxiong Sun
bullets: Problem: Step-wise imitation can overfit to demonstration paths and offers limited guidance after execution deviates from them.
Method: Relabels offline trajectories with semantic key states and uses goal-conditioned process rewards to optimize key-state reachability.
Contribution: Shifts VLA post-training from trajectory imitation toward recoverable, goal-directed behavior from feasible off-demonstration states.
Results: Improves performance over standard supervised fine-tuning on LIBERO and MetaWorld, with stronger robustness under shifts and perturbations on LIBERO-Plus and LIBERO-ReAct.

papers.abstract: Federated Direct Preference Optimization (FedDPO) enables privacy-preserving alignment of language models across distributed agents without centralizing sensitive preference data. However, existing FedDPO analysis assumes all clients converge to a single shared policy, which is fundamentally at odds with the heterogeneous preference distributions present in practice. We propose Personalized FedDPO (pFedDPO), in which each client maintains a small private LoRA adapter atop a shared global base model. In pFedDPO, the base model is synchronized via FedAvg each round, while LoRA adapters remain local and capture client-specific preference patterns. We prove that this decomposition replaces the gradient diversity $\kappa^2$ in the FedDPO bound with a residual heterogeneity $\kappa^2_{\mathrm{eff}}$, which is no larger than $\kappa^2$ when adapters absorb client-specific directions, at the cost of an additive adapter-bias term that vanishes as adapters converge. Experiments on preference datasets show that pFedDPO consistently attains a lower gradient norm than vanilla FedDPO while remaining competitive in training loss and per-client reward accuracy.
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between single-policy FedDPO and heterogeneous client preferences.
Synchronizes a shared base model with FedAvg while keeping small client-specific LoRA adapters private.
Theoretical analysis replaces gradient diversity with lower residual heterogeneity, plus an adapter-bias term that vanishes as adapters converge.
Experiments report lower gradient norms than vanilla FedDPO while remaining competitive in training loss and per-client reward accuracy.

Only the base model updates ∆θi are uploaded to the server for FedAvg aggregation, while adapters and data remain local. This design is intended to reduce effective gradient diversity (κ2 eff ≤ κ2 under the conditions in the Appendix) and enables personalization without additional communication overhead.

papers.abstract: Understanding and manipulating spatial relations is fundamental to AI systems that reason about physical environments and construct grounded world models. However, existing evaluations of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) for spatial reasoning rely predominantly on static question-answering (QA) over small-scale or synthetic scenes, rarely probing whether models can modify spatial configurations while satisfying explicit geometric constraints. We introduce GeoSpatialBench, a benchmark designed to evaluate an escalating progression of spatial cognition, ranging from spatial relation understanding and geometric reasoning to constrained spatial editing. Grounded in real-world urban data across six geographically diverse cities, GeoSpatialBench evaluates a comprehensive taxonomy of 28 topological, directional, metric, and ordering relations across structured GeoJSON and map image modalities, with ground-truth references and constraints verified via GIS operations. Our empirical evaluation across frontier MLLMs uncovers a stark spatial gap: structured GeoJSON consistently outperforms map images, with multimodal combinations offering no reliable gain over GeoJSON alone, and while models show reasonable competence on qualitative topological and ordering, performance drops on quantitative metric relations. Crucially, editing performance on ordering relations declines relative to QA, and most failed edits violate at least one specified spatial constraint. These results highlight a gap between passively recognizing spatial relations and actively manipulating geometric configurations. GeoSpatialBench provides an open, rigorous diagnostic testbed to benchmark these spatial limitations, laying essential empirical groundwork for physically grounded world models and embodied spatial AI.
authors: Zheng Ren, Yanning Wang, Ziheng Huang, Fei Huang, Shiqi Wang, Ziqian Ye, Yang Yue

papers.abstract: Diffusion language models generate tokens in parallel, but still require multiple sampling steps to produce high-quality text. In this paper, we investigate whether a model can learn to generate an entire sequence in a single forward pass. We propose Seq-Drifting, a framework that applies drifting to sequences of continuous token representations and directly learns a map from Gaussian noise to text. Unlike existing DLMs that derive the supervision at each position directly from the observed token in a training sequence, Seq-Drifting builds a drift field whose position-wise targets adapt to the current generated context. At each position, attraction guides each output toward a set of contextually plausible token representations, while repulsion discourages collapse across samples and repetition within sequences. The generator learns from this drift field during training and produces all tokens jointly in one pass at inference. Empirically, Seq-Drifting achieves a generative perplexity of 36.01 on LM1B in one step and performs competitively in both unconditional and conditional generation. Experiments on translation, summarization, and reasoning further demonstrate the applicability of the framework beyond open-ended generation. These results suggest that drifting over token sequences offers a promising path toward effective one-step text generation. Our code is available at https://github.com/jyliu-ai/Seq-Drifting.
authors: Jiayu Liu, Ruizhi Zhao, Tianyun Ji, Yee Whye Teh, Zhenya Huang, Ning Miao

papers.abstract: Agile and reliable navigation is a core capability for embodied robots navigating complex spatial constraints and dynamic interactions. However, a single policy often struggles to accommodate the distinct decision-making demands of diverse scenarios. We present TAME-Nav, an asymmetric Teacher-Student navigation framework built around a temporal soft mixture of experts (Soft-MoE). The Teacher combines clean observations with causally maintained dynamic-obstacle tracks to construct privileged representations, while the Student learns complementary navigation features from corrupted observation histories through temporal encoding, soft expert routing, and latent distillation. Procedural scenario generation and parallel task-level simulation broaden training coverage, while deployment-informed asymmetric domain randomization supports sim-to-real transfer. Across in-distribution and unseen compositional scenarios, TAME-Nav achieves higher success rates, lower collision rates, and higher navigation scores than representative baselines. On a real quadruped robot, it completes all twenty trials across local-trap escape and narrow-passage navigation with sudden dynamic obstacles, with only one minor contact.

Procedural scenario generation, parallel simulation, and deployment-informed domain randomization support broad training and sim-to-real transfer.
Outperforms representative baselines in success, collision, and navigation scores; a real quadruped completed 20 trials with one minor contact.

papers.abstract: Long-term memory has been widely adopted in LLM-based agents to support persistent interaction and personalized assistance. Long-term multi-party interactions, however, accumulate substantially more detailed information, with decisions repeatedly updated and states evolving across participants and interaction stages. Temporal structure is therefore crucial for tracing such memories: relevant information often appears densely within short intervals, while transitions among different states are anchored by a strict temporal order. Existing temporally aware memory frameworks primarily store time as metadata or use temporal signals to guide retrieval over preconstructed memory structures, without using temporal structure to both recover locally concentrated evidence and reconstruct its complete event progression. To address these limitations, we propose T-Mem, a temporal-structure-based memory framework that preserves interactions and organizes query-relevant evidence through two temporal mechanisms. Temporal Evidence Discovery exploits the local concentration of related messages to recover overlooked evidence, while Temporal Memory Structuring models state transitions and supporting relations over time and compresses low-information spans within the resulting forest. Evidence Forest Linearization then serializes the structured evidence for answer generation. Experiments on two long-term multi-party memory benchmarks demonstrate that T-Mem consistently outperforms competitive memory frameworks across LLMs, parameter settings, domains, and query types.
authors: Junyou Guo, Chongyang Tao, Yan He, Yong Wang, Shuai Ma
bullets: Addresses the challenge of tracking evolving decisions and participant states in detailed, long-term multi-party interactions.
Uses Temporal Evidence Discovery to recover relevant messages concentrated within short time intervals.
Builds a temporal evidence forest that models state transitions and supporting relations while compressing low-information spans.
Linearizes the structured evidence into a format suitable for answer generation.
Outperforms competing memory frameworks across two benchmarks, multiple LLMs, domains, settings, and query types.

papers.abstract: Existing sequence models share a critical limitation: they lack an explicit, interpretable mechanism for content-aware temporal recall. LSTMs compress everything into a single hidden state, thereby losing information about specific past events. Transformers attend to all tokens indiscriminately at quadratic cost, while state-space models like Mamba compress history into a fixed-dimensional state without explicit content-addressable memory. To address this gap, we introduce a novel framework grounded in nonlinear time-delay systems, in which the effective delay is dynamically estimated based on the semantic similarity between current and historical inputs. Our approach features three key innovations: (i) a differentiable semantic lag estimator that computes content-aware soft attention weights over history, producing a weighted historical context and similarity score; (ii) a diagonal state space with closed-form cumulative sum solution, achieving O(1) per-step complexity with no sequential loops; and (iii) an interpretable fuzzy semantic modulation mechanism that learns context-dependent rules for balancing instantaneous processing versus historical recall, where rule centers correspond to prototypical semantic contexts. Experimental results on text classification and generation outperform state-of-the-art methods.
bullets: Addresses the lack of explicit, content-aware temporal recall in LSTMs, Transformers, and state-space models.
Uses a differentiable semantic lag estimator to assign soft attention weights over historical inputs.
Employs a diagonal state space with a closed-form cumulative-sum solution for O(1) per-step computation without sequential loops.
Adds fuzzy semantic modulation to balance current-input processing with historical recall using interpretable context rules.
Outperforms state-of-the-art methods on text classification and generation tasks, according to the abstract.

papers.abstract: In the practical deployment of vision--language--action policies, handling long-tailed task distributions is a common challenge due to the highly imbalanced composition of robot demonstration datasets. To investigate this issue, we study the head-task action bias in shared robot policies, particularly focusing on its relationship with task-specific visual evidence. Our experimental analysis shows that, when the visual evidence required by a tail task is insufficient, the policy increasingly falls back on action patterns reinforced by data-rich head tasks, resulting in degraded performance on under-represented tasks. Motivated by this observation, we propose Evidence-Guided Counterfactual Learning, a training framework for long-tailed robot policies. Our method identifies decision-relevant visual evidence using instruction-related and action-related signals, and constructs counterfactual observations by removing the selected evidence. The resulting counterfactual predictions are used to strengthen the association among task instructions, visual evidence, and actions, with the supervision adaptively adjusted according to the number of demonstrations available for each task. The proposed framework requires neither additional training data nor region-level annotations and incurs no additional computation during deployment. Extensive experiments across simulated benchmarks, different VLA architectures, and real-world robot platforms demonstrate that our method robustly and consistently improves long-tailed robot policy learning, particularly for tail tasks, while maintaining reliable performance on head tasks.
authors: Weiwei Chen, Chenghao Xu, Meiling Yu, Xu Yang, Cheng Deng
bullets: Long-tailed demonstration data can cause shared policies to favor action patterns from data-rich head tasks, harming under-represented tail tasks.
The method identifies decision-relevant visual evidence from instruction- and action-related signals, then removes it to create counterfactual observations.
Counterfactual predictions reinforce links among task instructions, visual evidence, and actions, with supervision adjusted by task demonstration frequency.
It requires no additional data or region-level annotations and adds no deployment-time computation.
Experiments across simulated benchmarks, multiple VLA architectures, and real robots show improved tail-task learning while maintaining head-task performance.

papers.abstract: On-Policy Self-distillation is a self-improvement paradigm that enables large language models (LLMs) to improve their capabilities by leveraging the same model as both teacher and student under different conditioning contexts. However, we find that OPSD methods can progressively degrade previously acquired capabilities: queries that are correctly responded at earlier training stages may become incorrectly responded as optimization proceeds, even the overall performance continues to improve. Further analysis reveals that this degradation coincides with a deterioration of the geometry of hidden representations, characterized by reduced intra-cluster compactness and diminished inter-cluster separation. Motivated by this observation, we propose Representation Geometry Regularization (RGR), which preserves representation geometry during post-training by encouraging compactness within cluster and separation across cluster. RGR can be seamlessly integrated into existing OPSD methods without altering their core optimization procedures. Extensive experiments on multiple OPSD methods and benchmarks show that RGR generally alleviates capability degradation while retaining capability improvements. Our code is available in https://github.com/supermachinelearner/RGR.
bullets: OPSD can improve overall performance while causing previously correct responses to become incorrect.
Capability degradation is associated with less compact within-cluster and less separated between-cluster representations.
RGR regularizes hidden representations to maintain intra-cluster compactness and inter-cluster separation.
It integrates with existing OPSD methods without changing their core optimization procedures.
Experiments across multiple OPSD methods and benchmarks show reduced degradation while preserving capability gains.

papers.abstract: In maximum entropy and behavior-constrained reinforcement learning (RL), the optimal policy is given by a Boltzmann distribution. Generating samples from this distribution can be challenging, as it is often complex and multimodal. While flow policies trained with flow matching provide a powerful framework for representing such distributions, they traditionally rely on access to training data, which is generally unavailable in online RL. To address this limitation, we propose fixed-point flow matching (FFM), a data-free procedure for training and fine-tuning flow policies in RL. FFM leverages the target flow identity to formulate the actor update as a fixed-point iteration, utilizing a flow-matching-style regression objective where the critic's action gradients serve as regression targets. We show that the optimal policy is a fixed point of this iteration. Through extensive experiments, we demonstrate that FFM effectively fine-tunes pretrained flow policies in the offline-to-online setting and enables efficient and accurate training of flow policies from scratch in online RL. These results establish fixed-point flow matching as a principled approach for learning expressive flow-based policies without requiring training data.
authors: Denis Blessing, Onur Celik, Gerhard Neumann
bullets: Targets maximum-entropy and behavior-constrained RL, where optimal policies are complex Boltzmann distributions.
Uses a fixed-point iteration based on the target flow identity to update the actor.
Trains flow policies with a regression objective whose targets come from critic action gradients.
Supports fine-tuning pretrained flow policies offline-to-online and training them from scratch in online RL.
Experiments show effective and accurate learning, though the abstract does not specify numerical results or limitations.

We have run FFM on all 20 MJX Playground tasks and on the four MJX humanoid tasks and present the aggregated results over all Playground tasks (left two panels) and the aggregated results over the humanoid tasks (right two panels). We have evaluated all methods on 10 seeds for every single environment (see Figure 4 and Figure 5 for results) and report the IQM with 95% stratified bootstrapped confidence intervals following Agarwal et al. (2021). FFM performs on par with the baselines on the Playground tasks (left two panels) but converges to the highest return much faster than TRUDI on the high-dimensional humanoid tasks. This result indicates that FFM’s benefits are most pronounced on high-dimensional tasks. Furthermore, we can boost FFM’s performance by leveraging its deterministic mapping properties and incorporating correlated exploration (FFM + OU), which leads to a significantly faster convergence to a similar return value as the best-performing baseline DIME (left two panels) (see Figure 15).

Figure 1: The FFM policy-improvement step. FFM repeats: (1) Clean actions X1 are generated from the current policy by integrating Equation (5) (forward only, no gradients); the grey curves are sampling trajectories. (2) Critic action gradients are required for the FFM regression target of Equation (12). (3) Fresh noise ε and the clean action X1 are used to sample a noised action Xt via Equation (3). (4) A flow-matching-style regression pulls vθ toward the FFM target. The optimal policy π⋆ ∝ eQ/λ is a fixed point of this loop.

However, we observe that there are some tasks such as AcrobotSwingupSparse, HopperHop, HopperStand, where FFM (and most of the baselines) perform badly, indicating that a more sophisticated exploration strategy is required. papers.abstract: A simulator summarizes an environment in a state that users can read and change. Generative models learn representations of the world without explicit specification, but offer no built-in way to edit that world's state. We investigate the conditions under which a generative model can act as a simulator through $\textit{editability}$: whether changing a model's latent representation produces the next-step outputs we get by editing a simulator's state. Plainly stated, our goal is to find a mapping between a generative model's latent state and the simulator state, where the model is trained on observations alone and the mapping is learned afterward. We test two kinds of mappings, both learned from observations paired with simulator states. In one, we train probes to decode the simulator state from the model, then steer along them. In the other, we learn the mapping directly with an inverse map, which can succeed even where steering fails. We study both in two contrasting environments: the discrete board game Othello, and Rayworld, our own continuous world of moving discs seen through partial renderings, closer to physical scenes and video. We find that which mapping succeeds depends strongly on the environment, even though the state is decodable in every variant. In Othello, editability falls smoothly as the game is simplified, and even small rule changes have large consequences. In Rayworld, probes fail to steer along the simulator's continuous state, yet an inverse map sets the model from that state anyway. A model can therefore be driven by a simulator it may have never learned.
authors: Sevan Brodjian, Michael Hobley, Pietro Perona
bullets: The study defines editability as whether changing a model’s latent representation produces the next-step outputs expected after editing a simulator state.
It learns mappings from observations paired with simulator states using either probe-based steering or a direct inverse map.
Experiments cover Othello and Rayworld, a continuous partially observed world of moving discs.
State decodability does not guarantee editability: probes work differently across environments, while inverse mapping succeeds in Rayworld where steering fails.
Small rule changes substantially affect Othello editability, and a simulator can drive a model even when the model has not learned that simulator.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of our evaluation procedure. The environment simulator renders state st into observation ot. papers.selection_reason: Investigates latent editability of generative models as environment simulators, directly relevant to world-model state manipulation.
papers.title: When Generative Models Act as Simulators
papers.tldr: Generative models can function as editable simulators when their latent states are mapped to simulator states, but the successful mapping depends strongly on the environment.

papers.abstract: Fewer latent tokens promise cheaper diffusion. Yet aggressive latent compression creates a reconstruction-generation dilemma: adding channels improves reconstruction but makes generation harder. We introduce APEX, short for Asynchronous Prefix denoising for EXtreme compression, which pairs a hierarchical latent space with asynchronous denoising over channel groups. Our autoencoder orders channel prefixes from structure to detail, while one shared denoiser generates them at staggered local times without adding tokens. On ImageNet-512, APEX outperforms existing methods at every evaluated channel count under 64x and 128x compression. At matched training and guided sampling compute, it also outperforms a 256-token model at every evaluated budget, with larger gains at lower compute. Code is available at https://daviddinkevich.github.io/APEX.
authors: David Dinkevich, Nisan Chiprut, Yoav HaCohen, Dani Lischinski
bullets: Addresses the reconstruction–generation trade-off in aggressively compressed latent spaces.
Uses an autoencoder with channel prefixes ordered from global structure to fine detail.
A shared denoiser generates channel groups at staggered local times without adding tokens.
On ImageNet-512, it outperforms prior methods across evaluated channel counts at 64× and 128× compression.
It also surpasses a 256-token model at matched compute, with larger gains at lower budgets.

figures.caption: Figure 6: APEX makes high compression advantageous under constrained compute. (a) Guided gFID versus relative denoiser inference FLOPs, where 1× matches f64 at 250 NFE with f32 at 64 NFE. (b) CFG sweep at the 1× budget. Stars mark the selected guidance scale for each model.

Figure 2: Channel hierarchy. We divide the channels of each latent token into ordered groups. The cumulative prefix through group ℓ defines level Lℓ. Resolution-supervised autoencoder. We sample a level, zero all later groups, and decode the retained prefix at full resolution. Reconstruction and target are then resized to that level’s assigned resolution before computing the autoencoder loss. Diffusion training. A global clock τ is sampled from q(τ) and mapped to one local timestep per group. Unstarted groups are zeroed, and the shared DiT predicts velocities for the denoising groups. Inference. Groups start in sequence along the same clock. Each newly active group is initialized from Gaussian noise, and generation continues until the full latent is clean.

Figure 5: APEX degrades far more slowly as latent width increases. Left: 64-token f64 latents; right: 16-token f128 latents. At f64, APEX changes from 2.85 → 3.15 → 4.90 gFID as channels increase 128 → 256 → 512, while DC-AE degrades from 3.22 → 9.19 → 26.10. At f128, increasing channels from 512 → 1024 changes APEX from 8.98 → 18.77, compared with DC-AE 14.44 → 89.47 and DC-AE 1.5 11.86 → 51.47. The boxed values summarize performance at f64c128 and f128c512. All runs use matched denoiser-training FLOPs and total NFE.

Figure 8: Gap, allocation, and level contribution. (a) We vary the stagger gap while using pL0 = 0.9. At g = 0, the tail interval is absent and the process reduces to synchronous diffusion. (b) Holding g = 0.25, we vary pL0 , the training probability assigned to the interval where L0 is denoising. Uniform clock sampling corresponds to pL0 = 2/3. (c) For the g = 0.25, pL0 = 1 checkpoint, we stop inference when L0, L1, or L2 completes and redistribute the same 250 NFEs over the retained clock interval. Generation improves at every endpoint, showing that all three levels contribute.

papers.tldr: APEX enables extreme latent compression by asynchronously denoising hierarchical channel groups, improving image generation quality without increasing token count.

papers.abstract: Knowledge distillation aims to train a smaller student model to mimic a larger teacher model for resource-constrained environments. However, the process of distillation is typically data-intensive and computationally expensive, particularly for generative tasks. Few-shot distillation offers an alternative by transferring teacher knowledge using limited training samples. However, we observe that few-shot distillation performance is heavily dependent on the choice of these training samples. In fact, we demonstrate that using more uncertain samples near the teacher's decision boundary can significantly deteriorate distillation performance. Motivated by this observation, we propose Counterfactual-guided Few-shot Distillation in Open-book Question Answering (COFFEQA), a novel strategy that aptly uses counterfactuals to provide additional supervision around challenging factual samples. In the generative QA setting, we define a counterfactual as a minimally modified context that induces the teacher to change its response to an alternative answer. We provide geometric insights on how factual-counterfactual pairs can constrain the deviation between the teacher's and student's decision boundaries. We further introduce a new metric, Context Following Difficulty (CFD) that further validates counterfactuals prior to distillation based on agreement with the intended alternative answer and dependence on the modified context. COFFEQA uses CFD-validated factual-counterfactual pairs for few-shot distillation. Experiments across five in-domain and three out-of-domain QA benchmarks using T5 and Qwen2.5 families show that COFFEQA outperforms factual-only distillation baselines under the same few-shot budget. For instance, on TriviaQA, COFFEQA improves over the factual-only baseline by 8.77 average EM points and 9.98 average F1 points under the T5 setting with 32 few-shot pairs.
bullets: Few-shot distillation is highly sensitive to training-sample selection; uncertain samples near the teacher’s decision boundary can harm performance.
The method creates minimally modified contexts that cause the teacher to switch to an alternative answer, forming factual–counterfactual pairs.
A Context Following Difficulty (CFD) metric validates pairs based on teacher agreement and reliance on the modified context.
Across five in-domain and three out-of-domain benchmarks with T5 and Qwen2.5, COFFEQA outperforms factual-only distillation under the same few-shot budget.
On TriviaQA with T5 and 32 few-shot pairs, it improves average EM by 8.77 points and average F1 by 9.98 points.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Counterfactual-guided few-shot distillation framework. We begin with (1) a few-shot factual QA dataset Df and (2) generate a counterfactual candidate for a factual sample. (3) The generated counterfactual is evaluated using the teacher model with (4) our proposed Context Following Difficulty (CFD) metric and accepted if it satisfies the CFD threshold τ . (5) The CFD-validated counterfactuals are then paired with their corresponding factuals and used to distill the student model.
Figure 2: Counterfactual context generation prompts. System and user prompts used to minimally modify the factual context C into a counterfactual context C ′ that supports the target answer A′.

We compare COFFEQA without CFD verification against the full COFFEQA framework with CFD verification (τ = 0.3). Panels (a) and (b) report accuracy EM and F1 gains, while panels (c) and (d) report teacher-student agreement EM and F1 gains. CFD verification generally yields larger improvements, demonstrating the benefit of validating generated counterfactuals before distillation.

Figure 4: Illustrative examples of CFD-based counterfactual evaluation from the NQ dataset. The four cases demonstrate how Answer Agreement (AA) and Contextual Loss Ratio (CLR) complement each other in evaluating generated counterfactual candidates.

The final stage uses a system prompt and a user prompt to minimally modify the original context to support the alternative answer.

papers.selection_reason: Few-shot distillation with counterfactual supervision reduces the cost of deploying smaller QA models, aligning with efficient AI goals.
papers.title: COFFEQA: Counterfactual-Guided Few-Shot Distillation for LLM Question Answering

papers.abstract: Pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) already exhibit strong visual, spatial and reasoning capabilities relevant to robotic manipulation. The key challenge in turning pretrained VLMs into generalist manipulation policies is to expose these capabilities through an appropriate action interface. Vision-language-action (VLA) models provide a unified trainable policy, but typically introduce learned action tokens, action heads, or action experts whose semantics must be learned from robot data pretraining. In contrast, modular foundation-model-based manipulation methods can exploit pretrained VLM capabilities for zero-shot manipulation, but rely on external planning and control scaffolds that are not end-to-end trainable as a unified continuous-action policy. In this work, we introduce EASG, an Explicit Action-Space Grounding framework that bridges these two paradigms. By projecting a tool center point (TCP)-centered action frame into the wrist camera observation and expressing actions in the form of VLM's native textual generation interface, EASG makes the semantics of a continuous robot action space directly observable in the VLM's perceptual context. This allows pretrained VLMs to directly generate executable robot actions using their existing visual-spatial reasoning capabilities, without robot-action pretraining or additional action modules. Besides, the same action interface supports direct fine-tuning with robot trajectories, allowing the models to continuously improve beyond their manipulation capabilities unleashed by EASG. Overall, EASG enables zero-shot manipulation and generalization across object positions, categories, and robot embodiments, while supporting effective fine-tuning in the same continuous action space. These results demonstrate that, given an appropriate action interface, pretrained VLMs can themselves serve as native action models for robotic manipulation.
authors: Jingkun Yi, Shujie Zhang, Zirui Zhou, Haoxiao Wang, Haiyang Sun, Yuhang Dong, Xudong Xu, Xing Shen, Tao Zhang, Yong Liu, Jiangning Zhang
bullets: Addresses the challenge of exposing pretrained VLM reasoning capabilities through a unified continuous-action interface.
Projects a tool-center-point action frame into the wrist-camera view, making action semantics visible in the VLM’s perceptual context.
Represents robot actions through the VLM’s native textual generation interface, avoiding robot-action pretraining and extra action modules.
Supports both zero-shot manipulation and trajectory-based fine-tuning in the same continuous action space.
Enables generalization across object positions, categories, and robot embodiments, as described in the abstract.

papers.abstract: Reasoning post-training draws on offline demonstrations and policy-generated rollouts, yet conventional supervised fine-tuning (SFT) followed by reinforcement learning (RL) separates their objectives and limits continued reuse of collected responses. We propose \textbf{Cross-Behavior Policy Optimization} (CBPO), which makes these sources compatible with one regression loss through a fixed-reference target. Because the generating policy does not enter this target, positive and negative offline completions, reference responses, and current and historical rollouts can share a common reward-labeled record format and replay buffer. As new responses enter the buffer, optimization retains the same regression objective without coordinating separate SFT and RL objectives or requiring stored behavior-policy probabilities, importance weighting, or a learned critic. Restricting the available sources gives offline, on-policy, and off-policy variants, while CBPO-Unified combines them. Across two model scales and four mathematical reasoning benchmarks, CBPO delivers leading \texttt{avg@32} and \texttt{pass@32} performance across benchmarks and data regimes. On Qwen3-1.7B, CBPO-Unified improves benchmark-averaged \texttt{avg@32} and \texttt{pass@32} over SFT DAPO by 2.33 and 4.44 percentage points, respectively. In the replay ablation, retaining historical rollouts improves these metrics by 1.87 and 3.72 percentage points over the no-history configuration.
authors: Du Cheng, Junyu Lu, Jingfan Zhang, Yuzhuo Zhang, Haoxuan Jia, Shichao Weng
bullets: Addresses the separation between supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning, which limits reuse of collected responses.
Uses a generating-policy-independent target so positive/negative completions, reference responses, and current or historical rollouts share one reward-labeled replay format.
Supports offline, on-policy, off-policy, and unified training variants without stored behavior-policy probabilities, importance weighting, or a learned critic.
Across two model scales and four mathematical reasoning benchmarks, CBPO reports leading avg@32 and pass@32 performance across tested benchmarks and data regimes.

papers.abstract: Outcome-supervised group-relative policy optimization (GRPO) assigns the same advantage to every token in an LLM agent trajectory, leaving useful and unhelpful decisions undifferentiated. Hindsight credit assignment (HCA) can refine this feedback, but its estimates rely on trajectories containing informative alternatives at consequential histories. We introduce TreeHCA, which couples hindsight-guided exploration with hindsight credit assignment. TreeHCA uses changes in reference-answer likelihood to revisit intermediate histories and sample alternative continuations, forming a tree of reasoning and tool interactions. Because this exploration changes the distribution of sampled continuations, we derive the corresponding inverse-hindsight importance correction, including an exact finite-pool identity. We use this structure in a normalized tree backup that propagates terminal outcomes into turn-level advantages. This shared hindsight structure is TreeHCA's central design principle, linking informative exploration with hindsight-guided credit assignment. Across seven question-answering benchmarks and three Qwen backbones, TreeHCA outperforms all baselines in aggregate exact match, validating the effectiveness of paired exploration and credit assignment for multi-turn LLM agent training. Our code is available at github.com/TheBlackCat22/TreeHCA.
authors: Debajoy Mukherjee, Jeremy Carleton, Sushil Vemuri, Srinivas Shakkottai, Dileep Kalathil
bullets: Addresses GRPO’s limitation of giving every trajectory token the same advantage, which obscures useful versus unhelpful decisions.
Revisits intermediate reasoning and tool-use histories using changes in reference-answer likelihood to sample alternative continuations.
Introduces inverse-hindsight importance correction to account for the altered continuation distribution, including an exact finite-pool identity.
Uses normalized tree backups to propagate terminal outcomes into turn-level advantages.
Outperforms all baselines in aggregate exact match across seven question-answering benchmarks and three Qwen backbones.

papers.abstract: Joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) learn compact latent world models without pixel reconstruction. Existing JEPA pipelines typically train visual representations and action-conditioned dynamics before adding a control policy or solver. We introduce LeWAM, an end-to-end JEPA for control with: (1) a joint training objective over next latent state prediction and action flow matching, and (2) an isotropic Gaussian constraint on the latent state, enabling a single model to support direct policy execution and efficient planning by evaluating sampled actions with its learned latent dynamics. Compared with prior JEPAs in visual planning, LeWAM improves success rate from 28.6% to 89.7% on contact-rich tasks and from 10.9% to 46.2% on long-horizon tasks, and plans 32.3 times faster. On behavior cloning tasks in simulation and physical robots, LeWAM is also competitive with established methods. Interpretability analyses show that LeWAM learns control-relevant representations and action distributions effectively guiding test-time planning and control.
authors: Minghao Fu, Tavis Siebert, Eryk Halicki, Randall Balestriero
bullets: Addresses the separation of representation, dynamics, and control training in prior JEPA pipelines.
Jointly trains next-latent-state prediction with action flow matching under an isotropic Gaussian latent constraint.
Supports direct policy execution and test-time planning by scoring sampled actions through learned latent dynamics.
Improves visual-planning success from 28.6% to 89.7% on contact-rich tasks and from 10.9% to 46.2% on long-horizon tasks.
Plans 32.3× faster than prior JEPAs and remains competitive on simulated and physical-robot behavior cloning tasks.

papers.abstract: LLM agents increasingly operate over sensitive resources, such as private documents and mutable system states, which can create serious safety and security risks. Runtime guardrails should therefore make inspectable, reproducible, and deterministic allow or refuse decisions before potentially irreversible agent actions are executed. However, safety and security requirements are rarely complete before deployment, so guardrails need to keep adapting as new risks emerge. Existing adaptive guardrails learn from deployment experience, but they usually apply safety policies through LLM inference, which can lead to inconsistent decisions and ambiguous policy interpretations. Formal guardrails, on the other hand, enforce policies deterministically, but they usually rely on pre-deployment or task-specific policies and have no mechanism to adapt to newly observed risks. We introduce VEPA, a framework for the verified evolution of formal agent guardrails. VEPA represents the guardrail as a formal policy of executable symbolic rules over typed agent events. During deployment, we use an LLM guided by deployment feedback to propose policy patches that fix newly observed failures while preserving previously correct behavior. Then, a deterministic verifier only accepts policies that are structurally valid and conflict-free. Finally, an evidence-aware authority layer activates a verified rule only when it has enough supporting evidence, so uncertain updates cannot directly affect guardrail decisions. Across ASSEBench-Safety, ASSEBench-Security, and ATBench, VEPA consistently outperforms baselines while expanding the scope of deterministic formal-policy enforcement. These gains also hold under more challenging deployment conditions, including mixed streams, corrupted feedback, and longer horizons.
authors: Duy Nguyen, Lesly Miculicich, Bhavana Dalvi Mishra, Shuo Li, Krishnamurthy Dj Dvijotham, Mohit Bansal, Tomas Pfister, Long T. Le
bullets: Targets safety and security risks when agents access sensitive documents or mutable system states.
Represents guardrails as executable symbolic rules over typed agent events.
Uses an LLM to propose policy patches from deployment feedback, then accepts only structurally valid, conflict-free updates.
An evidence-aware authority layer prevents insufficiently supported rules from affecting decisions.
Outperforms baselines across three benchmarks and under mixed, corrupted-feedback, and longer-horizon conditions.

figures.caption: Figure 2 | Overview of VEPA. Figure 1 | Motivation for evolving formal policy. Static formal policy cannot adapt. Across a sequence of deployment tasks, natural-language memory can accumulate ambiguous or conflicting guidance and overgeneralize from feedback, causing regression on previously correct behavior. In contrast, VEPA represents policy as executable symbolic rules, verifies new rules for conflict-freedom, and preserves previously correct rules while adapting to newly observed cases.

papers.abstract: We study byte-level autoregressive language models whose hidden state is a small quantum register, whose transitions are learned token-conditioned quantum channels, and whose next-byte probabilities come directly from Born-rule measurements without a learned classical vocabulary projection or softmax. In the fixed-width recurrent setting, unitary dynamics cannot contract or reset stored distinctions; experimentally, unitary recurrence loses to its retrained one-token control in every tested variant. Introducing learned dissipation, then token-conditioned dissipative gating, yields useful memory beyond one token. The gated model improves test negative log-likelihood by 0.20 +/- 0.03 nats/byte over retrained parameter-matched one-token controls at context length 12, and by 0.29-0.33 at longer contexts, but never beats retrained two-token controls. A key-value recall benchmark shows a width-dependent threshold: one stored pair meets the pre-registered accuracy bar at 4-5 memory qubits, two pairs at 6-7, and three pairs remain unsolved. This is consistent with, but does not establish, a capacity explanation for the short effective memory horizon. As a secondary result, one-qubit models reach lower stationary memory entropy than a heuristically optimized classical predictive frontier at matched error in 9/9 seeds. On IBM Heron hardware, computational-basis memory-register distributions show signal against a uniform null in 12/12 circuits across prefixes of up to 12 tokens, next-bit probabilities pass pre-registered accuracy bars at four-token prefixes, and bytes are generated autoregressively by sampling physically measured bit probabilities. The tested models are classically simulable and substantially worse than classical n-gram baselines. We claim no computational quantum advantage.
bullets: The models use small quantum registers with token-conditioned quantum channels and Born-rule measurements for next-byte prediction, without a classical vocabulary projection or softmax.
Unitary-only dynamics fail to contract or reset memory and underperform retrained one-token controls; learned dissipative gating provides useful longer-context memory.
At context length 12, gating improves test negative log-likelihood over matched one-token controls, but never surpasses retrained two-token controls.
Recall capacity grows with memory width: one key-value pair succeeds at 4–5 qubits, two at 6–7, while three remain unsolved; this supports but does not prove a capacity-based memory limit.

IBM Heron experiments detected memory signal and generated bytes autoregressively from measured probabilities, but the models showed no claimed quantum advantage and remained worse than classical n-grams.

Grey curves: the attacked classical frontier per p; dashed: Cµ = ln 2; dotted: the quantum optima Cq(p).

The model is defined with a single 256-outcome vocabulary POVM; the hardware implements a distilled binary-tree approximation in which each of eight conditional bit probabilities is physically measured and their product defines the token probability. papers.abstract: Audio-visual speech enhancement (AVSE) improves speech intelligibility in noisy environments but often relies on computationally expensive models unsuitable for resource-constrained edge devices. This paper introduces a reinforcement learning-driven neural architecture search (RL-NAS) framework to discover compact, efficient AVSE architectures. The search space preserves temporal alignment between audio and visual streams, while a novel reward function jointly optimises speech enhancement performance, measured by SI-SNR improvement, and model compactness. Using proximal policy optimisation with constraint-aware action masking, the framework evaluates only 35 candidate architectures and identifies a model with 2.9 million parameters, compared with 22 million in the baseline. The proposed architecture achieves a 14.5 dB SI-SNR improvement, only 0.7 dB below the baseline, while reducing model size by approximately nine-fold. Evaluation on commercial mobile CPUs demonstrates a 4.3-fold reduction in real-time factor, supporting practical on-device deployment. Compared with random search, RL-NAS achieves 92% higher search efficiency. Architectural analysis reveals that shallower but wider temporal convolutional blocks and aggressive visual pathway pruning can maintain enhancement performance while substantially reducing computational requirements. These findings demonstrate the potential of reinforcement learning-guided architecture search for developing lightweight, efficient and deployable multimodal speech enhancement systems.

papers.abstract: Pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) policies fail on memory tasks, behaviour that depends on events observed long before the current frame, because their training data is overwhelmingly Markov and mapping episodic memory directly to action chunks is hard. Yet the same policy, finetuned once to follow a privileged oracle's grounded-subgoal text, nearly solves these tasks: the difficulty lies entirely in mapping memory to a grounded symbolic subgoal. Existing work entrusts this stage to a single VLM that selects keyframes and reasons over raw frames, and falls far short of the oracle: key identities and dynamics are buried in noisy pixels, the reasoning spans hundreds of frames in an unbounded context, and hallucination corrupts the memory itself. We instead present GAMMA (Grounded multi-Agent Memory with Mechanical Audit), which builds the stage as a collaborating two-agent memory system: a detector tool (SAM-3) for spatial grounding, a VLM writer that distils each replan window into one grounded text line, an append-only text memory bank, and a VLM reasoner that reads the bank and emits the next grounded subgoal at the oracle's cadence, wrapped in a propose-verify harness that admits, defers, corrects, or rejects every agent claim against mechanical visual evidence, at training-corpus construction and at deployment alike. On a sixteen-task memory-manipulation suite GAMMA recovers a large fraction of the oracle ceiling with the policy held fixed, reaching the ceiling on several tasks, and transfers with unchanged contracts to a second benchmark.
authors: Yudong Liu, Yueqian Lin, Zijia Tang, Yuxi Zheng, Yuan Li, Shuai Zhang, Yi Li, Taotao Jing, Shuangjun Liu, Dashan Gao, Ning Bi, Jingwei Sun, Yiran Chen, Hai Helen Li
bullets: Addresses VLA failures on tasks requiring information from events far before the current frame.
Uses SAM-3 for spatial grounding, a VLM writer for concise episodic summaries, and a VLM reasoner to produce grounded subgoals.
Maintains an append-only text memory bank and verifies, corrects, defers, or rejects claims using mechanical visual evidence.
Recovers much of the privileged-oracle performance on a 16-task suite, reaching the oracle ceiling on several tasks.
Transfers to a second benchmark without changing its contracts; performance is scoped to the tested memory-manipulation tasks.

papers.abstract: Reliable robotic manipulation requires maintaining a firm grasp while strictly avoiding both contact slip and structural damage to the object. Satisfying these inherent \textit{secure-and-gentle} grasping constraints is challenging for unknown objects. We present a novel online data-driven predictive control framework for safe dynamic robotic grasping of unknown objects. The proposed system features a pair of compact, single-channel tactile-sensing modules that characterize the gripper-object dynamic interaction in real time, entirely bypassing the need for prior knowledge or offline training. A finite-state-machine-based grasping force probing mechanism is developed to establish the initial grasping force and explicitly identify grasping force constraints. Through online dynamics learning, a Gaussian Process (GP) model captures gripper-object interaction dynamics. The model uncertainties are further used to form robust grasping constraints, which are embedded into a model predictive control scheme. We demonstrate error convergence in a probabilistic sense. The proposed control framework runs at 100~Hz in real time to dynamically manipulate and handle objects rather than static holding. Extensive experimental evaluations across diverse contact surface topologies and various types of objects validate superior performance and efficiency compared to baseline strategies. The proposed method is able to manipulate objects ranging from delicate items, such as raw tofu and marshmallows, to rough objects, such as rocks.
bullets: Uses compact single-channel tactile sensors to monitor gripper–object interactions in real time.
Probes for an initial grasp force and identifies force constraints with a finite-state machine.
Learns interaction dynamics online with a Gaussian Process and incorporates uncertainty into robust MPC constraints.
Runs at 100 Hz and demonstrates probabilistic error convergence during dynamic manipulation.
Experiments cover delicate and rough objects across varied contact surfaces, including tofu, marshmallows, and rocks.

papers.abstract: Self-evolving LLM agents typically improve how they act through accumulated experience, reflection, or skills. Yet even procedurally capable agents can fail when their beliefs about environment dynamics are incomplete, incorrect, or outdated. We study a complementary axis of self-evolution: evolving those beliefs during deployment. Such beliefs can support multiple tasks, but incorrect ones can also propagate across them. We introduce EvoBelief, a self-evolving world model that represents environment knowledge as falsifiable hypotheses. Unexpected outcomes and decision-relevant unknowns trigger hypothesis formation. Later observations and controlled experiments provide independent validation before a rule can guide predictions or plans within its supported scope. Counterexamples narrow or retire rules as the environment changes. The language model remains frozen, and each rule remains linked to its evidence and the decisions it changes. Across four benchmarks spanning static dynamics, hidden drift, and scientific discovery, EvoBelief improves task performance and reuses learned rules across tasks. On ALFWorld without actor-side transition memory, it improves success over the matched Frozen World Model by 23.9% and 31.3% with Claude Haiku 4.5 and GPT-5.4, respectively. On MiniGrid, it revises stale rules and recovers after unannounced dynamics changes. In DiscoveryWorld's Reactor Lab, it discovers and validates quantitative laws, completing 83.3% of Normal-tier and 58.3% of Challenge-tier instances, versus 0% for each evaluated baseline. These results demonstrate self-improvement through testable, revisable environment knowledge rather than model-parameter updates.
authors: Janet Wang, Jiang Guo, Yi Xiang, Jiaqing Yuan, Mingwen Dong, Hideo Kobayashi, Shuaichen Chang, Chandan K. Reddy, Jiarong Jiang
bullets: Targets failures caused by incomplete, incorrect, or outdated beliefs about environment dynamics.
Creates hypotheses from unexpected outcomes or decision-relevant unknowns, then validates them through observations and controlled experiments.
Links each rule to supporting evidence and affected decisions; counterexamples narrow or retire stale rules.
Across four benchmarks, it improves task performance, reuses rules across tasks, adapts to hidden dynamics changes, and discovers quantitative laws.
Reported gains include 23.9% and 31.3% higher ALFWorld success than a matched Frozen World Model, and nonzero DiscoveryWorld completion where baselines achieved 0%.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Illustrative example. (a) Following its frozen prior, a capable agent heats compound X to 100 ◦C and gets decomposition products. (b) The mismatch triggers a hypothesis, which controlled experiments test. (c) The verified belief is stored in the persistent world model W and changes later actions in the original task and in new ones, without any parameter update. Based on the updated belief, the agent avoids gas chromatography (GC), whose operating temperature exceeds the supported range, and correctly chooses to use liquid chromatography (LC) instead.

Only the ringed key unlocks the door, blue for episodes 1–20 and green for 21–40. The switch is silent, and the red key that matches the door is a decoy. Right: the preconditions each family requires to complete the task of lifting the box. In MG-C the box lifts only with the door shut and hands empty. A grounded prediction mismatch or a decision-critical unknown opens an evidence loop that forms falsifiable hypotheses, gathers evidence, and verifies their scope. Figure 8: What each MiniGrid family requires. In every family the red key matches the door and never works, the blue key opens the door for the first twenty episodes, and after episode 20 the green key does instead; the ring marks the key that opens the door and the switch is never announced. In MG-R (R for rebind) one toggle with the working key unlocks and opens the door, and nothing more is asked. In MG-C (C for conjunctive) the door behaves the same, but the box lifts only with the door shut and the agent’s hands empty, so after entering the agent must drop the key and close the door it just opened. In MG-M (M for multi-stage) toggling with the working key only unlocks the door, which stays shut until a second toggle with empty hands. The switch is the only change within a stream; the family rules hold in both halves. The steps in dark red are the ones the pretrained prior does not expect.

papers.abstract: Aligning two independently pretrained unimodal encoders typically demands millions of paired examples. In this paper, we study the regime where only $N \sim 100$--$500$ pairs are available, while unpaired data on either side is abundant. Our method expresses every representation by its similarities to the $N$ paired anchors, which places both modalities in a common coordinate system; matches the two point clouds with a single entropic optimal transport problem solved over the entire pool, whose marginal constraints counteract the hubness that defeats nearest-neighbor matching; and distills the resulting plan into two lightweight encoders, so that the correspondence becomes inductive. We additionally put this marginal constraint in relation with the one-step hub corrections of the bilingual lexicon induction literature. Pairing is required only for the anchors: the unpaired collections may be drawn independently from the two marginals, so that no item outside the anchor set needs to have both of its modalities observed. We evaluate on image-text and molecule-text alignment, where our method outperforms existing approaches at the same anchor budget on Flickr30k, MS-COCO and ChEBI-20.
bullets: Targets cross-modal alignment when only about 100–500 paired examples are available.
Represents each item by its similarities to paired anchors, creating a shared coordinate system.
Uses entropic optimal transport with marginal constraints to reduce hubness and match the full representation pools.
Distills the transport plan into lightweight encoders, making the learned correspondence inductive.
Outperforms existing methods at the same anchor budget on image–text and molecule–text benchmarks, including Flickr30k, MS-COCO, and ChEBI-20.

Step 3: this coupling is used as a pseudo-pairing signal to train two lightweight encoders fθ and gψ, via contrastive learning directly on the original pretrained embeddings, distilling the transport plan into a shared aligned space that requires no anchors and no optimal transport at inference time.

papers.abstract: Humans effortlessly react to the world; they adeptly return a tennis shot, catch a falling cup, step aside from a passing cart, or pass a box tossed during truck unloading. These everyday actions require anticipating a moving target and reflexively responding with the whole body within about a second. Such visual reactive whole-body control remains challenging for humanoids, which must (1) coordinate whole-body control, (2) react to object dynamics in real time, and (3) ground perception in egocentric vision. We study catching thrown boxes as a representative task that demands all three capabilities; existing systems cover only part of it, relying on end-effectors, motion capture, or marked objects. We present Reflex, a three-stage framework that learns these capabilities stage by stage while connecting them through a compact representation of object dynamics. First, a state-based policy learns whole-body catching with reinforcement learning. Second, the policy learns to infer the dynamics of a moving box from delayed and incomplete observations. Third, an egocentric RGB-D encoder learns to recover this dynamics representation directly from visual observations while keeping the whole-body controller fixed. This decomposition provides each capability with a direct training signal and makes visual learning substantially more scalable. In simulation, Reflex achieves 85.7% catch success from egocentric RGB-D, compared with 87.9% when given privileged box observations. Temporal visual history is critical: removing it reduces success by 35.6 and 39.8 points on centered and laterally offset throws. On a real Unitree G1, Reflex catches human-thrown boxes with 65% and 40% success at 2.5 and 5 m, reaching 76% and 59% of human catchers' success at the same distances.
authors: Taoyang Jia, Weikai Huang, Linxin Song, Jared Darlington, Jieyu Zhao, Yue Wang, Jiafei Duan, Zhongzheng Ren, Ranjay Krishna
bullets: Addresses the challenge of combining whole-body control, moving-object dynamics prediction, and egocentric visual grounding.
Uses a three-stage framework: reinforcement-learned catching, dynamics inference from delayed observations, and RGB-D perception of that dynamics representation.
In simulation, achieves 85.7% catch success from egocentric RGB-D, close to 87.9% with privileged object observations.
Temporal visual history is essential, with its removal reducing success by 35.6–39.8 percentage points.
On a Unitree G1, catches human-thrown boxes at 65% success from 2.5 m and 40% from 5 m.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Training pipeline and policy architecture. Stage 1 learns whole-body control by training the state-policy teacher with PPO. Stage 2 learns the object dynamics: it initializes the privileged encoder and decoder latent-input weights by matching teacher actions, then jointly refines the encoder and decoder with PPO. Human motion examples supply reference tracking and an AMP style reward. Stage 3 learns visual grounding by predicting the latent from RGB-D histories and camera ego-motion, using box-state supervision and DAgger rollouts. The pretrained CNN and heatmap head stay fixed during GRU training; the privileged encoder and decoder remain fixed throughout Stage 3. The decoder also receives robot/reference observations. Because Stage 3 learns only the latent predictor, the visual controller reuses the PPO-trained decoder without modification.

papers.abstract: Foundation models are increasingly used for high-level multi-robot task planning, yet independently generated symbolic plans can become jointly infeasible after geometric grounding because of shared spatial and temporal constraints. We study execution-aware coordination of large-language-model (LLM) planners for multi-robot navigation. We compare a centralized architecture, in which one LLM jointly reasons over the robot team, with a decentralized multi-LLM architecture in which each robot independently proposes a task plan. A geometric verifier grounds the candidate plans into robot trajectories, detects predicted inter-robot conflicts, and converts conflict information into structured feedback for targeted replanning. This verifier-mediated architecture separates semantic task reasoning from execution-level feasibility while enabling iterative coordination among LLM planners. Experiments in CARLA and on Crazyflie aerial robots evaluate coordination performance as task complexity increases and characterize the trade-offs between centralized reasoning, decentralized verifier-mediated coordination, and physical executability.
authors: Vivek Khatana, Zijian Song, Naira Hovakimyan, Petros Voulgaris
bullets: Addresses the gap between independently generated symbolic plans and jointly feasible robot trajectories.
Compares centralized joint planning with decentralized, per-robot LLM planning.
Uses geometric grounding to detect inter-robot spatial and temporal conflicts.
Feeds structured conflict information back to LLM planners for iterative coordination.
Evaluates increasing task complexity in CARLA and with Crazyflie aerial robots, including physical executability trade-offs.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Verifier-mediated multi-robot planning architecture. In the centralized architecture, a single LLM jointly generates symbolic plans for the robot team, whereas in the decentralized architecture each robot is assigned an independent LLM planner. The resulting symbolic plans are grounded into robot trajectories and evaluated by a shared execution-level verifier. Predicted obstacle or inter-agent conflicts are converted into structured feedback and returned to the affected LLM planner for targeted replanning.

Fig. 4: Cross-platform evaluation on Crazyflie aerial robots. (a) Two-Crazyflie coordinated navigation in simulation with obstacle and predicted inter-agent conflict checking (demo video: https://tinyurl.com/cn3anffv). Multi-robot coordination is evaluated in simulation, while the hardware experiment evaluates the planning pipeline under tracking, localization, actuation, and physical execution effects.

Results compare centralized single-LLM planning with coordinate and neighbor-list representations against decentralized two-LLM planning with the neighbor-list representation. Metrics are (a) mean planning time of successful trials, (b) mean successful path length, and (c) mean planning time over all trials.

papers.abstract: Ego-trajectory prediction in urban roadway work zones remains an underexplored topic in autonomous-driving research, with limited dedicated data and systematic evaluation. Roadway work zones involve temporary changes in the lane layouts and connectivity of the roads, complicating interactions with surrounding vehicles and workers. These changes make future vehicle trajectories difficult to predict. To address these challenges, we collect WZDrive-Data, a multimodal dataset comprising 1,183 work-zone driving segments from 33 drivers, using a human-in-the-loop driving simulator with prerecorded worker animations and VR-controlled workers. Driver control and gaze signals are recorded from human participants, while vehicle trajectories and scene information are obtained from the simulator. Our proposed multimodal ego-trajectory predictor, WZDrive, achieves a mean minADE (K=6) of 1.09 m and minFDE (K=6) of 2.12 m. Compared with the best-performing state-of-the-art baseline for each metric in our benchmark, WZDrive reduces minADE (K=6) by 7.18% and minFDE (K=6) by 13.18%. This research addresses a gap in autonomous-driving research on urban work zones by combining human-in-the-loop data collection with multimodal learning from human driving signals and in the context of work zones.
authors: Shuo Zhang, Aman Sunesh, Semiha Ergan, Kaan Ozbay
bullets: Work zones introduce temporary lane changes and altered road connectivity, making vehicle-trajectory prediction difficult and underexplored.
The WZDrive-Data dataset contains 1,183 work-zone driving segments from 33 drivers, including vehicle, scene, control, and gaze signals.
The WZDrive predictor uses multimodal human-driving and scene information to forecast multiple possible ego trajectories.
It achieves minADE@6 of 1.09 m and minFDE@6 of 2.12 m, improving on the strongest benchmark baselines by 7.18% and 13.18%, respectively.
The study focuses on urban roadway work zones and relies on human-in-the-loop simulator data.

papers.abstract: Parameter-efficient continual learning updates a restricted subset of adapter parameters to incorporate sequential tasks while limiting catastrophic forgetting. Gradient attribution is a common rule for selecting that subset, but it requires an additional backward pass over calibration data. We identify a parameter-pool confound in comparisons between initialization-time gradient masks and unrestricted random masks under standard zero-initialized LoRA ($B=0$): the gradient with respect to $A$ is identically zero ($\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial A=0$), so gradient masks select strictly from the $B$ matrix whereas unrestricted random masks draw from both $A$ and $B$. Such a comparison changes both the selection rule and the candidate parameter pool. Isolating the selection criterion by restricting both approaches to the same parameter pool, we find a negative result: a uniform random mask consistently achieves lower loss-based backward transfer than gradient attribution across seven seeds on Qwen2.5-3B. The effect is concentrated on the medical task, which contributes 80\% of the aggregate; code and math move in the same direction, and legal shows no reliable difference. This advantage is consistent with a stability--plasticity trade-off under the tested task sequence, in which random masking slightly reduces single-task fitting. On the two discrete-option tasks (Medical and Legal), the mean accuracy-BWT difference is not statistically distinguishable from zero.
authors: Yu Sun, Junwei Zhou, Zuodong Xiang, Yike Zhang, Pengcheng Xu, Xinyu Guan, Ruoyun Ma, Hailu Xu
bullets: Zero-initialized LoRA makes gradients with respect to A identically zero, causing gradient masks to select only B while unrestricted random masks sample both A and B.
Restricting both methods to the same B-matrix pool isolates the selection rule rather than the candidate-parameter pool.
Across seven seeds on Qwen2.5-3B, random masking consistently produces lower loss-based backward transfer than gradient attribution.
The effect is driven mainly by the medical task; code and math follow the same trend, while legal shows no reliable difference.
On Medical and Legal, mean accuracy-based backward-transfer differences are not statistically distinguishable from zero.

papers.abstract: We interpret Transformer networks as learned approximations to a hybrid probabilistic-inference procedure that combines max-product Loopy Belief Propagation (LBP) with Expectation--Maximization (EM). In this view, a Transformer performs inference in partially observed Markov Random Fields (MRFs) whose structure and parameters are not given a priori but are inferred from data. We show that self-attention implements a differentiable approximation to max-product LBP on an input-conditioned, dynamically structured MRF, with attention weights encoding learned structural affinities. We further establish an EM correspondence at the level of depth: each layer updates latent representations in an E-step-like forward pass, while the transition $\theta^{(l)} \to \theta^{(l+1)}$ across layers acts as an implicit M-step. Building on this interpretation, we introduce \emph{meta-models}, a design paradigm in which inputs generate instance-specific parameters, unifying mechanisms such as self-attention, mixture-of-experts, and gated units within a single framework. Empirical results support the proposed perspective.
bullets: Reinterprets self-attention as differentiable max-product LBP on input-conditioned Markov Random Fields.
Maps Transformer depth to EM: layerwise representation updates resemble E-steps, while parameter transitions resemble implicit M-steps.
Introduces meta-models, where inputs generate instance-specific parameters.
Unifies self-attention, mixture-of-experts, and gated units under this meta-model perspective.
Reports empirical support for the proposed interpretation, without specifying results in the abstract.

papers.abstract: Indoor navigation to task-relevant targets remains difficult when the target is small, occluded, or visually indistinct. Meanwhile, smart appliances, mobile devices, and IoT tags emit Wi-Fi signals during everyday communication, providing a pervasive but underused spatial cue. We study visual-Wi-Fi navigation, where a robot reaches a signal-emitting device in an unmapped environment using onboard visual observations and Wi-Fi packets overheard from the device, without connecting to the device or modifying infrastructure. Realizing this requires pose-dependent Wi-Fi observations during closed-loop policy learning and reliable spatial cues from bearing measurements corrupted by indoor multipath propagation on a moving robot. We present WiFiSpaces, which extends the Habitat embodied simulator with online ray-traced Wi-Fi sensing, rendering Wi-Fi observations for a robot-mounted antenna array at continuous poses during policy rollouts. On top of it, we build ViFiNav, a localization-aware navigation framework: an online source-localization algorithm exploits robot motion to disambiguate and robustly aggregate bearings from multiple viewpoints into a confidence-aware source estimate, and a learned policy fuses this evolving estimate with depth observations and learns to act on it as it is refined. Experiments show that exploiting robot motion is key to accurate source estimates, and that fine-tuning on ray-traced Wi-Fi observations in WiFiSpaces improves the success rate of ViFiNav. The policy transfers zero-shot to unseen scene datasets, and we deploy it on a real robot with a Wi-Fi sensor built from a commodity router, without any real-world training.
authors: Lihao Wang, Tianjian Xu, Tianmin Shu, Renjie Zhao
bullets: Addresses navigation to small, occluded, or visually indistinct devices using Wi-Fi signals as a spatial cue.
Introduces WiFiSpaces, a Habitat extension that simulates pose-dependent, ray-traced Wi-Fi observations during policy rollouts.
Uses robot motion to aggregate noisy multi-view bearing measurements into a confidence-aware source estimate.
A learned policy fuses the evolving Wi-Fi estimate with depth observations for closed-loop navigation.
Improves with ray-traced Wi-Fi fine-tuning, transfers zero-shot to unseen scenes, and runs on a real robot without real-world training.

They form a closed loop: the policy’s motion selects the localizer’s viewpoints, and the policy is trained on the evolving estimate rather than on a fixed goal. The policy is trained with reinforcement learning (RL) in WIFISPACES, using a reward available only in simulation, and deployed zero-shot on a real robot.
