papers.abstract: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning has hundreds of methods, usually compared by parameter count and benchmark score. We compare them as maps. A pretrained checkpoint is a base point in weight space, and a weight-space method is a smooth map from a small parameter space that starts at that point. These maps form a slice category in which the frozen model is initial and full fine-tuning terminal. Three invariants of the map do most of the work. Its image near the base point governs expressivity, through the first-order image, the dimension, a min-cut bound on rank and whether that point is smooth or an apex. Its fibres, with the optimizer's metric, govern training dynamics. Base change moves the base point and covers splitting initialisations, quantisation, restarts and merging. We prove, for example, that zero-initialised LoRA, and Householder reflection adaptation at its default start under stated rank and parity conditions, begin at the apex of a cone; that no exact initialisation lets LoRA reach an update of rank above twice its own; that exactly orthogonal methods never change a weight's singular values in exact arithmetic, however often they are merged; that under Adam with no epsilon, weight decay or clipping and one shared schedule, LoRA+ from the standard zero initialisation follows exactly the trajectory of plain LoRA with its scale multiplied by the learning-rate ratio; that Adam with shared hyperparameters respects only the signed permutations inside LoRA's continuous symmetry group of full-rank factors; and that the activation function decides when a scaling adapter folds into preceding weights. We classify 382 methods from 138 papers by seven coordinates read off their formulas, with 403 simulation arrows and 485 obstructions. Every numbered result is proved in full, and results due to others are credited where we re-derive them.
authors: Xiaoyu Li, Zhizhou Sha, Chiwun Yang, Dai Shi
bullets: Models fine-tuning methods as smooth maps from low-dimensional parameter spaces into weight space, forming a slice category from frozen to full fine-tuning.
Characterizes methods using image geometry, fibres with optimizer metrics, and base changes such as quantization, restarts, splitting, and merging.
Proves structural results for LoRA, Householder adaptation, orthogonal methods, LoRA+, Adam symmetries, and scaling adapters.
Classifies 382 methods from 138 papers using seven formula-derived coordinates, supported by 403 simulation arrows and 485 obstructions.
Results often depend on stated assumptions, including initialization, rank and parity, optimizer settings, exact arithmetic, and activation functions.

papers.abstract: Feed-forward 3D foundation models reconstruct scenes from unposed images, but the quadratic cost of global attention limits their scalability to large view sets. We present Zebra3D, a layerwise sparse-linear hybrid attention framework that improves the efficiency of pretrained 3D foundation models without training from scratch. Across VGGT, HunyuanWorld-Mirror, and $\pi^3$, we observe a broadly consistent depth-wise pattern: early stages are relatively tolerant to linear replacement, while sensitive middle-to-late stages tend to exhibit more concentrated attention. Zebra3D exploits this structure by assigning linear-centered attention to tolerant stages and tile-sparse attention to sensitive stages, using landmark summaries to preserve unselected context. Closed-form affine fitting enables training-free conversion, while optional post-conversion training combines task supervision with output and relational feature distillation. Across all three backbones, Zebra3D achieves strong reconstruction and camera-pose accuracy at high attention sparsity, with training-free variants remaining close to their dense counterparts. End-to-end speedups increase with input view count, reaching up to $7.1\times$ at 1,024 views. After post-conversion training, Zebra3D-VGGT reaches 80.5\% RealEstate10K AUC@30 at 94\% mean attention sparsity, within 1.1 percentage points of dense VGGT fine-tuned on the same data and schedule.
authors: Utkarsh Saxena, Ruijing Yang, Mehdi Rezagholizadeh, Akash Haridas, Vikram Appia, Emad Barsoum
bullets: Addresses the quadratic cost of global attention in feed-forward 3D foundation models for unposed-image reconstruction.
Assigns linear-centered attention to tolerant early stages and tile-sparse attention with landmark summaries to sensitive middle-to-late stages.
Converts models without training from scratch using closed-form affine fitting; optional distillation-based post-conversion training further improves performance.
Across VGGT, HunyuanWorld-Mirror, and π³, maintains strong reconstruction and camera-pose accuracy at high attention sparsity.
Zebra3D-VGGT reaches 80.5% RealEstate10K AUC@30 at 94% mean sparsity, within 1.1 percentage points of dense fine-tuned VGGT; speedup reaches 7.1× at 1,024 views.

papers.title: Zebra3D: Efficient Hybrid Foundation Models For Scalable 3D Reconstruction
papers.tldr: Zebra3D makes pretrained 3D reconstruction models scalable to many views by replacing dense attention with layerwise hybrid sparse-linear attention, achieving up to 7.1× speedup with limited accuracy loss.

papers.abstract: Neural surrogates that forecast a physical field from sparse, noisy sensors read a window of nearby sensors and a history of past snapshots. Practitioners choose both by comparing fitted models with each other. Such comparisons cannot tell a model's shortfall from missing information. We measure the trade-off between window and history against the Bayes-optimal error of the same readings. An exact Gaussian analysis shows that noisy or sparse observation of a field with local dynamics makes the optimal forecast read distant sensors only through spatial correlation. On a forced linear field with a known optimum, trained models that read only the window come within 1% of it. We then train such models on viscous Burgers flow and the chaotic Kuramoto-Sivashinsky (KS) equation, with every deciding comparison fixed before any test evaluation. In every field except KS, eight snapshots remove a smaller fraction of the one-snapshot error as the lead time, the number of steps to the forecast target, grows. In KS, for windows up to one correlation length, they remove a larger fraction. This lead-time inversion persists across sensor densities, three architectures and a two-dimensional domain. It shrinks as damping lowers the Lyapunov exponent. Damping also removes the linear instability of KS. We therefore tie the inversion to instability and leave chaos and linear amplification unseparated. For surrogate design the results give two rules. Size the window in correlation lengths of the field. Split a fixed input budget between window and history for the lead time the model will serve, because the best split moves toward wider windows as the lead time grows. In Burgers flow the split chosen at lead time one ends with 13.5 times the best error at lead time eight.
bullets: Bayes-optimal analysis finds that distant sensors help mainly through spatial correlation when observations are sparse or noisy.
For a forced linear field, window-only models approach the known optimum, coming within 1%.
In most tested fields, history becomes relatively less useful at longer lead times; chaotic Kuramoto–Sivashinsky flow shows the opposite for short windows.
The lead-time inversion persists across sensor densities, architectures, and a two-dimensional domain, but weakens with damping.
Choosing the input split for one-step forecasting can be highly suboptimal at longer horizons; in Burgers flow, it yields 13.5× the best error at lead time eight.

papers.abstract: Large language models are stochastic by nature. Repeated executions under the same experimental conditions may produce different responses. We propose a framework that can be applied across the model lifecycle, from task design to residual behavior and continuous monitoring. The method consists of building an empirical response distribution estimated through Monte Carlo simulation. Semantic interventions are introduced to study how these distributions change. We illustrate the framework with two different tasks, borrower classification and music album recommendation, and quantify the resulting distributional changes. The framework is linked to model risk management and governance by measuring robustness and control effectiveness, and characterizing residual behavior. Since it relies only on observed responses, it can also be applied to black-box models accessed through commercial APIs.
bullets: Addresses variability in LLM outputs across repeated executions under identical conditions.
Estimates response distributions via Monte Carlo simulation across the model lifecycle.
Uses semantic interventions to measure changes in behavioral distributions.

Connects distributional measurements to robustness, control effectiveness, governance, and residual behavior.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon manipulation requires robots to retain task-relevant history while revising conclusions no longer supported by physical evidence. Retaining observations alone does not specify which completed conditions should be withdrawn after a disturbance or which obligations require repair. We introduce REMM, Revisable Embodied Memory for Manipulation, a supervisory memory layer for a frozen G0.5 vision-language-action executor. REMM separates an append-only evidence history from revisable task state and explicitly links derived relations and completed conditions to their supporting facts. When accepted evidence changes a supporting fact, it withdraws dependent conclusions and schedules targeted recovery at verified skill boundaries without updating the executor. Across 51 physical trials, including operator-assisted runs, REMM improves mean recorded task progress over the strongest baseline from 57% to 91% in intervention recovery and from 43% to 70% in sequence recall. Complementary video diagnostics show improved grounding of retained history into the next instruction, including comparisons with $\pi_{0.5}$-compatible high-level planner adaptations. These results support revisable memory as a practical interface for continued manipulation without policy retraining. Project: https://revanthsenthil.github.io/remm/.
authors: Revanth Krishna Senthilkumaran, Ruwan Wickramarachchi, Alessandro Oltramari, Jonathan Francis
bullets: Targets long-horizon manipulation, where robots must retain useful history while retracting unsupported conclusions.
Uses a supervisory memory layer for a frozen G0.5 vision-language-action executor, without policy retraining.
Links derived relations and completed conditions to supporting facts, then withdraws affected conclusions when evidence changes.

Across 51 physical trials, mean recorded progress improved from 57% to 91% for intervention recovery and from 43% to 70% for sequence recall.

papers.abstract: Vision-language reward models are trained on annotated preference pairs, which are expensive to collect, can disagree, and are ranked by benchmark accuracy. We build one with no human preference label: a linear head on an intermediate layer of a frozen Qwen3-VL backbone, trained to score a web caption above a perturbed version of the same caption; labeled data enters only to select the layer. The layer is the decisive choice, worth 5.8 points over the last layer, and one recipe transferred without re-tuning beats or at least matches GPT-4o on three benchmarks at 32B, 6.6 points ahead on VL-RewardBench, from a few thousand parameters at about a thousandth of fine-tuning compute. At an equal pair budget, perturbations teach a frozen head 3 to 5 points more than curated RLAIF-V pairs. Because the backbone is frozen, the objective is convex, and the perturbation sampler specifies the reward, which the benchmark does not identify: two heads trained on disjoint halves of the same perturbations tie on the benchmark and differ by 6.4 points in hallucination judging. Retraining the head on the policy's own verifier-labeled candidates cuts caption hallucination by 5.1 CHAIR points and lifts image-generation pass rate by 5.4, while scoring lower on every reward benchmark. Together, an intermediate-layer probe, free same-image perturbations, and a verifier-driven bootstrap turn give a recipe for multimodal reward modeling that needs no annotator, costs a fraction of fine-tuning, and is specified by the comparisons it is trained on rather than by a benchmark rank.
authors: Yueying Li, Jingxuan Fan, Kiant\'e Brantley, Sham M. Kakade, Hanlin Zhang
bullets: Uses a linear head over a frozen Qwen3-VL intermediate layer, training original web captions to outrank perturbed versions.
Selecting the intermediate layer is critical, improving performance by 5.8 points over using the last layer.
A single recipe matches or exceeds GPT-4o across three benchmarks at 32B and leads VL-RewardBench by 6.6 points.
With equal pair budgets, perturbation-based training outperforms curated RLAIF-V pairs by 3–5 points.

Benchmark scores do not fully identify reward behavior: perturbation choice affects hallucination judgments, while verifier-driven bootstrapping improves CHAIR and image-generation pass rate despite lower benchmark scores.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action models (VLAs) offer a promising route toward general-purpose robotics by transferring semantic knowledge from large-scale vision-language pretraining into language-conditioned control. However, most VLA evaluations emphasize aggregate manipulation success under changes in objects, instructions, or environments, leaving unclear how reliably these policies ground spatial descriptions in the physical scenes where they act. We therefore ask a sharper question: how reliably can current VLAs translate spatial descriptions into appropriate real-robot behavior? To investigate this, we introduce Spa-Bench, a real-robot benchmark that evaluates spatial grounding across six tabletop tasks covering Object State, Relative Size, Referential Description, Relational Placement, Ordinal Position, and Counting. Our primary evaluation compares in-distribution (ID) and out-of-distribution (OOD) spatial configurations while retaining training support for the relevant objects, concepts, and actions, reducing object and motor unfamiliarity as alternative explanations for failure. Four diagnostic conditions further probe physical execution, sensitivity to wording, object-task associations, and recognition that no action is required. We release 4,092 episodes collected on the SO-101 robot arm: 1,200 human-teleoperated demonstrations and 2,892 real-robot evaluation rollouts from five state-of-the-art VLA policies. Across the three fully evaluated policies, success falls from 67.5-73.3% on ID spatial configurations to 40.7-52.0% on OOD spatial configurations, while matched direct instructions improve success by 28.3-40.0 percentage points. These results show that the evaluated VLAs can often execute the required manipulations but lack robust spatial grounding. Project materials, including videos, code, and benchmark data, are available at https://justintiensmith.github.io/Spa-Bench/.
authors: Justin Tien-Smith, Matthew Pidden, Rolandos Alexandros Potamias
bullets: Introduces a real-robot benchmark spanning six tabletop spatial tasks: object state, relative size, referential description, relational placement, ordinal position, and counting.
Compares in-distribution and out-of-distribution spatial configurations while controlling for object and motor unfamiliarity.
Adds diagnostics for physical execution, wording sensitivity, object-task associations, and recognizing when no action is needed.
Evaluates 4,092 episodes on the SO-101 robot arm, including demonstrations and rollouts from five VLA policies.

Across three fully evaluated policies, success drops from 67.5–73.3% on in-distribution configurations to 40.7–52.0% on out-of-distribution configurations; direct instructions improve success by 28.3–40.0 percentage points.

papers.abstract: Non-prehensile manipulation with mobile robots has primarily targeted placement in coarse goal regions. Precision placement has been studied with manipulators on benchmarks such as Push-T, where an omnidirectional end effector can readily re-approach an object from any side. For a mobile robot, correcting the same placement errors may require wide repositioning maneuvers around the object. We formalize multi-object pushing with a mobile robot as a multi-target assignment problem at tight tolerances. We propose a diffusion planner with a causal factorization: each robot denoising step is followed by an object step conditioned on the current clean robot estimate. This factorization allows us to sample multiple object outcomes for a single robot plan, capturing the multi-modality of pushing. We also design a set of pushing-specific costs for mobile robots, used for both guidance and best-of-$N$ sampling at inference. On Push-T, our planner attains the highest success rate of the methods we compare, while having the lowest rate of implausible object motion. Across three multi-box pushing environments resembling warehouse scenarios, it raises the fraction of boxes placed by $21.5$ percentage points over an unguided baseline, and replans $1.8\times$ faster than a planner that denoises the two trajectories together. Lastly, we deploy the guided planner on a TurtleBot 3 Burger with object shapes absent from the training data, where it places $85.0\%$ of objects within tolerance against Diffusion Policy's $37.5\%$.
authors: Lance Pharand, Megnath Ramesh, Mark Chiu, Yash Vardhan Pant, Stephen L. Smith
bullets: Formulates tight-tolerance multi-object pushing as a multi-target assignment problem for mobile robots.
Uses causal diffusion: each robot denoising step is followed by an object step conditioned on the robot estimate, capturing multiple possible pushing outcomes.
Introduces pushing-specific costs for guidance and best-of-N trajectory selection.
Achieves the highest compared success rate and lowest implausible-motion rate on Push-T; improves box placement by 21.5 percentage points over an unguided baseline.
Replans 1.8× faster than joint trajectory denoising and places 85.0% of objects within tolerance on a TurtleBot 3 Burger with unseen shapes.

papers.abstract: Large language models are becoming central to GeoAI systems, yet their evaluation rarely considers the elicitation of geospatial data requirements. This omission is critical as retrieval oriented geo-analytic tasks cannot be supported reliably without first identifying the necessary datasets and constraints. GeoFitBench-LLM is introduced as a benchmark for assessing whether LLMs can infer the datasets, the supporting resources and the constraints required by geo-analytic requests in natural language. The benchmark is structured around two reasoning dimensions, Spatio-Temporal Relational and Semantic Grounding, reflecting long-standing challenges in geospatial information retrieval and related natural language tasks. Ground truth requirements are encoded in a fixed, provider-independent schema for reproducible evaluation of resource identification and attribute-level specification. Experiments on seven models under minimal prompting indicate that identifying the necessary resources is often achievable, with GPT-5.4 Thinking achieving the best result by recovering the complete set of resources in 66.67% of benchmark requests. Results further indicate that accurate fitness-for-use specification remains more difficult as inferential demands increase.
authors: Amirhossein Vahdat, Thierry Badard, Luc Lamontagne
bullets: Targets a gap in LLM evaluation: geospatial data-requirements elicitation for retrieval-oriented analysis.
Evaluates two reasoning dimensions: Spatio-Temporal Relational and Semantic Grounding.
Uses a fixed, provider-independent schema to encode ground-truth resource and attribute requirements.
In minimal-prompt experiments across seven models, GPT-5.4 Thinking recovered all required resources for 66.67% of requests.
Resource identification was more achievable than accurate fitness-for-use specification, especially when inference demands increased.

papers.abstract: Language model agents increasingly operate over long interaction streams, requiring online adaptation to distribution shifts through continual learning. However, existing agent harnesses typically either evolve their states only through forward information flow or rely on additional replay or validation data for harness optimization. To address this, we propose ReHarness, a recurrent harness framework for agentic continual learning that complements forward read and write with backward revision under a strictly online streaming protocol. We ask what information could have been captured differently in the harness state to better inform the current instance in the stream. Specifically, after each instance, we leverage the resulting trajectory as feedback to revise the reflections retrieved for that instance, thereby propagating feedback backward through the textual harness state. Across three continual learning benchmarks and three language model backbones, ReHarness consistently outperforms strong raw-context baselines, memory- and reflection-based methods, and prompt optimization approaches. Further analysis shows that ReHarness produces source-grounded and meaningful revisions, corrects overgeneralized or outdated experience under distribution shifts, and improves both stability and plasticity during continual learning.
authors: Yuxin Xiao, Zhiyun Lu, Jianyu Wang, Yangtian Zhang, Yang Song, Qifan Wang, Bailin Wang
bullets: Addresses adaptation to distribution shifts in long, streaming agent interactions.
Adds backward revision to the usual forward read/write updates of agent harnesses.
Uses each completed trajectory to revise the reflections retrieved for the current instance, without replay or validation data.
Outperforms several baseline families across three benchmarks and three language-model backbones.
Revisions are source-grounded, correct outdated or overgeneralized experience, and improve stability–plasticity balance.

papers.abstract: We introduce iRAG, a human-in-the-loop decision-support system combining Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) with Hybrid Decision-Making. Unlike conventional RAG systems, relying on static Knowledge Bases (KBs), our proposal addresses settings where the KB is initially empty and is progressively populated through human decisions. The system stores previous decisions as retrievable precedents and moves from silent observation to evidence-grounded contestation and, finally, to autonomous handling with abstention. Against an independent baseline, iRAG matches final-decision error under 10% drift without retrieval decay and reduces it under 40% drift across all configurations. Retrieval decay improves performance on changed knowledge while increasing error on stable knowledge, evidencing a stability--plasticity trade-off rather than a general advantage. Human oversight is an architectural provision of the workflow; its usability with real human users remains to be evaluated.

The workflow includes human oversight, but usability with real users has not yet been evaluated.

papers.abstract: Efficient autoregressive generation is increasingly limited by the memory footprint of the key-value (KV) cache, which grows linearly with sequence length, batch size, and model depth. Existing approaches such as Multi-Query Attention (MQA), Grouped-Query Attention (GQA), Multi-Head Latent Attention (MLA), and Tensor Product Attention (TPA) reduce this cost through different trade-offs, but often sacrifice expressivity, require additional positional-encoding machinery, or impose restrictive low-rank structure. We propose Kronecker Product Attention (KPA), which represents key and value activations as sums of Kronecker products of compact, token-dependent matrix factors. KPA strictly generalizes TPA: rank-one vector-outer-product factorization arises as a degenerate Kronecker split, while non-degenerate matrix factors can represent richer block-structured patterns. We further show that a structured rotary embedding operator matched to the Kronecker representation preserves the relative-position property of RoPE while rotating only the compact factors, removing the need for a decoupled RoPE branch as in MLA. Empirically, KPA matches or exceeds TPA, MHA, MQA, GQA, and MLA across four model scales and nine downstream benchmarks under identical training conditions, while achieving up to 10x KV cache compression. The Kronecker head split is a tuneable hyperparameter that allows practitioners to navigate the compression-accuracy trade-off at design time without architectural changes.
authors: Bahareh Nikpour, Hossein Rajabzadeh, Maryam Dialameh, Vahid Partovi Nia, Parsa Omidi
bullets: Targets KV-cache memory growth with sequence length, batch size, and model depth.
Represents key/value activations as sums of Kronecker products, strictly generalizing Tensor Product Attention.
Introduces a matched structured rotary embedding that preserves RoPE’s relative-position property without a separate positional branch.
Matches or exceeds several attention baselines across four model scales and nine benchmarks, with up to 10× KV-cache compression.
A tunable Kronecker head split controls the compression–accuracy trade-off without architectural changes.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of Multi-Head Attention (MHA), Tensor Product Attention (TPA), and Kronecker Product Attention (KPA, ours). MHA projects x directly into dense Q,K, V . TPA and KPA instead factor each projection into two components, combined via an outer product (×) for TPA or a Kronecker product (⊗) for KPA. RoPE is applied only to Q and K (never V ), and rotates only the B factor in both methods (Theorem 2.4 formalizes this for KPA); A is cached unrotated. Since TPA’s A,B are vectors, their outer product is a flat, unstructured matrix; since KPA’s A,B are matrices, their Kronecker product is block-structured with a two-level head/feature hierarchy (shown by the internal grid lines). Only K,V factors enter the KV cache; Q is not cached. The token index t is omitted throughout except on the final Qt,Kt, Vt, for clarity.

papers.abstract: Motion retargeting is a critical preprocessing step for transferring human motion data to humanoid robots. While existing methods are effective for single-character motions, interactions involving multiple characters and objects introduce additional contacts and spatial relationships that must be preserved. Retargeting is commonly formulated as a weighted multi-objective optimization problem, where conflicting objectives can require careful tuning of relative weights and can still compromise important motion characteristics. We introduce PriMoRetarget, a prioritized motion-retargeting framework that replaces relative objective weighting with an explicit priority hierarchy. Lower-priority updates are constrained to preserve higher-priority objectives, allowing critical characteristics such as foot placement and interaction contacts to take precedence over lower-priority pose objectives. The method is evaluated on four datasets spanning single-character motion, character-object manipulation, and character-character interactions. The resulting motions better preserve task-relevant interactions and provide reference trajectories that can be tracked more reliably than those produced by widely used retargeting methods.
authors: Nicholas Ioannidis, Dun Yang, Max Smith, Tue Vu, Ziyu Zhang, Shayegan Omidshafiei, Xue Bin Peng
bullets: Addresses motion-retargeting failures in multi-character and character-object interactions, where contacts and spatial relationships must be preserved.
Replaces manually tuned weighted objectives with prioritized optimization: lower-priority updates cannot compromise higher-priority objectives.
Prioritizes task-critical features such as foot placement and interaction contacts over lower-priority pose matching.
Evaluated across four datasets covering single-character motion, manipulation, and character-character interactions.
Produces motions that better preserve interactions and yield more reliably trackable reference trajectories than widely used retargeting methods.

papers.abstract: Recently, soft robotic procedures are being developed aiming at achieving targeted minimally invasive operations or drug administration in specific locations in the human body. Accordingly, specialized path-planning algorithms need to be investigated for the estimation of efficient paths that would protect the delicate tissue structures and simultaneously satisfy a set of requirements for the efficient navigation of the robot. In this context, we propose an image-based 3D pathplanning algorithm, which is an extension of the A* algorithm, for the navigation of a soft-growing robot inside the spinal subarachnoid space (SSS). The proposed algorithm is capable of estimating a safe pathway towards the goal location, while ensuring the establishment of anchor points that facilitate the efficient steering of the soft robot. The algorithm is evaluated using a highly detailed model of the SSS with respect to its capacity to satisfy the robot movement requirements and path efficiency.
authors: George Dimas, Panagiotis G. Kalozoumis, Panagiotis Vartholomeos, Dimitris K. Iakovidis
bullets: Targets minimally invasive procedures and drug delivery in delicate anatomical environments.

papers.abstract: Physics foundation models are an increasingly popular approach for building versatile emulators for spatiotemporal systems. They require tokenisation layers that lift physical field data into a latent representation suitable for dynamic processing. A typical choice for this layer is a convolutional encoder, which lifts field information in a locality-aware way and can be trained very efficiently. However, this choice cannot be applied to a large class of scientific computing problems where data are represented on unstructured meshes, for example simulations on domains with curved boundaries. Such data typically require graph neural network architectures, which are more expensive to train and, in the form currently used, encode information differently from their CNN counterparts, thus limiting the portability of physics emulators between these data regimes. In this work we introduce Mesh-Native Convolution (MNC), a locality-aware tokenisation layer that encodes unstructured mesh-based data in a way that is analogous to CNNs. This approach leads to models that can be trained once on mesh data and then deployed to arbitrary unstructured meshes, even if these are irregular, with minimal retraining. We show that this tokenisation approach can be used to retrofit grid-pretrained foundation models efficiently on unstructured meshes and provide theoretical results to confirm the consistency of this approach with classical CNN encoders. We demonstrate the favourable performance of this retrofitting approach, which in many cases reaches acceptable accuracy even in zero-shot deployment, and outperforms existing baselines after only a few epochs of fine-tuning, thus providing an efficient bridge between the two data regimes.
authors: Georg Maierhofer, Miles Cranmer, Payel Mukhopadhyay
bullets: Unstructured meshes arise in scientific problems such as simulations with curved boundaries, but standard CNN tokenisers are limited to regular grids.
The proposed Mesh-Native Convolution (MNC) provides locality-aware, CNN-analogous tokenisation for mesh-based data.
Models trained on mesh data can be deployed across arbitrary irregular meshes with minimal retraining.
MNC can retrofit grid-pretrained foundation models to unstructured meshes, achieving acceptable accuracy in some zero-shot settings and outperforming baselines after brief fine-tuning.
The approach is supported by theoretical consistency results with classical CNN encoders.

papers.abstract: Humanoid and service robots operating in clut- tered human environments may encounter motion planning problems that are infeasible when all surrounding objects are treated as fixed obstacles. The Minimum Constraint Removal problem, which we refer to as MCR, addresses this situation by identifying the minimum number of constraints, such as movable objects, whose removal enables a collision-free path. However, computing an optimal MCR solution is NP-hard. In this work, we propose a graph-based heuristic pipeline that combines bidirectional feasible-set generation with fixed- length searches over reduced MCR graphs. We further derive an extended feasible-set generator for instances in which the candidates produced by the first generator do not contain a complete optimal removal set. Across six benchmarks, the evaluated pipeline matches the exact solution in three cases and, in the remaining cases, selects at most 31.25% more obstacles than the optimum, while being between 3.4 and 33.7 times faster than exact search. In one of the benchmarks, involving a manipulation task amidst clutter, selecting two rather than seven obstructing objects reduces the combined MCR, inverse- kinematics, and motion planning time from 84.72 s to 30.59 s. These results indicate that the proposed approach provides a practical compromise between computational efficiency and solution quality for motion planning among movable obstacles.
authors: Antony Thomas, Fulvio Mastrogiovanni, Marco Baglietto
bullets: Targets Minimum Constraint Removal (MCR), which is NP-hard in cluttered environments with movable obstacles.
Combines bidirectional feasible-set generation, fixed-length searches, and an extended generator for difficult instances.

papers.abstract: Continual learning (CL) seeks to adapt pretrained models while preserving prior capabilities. Yet the tasks supplied for preservation cover only part of what a model knows, while forgetting can extend beyond them. Recent work shows that language models can supplement this limited evidence by generating useful replay without access to their original training data. This raises a question about self-preservation: can a model help choose preservation targets that protect its own capabilities more broadly? To study this question, we organize task descriptions and their examples into Task Banks, whose entries can be selected and combined to guide replay generation by a frozen model. Continual instruction tuning with Qwen models of varying sizes yields three findings. First, the new task and learning rate shape which prior capabilities degrade, while tracking previously correct answers reveals losses that average accuracy can conceal. Second, generated replay reduces forgetting on tasks outside the bank. Combining partial banks strengthens this protection, improving mean retention of previously correct answers over either bank alone across the tested sizes. Third, the model can also help choose replay targets: selection informed by the new task improves mean held-out retention over random selection at 4B, with similar new-task gains, although smaller models show no corresponding advantage. Under a fixed example budget, however, replacing new-task examples with replay improves preservation at the cost of smaller new-task gains. Together, these findings show that models can support broader self-preservation by generating replay data and, in some settings, choosing which tasks to replay.
authors: Dongkyu Cho, Rumi Chunara, Ali Behrouz
bullets: Continual learning may forget capabilities not represented in the available preservation tasks.

Using a fixed example budget, more replay improves preservation while reducing gains on the new task.

papers.title: Self-Preservation in Language Models

papers.abstract: Sparse computation can scale the parametric capacity of LLMs without proportionally increasing active computation, but pretraining sparse architectures remains expensive and data-hungry. Existing sparse upcycling methods mainly target Mixture-of-Experts models, where expert homogeneity, sample inefficiency, and system overheads can limit practical scalability. Static sparse memory offers predictable access and token-specific updates that can help address these challenges, but naively integrating it into pretrained computation yields poor returns. In this work, we introduce STAPLE, a recipe built upon STEM for integrating static sparse memory into pretrained models. Whereas STEM replaces FFN up-projections with token-indexed embeddings, STAPLE retains them and adds the embeddings as a residual pathway, preserving pretrained computation while learning complementary token-specific information in a scalable manner. On OLMo-2 1B, STAPLE improves over continued dense training by 4.27 points on HumanEval, 2.80 on MBPP, 2.27 on GSM8K, and 1.65 on DROP. Average performance increases with static capacity, and improvements persist on the larger OLMo-2 7B backbone. STAPLE also outperforms static sparse baselines such as STEM and an Engram-style model, and achieves a higher average score than an MoE upcycling baseline while decoding 2x faster with less than half its GPU model memory and measured GPU energy per token in our throughput-oriented decoding evaluation. Importantly, despite introducing billions of parameters late in training, our host-offloaded implementation keeps generation throughput within 1.5% and training throughput within 3% of the dense baseline, while caching only the ~5% most frequent embeddings on GPU. These results show that static sparse memory can provide a sample-efficient, scalable, and sustainable path for expanding pretrained models without sparse pretraining from scratch.
authors: Ranajoy Sadhukhan, Euijin Hong, Sheng Cao, Zechun Liu, Shuowei Jin, Sha Li, Changlong Yu, Xin Liu, Qin Lu, Zhenyu Shi, Priyanka Nigam, Beidi Chen

papers.abstract: Agentic large language models now tackle complex tasks, yet strategic reasoning over long horizons is under-studied: most agentic benchmarks are short and episodic, and performance on long tasks is hard to dissect into stored knowledge, reasoning and luck. We introduce SpireBench, in which models play the complete commercial deck-builder Slay the Spire (StS), where early decisions decide long-term success. Across 20 large language models (LLMs) at the game's highest difficulty, frontier models beat heuristic baselines and match the average human player but remain far behind experts. This gap widens as the run lengthens: the strongest models win the first act as often as experts, then fall behind. What separates strong models from weak is how well they play each fight; all of them misjudge risk over a run, preserving health rather than spending it to grow stronger. A comprehensive, self-consistent renaming of every game term shows that part of their performance rests on prior knowledge of the game, and models do not improve from the memories they write across runs, which are often wrong and overly cautious. Our harness is the first to give a model the complete original game, and we compare it with existing harnesses. Overall, SpireBench offers an unsaturated long-horizon benchmark with tools to locate where and why agents fail.
authors: Scott C. Lowe, Sander W. Keemink
bullets: Tests 20 LLMs at Slay the Spire’s highest difficulty against heuristic baselines and human performance.
Models win the first act about as often as experts, but their performance declines as runs become longer.
Stronger models distinguish themselves mainly through better fight-by-fight play, while all models misjudge long-term risk.
Agents tend to preserve health instead of spending it to become stronger, and written memories across runs are often incorrect, overly cautious, and unhelpful.
Renaming game terms shows that performance partly depends on prior game knowledge; the benchmark is designed to diagnose long-horizon failure modes.

figures.caption: Figure 6: The harness as a sequence of messages, with time running downwards. In combat the model returns a whole turn as several tool calls in one reply; the harness sends them to the game one command at a time, diffs the state after each, and returns each call’s own effect as that call’s result, followed by each enemy’s action and the next turn’s state. At the end of each floor the model forecasts its chances and may update its run notes; at the end of the run it consolidates them into the memory bank that the next run’s system prompt carries. Code on the right is the shape of what the model sends and receives, with names as it sees them under the reskin.

Figure 1: Multiple time horizons at play in Slay the Spire. Cohort: the model plays a series of runs on different seeds, carrying memories it writes between them. Run: four acts of escalating difficulty, each ending in a boss; the player must grow stronger fast enough to keep up. Act: about 17 floors (Act 3 ends in two bosses at this difficulty; Act 4 has 4) through which the player plans a route, trading safer floors against riskier ones with larger rewards. Floor/Combat: most floors are fights of several turns, each followed by a deck choice that persists for the run; a card weak now may matter later, and a generally good one may be wrong for what lies ahead. Turn: the player draws part of the deck; the model plans the turn and plays it in one response of several tool calls (purple). Sometimes the best play takes more damage now to end the fight sooner. Magenta: choices made during the example Turn, and the part zoomed into for the other rows.

Figure 2: Mean acts cleared per run for the LLM agents of Table 1. (a) Against mean dollar cost per run (log scale), across reasoning-effort levels. Only points on the Pareto front (blue step line) are named; see Fig. 20 for other names. Dashed lines: the non-LLM baselines (no cost). (b) Against the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, at their highest effort and at low effort (low). Dashed line: least-squares fit. Only models on the cost Pareto front of (a) are named. For correlations with each Artificial Analysis evaluation, see Table 18.

Figure 3: Do models use HP as a resource? (a) Rest sites can be used to heal or upgrade a card; both top (blue) and other (grey) tier LLMs nearly always rest if they are missing any HP, whereas Twitch streamers (magenta) favour upgrading much more heavily. Bars are labelled with their number of visits. (b) Relative HP left at the end of each floor. Each act is drawn over the runs that reached the act boss (runs that die to the boss count as 0 HP for the boss floor); run counts are above each act. Lines: medians; bands: interquartile range. Streamers spend their HP in Act 1 to get stronger, reducing the amount of damage they take in future floors as a result.

Figure 4: Survival over a run. The share of each agent’s runs that reached each floor. Every LLM agent in Table 1 with all 10 seeds is shown; models on the cost Pareto front (Fig. 2a) are shown. Floor 57 indicates a win of the full game (defeating the Heart at the end of Act 4); a win at the Act 3 boss without the keys to unlock Act 4 stops at floor 52. Dark grey dash-dot: the random-choice policy. Purple: the mean of four Twitch streamers (band spans the four, weighted equally). Black: the 3,641 A20 Ironclad telemetry runs that follow an earlier A20 Heart kill in the same session chain (Appx. D). Shading marks the acts.

Figure 19: How the memory bank grows over a 10-run chain. For each model, top: the number of xml memories held after each run (line), with the memories added (blue, up) and deleted (grey, down) in that run’s consolidation. Bottom: the size of the bank carried into the next run, in thousands of characters, for xml consolidation, the single compact summary, and notes kept verbatim. Size is measured exactly, from the system prompt of the following run, relative to the first run’s empty bank; the bank after run 10 is never read, so that curve ends at run 9.

Figure 5: Our harness. Game states become text, each action’s effect attributed to its tool call; a router sends each part of the game to the model or a symbolic player; in-game names are (optionally) reskinned; tool calls are mapped back and validated. The prompt runs from cached layers to turn messages. Bottom: when the model plans, forecasts and writes notes.

Figure 10: Act 1 choices and combat against mean acts cleared, one point per LLM agent of Table 1 with at least three runs reaching the Act 1 boss (16 models), over those runs; lines are the telemetry population (dashed) and the four Twitch streamers. 𝜌 is Spearman's correlation across the models and 𝑝 a two-sided permutation test. HP change per hallway fight is the net HP change over a hallway-fight floor, including the relic heal after it, computed the same way for humans. Last panel: each model's rate of beating the Act 1 boss against the rate expected from its runs' states on reaching it, by a logistic model fitted on the 143,071 telemetry runs that reached it with a complete state record; the dotted line is equality.

Figure 15: Prediction error against distance from the outcome, for the runs of Table 1. Left: Brier score of the act-survival prediction against the number of floors before the act resolves (at its end if the run cleared it, otherwise where the run died). Middle: the same for the run-win prediction, against floors before the run ends. Right: mean absolute error, in HP, of the predicted HP at the end of the fight against the number of turns still to be played in it. Darker is worse, on a scale per panel; blank cells have fewer than 5 predictions. The bottom row pools all models, and its mix of distances is the one each model is scored over in Table 15. Fight-end predictions sharpen steeply as the fight ends; act-survival predictions barely sharpen before the act resolves.

Figure 16: As Fig. 14, for the forecasts made within a floor: the HP a model expects at the start of its next turn and at the end of the fight, both optional when ending a turn. Each is scored by its mean absolute error in HP, divided by that forecast's mean error over the predictions of every model in Table 1 (so 1 is average), and the two are averaged for each run. The division matters: fight-end errors are about ten times next-turn ones, so without it a run that made only next-turn predictions would look excellent. A run with no HP predictions has no score. Within-floor error tracks play more closely than end-of-floor calibration (Table 16).

Figure 17: Each ablation, model by model. Each grey line is one LLM agent: its mean over the 10 seeds in each condition, shown only where it has all 10 seeds in both that condition and the condition’s baseline, so every comparison is paired. Bars are the mean over those agents, and 𝑛 beneath each bar is how many there are. Baselines are the first bar of each panel, except that the compact summary is read against no memory bank with compact notes. Panels show mean acts cleared per run; the pooled tables are Tables 2, 27 and 29. Brackets test each condition against its baseline with a paired sign-flip permutation test over agents (* 𝑝 < 0.05; n.s. not significant). Orak is shown for the four models with all 10 of its seeds scored; its full paired comparison is in Table 2.

Figure 11: Do models learn from their memories? Mean acts cleared per run over the first five runs of each chain (open circle) against the last five (arrowhead), by memory mechanism; a circle alone means no change. The two halves are different seeds, so the no-memory cohort on the same seeds (grey) is the control for how hard each half is: learning shows as an arrow further right than the grey one. Only cohorts with all 10 seeds are shown. For reference, the top row is one of the authors (a non-professional player) over their first ten A20 Ironclad runs, playing the unmodified game without a harness or memory bank; with five runs per half, a single win moves a half’s mean by 0.8 acts.

Figure 12: Effect of difficulty on performance. Final floor reached against the pinned ascension level, for every agent in Table 1 with runs at more than one level, on the held-out seeds under the same configuration as the table. Each level is a separate cohort (its own memory chain). The solid line is the median floor at each level, the blue band the interquartile range, and the dotted lines the lowest and highest floor reached. Background shading marks the floors of each act. Levels with fewer than 10 completed seeds are annotated with their seed count. The last panel is every Ironclad run in Mega Crit’s released telemetry (October–November 2020, final content build; abandoned runs excluded), with the dotted lines at the 5th and 95th percentiles instead, since over tens of thousands of runs per level the extremes are always the first and last floors reachable. Each level there is a different population: a level is unlocked by winning at the one below it, so higher levels hold more experienced players, and only Ascension 20 includes runs that continue to the Heart.

Figure 14: Calibration against play, for each LLM agent in Table 1. Calibration error is the reliability term (Murphy, 1973) of the Brier score (Brier, 1950), in percentage points, over ten bins of stated probability, for the two forecasts made at the end of every floor (surviving the act, winning the run), scored separately and averaged. It is computed per run, not adjusted for how far ahead a prediction was made (Table 15); points are the median over a model's runs and bars the interquartile range. Lower effort levels are drawn smaller and paler, joined to the same model. The Spearman correlation is over the levels in Table 1, one per model.

Figure 8: What runs did on each act's 15 map floors, over the runs that reached that act's boss (floors 16, 33 and 50): the telemetry population (143,146, 47,619 and 22,729 runs), the four Twitch streamers (788, 671 and 603) and the LLM agents of Table 1 in three groups by mean acts cleared: the top 4 (36, 23 and 10 runs), the next 8 (65 and 7) and the bottom 8 (26). A group is drawn for an act only when at least five of its runs reached that boss. Shops and unknown rooms count the map nodes entered; elites fought and hallway fights the rooms entered. Rest-site and card-reward shares pool the visits and fights of all runs in the group.

Figure 7: Human performance at A20 with the Ironclad against hours of the game played, from the telemetry in Table 10: mean acts cleared per run (left) and the share of runs that kill the Heart (right). Each point is a bin of Table 10 at its median hours; bins with fewer than 2,000 runs are labelled with their count. Play time resets with a new save profile, so the lowest bin likely holds experienced players on fresh profiles.
Figure 18: Performance against thinking: mean acts cleared per run against thinking tokens per floor (log scale), for the same points as Fig. 2a.

Figure 21: Performance against cost per floor: mean acts cleared per run against mean cost per floor (log scale), for the same points as Fig. 2a. †Self-hosted; priced at Artificial Analysis headline rates. ‡Peak-rate list price, an upper bound.
Figure 20: Figure 2a with every point named, with its reasoning-effort level and, where it has fewer than 10 seeds, its seed count.

Figure 13: Where runs end. For each agent in Table 1, the share of its runs that ended in each act, sorted by mean floor (right). Agents with a similar mean floor can differ in whether they reliably reach the next act or split between early deaths and deep runs.

Figure 9: Relics, cards in the deck and upgraded cards at the end of each floor survived: median (lines) and interquartile range (bands), for the telemetry population (dashed), the four Twitch streamers, the top 4 LLM agents of Table 1 by acts cleared and the other 16. A floor is drawn only while at least 20 human or 8 LLM runs are alive on it. Human counts are reconstructed backward from each run's final deck and relics, removing every change the record itemizes after the floor.

Table 1: Benchmark results. Ascension 20 with the Ironclad. Each LLM is run at its highest reasoning setting (grey), played under the themed reskin, with model note-taking across floors within a run, and between runs within a cohort. Runs: number of runs used. Act 𝑘 win rate: share of runs that cleared Act 𝑘 . Acts cleared: mean number of acts cleared per run. Floor: final floor reached. BottledAI: symbolic agent (Bottled AI contributors, 2022). Human experts: public run histories of Twitch streamers who play Slay the Spire professionally (see Appx. D for details). An author: non-professional player. All humans: Mega Crit released run telemetry (Oct–Nov 2020, final content build) (Appx. D). Best and second best over LLMs. Among the streamers, bold marks the best value on each column among the averages. †Self-hosted; priced at Artificial Analysis headline rates. ‡Peak-rate list price (upper bound).

Table 32: What the system prompt carries, per model, on the 10 evaluation seeds (disjoint from those of Table 1). The baseline is our themed reskin; each other arm adds one thing to the reskinned prompt: the enemy compendium (Bestiary), the Reddit high-ascension strategy guide, or the Jorbs transcript set (his tutorial series and six hours on the Ironclad, 7 h in all; Appx. C.6). Guides and transcripts are renamed by the reskin. All arms take xml notes within a run, write no memory bank, and use generic guidance, with each model at its main-table reasoning setting (grey). Acts is the mean number of acts cleared per run and Floor the mean final floor. A superscript gives the seed count where fewer than 10 seeds completed, and – marks an arm with no valid runs. Best and second best are per row, among cells with all 10 seeds. Pooled over models in Table 31.
Table 3: Real game names against our themed reskin, for models with all 10 seeds under both; Δ is themed minus real. Control mappings are in Table 29.

Table 31: Effect of adding material to the system prompt. Reskin is the themed reskin with nothing added and is the baseline; Bestiary adds the enemy compendium, Reddit guide the Reddit high-ascension strategy guide and Jorbs the Jorbs transcript set, each renamed by the reskin (Appx. C.6). All with xml notes, no memory bank and generic guidance. Pooled over models: each method is compared with its baseline only on matched runs (the same model on the same seed; Pairs, over Agents models), and Acts, Floor and A1 (mean acts cleared, mean final floor and Act 1 win rate) are over those runs. Usage is compared on like-for-like floors only: the same model, seed, act and room type, and the same occurrence of that room type within the act, kept only where every method run on that model and seed completed it (Floors), so a method is neither credited with cheap early floors nor charged for expensive late ones. Calls and k tokens (input, including cached, plus output, in thousands) are means per floor; the token difference is the ratio of totals. Each Δ is the method minus its baseline. All runs are A20 on the 10 evaluation seeds, each model at its main-table reasoning setting. Per-model results are in Table 32.

Table 18: SpireBench against Artificial Analysis's public benchmarks, over the 20 LLM agents of Table 1 with all 10 seeds at their highest reasoning effort, and 10 of them again at low effort (30 points), each matched to the Artificial Analysis entry for the reasoning setting it ran at (scores retrieved 2026-09-24). A low rung is included where it has all 10 seeds and Artificial Analysis lists that setting. Left: correlation of each benchmark with mean acts cleared, over both rungs together and within each rung (𝑛 is the number of points with that evaluation). Right: how substitutable each benchmark is by the rest of the suite, with SpireBench added as one more row: its strongest correlation with any other single evaluation, its mean correlation with the others, and the share of its variance across points that the first principal component of the others predicts for a model left out of the fit, both rungs of it together (𝑅2 LOO; negative is worse than predicting the mean). The Intelligence Index is a composite of evaluations like these, so it is left out of the right-hand block, which uses the points with every evaluation (25).

Table 5: Which parts of the game each harness covers. ✓: covered (for our harness and Orak, the LLM sees/decides it) rule bot: Orak’s rule-based bot decides it, without the LLM. ✗: not covered. For Bottled AI, a symbolic player with no model, ✓ means it handles it, and a percentage is the share it handles.

Table 33: What a run costs, for the agents of Table 1: wall-clock minutes per seed (one game instance, seeds in series), dollars per run and per 10-seed cohort (priced as in Table 1), model calls and tokens per run (input including cached, plus output, in thousands); tool-call errors are in Table 23. Time depends on the provider's throughput on the day as well as on the model.

Table 24: Excerpts from the runs of Table 1, verbatim. Names are as the model saw them under the reskin, with the real game term in brackets. Excerpts are taken from the full run logs and cut at the ellipsis.

Table 19: Which models play below, or above, what their public agentic scores predict. For each Artificial Analysis evaluation, mean acts cleared (Table 1, highest reasoning effort, all 10 seeds) is regressed on the evaluation score across models, one point per model; cells are internally studentized residuals (𝑧; negative means fewer acts than the evaluation predicts). The top rows give each evaluation's correlation with acts cleared, with two-sided permutation 𝑝 (200,000 permutations) and 𝑛 models. Models are sorted by their mean residual over the agentic evaluations (left block). Artificial Analysis scores retrieved 2026-09-24. Terminal: Terminal-Bench. HLE: Humanity's Last Exam.

Table 27: Effect of cross-run memory. Within a run the model writes either keyed xml notes or a single compact summary; between runs they are consolidated into the memory bank (xml memories or one compact summary), kept verbatim (xml notes only), or discarded (None, the baseline for its kind of notes). All with the themed reskin and generic guidance. Pooled over models: each method is compared with its baseline only on matched runs (the same model on the same seed; Pairs, over Agents models), and Acts, Floor and A1 (mean acts cleared, mean final floor and Act 1 win rate) are over those runs. Usage is compared on like-for-like floors only: the same model, seed, act and room type, and the same occurrence of that room type within the act, kept only where every method run on that model and seed completed it (Floors), so a method is neither credited with cheap early floors nor charged for expensive late ones. Calls and k tokens (input, including cached, plus output, in thousands) are means per floor; the token difference is the ratio of totals. Each Δ is the method minus its baseline. All runs are A20 on the held-out seeds, each model at its main-table reasoning setting. Models: Qwen3.8 27B, Qwen3.6 35B-A3B, Qwen3.5 122B-A10B, Gemini 3.8 Flash (low), Nemotron 3 Nano Omni, GPT-5.6 Luna, gpt-oss-120b, GLM-5.3 Flash. Per-model results are in Table 28.

Table 14: Combat play in Act 1 by tier of Table 1 (top four, next eight, bottom seven with full logs), with Spearman's 𝜌 against mean acts cleared over the 19 models and its permutation 𝑝 . Hallway fights are ordinary combats. Block into no attack: turns on which a block card is played although no enemy intends to attack. Over-block: a block-only card played beyond the incoming damage while an attack was playable. Missed lethal: turns with one enemy left and enough damage in hand to kill it. The lower block shows measures that do not separate the tiers (𝑝 > 0.4).

Table 15: How well the models predict their own game. At the end of every floor each model is asked for its chance of surviving the current act and of winning the run; when ending a turn it may also predict its HP at the start of the next turn and at the end of the fight. Same runs as Table 1. Pred. and Obs. are the mean predicted and observed rates (a floor's act counts as survived if the run went on to clear it; a run is won at the Heart). A prediction is easier the closer it is made to the moment it resolves, and stronger models make more of theirs close to an act's end, so the Brier scores (0 is perfect; always answering 50% scores 0.25), the AUC (0.5 is chance; – where every act had the same outcome) and the fight-end HP error are adjusted for that distance: each is scored over the same mix of distances, pooled over all models (Fig. 15). HP: mean absolute error and signed bias (predicted minus actual; positive is optimistic) in hit points, with a prediction made in the fight that killed the player scored against 0. Next-turn HP is always one turn ahead, and close to arithmetic since enemy intents show the incoming damage. Best and second-best scores among models with all 10 seeds are highlighted.

Table 23: Tool-call errors per 100 model calls, for the LLM agents of Table 1. No usable call: a response in which no tool call could be executed, because every call was malformed or refused or none could be parsed; the harness asks again. Refused call: one call refused before it reached the game, as illegal on the current screen or with invalid arguments; the model is told why. Energy mismatch: a turn ended with a different amount of energy left than the model declared when ending it, a sign that it lost track of its own turn. Recovered from prose: a call the model wrote as text rather than through the tool interface, which the harness recovered and executed. Errors sums the first three, which are the ones the model is told about. Rates are totals over the cohort divided by its calls. Lowest and second lowest in each column, among agents with all 10 seeds.

Table 7: The models of Table 1: developer, how each was reached, the model ID sent, and the reasoning setting it ran at in the main table (an effort level, or a thinking budget for Claude Haiku 4.5). Self-hosted models were served through an OpenAI-compatible endpoint under the deployment name given. Every main-table run was played between 19 and 25 September 2026. N/A: No reasoning control available; the model runs at its default.

Table 20: What the models keep in their memory bank after the tenth seed of Table 1, classified by hand. Bank is the final number of memories; Created, Rewritten and Deleted count consolidation operations over the ten runs (Rewritten excludes verbatim re-saves). Composition is the share of the final bank in each category (a random 30 per model where the bank is larger): a game fact describes how the game works, a heuristic advises, an absolute rule prescribes without condition, an observation recounts one run; Other is route plans and notes about the harness. Wrong is the share stating a false game fact or a rule that fails in common situations, and H. how many of the coded wrong memories trace to harness text that was itself wrong (a rest-site key label, a state diff across the two final bosses, and debuff expiry shown as an enemy’s action); Absolute the share phrased as ALWAYS, NEVER or MUST anywhere; One run the share drawn from a single run. Models are ordered by mean acts cleared. Operations are read from the full run logs, except for Gemma 4 E4B, whose are read from the harness output log (its full logs are not available).

Table 30: Effect of the knowledge reskin, per model (supplementary to Table 29). None shows the real game names; Themed is our default Lich's Lair reskin; Random replaces every name with pronounceable nonsense; Permuted swaps each name for another real game name of the same kind; Perm.+themed applies the same permutation in the themed vocabulary. All with xml notes, a read-write memory bank and generic guidance. All cells are A20 on the held-out seeds, with each model at its main-table reasoning setting (grey). Acts is the mean number of acts cleared per run, Floor the mean final floor, and A1 the Act 1 win rate (%). A superscript gives the seed count where fewer than 10 seeds completed. Best and second best are per row, among cells with all 10 seeds.

Table 28: Effect of cross-run memory, per model (supplementary to Table 27). Within a run the model writes either keyed xml notes or a single compact summary; between runs they are consolidated into the memory bank (xml memories or one compact summary), kept verbatim (xml notes only), or discarded (None). All with the themed reskin and generic guidance. All cells are A20 on the held-out seeds, with each model at its main-table reasoning setting (grey). Acts is the mean number of acts cleared per run, Floor the mean final floor, and A1 the Act 1 win rate (%). A superscript gives the seed count where fewer than 10 seeds completed. Best and second best are per row, among cells with all 10 seeds.

Table 2: Comparison of Slay the Spire harness designs. Actions/call: how many game actions one model response may issue; Effects: whether each action's result is returned to the model; Context: what the model sees of earlier decisions; Choices: what resolves card choices opened mid-fight (e.g. select a card to put in your hand, on top of your draw pile, or upgrade). Measured rows are paired with our harness on the same models and seeds without the reskin or a cross-run memory bank for consistency with Orak which does not support either. Not run here: MiniStS (Bateni & Whitehead, 2024) (a reimplementation; one action per call, one fight) and AgenticSTS (Cheng et al., 2026) (the sequel; combat as a plan, a prompt rebuilt by retrieval, routine choices to a fast model tier). Calls are per floor on floors both arms played; cost is the run's API cost per floor it reached, priced as in Table 1 (cached input at its own rate), so the Orak row is comparable with the rest. †Orak keeps no per-floor record: calls and cost per floor reached over whole runs, not floor-matched, and over the 40 of its 51 runs with a usage record, since a run Orak's harness ended records none; a run it ended counts as a loss at the floor reached; its rule bot plays non-combat floors with no model call. For further comparisons, see Table 25.

Table 26: Effect of reasoning effort. Each model at every effort level it was run at, A20 on the held-out seeds with the main-table configuration (themed reskin, xml notes, read-write memory, generic guidance). Columns as in Table 1, with Acts the mean number of acts cleared per run; Act 4 (a Heart kill) is not shown but counts in Acts. Only levels with all 10 seeds completed are shown, and only models with two or more such levels. Bold marks the best level per model on each column. †Self-hosted; priced at Artificial Analysis headline rates.

Table 22: Card-reward skip rate by act on the main-table cohorts (seeds 1–10, A20). A decision is a fight survived; it is a skip when no card joined the deck. 𝑛 is the number of decisions in the act. Δ is the model’s Act 2+ skip rate minus its Act 1 rate (pooled over its decisions), shown where it has at least 10 Act 2+ decisions. Humans are Mega Crit telemetry, A20 Ironclad, where a Singing Bowl pick also counts as a skip. The first- and random-option baselines never skip by construction; Bottled AI skips every card not on its strategy's wish list.

Table 17: Success at each decision scale of Fig. 1, for the LLM agents of Table 1 (10 runs each). Turn is the share of combat turns without a rejected action, format error or energy mismatch (a lower bound, since every error is charged to a different turn). Combat is the share of fights won; A1 hallway is the share of ordinary Act 1 fights (not elites or the boss) won, and Boss the share of boss fights won (superscript: boss fights played). Act is the share of acts cleared among acts entered, pooled over Acts 1–3. Run is the share of runs that cleared Act 3. ℎ50 is the human time at which a logistic in log time, fitted with each scale weighted equally, crosses 50%, with each scale placed at a human time from Mega Crit's telemetry: 10 s for a turn, 10 s per turn of an average fight, the mean of the median times to complete Acts 1–3 (8.8, 11.9 and 20.3min, taken from players who completed each act), and the median run that kills the Heart (50min). Human rows come from Appx. D and have no turn or combat data.

Table 29: Effect of the knowledge reskin. None shows the real game names and is the baseline; Themed is our default Lich's Lair reskin; Random replaces every name with pronounceable nonsense; Permuted swaps each name for another real game name of the same kind; Perm.+themed applies the same permutation in the themed vocabulary. All with xml notes, a read-write memory bank and generic guidance. Pooled over models: each method is compared with its baseline only on matched runs (the same model on the same seed; Pairs, over Agents models), and Acts, Floor and A1 (mean acts cleared, mean final floor and Act 1 win rate) are over those runs. Usage is compared on like-for-like floors only: the same model, seed, act and room type, and the same occurrence of that room type within the act, kept only where every method run on that model and seed completed it (Floors), so a method is neither credited with cheap early floors nor charged for expensive late ones. Calls and k tokens (input, including cached, plus output, in thousands) are means per floor; the token difference is the ratio of totals. Each Δ is the method minus its baseline. All runs are A20 on the held-out seeds, each model at its main-table reasoning setting. Models, by method: Themed: Qwen3.8 27B, Qwen3.6 35B-A3B, Qwen3.5 122B-A10B, Claude Haiku 4.5, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, Gemini 3.8 Flash, Gemini 3.8 Flash (low), Nemotron 3 Nano Omni, GPT-5.6 Luna, gpt-oss-120b, GLM-5.3, GLM-5.3 Flash; Random, Permuted and Perm.+themed: Qwen3.8 27B, Qwen3.6 35B-A3B, Qwen3.5 122B-A10B, Gemini 3.8 Flash (low), Nemotron 3 Nano Omni, GPT-5.6 Luna, gpt-oss-120b, GLM-5.3 Flash. Per-model results are in Table 30.

Table 21: Recognition of the reskinned game, from each run’s own text (reasoning, prose and tool-call arguments). Per arm: Rec. runs whose text names the real game or a real entity name the arm does not display; Game runs naming “Slay the Spire”/“StS”; Names median distinct real entity names per run. Themed also gives the first seed (floor) with recognition. The Permuted arm displays the title and real names (for the wrong entities), so there only undisplayed names and “StS” count. Memory, None: runs whose newly written memories use real names when the arm shows them (a sanity check; the real-names arm has no local logs).

Table 10: A20 Heart Ironclad by hours of Slay the Spire played, from Mega Crit’s run telemetry (build 2020-07-30). Hours is the player’s cumulative play time when the run ended (bin and bin median). Acts is the mean number of acts cleared per run.

Table 16: Which forecasts track play. The Spearman correlation, over the 20 models of Table 1, between mean acts cleared and the error of each forecast, pooled over each model's runs: mean absolute error for the two HP forecasts, made when ending a turn, and the calibration error of Fig. 14 for the two probability forecasts, made at the end of every floor. Negative means the models that forecast better play better. Every model plays Act 1, so the Act 1 column compares all of them on forecasts about the same part of the game, while the first column also counts later acts, which only the stronger models reach and where hits are larger. Next-turn HP is close to arithmetic once enemy intents are shown, so its error measures how well a model reads the fight rather than what it knows of its own play. Almost no run is won (1.5% of run-win forecasts), so the run-win error mostly measures how much chance a model gives itself. The bottom rows correlate the scores plotted in the two figures, which combine two forecasts each and are medians over runs.

Table 4: Example entries of the five reskin mappings (Table 29). Under none each entity keeps the name in the second column. Card names are shown verbatim. N.B. There are some in-game effects which act on “cards containing Strike”; a permutation would make that rule name a family the model cannot see, so in both permuted mappings the Strike family is marked with a dagger and the rule refers to it. papers.abstract: A latent recurrent language model applies a shared block of layers repeatedly, so one checkpoint can trade inference compute for accuracy by changing the loop count. At one loop, however, such models typically fall well short of a non-recurrent model of the same size, a one-loop tax that makes a separate non-recurrent model the better choice whenever latency matters. We present Elastic Latent Recurrence (ELR), a recipe for training looped language models without this tax. At one loop, an ELR model costs the same to serve as a non-recurrent model of the same size and, trained on the same data, reaches similar accuracy. Each additional loop then buys more accuracy for more inference compute. Three choices make this work: a gated state update with a learned step size, loop counts mixed within each optimizer update, and conditioning each pass on its loop index and budget. The first two preserve one-loop accuracy, and the third lowers loss at every additional loop. Mixed depths can be introduced late in pretraining to limit the added training cost, and with zero-initialized conditioning added at the switch, this late schedule reaches lower loss than mixed-depth training from scratch. In MoE models, reusing first-loop expert routes on later loops cuts mixed-depth update time by 11.7% with no measurable change in accuracy. At inference, keeping only the last loop's attention KV cache holds attention KV memory at its one-loop level while retaining most of the gain from additional loops. On 4B dense and 30B-A3B MoE hybrid models, ELR at one loop is 0.52 points below and 1.04 points above its matched baseline on a ten-task average, and four loops add 7.25 and 4.75 points. Carried through post-training, the recipe yields Koi-4B, a single checkpoint that scores an estimated 18 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at one loop, matching Qwen3.5-4B, and 29 at four loops.
authors: Faisal Ladhak, Shantanu Acharya, Santiago Akle Serano, Simeng Sun, Boris Ginsburg, Krishna C Puvvada
bullets: Addresses the one-loop accuracy tax that often makes recurrent models unattractive under latency constraints.
Uses gated state updates with learned step sizes, mixed loop counts during training, and loop-index/budget conditioning.
Late mixed-depth training can reduce added training cost; reusing MoE expert routes cuts update time by 11.7% without measurable accuracy loss.
Retaining only the final loop’s attention KV cache keeps KV memory at the one-loop level while preserving most multi-loop gains.

On 4B dense and 30B-A3B MoE models, four loops improve ten-task averages by 7.25 and 4.75 points, respectively; the post-trained Koi-4B reaches estimated Intelligence Index scores of 18 at one loop and 29 at four.

papers.abstract: Modern video-language models are increasingly treated as general-purpose video reasoners, yet it remains unclear whether they robustly capture temporal dynamics in safety-critical settings such as driving. We study this question through controlled ego-motion tasks that require identifying actions from driving videos. Across video-language models, we find that standard prompting, visual prompting, few-shot prompting, and chain-of-thought prompting remain unreliable and highly task- and model-dependent, with persistent class biases, although newer models show substantial task-specific few-shot gains. In contrast, lightweight LoRA finetuning and simple probes trained on intermediate visual features recover strong motion-discriminative performance, indicating that motion-relevant cues are often present inside the models but are not reliably used by the final video-to-language pathway. These results suggest that, in driving, current video-language models remain unreliable temporal reasoners and often behave more like frame-level, bias-driven recognizers than dependable temporal world models.
authors: Shiva Sreeram, Erfan Aasi, Tsun-Hsuan Wang, Alaa Maalouf, Daniela Rus
bullets: The study evaluates temporal understanding through controlled ego-motion action-identification tasks in driving videos.
Standard, visual, few-shot, and chain-of-thought prompting are unreliable and strongly dependent on the task and model.
Models exhibit persistent class biases, though newer systems can gain substantially from task-specific few-shot examples.
Lightweight LoRA finetuning and probes on intermediate visual features achieve strong motion discrimination.
Findings suggest final video-to-language pathways underuse temporal cues, causing models to act more like frame-level recognizers than temporal world models.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Pipeline for probing ego-motion understanding in video-language models. We evaluate increasingly structured approaches, from training-free prompting to lightweight learning-based probes. In standard prompting, the model directly classifies the vehicle’s motion. Visual prompting adds a green bounding box around a static reference object to test whether explicit spatial grounding improves motion inference. In fusion of visual and text, labeled few-shot video examples are provided before the query. Chain-of-thought prompting explicitly relates temporal changes in the reference object’s position or size to ego-motion. We then apply LoRA finetuning to test whether motion distinctions can be learned under lightweight supervision, and feature extraction to train simple classifiers on intermediate visual representations and examine where motion information remains decodable. Overall, prompt-level methods remain strongly model- and task-dependent, whereas learning-based approaches recover substantially stronger motion discrimination.
