papers.abstract: Online reinforcement learning (RL) fine-tunes diffusion models with black-box rewards, but reverse-process methods such as Flow-GRPO are limited in efficiency by poor credit assignment, while forward-process methods such as DiffusionNFT are efficient yet unstable without carefully tuned exponential-moving-average (EMA) off-policy training. We show that NFT-style objectives contain a hidden forward--reverse consistency force that joint positive--negative training cancels only partially, and that EMA stabilizes training through restoration rather than off-policy rollouts. We introduce DiffusionART (Diffusion Reinforcement with Aggregation-First Reward Tilting), which aggregates each prompt's rewards into a shared reward-improving direction for reverse-process states, removing the consistency force by construction, and adds a trust-region-masked second update for drift-adaptive restoration without EMA tuning. It requires no differentiable reward model, remains effective with fewer samples per prompt, and supports pairwise reward models (DiffusionART-Pairwise). Across image and video generation, DiffusionART trains efficiently and stably without per-task tuning. In particular, on HunyuanVideo-13B with equally weighted visual and motion quality rewards, DiffusionART reaches the late-stage mean reward levels of DiffusionNFT and Flow-GRPO-Fast with 12.02 and 11.72 times fewer GPU hours, respectively, while achieving 28.8% and 53.0% higher mean training rewards.
authors: Zhenglin Wan, Jiayu Chen, Zhengfeiyang Zhang, Pengfei Zhou, Wangbo Zhao, Fangyuan Kong, Pengfei Wan, Kun Gai, Yang You
bullets: Addresses inefficient credit assignment in reverse-process RL and instability in forward-process methods.
Aggregates per-prompt rewards into a shared reward-improving direction for reverse-process states, eliminating a conflicting consistency force.
Uses a trust-region-masked second update for drift-adaptive restoration instead of carefully tuned EMA training.
Requires no differentiable reward model, works with fewer samples per prompt, and supports pairwise rewards through DiffusionART-Pairwise.
Across image and video generation, it achieves comparable late-stage rewards with substantially fewer GPU hours and higher mean training rewards on HunyuanVideo-13B.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates large language model inference by using a lightweight drafter to propose multiple tokens that are subsequently verified in parallel by the target model. Recent diffusion-based drafters make this paradigm particularly attractive: deep attention-based neural backbones provide strong predictions, while drafting multiple future positions in parallel avoids the sequential cost of autoregressive generation. This parallelism, however, comes at a cost. Tokens within a draft block are predicted without access to the realized identities of preceding draft tokens, removing intra-block dependencies that would naturally be available under autoregressive generation. We introduce DCOCO (DFlash Contextual Corrector), a lightweight mechanism that restores these dependencies while preserving parallel drafting. Rather than committing to each position's top prediction, DCOCO retains multiple candidate tokens and evaluates their contextual compatibility across adjacent draft positions in parallel, enabling contextually informed token selection at low additional cost. Across four verifier backbones and ten benchmarks, DCOCO achieves the highest average throughput in every evaluated configuration, spanning greedy and stochastic decoding with and without extended reasoning, with speedups of up to 6.6x over vanilla decoding. Its advantage persists under concurrent serving: DCOCO outperforms the strongest competing method by 6-23% across 4-32 concurrent requests, while other sequential correctors fall below uncorrected DFlash at these loads. These results demonstrate that recovering intra-block dependencies through parallel contextual scoring delivers consistent acceleration across decoding regimes and serving loads.
authors: Roy Eisenstadt, Harel Lidar, Tal Gonen, Omer Luxembourg, Itamar Zimerman, Lior Wolf, Eli David, Ilan Naiman

Speedups reach up to 6.6× over vanilla decoding and remain 6–23% better than the strongest competitor under 4–32 concurrent requests.

papers.abstract: Prior research on learning from humans often requires real human demonstrations. But advances in video generation models offer a new paradigm: we can now prompt these generators to make synthetic videos of the task. On the plus side, these synthetic videos take place in the robot's current environment, and do not require actual human teaching. However, while the generated videos appear to show plausible motions, they lack both physical consistency and robot grounding, and thus the robot cannot directly roll out the trajectory shown by the video. In this paper we seek to formalize the process of going from synthetic video generation to real-world robot trajectories for zero-shot manipulation tasks. We recognize that this problem is an instance of constrained optimization. The object trajectories extracted from the synthetic video provide an initial guess at the correct motion, and the robot must refine these trajectories (for instance, within a digital twin) while enforcing physical feasibility and semantic consistency. Our optimization-based formalism provides insights into the video generation properties necessary for success. Specifically, we show that the video generation must probabilistically seed the search within a semantic basin of attraction where the trajectory can be locally modified without losing its task alignment. Our analysis further reveals that state-of-the-art approaches can be viewed as instances of our unified formalism with key simplifications. In our experiments we remove these simplifications to more closely match the underlying optimization, leading to more robust zero-shot trajectories from synthetic videos and improving average task success by 34.1% compared to the best-performing baseline. See videos at our project website: https://collab.me.vt.edu/CASTER
authors: Yinlong Dai, Homanga Bharadhwaj, Dylan P. Losey
bullets: Synthetic videos avoid real human demonstrations and can depict tasks in the robot’s environment.
Video-derived object trajectories serve as initial guesses, which are refined under physical-feasibility and semantic-consistency constraints.
Success requires generated videos to seed trajectories within a task-aligned semantic basin of attraction.
The framework unifies existing approaches and removes simplifying assumptions to better match the underlying optimization.
Experiments report a 34.1% improvement in average task success over the best-performing baseline.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of CASTER. From the synthetic videos we extract the object trajectories, which then serve as initial guesses for trajectory optimization within the digital twin. (Bottom) The trajectories extracted from synthetic videos do not need to be perfect: instead, they must lie within a semantic basin of attraction where the optimization can locally modify the trajectory shape without removing its semantic meaning. (Bottom Right) We perform constrained optimization so that the robot’s actions in the digital twin cause the objects to move similarly to their video trajectories, while enforcing kinematic constraints so that the output can be directly executed by the real robot.

We bridge the gap between generation and deployment by developing an optimization-based formalism. Under this formalism the robot uses multiple synthetic videos to seed its search and identify task-critical features. By matching these features while enforcing semantic consistency and physical feasibility, we can transfer erroneous videos to successful zero-shot trajectories.

papers.abstract: Zeroth-order (ZO) optimization offers a memory-efficient alternative to backpropagation for fine-tuning large language models. However, existing ZO methods typically sample training examples uniformly, overlooking their evolving importance and leaving avoidable estimation variance. To address this limitation, we propose Sample-Adaptive Zeroth-Order Optimization (SAZO), which learns sample importance online and adaptively allocates queries to accelerate convergence. SAZO extracts gradient-norm information from existing directional differences to estimate sample importance without access to true gradients. Furthermore, to track evolving importance from sparse minibatch feedback, SAZO maintains per-example exponential moving averages that aggregate observations across updates. The method requires no additional model evaluations and only $O(N)$ additional scalar state compared with MeZO. We prove that SAZO asymptotically matches the leading convergence term of the minimum-variance sampling oracle, and achieves a strictly faster convergence rate than standard methods. Extensive experiments across four model families demonstrate improved average downstream performance and up to $6\times$ faster convergence to the same training loss in terms of query count.
authors: Haiyuan Wan, Yanyi Li, Weicheng Lin, Cong Fang
bullets: Uniform sampling in existing zeroth-order methods can waste queries and increase estimation variance as sample importance changes.
SAZO estimates sample importance from directional differences, without requiring true gradients.
Per-example exponential moving averages track importance under sparse minibatch feedback.
It adds only O(N) scalar state over MeZO and theoretically approaches minimum-variance sampling convergence.
Experiments across four model families show improved average downstream performance and up to 6× faster convergence by query count.

papers.abstract: Memory allows large language model (LLM) agents to use past experience, often stored as textual records, when responding to requests. For embodied agents that control robots, visual and spatial observations introduce a broader choice of memory modalities, affecting both the information available for subsequent tasks and the model inference costs of constructing and using memory. We introduce MeMoREval, a benchmark for studying this problem through a controlled experience-request protocol. Agents first experience a sequence of events without knowing the subsequent tasks, and subsequently they use memory to respond to information and action requests without receiving new observations. The benchmark comprises 53 tasks across four simulated indoor environments and measures task success alongside the inference costs of memory construction and use. Our reference evaluations reveal that storing frames outperforms storing generated descriptions at lower write-time inference cost for the primary model, while storing frames with scene graphs achieves the highest aggregate task success for every tested model. Extensions to accumulated experience, selective frame retention, and visual input to memory writers demonstrate how the benchmark accommodates further memory-design investigations. Two physical-robot demonstrations establish the feasibility of applying its protocol beyond simulation.
authors: Junxiang Wang, Yuchen Liu, Yi Wu, Guofei Chen, Nir Pechuk, Tao Chen, Zackory Erickson, Yuzhe Qin, Tianyu Li
bullets: Evaluates memory through a controlled protocol: agents observe events first, then answer information and action requests without new observations.
Covers 53 tasks across four simulated indoor environments, measuring success plus memory construction and usage costs.
For the primary model, storing frames outperforms generated descriptions while requiring lower write-time inference cost.
Combining frames with scene graphs achieves the highest aggregate task success across all tested models.
The protocol also supports studies of experience accumulation, selective frame retention, visual memory writers, and physical-robot deployment.

papers.abstract: Humanoid robots have many degrees of freedom and contact surfaces, yet most loco-manipulation research restricts manipulation to the hands and avoids other body contacts with the environment. To extend manipulation beyond the hands, we present PanTact, a system that learns humanoid whole-body dexterity, the capability to manipulate with any suitable body surface, directly from robot-free human demonstrations. Our key idea is to use contact as manipulation-centric information that transfers across embodiments. Contact locations and timing specify the interactions needed to accomplish a task, while the robot chooses how to coordinate its body to realize them within its own physical constraints. Specifically, PanTact captures, learns, and executes whole-body contact via: 1) a wearable, robot-free data collection interface that augments egocentric vision and bimanual UMI grippers with whole-body modular contact patches to record body contact locations and states; 2) a visuomotor policy that mitigates the egocentric observation gap and predicts whole-body contact goals; and 3) contact-aware whole-body control formulations that realize active contact goals using suitable robot surfaces. We deploy PanTact on a Unitree G1 humanoid without additional body contact sensors, demonstrating whole-body dexterity involving body support, pushing, sweeping, and load-sharing. Website: https://pantact.github.io
authors: Xiaomeng Xu, Han Zhang, Zhian Ruan, Xiaofeng Guo, Jinkun Cao, Ruihan Yang, Carmelo Sferrazza, Shuran Song, Guanya Shi

Uses a wearable interface combining egocentric vision, bimanual grippers, and modular whole-body contact patches to capture demonstrations.
A visuomotor policy predicts whole-body contact goals while accounting for the egocentric observation gap.
Contact-aware whole-body control realizes these goals within the robot’s physical constraints.
Demonstrated on a Unitree G1 for support, pushing, sweeping, and load-sharing without additional body contact sensors.

papers.abstract: Embodied coding agents construct robot policies from natural-language instructions by generating executable programs and refining them from execution feedback. This refinement assumes that execution feedback reveals whether the task succeeded and, after a failure, provides sufficient evidence to guide program revision. Aerial manipulation violates this assumption in two ways. Payload constraints restrict onboard camera coverage and leave task-critical outcomes outside the robot's view (partial observability), while strong dynamic coupling and limited control margins make physical interactions fragile (limited interaction robustness) and leave failure causes unresolved. Re-examining the same feedback cannot recover observations that were never collected or separate failure causes that the available evidence does not distinguish. To acquire this missing evidence, we introduce Active Feedback (AF), an active "View and Probe" framework. When execution feedback leaves unresolved questions, the agent synthesizes a separate diagnostic program that runs in simulation to inspect unseen outcomes from informative viewpoints (View) or test hypotheses about failure causes through targeted physical interactions (Probe). Across six simulated aerial manipulation tasks with 60 trials per condition, AF reduces false completion declarations from 25 to 5 and raises final task success from 31.7% to 75% compared with terminal feedback under the same coding-agent configuration and task-execution limit. Using shared robot APIs, task programs refined with AF in simulation run on a physical aerial manipulator without task-program source-code modification and complete multi-stage manipulation tasks in the real world. These results show that executable diagnosis fills gaps in execution feedback for embodied coding agents, improving both completion assessment and program refinement in aerial manipulation.
authors: Jaewoo Lee, Jeongyeon Seo, Sihyun Cho, Gyeongrak Choe, Yutong Wang, Bavin Saravanan, Jia-Bin Huang, Furong Huang, Sebastian Scherer, Guanya Shi, H. Jin Kim, Seungjae Lee, Dongjae Lee
bullets: Aerial manipulation suffers from partial observability and fragile physical interactions, making ordinary execution feedback insufficient for program refinement.

Across six simulated tasks, false completion declarations fell from 25 to 5, while final success increased from 31.7% to 75% under the same agent configuration and task limit.
Programs refined with Active Feedback in simulation transferred to a physical aerial manipulator without source-code changes and completed multi-stage tasks.
The approach is demonstrated within the scope of simulated evaluation and selected real-world aerial manipulation tasks.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive decoding is less suited to non-causally ordered data, e.g., cross-references or future dependencies, since their outputs cannot be revised post hoc, unlike iterative human reasoning. Diffusion LLMs partially mitigate this limitation but still cannot flexibly insert or remove arbitrary numbers of tokens from a pre-generated context. We design AutoIndexer as a generative model with a novel training and decoding mechanism that simulates a Chain of Edits, allowing the model to flexibly modify its prior outputs in hindsight via token insertions, substitutions, and deletions. The model learns to predict marker tokens for opening and closing edits, simultaneously moving a cursor to positions in the existing token sequence, analogous to a text editor. Training sequences are obtained by perturbing ground-truth labels with inverse chained edit operations, and the model learns to edit by undoing those inverses. The perturbation training allows AutoIndexer to be robust to erroneous context and adaptable to editing tasks such as code correction. We demonstrate that our method exhibits post-generation context-editing capabilities that most autoregressive and diffusion models lack without compromising performance on standard LLM benchmarks. The code is available at https://github.com/AutodeskAILab/autoindexer.
authors: Shu Ishida, Aliasghar Khani, Tianyu Zhang, The Cong Luong, James Seale Smith, Adam Gaier
bullets: Addresses causal decoding’s difficulty with non-causal dependencies and outputs that require hindsight revision.
Trains models on perturbed sequences created through inverse chained edits, teaching them to undo errors.
Predicts edit markers while moving a cursor through the existing token sequence, like a text editor.
Supports flexible post-generation context editing and potential applications such as code correction.
The abstract reports retained performance on standard LLM benchmarks, but gives no quantitative results or detailed scope limits.

papers.selection_reason: Novel decoding mechanism for LLMs with edit operations; fits language foundation model architecture research.
papers.title: AutoIndexer: Flexible-Order Decoding by Training Causal Models on Chains of Edits
papers.tldr: AutoIndexer augments causal language models with chain-of-edit decoding so they can revise generated text through insertions, substitutions, and deletions.

papers.abstract: Masked diffusion models (MDMs) generate discrete data by iteratively unmasking multiple tokens in parallel using a learned mask predictor. Their output carries two errors: parallelization error due to parallel sampling, and estimation error from the mask predictor learned with finite samples. Existing theory treats these errors separately, and the available statistical bounds typically scale with the number $V^L$ of length-$L$ sequences over a vocabulary of size $V$, suffering from the curse of dimensionality. In this work, we establish end-to-end statistical guarantees showing that transformer-based MDMs learn structured distributions with a sample complexity governed by their latent structure. Specifically, we model this structure through mixtures of hidden Markov trees, which capture latent dependencies within components and heterogeneity across components. When the data distribution is well approximated by such a mixture, a transformer-based MDM with parallel unmasking schedules achieves $\varepsilon$-accurate sampling in KL divergence with $\widetilde{O}(LK_{\mathrm{par}}/\varepsilon)$ training samples, where $K_{\mathrm{par}}$ is polynomial in $L$, $V$, the number of hidden states, and the number of mixture components. The transformer network and sampling procedure require no knowledge of the tree topologies or component parameters, thereby adapting to the unknown latent structure automatically. Overall, our results provide theoretical justification for the empirical effectiveness of MDMs on real-world data.
bullets: Addresses both parallelization and finite-sample estimation errors in masked diffusion models.
Models structured data as mixtures of hidden Markov trees, capturing latent dependencies and component heterogeneity.
Proves end-to-end ε-accurate sampling in KL divergence with approximately O(LK_par/ε) training samples.
The polynomial factor K_par depends on sequence length, vocabulary size, hidden states, and mixture components.
The method adapts to unknown tree topologies and component parameters without requiring them as input.
papers.selection_reason: Provides theoretical guarantees for transformer-based Masked Diffusion Models learning structured distributions, bridging video understanding and latent dynamics prediction.
papers.title: Transformer-Based Masked Diffusion Models Provably Learn Distributions with Latent Structure
papers.tldr: Transformer-based masked diffusion models can learn discrete distributions with latent structure using sample complexity that depends on the structure rather than the full sequence space.

papers.abstract: Boundary-value problems for the Laplace equation develop singular behaviour near corners, edges and junctions that smooth approximators resolve poorly. We combine holomorphic neural networks with singular functions derived from the local geometry and boundary conditions. The representation is harmonic by construction, so no interior residual is needed: the network fits the smooth remainder from boundary data alone, and the enrichment terms capture the singular behaviour. Singular exponents are trainable, so the construction also applies when the local expansion is not known in advance. We extend the approach to three dimensions using independent networks evaluated along complex null directions. The enriched model is the most accurate tested method on every problem. Its margin is several orders of magnitude where the enrichment captures the singularity exactly, and a factor of about 1.7-2.1 over the next-best method on a CdZnTe radiation detector with many singular sites, in both two and three dimensions.
authors: Kalp Shah, Andrei Vlad Nicula, Mihnea Andrei B\^arsan, Robert-Stefan Sofroni, Agneya Bhardwaj, Jan Jel\'inek, Alejandro Valverde Mahou
bullets: Targets the poor performance of smooth approximators near geometric and boundary-induced singularities.
Combines holomorphic neural networks with geometry- and boundary-informed singular functions.
Produces harmonic solutions by construction, avoiding interior residual evaluation and fitting only the smooth remainder at the boundary.
Trains singular exponents when the local expansion is unknown and extends the method to 3D via complex null directions.
Achieves the best tested accuracy on all problems, with especially large gains for exactly captured singularities and about 1.7–2.1× improvement on a CdZnTe detector problem.

papers.selection_reason: Applies enriched holomorphic neural networks to solve 2D and 3D Laplace boundary value problems, relevant to 3D vision and geometric modeling.
papers.title: Enriched Holomorphic Neural Networks for 2D and 3D Laplace Problems
papers.tldr: Enriched holomorphic neural networks solve 2D and 3D Laplace problems more accurately by explicitly modeling corner, edge, and junction singularities from boundary data alone.

papers.abstract: EliteTable is a self-improving program-search algorithm guided by large language models (LLMs) that uses a fixed-capacity table of high-scoring solutions to guide new proposals, edits of existing solutions, and remixes of several solutions. Performance was evaluated across six Gymnasium control tasks, each with ten generations and fifty candidate slots per generation. Each task was evaluated across ten independently initialized searches. Candidate-score medians rose between the first and final generations in all six tasks, and selected-winner search-score medians rose in five. In CartPole-v1, the selected winner reached the search-score ceiling in the first generation of all ten searches. All ten paired held-out endpoints improved in four of the six tasks. BipedalWalker-v3 and CarRacing-v3 improved without reaching their reporting targets. Six of ten Acrobot-v1 searches declined on held-out episodes, and the median paired change was negative. The results document improvement during program search and the transfer of selected-winner gains to new episodes in some tasks. Comparisons and ablations are needed to establish EliteTable's relative performance and the contributions of its components.
bullets: Maintains a fixed-capacity table of strong solutions to guide new proposals, edits, and multi-solution remixes.
Evaluated over ten generations with fifty candidates per generation across ten independent searches for each of six tasks.
Candidate-score medians increased from the first to final generation in all tasks; selected-winner medians increased in five.
All held-out endpoints improved in four tasks, while Acrobot-v1 often declined and some tasks did not reach reporting targets.
Comparisons and ablations remain necessary to assess relative performance and component contributions.

papers.abstract: Training-free feature reuse accelerates diffusion transformer inference by replacing full denoising computation at selected steps with cached approximations. Existing methods mainly improve the reconstruction of skipped features, but we find that once a stable first-order reconstructor is used, increasing reconstruction complexity brings limited gains, whereas the placement of exact-computation steps has a much larger effect on fidelity. More importantly, absolute shallow-probe variation is jointly affected by input-trajectory displacement and network response strength, and therefore does not directly reflect cache risk. We address this confounding by normalizing probe-output variation with the corresponding input displacement, yielding a directional gain per unit trajectory movement. Based on this signal, we propose CacheScope, which identifies high-risk reuse steps online and selectively falls back to full denoising computation while leaving the underlying cache reconstructor unchanged. CacheScope requires no additional training, gradients, auxiliary networks, or prompt-specific offline schedule optimization. Across FLUX.1-dev, Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B, and Open-Sora 1.2, CacheScope achieves up to 3.57x acceleration and reduces median LPIPS by up to 70.1% over the strongest probe-based baseline.
authors: Qinhan Lyu, Jusheng Zhang, Zhixing Zhang, Hao Liu, Zijie Liang, Jin Jiang, Keze Wang
bullets: Exact-step placement matters more than increasing the complexity of a stable cache-feature reconstructor.
Raw shallow-probe variation confounds input-trajectory movement with network response strength and can misestimate cache risk.
CacheScope normalizes probe-output variation by input displacement to estimate directional gain per unit movement.
It selectively falls back to full denoising at high-risk steps while keeping the existing cache reconstructor unchanged.
Across three diffusion models, it reduces median LPIPS by up to 70.1% versus the strongest probe-based baseline.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of the CacheScope insight. Under a fixed cache reconstructor and a fixed exact-compute budget, more flexible reconstruction rules do not consistently outperform a bounded first-order reconstructor, while the placement of exact evaluations dominates fidelity. Raw probe variation ∆yt conflates trajectory displacement with network response; CacheScope instead schedules exact computation using the trajectory-conditioned sensitivity st = ∆yt/(∆xt + ϵ).

Figure 3: Overview of CacheScope. At every denoising step, the first transformer block is executed as a shallow probe. From its input and output we compute the relative trajectory movement ∆xt and probe response ∆yt, and accumulate the trajectoryconditioned sensitivity st = ∆yt/(∆xt+ ϵ) — the only change relative to raw probe scheduling. When the accumulator reaches the threshold τ , the remaining blocks are evaluated exactly and the cache is refreshed; otherwise the step is reconstructed by the unchanged bounded first-order reconstructor. Under classifier-free guidance, the two branches maintain independent accumulators and cache states.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes CacheScope, a method to accelerate diffusion transformer inference by identifying high-risk steps for exact computation, directly relevant to video diffusion acceleration.
papers.title: CacheScope: Exact-Compute Allocation for Training-Free Diffusion Acceleration
papers.tldr: CacheScope accelerates training-free diffusion inference by allocating exact computation to high-risk denoising steps identified through normalized probe variation, achieving up to 3.57× speedup with substantially better fidelity.

papers.abstract: Continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) foundation models encode each day as one vector that mixes who the person is, what happened that day and how the sensor measured it, so measurement differences travel with the representation into new cohorts. We ask whether pretraining can place the measurement component that harms transfer in known coordinates, so that deployment drops them with a fixed projection and no target data. GlucoPRISM supervises a GlucoFM backbone with response contracts, rules for how each part of the representation should change when only the day or only the sensor changes: a 64-dimensional Trait band should change with neither, a 48-dimensional State band only across days, and a 16-dimensional Sensor band should track the device. Synthetic sensor views calibrated on paired Dexcom and Libre recordings, different-day pairs and glucose-summary targets supply this supervision without clinical labels. Across twelve cross-cohort directions, dropping the Sensor band from the same frozen encoder raises mean transfer AUROC from 68.75 to 73.57, against 69.3 for GlucoFM. The gain has two parts. Into CGMacros, the one target cohort recorded with two sensor types, filtering adds 11 to 19 points, and this holds when the generator is recalibrated on half of the participants and scored on the other half. On the other eight directions filtering is neutral and the encoder itself exceeds GlucoFM by 3.5 points. The device remains linearly decodable after filtering, so the filter removes a device-related component that harms transfer rather than all measurement information. The retained bands improve window AUROC on thirteen of fourteen public task--cohort cells (Holm-adjusted p=0.031) and correlation on fourteen of fifteen clinical endpoints in an external cohort of 9,303 participants.
authors: Adinath Madhavrao Dukre, Abdullah Mohammad, Yifan Lu, Eran Segal, Ahmed Metwally, Imran Razzak
bullets: CGM representations entangle person traits, daily state, and sensor effects, allowing device differences to harm transfer.
Protocol-supervised pretraining organizes representations into Trait (64D), State (48D), and Sensor (16D) bands with distinct invariance/change rules.
Supervision uses synthetic sensor views, different-day pairs, and glucose-summary targets rather than clinical labels.
Across 12 transfer directions, removing the Sensor band increased mean AUROC from 68.75 to 73.57, versus 69.3 for GlucoFM.
Filtering produced 11–19 point gains in the dual-sensor CGMacros cohort; other directions were neutral, while the encoder itself improved by 3.5 points.

papers.abstract: Distribution operators need visibility of behind-the-meter photovoltaic (PV) generation, yet most residential customers are observed only through net smart meters. Deep-learning-based PV disaggregation can restore this visibility, but its operational value depends on whether the model serves known customers, new customers, future periods, or new regions. We quantify this dependence using four deployment regimes that separate household transfer from temporal extrapolation, applied to Ausgrid smart-meter data with cross-dataset adaptation to the Pecan Street data. Using a fixed training protocol, we benchmark representative deep sequence architectures for PV disaggregation under regime-matched evaluation. At a fixed 48-hour context length, daylight mean absolute error (MAE) of the best model rises from 0.104~kW on seen households in the future test period to 0.185~kW on unseen households over the same period, and under a fixed training contract the deployment regime explains far more of the error variation than model choice. Under target-domain normalization, fine-tuning on five target-region households reduces source-model transfer error by 28\%--36\%. Long input windows help known-customer extrapolation, while their new-customer benefits vary by model. These findings suggest regime-matched error budgets, limited target supervision for model adaptation in new regions, and use-case-dependent context selection for energy data analytics.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in molecular discovery and structure elucidation, where decisions depend on physical observations. Existing evaluations primarily focus on end-to-end molecular reconstruction, where correct predictions do not necessarily indicate reliance on the supplied properties. We introduce MolP2SBench, a benchmark for molecular property-to-structure (P2S) reasoning in LLMs. Each task presents a masked molecular scaffold with given properties and asks the model to select the missing structure from plausible candidates. We shuffle or replace properties to test reliance on correct property-structure pairing and responsiveness to counterfactual property changes. A channel-wise leaderboard uses Property-Grounded Recovery (PGR), giving equal weight to source and counterfactual recovery. Evaluating seven models, we find that LLMs can use physical properties for structure prediction, but performance varies substantially across property types. Higher accuracy with a property does not necessarily imply greater responsiveness to it: a model may benefit more from $^1$H NMR than from $^{13}$C NMR, yet be less likely to change its prediction when the $^1$H data is replaced. LLM performance also need not reflect the relative difficulty of these properties for human chemists. Although UV-Vis spectra provide less direct structural information than NMR spectra, Astra achieves higher accuracy with UV-Vis data than with NMR peaks. MolP2SBench supports studying how LLMs extract and use physical-property information, revealing patterns that may differ from conventional chemical intuition and providing a foundation for more reliably property-grounded models for molecular and quantum-chemical inference. Code and dataset: https://github.com/DUAL-Xiao/MolP2SBench.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive video diffusion models maintain a growing attention key-value (KV) cache, making memory a key bottleneck for long video generation. Recently, clustering-based quantization has emerged as an effective method to compress video KV caches by grouping similar key and value vectors then quantizing residual errors. However, when later frames attend to the compressed history, small reconstruction errors can compound as the video grows. Beyond the within-layer similarity exploited by clustering, we find strong dependencies across cache layers in video models. This motivates Coral-KV - Calibrated Offline, Residual-coded, and Adapted Locally - a KV-cache compression framework that uses cache states in each layer to predict keys and values in subsequent layers, then quantizes the remaining prediction residuals. We construct compact block-diagonal-plus-low-rank (block-DPLR) predictors: block-diagonal components model channel relationships within each attention head, while a global low-rank term models dependencies between heads. Coral-KV exposes a flexible fidelity-memory trade-off: it can reuse its predictors across videos or refit lightweight block-diagonal predictors to the current video for higher fidelity. Across extensive evaluations on both HY-WorldPlay and MAGI-1, our reusable configuration improves PSNR over QVG-4 by 0.32 dB and 4.95 dB, respectively, while using 48% and 37% less cache memory. Against QVG-Pro, our video-adapted configuration improves MAGI-1 PSNR by 3.77 dB while using 33.7% less cache memory. Coral-KV also maintains higher reconstruction fidelity over extended generation and reduces temporal discontinuities while retaining comparable generation latency.
authors: Albert Ge, Akash Haridas, Utkarsh Saxena, Ruijing Yang, Ian Colbert, Frederic Sala, Vikram Appia, Emad Barsoum
bullets: Addresses growing KV-cache memory and error accumulation in long video diffusion generation.
Uses block-diagonal-plus-low-rank predictors to capture within-head channel and across-head dependencies.
Supports reusable predictors for efficiency or lightweight video-specific refitting for higher fidelity.
Improves PSNR while reducing cache memory versus QVG-4 and QVG-Pro across HY-WorldPlay and MAGI-1.

(a) average PSNR versus total compressed KV storage across 32 prompts per model, using the same storage accounting as in Table 1; stars mark our selected reusable codec. (b) Qualitative comparisons of BF16, QVG-1, QVG-Pro, and reusable CORAL-KV on matched frames.

Figure 2: Cross-layer prediction and quantization-boundary effects. (a) Linear maps predict current-layer keys from previous-layer keys and current-layer values from previous-layer values. Adding current-layer keys improves value prediction. The key and augmented value maps explain over 80% of the variance on both models. (b) We compare reconstruction MSE from predictors and centroids on the same keys and values before residual quantization. Bars show relative MSE normalized to the centroid result. Predictors significantly reduce reconstruction MSE compared with centroids. (c) QVG fits video-specific centroids online when a cache block reaches its token limit, whereas CORAL-KV reuses offline-calibrated predictors. The yellow box highlights facial distortion in QVG’s first frame generated from compressed history; visible degradation also appears in the clothing and ski pole.

Figure 3 illustrates how Coral-KV reconstructs each layer of a compressed cache block. Once a block is full, we encode its KV states and retain quantized codes and scales. When later chunks attend to that block, we reconstruct its keys and values layer by layer. At layer ℓ > 0, a tokenwise linear map PK ℓ predicts keys from reconstructed keys at layer ℓ − 1. A second map PV ℓ predicts values from reconstructed keys at layer ℓ and reconstructed values at layer ℓ−1. Section 4.2 gives their compact parameterization. We augment both predictions with quantized residuals, where QR denotes the residual quantizer formally defined in Appendix B.1:

Figure 3: CORAL-KV reconstruction. At layer ℓ > 0, reconstructed cache states from layer ℓ−1 feed the predictors. The key predictor maps K̂ℓ−1 to K̃ℓ; adding the quantized key residual gives K̂ℓ. The value predictor maps [K̂ℓ, V̂ℓ−1] to Ṽℓ; adding the quantized value residual gives V̂ℓ. Both predictors use a block-diagonal component and a rank-r low-rank component.

papers.selection_reason: KV-cache compression for autoregressive video diffusion models; directly relevant to memory-efficient inference and video generation.
papers.title: CORAL-KV: Compact Cross-Layer Prediction and Residual Coding for Autoregressive Video KV Caches
papers.tldr: Coral-KV compresses autoregressive video KV caches by predicting later-layer states from earlier layers and quantizing only the residuals, reducing memory while preserving video quality.

papers.abstract: Sensing-aided beam prediction can reduce the beam-training overhead of millimeter-wave (mmWave) systems by leveraging environmental information from complementary modalities such as vision and position. However, the resulting sensing and inference pipeline can be energy-intensive, motivating the use of energy-efficient spiking neural networks (SNNs) as an alternative to conventional artificial neural networks (ANNs). In this work, we develop SNN architectures for beam prediction and systematically compare them with ANNs using position-only, vision-only, and multimodal inputs. Our results show that compact ANNs consistently outperform SNNs for position-only sensing. In contrast, for vision and multimodal sensing, SNNs achieve higher accuracy than ANNs at similar energy costs and require up to an order of magnitude less energy at a comparable accuracy. For example, the multimodal SNN achieves 58.08% top-1 accuracy, outperforming the closest-energy ANN by 18.11 percentage points. We further show that SNN accuracy is limited by the binary communication between layers rather than by model size. These results demonstrate the potential of SNNs for energy-efficient sensing-aided beam prediction while highlighting their accuracy limitation.
authors: Nhan Thanh Nguyen, Phuong Nam Tran, Mengyuan Ma, Huy T. Nguyen, Ahmed Alkhateeb, Markku Juntti
bullets: Sensing-aided beam prediction reduces mmWave beam-training overhead by using position and/or vision information.
The study compares SNNs and ANNs with position-only, vision-only, and multimodal inputs.
Compact ANNs outperform SNNs for position-only sensing.
For vision and multimodal inputs, SNNs provide higher accuracy at similar energy or use up to an order of magnitude less energy at comparable accuracy.
The multimodal SNN reaches 58.08% top-1 accuracy, 18.11 percentage points above the closest-energy ANN.

papers.selection_reason: Energy-efficient SNNs for sensing-aided beam prediction; fits efficient AI energy reduction focus.
papers.title: Energy-Efficient Spiking Neural Networks for Sensing-Aided Beam Prediction
papers.tldr: Spiking neural networks can make vision- and multimodal sensing-aided mmWave beam prediction substantially more energy-efficient, though their accuracy is limited by binary inter-layer communication.

papers.abstract: Sequence models with a fixed-size state avoid the quadratic cost of attention, but face a design choice. An input-dependent state transition gives content-dependent memory at the cost of FFT-based training, while a fixed transition keeps the O(T log T) convolutional path but reads memory the same way for every input. ResonatorLM, a recent model of the second kind, reads a bank of damped complex oscillators through a fixed learned phase per head. We make that readout phase a function of the current token, which adds input dependence to the read only, keeps the convolution exact, and costs 0.2 percent more parameters. An analysis of the untrained bank shows that phase does encode elapsed time, but an ordinary token falls below the background within 2-8 steps and no choice of damping extends linear reconstruction beyond about 16 tokens. In 6M-parameter character-level models on WikiText-2, the input-dependent phase matches the original at the training length and removes its failure beyond it: trained on 256 tokens and tested on 1024, perplexity falls from 12.81 to 3.76. We trace the failure to long-memory heads that accumulate more history than training exposed them to. The learned phase tracks the current character rather than distance and does not improve retrieval.
bullets: Fixed-state sequence models retain efficient O(T log T) convolution but normally read memory identically for every input.
The proposed input-dependent readout changes only the phase, preserving exact convolution and adding 0.2% parameters.
Untrained oscillators lose ordinary-token information after 2–8 steps, with linear reconstruction limited to about 16 tokens regardless of damping.
In 6M-parameter WikiText-2 character models trained on 256 tokens and tested on 1024, perplexity drops from 12.81 to 3.76 versus the original model.
The learned phase follows the current character rather than elapsed distance and does not improve retrieval; long-memory heads explain the baseline’s extrapolation failure.

papers.selection_reason: Improves the long-context capabilities of ResonatorLM sequence models by making the readout phase input-dependent, relevant to LLM architecture and context handling.
papers.title: An Input-Dependent Readout Phase for Resonant Sequence Models
papers.tldr: Making ResonatorLM’s oscillator readout phase depend on the current token preserves efficient convolution while substantially improving extrapolation to longer sequences.

papers.abstract: Small language models trained on a single local machine leave little room for architectural trial and error. Kairos combines bidirectional gated-DeltaNet linear attention and sliding-window attention over shared projections (LiZAttention2), block-wise Attention-Residual aggregation, a sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) feed-forward layer and a multi-scale byte-level codec, trained with a uniform-noise denoising objective over one byte space shared by text, image, audio, video, lidar and control streams; this report asks whether the combination optimizes at all before asking whether it is useful. We give code-derived algorithms for each component, including a cross-session recurrent-state memory gate, then run convergence sanity checks: overfittinga single 440-byte sentence at 1--15M parameters, text only, with three seeds for codec and attention choices and single-run sweeps for seven further factors. The two attention variants tested at 3\,000 steps (LiZAttention2 and window attention alone) reach a minimum loss near $10^{-3}$. After 600 steps, the mean minimum loss ranges from 0.018 (patch codec) to 0.354 (depthwise convolutional codec) with an identical ranking on three seeds. An apparent advantage of shared over separate attention projections closes with more steps or more diverse data and reverses when the projections are frozen: it is a convergence-speed effect, not a capacity effect. These checks suggest that the implementation optimizes; they say nothing about generalization, multimodal training or comparison with existing models, which a planned pretraining run is meant to address. The Discussion sizes a 200M-total/25M-active target analytically; none of its throughput figures is measured. Code is available at https://github.com/fabienfrfr/Kairos . Python package at https://pypi.org/project/kairos-fm/ .
bullets: Combines bidirectional gated-DeltaNet and sliding-window attention, shared projections, block-wise attention-residual aggregation, sparse MoE layers, and a multi-scale byte codec.
Uses uniform-noise denoising across a shared byte space intended for text, images, audio, video, lidar, and control streams.
Convergence checks overfit one 440-byte sentence at 1–15M parameters; both tested attention variants reach minimum loss near 10⁻³ at 3,000 steps.
Codec choices produce different early optimization behavior, while the apparent shared-projection benefit is attributed to convergence speed rather than capacity.
Results do not establish generalization, multimodal training, model superiority, or the proposed throughput; larger pretraining is planned.

papers.selection_reason: Byte-level multimodal foundation model with linear attention and MoE; fits multimodal LLM and efficient attention interests.
papers.title: Kairos: Toward a Byte-Level Foundation Model for Every Modality
papers.tldr: Kairos proposes a byte-level multimodal foundation-model design and finds that its components can optimize on a tiny text-only memorization task, without yet demonstrating generalization or multimodal usefulness.

papers.abstract: In this article, we propose algebraic integer number formats (AINF) as a framework for highly configurable and accurate compressed computation. A key property of AINF is its straightforward reduction to purely integer arithmetic, enabling error-free multiply-accumulate operations. We develop a matrix multiplication engine that exploits this property, obtaining performance within a predictable factor of the most efficient numerical counterparts on modern hardware accelerators. Another key advantage of AIQ is the freedom to select algebraic integers tailored to the numerical characteristics of a given use case, offering optimization opportunities that are fundamentally unavailable in floating-point or fixed-point formats. Motivated by these properties, we introduce algebraic integer quantization (AIQ), a lossy compression format for large language model (LLM) inference, and provide results demonstrating that AIQ achieves competitive accuracy compared to the industry-standard MX format across a diverse set of models and benchmarks at equivalent bit-per-parameter budgets. The experiments presented in this article employ algebraic integers of degree two (quadratic integers); generalizations to higher-order and, in particular, multidimensional algebraic integers promise even greater computational advantages and remain a promising direction for future work.
authors: Anthony Kostal-Vazquez, Vassil Dimitrov, Branden Butler
bullets: Algebraic integer number formats reduce computation to integer arithmetic, enabling error-free multiply-accumulate operations.
The proposed matrix multiplication engine delivers performance within a predictable factor of efficient numerical alternatives on modern accelerators.
Algebraic integers can be selected to match the numerical properties of specific applications, offering flexibility beyond floating-point and fixed-point formats.
AIQ achieves competitive accuracy with the industry-standard MX format across diverse models and benchmarks at equivalent bits per parameter.
Experiments use quadratic integers; higher-order and multidimensional extensions are left for future work.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a novel number format (Algebraic Integer Quantization) for LLM inference, directly addressing computational efficiency and compression.
papers.title: Algebraic Integer Quantization for Machine Learning Applications
papers.tldr: Algebraic integer quantization enables configurable, integer-only compressed computation for LLM inference with accuracy competitive with MX at matched bit budgets.

papers.abstract: Zero-shot text-to-speech (TTS) can clone a voice from seconds of audio. Yet the quality comes from billion-parameter diffusion transformers whose size and multi-step sampling put them out of reach of the on-device, assistive, and real-time applications that need them most. Post-training quantization (PTQ) shrinks such models without retraining, but it has been built for language and vision, not speech. At 4 bits, a strong quantizer leaves intelligibility close to full precision but consistently erodes speaker timbre, so error rates stay low while the voice drifts from the target speaker. We ask why quantization hurts speech, where the damage lives, and whether it can be repaired without retraining. To find out, we run the first 4-bit weight-and-activation (W4A4) PTQ study of a TTS diffusion transformer at 1B and 3.5B. The timbre cost comes from both the weight and the activation quantization, but only the activation part has the timestep structure a precision schedule can exploit. We therefore introduce TTS-Q, which selects hard-to-quantize items from task-matched calibration candidates and applies a budget-balanced mixed-precision schedule that assigns higher precision to late-step feed-forward activations. TTS-Q recovers timbre best at both scales, at no cost to intelligibility. Separately, the deployed calibrated-W4A4 reference reduces peak memory on GPU, providing a practical reference for resource-constrained TTS deployment.
authors: Xiaoqin Feng, Yuqi Li, Weilun Feng, Yi-Cheng Lin, Kai Li, Xianglong Wang, Kuo Yang, Chuanguang Yang, Yingli Tian, Wei Li, Zhongwei Cheng, Lin Chen
bullets: Targets the memory and latency barriers of billion-parameter, multi-step zero-shot TTS models for on-device and real-time use.
A W4A4 study at 1B and 3.5B shows that quantization damages timbre through both weights and activations, while intelligibility remains relatively robust.
Only activation quantization has timestep-dependent structure that can be addressed with a precision schedule.
TTS-Q uses task-matched calibration candidates and budget-balanced mixed precision, assigning higher precision to late-step feed-forward activations.
It achieves the best timbre recovery at both model scales without reducing intelligibility; the calibrated-W4A4 reference also lowers peak GPU memory.

papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses efficient AI by proposing a post-training quantization method for large diffusion transformers, reducing model memory requirements and compute.
papers.title: TTS-Q: Perception-Guided Post-Training Quantization of Text-to-Speech Diffusion Transformers
papers.tldr: TTS-Q improves 4-bit post-training quantization of TTS diffusion transformers by preserving speaker timbre without sacrificing intelligibility.

papers.abstract: Satellite onboard computing faces an irreducible tension: mission intelligence requirements grow monotonically while power, mass, and radiation budgets remain fixed. This paper advances the state of the art on three fronts. First, we develop a formal mathematical model of spiking neural computation for satellite workloads, deriving closed-form expressions for energy consumption as a function of network sparsity, firing rate, and synaptic fan-out. Second, we propose three original algorithms -- a Spiking Kalman-Complementary Filter (SKCF) for attitude estimation, a Temporal Contrast Anomaly Detector (TCAD) for spacecraft health monitoring, and a Spike-Based Adaptive Modulation and Coding (SAMC) scheme for cognitive satellite links -- each with pseudocode and analytical complexity bounds. Third, we introduce a quantitative Energy-Accuracy-Latency (EAL) trade-off surface and populate it with numerical estimates derived from published silicon measurements of Loihi and SpiNNaker, enabling direct comparison with FPGA and GPU baselines. A taxonomy of four radiation-aware neuromorphic architecture classes is refined with fault-rate models. Continual on-orbit learning is formalized through a constrained Spike-Timing Dependent Plasticity (STDP) rule that provably bounds weight drift. Case studies for a 12U CubeSat Earth observation mission, a GEO communications payload, and an autonomous deep-space probe provide concrete, quantified design points. Our analysis shows that neuromorphic implementations can achieve 8 to 47 times energy reduction over GPU baselines while maintaining inference accuracy within 2.1\% for representative satellite workloads.
bullets: Models spiking computation energy from network sparsity, firing rate, and synaptic fan-out.
Introduces SKCF for attitude estimation, TCAD for health monitoring, and SAMC for adaptive satellite communications, with analytical complexity bounds.
Defines an Energy-Accuracy-Latency trade-off surface using published Loihi and SpiNNaker measurements against FPGA and GPU baselines.
Refines radiation-aware architecture classes and formalizes continual on-orbit learning with bounded weight drift.
Case studies estimate 8–47× lower energy than GPU baselines while keeping accuracy within 2.1% for representative workloads.

papers.selection_reason: Formalizes a continual learning rule (STDP) for on-orbit adaptation, directly fitting the continual and online learning subtopic, while also addressing energy-efficient AI.
papers.title: Neuromorphic Satellite Intelligence: A Formal Framework for Event-Driven Architectures, Spike-Based Algorithms, and Quantitative Energy-Accuracy Trade-offs
papers.tldr: A formal framework and three spike-based algorithms show how neuromorphic satellite computing can trade energy, accuracy, latency, and radiation resilience for onboard intelligence.

papers.abstract: Spatial coding agents significantly improve spatial reasoning in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) by using external tools to generate verified execution traces. However, this paradigm inherently suffers from prohibitive inference-time overhead and external dependencies. In this paper, we explore whether an MLLM can internalize this agentic capability to operate entirely tool-free. We begin with a simple observation: prompting an MLLM with summarized execution traces of a spatial coding agent naturally unlocks the model's internal spatial Chain-of-Thought (CoT). Motivated by this, we introduce SpatialOPSD, an on-policy self-distillation framework that internalizes spatial reasoning into a standalone MLLM by formulating verified agent traces as privileged information. To mitigate privileged-information leakage during distillation, we introduce Repetition-Aware Distillation, which combines repetition masking with unlikelihood regularization. Experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that self-distilling SpatialOPSD achieves higher average accuracy than SFT and GRPO on both spatial and OOD datasets, exhibiting superior performance and generalization.
bullets: Targets the inference overhead and external dependencies of tool-using spatial coding agents.
Uses on-policy self-distillation to treat verified agent traces as privileged reasoning information.
Introduces Repetition-Aware Distillation with repetition masking and unlikelihood regularization to reduce privileged-information leakage.
Experiments report higher average accuracy than SFT and GRPO across spatial and out-of-distribution benchmarks.
Scope: focuses on internalizing spatial reasoning in standalone MLLMs without external tools.

papers.title: SpatialOPSD: Self-Distilling Spatial Intelligence from Verified Coding Agent Traces
papers.tldr: SpatialOPSD distills verified spatial coding-agent traces into an MLLM, enabling tool-free spatial reasoning with improved benchmark performance and generalization.

papers.abstract: Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) achieve remarkable performance in video synthesis, but their iterative denoising process suffers from high inference latency. To address this, caching has emerged as an effective acceleration strategy by capitalizing on inter-step redundancy during denoising. Existing dynamic caching methods typically estimate the error that cache reuse would introduce at each denoising step (step error) to guide cache decisions, whereas our concern is how much quality loss cache reuse would cause in the final generated video (terminal error). We show that step error does not directly correspond to terminal error and that latent information helps capture their relationship, thereby informing cache decisions. Moreover, existing threshold-based methods cannot provide precise speedup control, making it difficult to meet practical requirements for user-specified acceleration targets. To address these limitations, we introduce MORCA, a cache scheduling framework trained through offline-to-online reinforcement learning to make latent-aware reuse/recompute decisions under user-specified acceleration targets. Extensive experiments on different video generation models across multiple target acceleration ratios demonstrate that MORCA achieves better generation fidelity than state-of-the-art caching methods under comparable computational budgets. Code is available at https://github.com/x10ngyx/MORCA.
bullets: Existing caching methods optimize per-step error, which does not reliably reflect final video quality loss.
MORCA learns the relationship between latent information, cache decisions, and terminal generation error.
Its policy makes reuse-versus-recompute decisions under explicit acceleration targets, offering finer speedup control than threshold-based methods.
Experiments across multiple video generation models and acceleration ratios show better fidelity than prior caching methods at comparable computational budgets.

papers.abstract: Tactile feedback provides embodied agents with physical information beyond visual observations, enabling more reliable interaction with the real world. However, despite the rapid progress of vision-tactile-language-action (VTLA) policies, there remains a lack of unified benchmarks for evaluating tactile-enabled robot manipulation across simulation and the real world. To address this gap, we introduce OpenViTac, a visuo-tactile manipulation benchmark for evaluating robot policies across simulation and the real world. OpenViTac organizes contact-rich manipulation into four tactile-relevant capability dimensions and provides paired simulation-real-world settings for consistent evaluation of VLA, WAM, and VTLA policies. Building upon this benchmark, we investigate how different tactile representations and integration strategies affect the performance of pretrained VLA models. Correspondingly, we introduce OpenVTLA, a tactile augmentation framework that combines the best-performing representation and integration strategy. Furthermore, we leverage the paired benchmark setting to study sim-real co-training and analyze factors affecting cross-domain policy learning. Together, OpenViTac provides a unified platform for evaluating and advancing visuo-tactile robot manipulation.
bullets: Targets the lack of consistent benchmarks for tactile-enabled manipulation across simulation and reality.
Organizes contact-rich tasks into four tactile-relevant capability dimensions with paired sim-real settings.
Evaluates VLA, WAM, and VTLA policies, including different tactile representations and integration strategies.
Introduces OpenVTLA, a tactile augmentation framework based on the best-performing design choices.
Uses the paired benchmark to study sim-real co-training and factors influencing cross-domain policy learning.

papers.abstract: Continual pre-training and fine-tuning in Large Language Models (LLMs) inevitably induce catastrophic forgetting, typically mitigated by replay using often-inaccessible original data. In this data-free regime, we analyze where forgetting occurs and why. Systematic parameter freezing across five settings up to 1.4B reveals that forgetting concentrates selectively in the output embeddings of tokens rarely seen in the new corpus, whereas the same sqrt(v-hat) band of the body is inert and new learning resides elsewhere. This localization is governed by the vocabulary deficiency of the corpus rather than the training mode, allowing pre-retraining risk ranking from token counts alone within a fixed base model. Mechanistically, absent tokens receive persistent one-sided softmax gradients that Adam's second-moment (sqrt(v-hat)) normalization amplifies into full-sized updates. We therefore propose an intervention: raising Adam's epsilon exclusively for the output projection during training. Across eight settings spanning 160M to 12B parameters and four model families, this removes 39.4% to 67.9% of forgetting across all seven stable configurations without degrading target learning or requiring per-model tuning. The defense combines additively or better with replay (79.8% on Qwen/Korean) and rescues released-head LoRA from a 23-fold forgetting surge. Because post-hoc editing of the drifted rows recovers under 5% of forgetting, the intervention must operate during training. Our findings indicate that a single-line optimizer adjustment may serve as the primary defense against catastrophic forgetting where the corpus starves the vocabulary.
bullets: Forgetting is localized to output embeddings of rarely or never-seen tokens, while comparable body parameters remain largely unchanged.
The underlying risk is driven by vocabulary deficiency, enabling pre-training risk ranking from token counts for a fixed base model.
Absent tokens receive persistent one-sided softmax gradients that Adam normalization converts into large updates.
Raising Adam’s epsilon only for the output projection reduces forgetting by 39.4%–67.9% across the reported stable settings without harming target learning.
The intervention complements replay and rescues released-head LoRA; post-hoc correction is ineffective, so protection must occur during training.

papers.selection_reason: Analysis and mitigation of catastrophic forgetting in continual pre-training; fits continual learning.
papers.title: A Deafening Silence: Catastrophic Forgetting Lives in the Output Embeddings of Tokens the Data Never Speaks
papers.tldr: Catastrophic forgetting during data-free continual LLM training concentrates in output-embedding rows for tokens absent from the new corpus, and increasing Adam’s epsilon for the output projection substantially reduces it during training.

papers.abstract: Mid-prefill pruning can reduce the sequence processed by deeper transformer layers, but attention concentration alone does not certify that discarded context is dispensable. We formulate EntroPrefill as a Renyi-guided proposal mechanism coupled to explicit constraints on discarded attention mass. Sink-isolated, regularized head pooling respects grouped-query attention while exposing a quantitative trade-off between specialization and worst-head coverage. We derive a mixture-to-head deletion envelope, a computable upper bound on feasible token removal, and a finite-sample observer guarantee that remains valid when the pruning layer is selected adaptively. We then establish a conditional transformer perturbation bound with explicit sufficient Lipschitz constants and a first-token decision-margin corollary. A counterexample shows why shallow observations alone cannot imply an unconditional future-output guarantee. The systems analysis distinguishes query-head unions, physical page allocation, and KV-transfer payload, and gives an arithmetic break-even condition for pruning. This manuscript is theoretical in scope: it defines the procedure, its assumptions, and its formal limits, but does not report measured acceleration or task-accuracy preservation. Experiments are reserved for subsequent validation of the assumptions, approximation tightness, and end-to-end resource trade-offs.
bullets: Addresses the lack of formal guarantees that low-attention context tokens are safely dispensable.
Uses Rényi-guided proposals, sink-isolated regularized head pooling, and constraints on discarded attention mass.
Derives deletion bounds, adaptive finite-sample observer guarantees, and conditional transformer perturbation and decision-margin bounds.
Separates attention-head unions, physical page allocation, and KV-transfer payloads, yielding an arithmetic break-even condition for pruning.
Theoretical only: no measured speedup or task-accuracy results are reported, and guarantees depend on stated assumptions.
papers.selection_reason: Context pruning with guarantees for RAG; directly fits token pruning and KV cache efficiency.
papers.title: EntroPrefill: Renyi-Guided Context Pruning with Conditional Stability Guarantees for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
papers.tldr: EntroPrefill provides a theoretically bounded method for pruning RAG context during prefill while clarifying when output stability and systems-level savings can—and cannot—be guaranteed.

papers.abstract: Persistent memory allows an LLM agent to carry experience across conversations, but it also turns a local reasoning mistake into a durable one. During deliberation, an agent may consider a plan, simulate a tool result, report another speaker's belief, and then reject all of them. If memory retains only the resulting sentences, those once-useful possibilities can later return as facts. The record is neither fabricated nor irrelevant; it has simply been detached from the context in which it was valid. We identify this missing context as \emph{discourse ownership}: the world, branch, or speaker that licenses a proposition. Our first finding is counterintuitive. Language models already carry a causally active signal for ownership, yet conventional memory interfaces discard it when they convert reasoning into records. We introduce CASK (Causally Anchored Scoping Keys), a commit rule that preserves this signal so that shared-world facts enter durable memory while provisional content remains available only within its original scope. Our second finding is that the most obvious way to preserve the signal---storing the discovered internal coordinates---is unreliable because equivalent representations need not keep the same coordinates. CASK instead preserves the stable relations that express ownership. Controlled long-conversation conflicts and tool-agent traces show that this design improves memory admission and prevents provisional content from contaminating later answers while complementing runtime provenance. The resulting commit boundary lets agents explore more possibilities without granting every intermediate sentence authority over future behavior.
bullets: Persistent memory can turn discarded plans, simulated tool results, or reported beliefs into misleading future facts when their context is lost.
The paper identifies this missing context as discourse ownership: which world, branch, or speaker licenses a proposition.
CASK preserves stable ownership relations rather than unreliable internal representation coordinates.
Controlled conflict and tool-agent traces show improved memory admission and reduced contamination from provisional content.
The approach complements runtime provenance and enables broader reasoning without granting every intermediate sentence durable authority.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Reasoning creates propositions that belong to different worlds. The agent considers Paris but rejects that branch, while committing to Sydney. CASK converts the model’s ownership-sensitive relational geometry into an explicit commit edge: Sydney enters actual-world memory, whereas Paris remains available only inside its scoped world. A later query may use committed evidence without turning the discarded branch into a fact.

Under a development-calibrated 95% actual-admission constraint, output logits define the stronger high-recall boundary. (c) The safety gain reduces adoption of the injected answer, while ordinary reader utility remains a separate trade-off.

papers.selection_reason: Scope-aware commit rules for persistent LLM memory; directly fits LLM memory.
papers.title: Whose Memory Is It? Scope-Aware Commit Rules for Long-Term LLM Memory
papers.tldr: CASK makes LLM long-term memory scope-aware, preserving only facts licensed by the correct world, reasoning branch, or speaker while keeping provisional content local.

papers.abstract: Recurrent neural networks typically compress information into a single vector-valued recurrent state, forcing short-term computation and long-term retention to share the same representation. Past extensions alleviate this bottleneck by increasing the memory capacity or separating timescales, but lack the combination of rapid neuron-level processing and longer-term retention found in biology. To that end, we introduce the Continuous Memory Machine (CMM), a recurrent architecture with matrix-valued short- and long-term memory states serving distinct functional roles. Building on the Continuous Thought Machine (CTM), the CMM's short-term memory tracks recent neural activity, with uniquely parameterized neuron-level models learning to use these activity patterns for computation. A persistent long-term memory stores information for later use, with a Transformer jointly updating both memory stores, providing an expressive bidirectional read--write mechanism such that each store can reorganize its own contents and both read from and write to the other. Across algorithmic, in-context learning, and recurrent reasoning tasks, the CMM outperforms a broad suite of baselines, exhibiting stronger generalization than prior memory-augmented networks while preserving the CTM's interpretable attention patterns. Code is available at https://github.com/SakanaAI/continuous-memory-machines.
bullets: Addresses the bottleneck of compressing short-term computation and long-term information into one recurrent state.
Uses short-term memory for recent neural activity and persistent long-term memory for later retrieval.
A Transformer jointly performs bidirectional read–write updates across both memory stores, allowing them to reorganize and interact.
Outperforms broad baselines on algorithmic, in-context learning, and recurrent reasoning tasks, with stronger generalization and interpretable attention patterns.

figures.caption: Figure 1: The Continuous Memory Machine. At timestep t, the current observation ot and previous activated state zt are processed by the feedforward synapse model to produce a pre-activated state at. This state is appended to the sliding short-term memory (STM) At. At and the long-term memory Bt are jointly processed by a Transformer, producing updated memories Ãt and B̃t. Ãt is passed through the neuron-level models to produce the next activated state zt+1. From the activated-state history, the model computes the synchronization St+1 and output yt+1. At, B̃t = Bt+1, and zt+1 are carried forward to the next iteration.

Figure 7: Comparison of the Continuous Thought Machine (top), the Continuous Memory Machine (middle), and CMM-LSTM (bottom). The CTM maintains a sliding short-term memory (STM) of recent pre-activations, which is processed by independent neuron-level models, while the synchronization module computes time-decayed outer products of activation histories that are projected to output logits. The CMM extends the CTM with a persistent long-term memory (LTM) that is jointly updated with the STM through the memory-update Transformer before the neuron-level models are applied. CMM-LSTM replaces the CTM backbone with a LayerNorm LSTM while retaining the same LTM and memory-update Transformer. Consequently, the Transformer receives a single hidden-state token instead of the CTM’s sliding window of MS STM tokens, and there are no neuron-level models or synchronization representation. Comparing the CMM and CMM-LSTM isolates the contribution of the CTM’s distributed short-term representation and per-neuron processing.

Figure 8: Memory-update modules for the CMM (a) and CMM-LSTM (b). Both apply a Transformer over a sequence consisting of a sink token, the LTM tokens, and STM tokens, with learned positional embeddings. The CMM (a) attends jointly over MS STM tokens drawn from the sliding window of recent pre-activations, giving the Transformer a multi-token view of recent activity. CMM-LSTM (b) replaces the sliding window with the LSTM’s single hidden vector, so only one STM token is passed to the Transformer. Comparing the two isolates the effect of the CTM’s distributed short-term representation on the memory update.

papers.title: Continuous Memory Machines
papers.tldr: Continuous Memory Machines combine distinct matrix-valued short- and long-term memories with neuron-level processing to improve recurrent computation and retention.

papers.abstract: Mobile manipulators such as humanoid robots are increasingly deployed in dynamic, unstructured environments to perform dexterous manipulation tasks. However, end-to-end manipulation policies trained to imitate demonstration data collected from a single robot pose are brittle: even centimeter-scale deviations in robot pose at deployment can drive ego-centric observations and end-effector trajectories out of the training distribution, leading to sharp drops in performance. We introduce MobileVISTA, a data generation framework that transforms demonstrations captured at canonical poses into diverse, pose-perturbed training data by jointly (1) augmenting egocentric visual observations and (2) retargeting actions to compensate for base pose changes. Unlike prior methods, which assume a camera rigidly mounted off the actuated chain or non-trivial articulated robot geometry largely out of frame, MobileVISTA targets compatibility with egocentric platforms (e.g., humanoids) where the camera is both influenced by and must observe the robot's kinematic chain as it moves. We study MobileVISTA in simulated tasks spanning humanoid and bimanual embodiments, and on a real Galaxea R1 Pro. We find policies trained on MobileVISTA-augmented data demonstrate improved robustness to previously out-of-distribution poses encountered at test time, without additional demonstration collection or a trained generative model. Additionally, we find MobileVISTA's benefit is largest on tested humanoids, where the camera rides the actuated chain and the robot fills much of the frame. Additional videos and appendix can be found on our website: https://mobilevista.github.io
bullets: Addresses brittleness caused by training demonstrations collected from a single robot pose.
Jointly generates pose-perturbed egocentric observations and compensating action trajectories.
Designed for egocentric robots, including humanoids whose cameras move with and observe the actuated body.
Evaluated in simulated humanoid and bimanual tasks and on a real Galaxea R1 Pro.
Improves robustness to previously unseen test poses without collecting more demonstrations or training a generative model; gains are largest on tested humanoids.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: The MobileVISTA framework. Given single-pose demonstrations, MobileVISTA jointly augments observations and actions under a sampled base pose perturbation ∆p ∈ SE(3). The visual branch removes the robot, reprojects the scene, and re-renders the robot at its retargeted configuration, while the action branch retargets actions in end-effector space via ∆p−1 to produce (ãt) T t=1. This augmented dataset is then used to train a pose-robust policy.

Fig. 6: Per-trajectory PSNR for synthesized images. Each point shows the PSNR (↑, dB) of a synthesized trajectory at its sampled base offset from canonical (cm, overhead view). MobileVISTA yields higher PSNR overall, with the largest separation on humanoid tasks. Tasks where the methods are closer in PSNR also show smaller gaps in downstream policy performance.

Fig. 7: Sampled offsets at reval = 15cm in real-world evaluation. Outcomes for each policy across sampled base offsets (cm, overhead view), for book stacking (a) and laundry sort (b). MobileVISTA succeeds across a wide range of offsets, while baselines fail to generalize beyond the canonical pose.

Fig. 4: Ablation results across tasks. Success rate vs. evaluation perturbation radius reval. We compare MobileVISTA against singlemodality augmentation—Aug. Images Only, Aug. Actions Only— and an augmentation that omits robot re-rendering at retargeted configurations, Fixed Robot Geom. MobileVISTA outperforms nearly all ablated variants, indicating that both coupled visual–action augmentation and explicit robot re-rendering contribute to pose robustness.
